stem: A pediatric nurse practitioner (PNP) is counseling a parent of a 3-month-old about the order in which motor skills emerge. The parent asks why the infant can lift her head before she can sit. Which principle of development best explains this sequence?

options.label: A
options.text: Cephalocaudal direction of neuromuscular maturation
options.rationale: Head control precedes trunk and lower-extremity control because myelination and motor maturation proceed cephalocaudal (head to toe); the professor emphasized this pattern as the organizing framework for the entire gross motor sequence (head lift 2 mo, roll 4 mo, sit 6 mo, crawl 9 mo, walk 12 mo).

options.label: B
options.text: Proximodistal direction of neuromuscular maturation
options.rationale: Proximodistal maturation explains why infants control the upper arm and shoulder before the wrist and fingers (reach before pincer), not the head-before-trunk sequence described.

options.label: C
options.text: General-to-specific refinement of voluntary movement
options.rationale: General-to-specific describes refinement from whole-hand raking to pincer grasp and from fist grasp to pencil grip, not the vertical head-to-trunk order.

options.label: D
options.text: Head-to-toe myelination of the corticospinal tracts beginning at birth
options.rationale: Corticospinal myelination is incomplete at birth and continues postnatally for months; stating it begins at birth in a head-to-toe fashion misstates both the timing and the named developmental principle.

questions.sourceMapping: Growth & Development Part 1, Slides 6, 9; Part 2, Slide 6; Transcript 2 (cephalocaudal/proximal-distal discussion)

stem: During a 4-month well visit, a parent reports that the infant rolled from back to front at 6 weeks of age and has done so repeatedly. Development is otherwise unremarkable. How should the PNP interpret this finding?

options.label: A
options.text: An expected variation within the normal range of motor development
options.rationale: Rolling at 6 weeks falls outside the expected window (front-to-back at about 4 months) and is listed among abnormal gross motor patterns, not normal variation.

options.label: B
options.text: A possible sign of hypertonia or limb rigidity warranting tone assessment
options.rationale: The professor explicitly flagged rolling before 3 months as a trap: stiff, hypertonic infants flop and roll early, so early rolling should prompt careful tone and neurologic assessment rather than praise (Part 2, Slide 10; Transcript 2).

options.label: C
options.text: Evidence of advanced development requiring no further assessment
options.rationale: Early milestone attainment is not automatically advanced development; rigid posturing that produces early rolling is a concerning mimic.

options.label: D
options.text: A normal finding because rolling front to back always precedes back to front
options.rationale: The expected sequence is front-to-back rolling first at around 4 months, but this infant rolled back-to-front at 6 weeks, so the statement does not normalize the finding.

questions.sourceMapping: Growth & Development Part 2, Slide 10; Transcript 2 (rolling before 3 months = possible stiff limbs)

stem: A parent brings a 9-month-old for a well visit. The infant sits only in a tripod position and cannot sit unassisted, but rolls both ways and bears weight on the legs when held. Which conclusion is most appropriate?

options.label: A
options.text: Observation at the 12-month visit is sufficient before acting
options.rationale: Deferring evaluation to 12 months delays identification of hypotonia or motor disorder and contradicts the course directive to evaluate missed milestones at the visit where they are identified.

options.label: B
options.text: Development is normal because tripod sitting is expected through 12 months
options.rationale: Tripod sitting is expected at about 6 months, not through 12 months; by 9 months independent sitting is the standard.

options.label: C
options.text: Unassisted sitting should be achieved by 9 months
options.rationale: ; delay warrants evaluation for tone and motor disorder: Tripod sitting is a 6-month skill and unassisted sitting is expected by 9 months; failure to sit alone at 9 months is a listed red flag (possible hypotonia) requiring evaluation, and the professor stated parents' concerns and missed milestones must be investigated, not watched (Part 2, Slides 6, 10; Transcript 2).

options.label: D
options.text: The infant meets criteria for isolated fine motor delay
options.rationale: The deficit described is gross motor (trunk control), not fine motor eye-hand coordination.

questions.sourceMapping: Growth & Development Part 2, Slides 6, 10; Transcript 2 (sit by 9 months; low tone discussion) | Parallel Form B (options re-randomized)

stem: Using the gross motor progression diagram shown, a PNP reviews a 10-month-old whose parents report the infant pulls to stand and cruises along furniture but does not walk alone. Which interpretation is correct?

images.alt: Figure 1: Growth & Development Part 2, Slide 7 reference asset - gross motor progression from head control through independent walking across the first 15 months.
images.caption: Figure 1: Growth & Development Part 2, Slide 7 reference asset - gross motor progression from head control through independent walking across the first 15 months.

options.label: A
options.text: Abnormal; independent walking is required by 10 months
options.rationale: Independent walking at 10 months is early, not required; the expected age is about 12 months.

options.label: B
options.text: Normal; walking alone is the goal of the first year, with a concern threshold at 15 months
options.rationale: The diagram and lecture sequence place pulling to stand and cruising at 8-10 months and independent walking at about 12 months, with concern triggered when walking is absent by 15-18 months; a cruising 10-month-old is on pattern (Part 2, Slides 6, 10; Transcript 2).

options.label: C
options.text: Abnormal; cruising should be achieved by 6 months at the latest
options.rationale: Cruising appears around 9-10 months on the diagram; a 6-month criterion is fabricated.

options.label: D
options.text: Normal only if the infant also crawls on hands and knees
options.rationale: Not all normally developing infants crawl on hands and knees (some bottom-shuffle or roll to move); absence of a hand-knee crawl alone does not invalidate an otherwise normal sequence.

questions.sourceMapping: Growth & Development Part 2, Slides 6-10, Figure (Slide 7); Transcript 2 (walk by 15 months; cruising reassurance)

stem: At a 16-month well visit, an infant is not walking alone but pulls to stand and cruises confidently around furniture. Tone, reflexes, and birth history are normal. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.text: Immediate referral for brain MRI
options.rationale: Neuroimaging is not indicated for an isolated, in-progression motor pattern with a normal examination.

options.label: B
options.text: Reassurance with routine follow-up, as cruising at 16 months suggests an intact progression
options.rationale: The professor's explicit teaching: a 16-month-old who is cruising is probably okay, because cruising demonstrates the pull-to-stand component of the walking sequence; the concern threshold is failure to walk by 15-18 months without such progression (Transcript 2).

options.label: C
options.text: Referral for developmental evaluation of gross motor delay
options.rationale: Cruising indicates the child is moving through the walking sequence; formal delay evaluation is reserved for absence of progression (not pulling up, not cruising) or walking absent by 15-18 months.

options.label: D
options.text: Serum creatine kinase and lead level screening
options.rationale: CK and lead testing are not indicated without focal findings, hypotonia, regression, or exposure history.

questions.sourceMapping: Transcript 2 (16-month-old cruising is probably okay; walk by 15-18 months)

stem: A 4-year-old continues to walk on his toes with a toe-only cadence and has tight Achilles tendons on examination. Which association should the PNP consider?

options.label: A
options.text: Normal variant requiring no follow-up after age 3
options.rationale: Persistence beyond age 3 is the definition of the abnormal pattern, not a normal variant.

options.label: B
options.text: Calf and Achilles tightness that may accompany cerebral palsy or autism spectrum disorder
options.rationale: Initial toe walking is normal in new walkers, but a heel-toe cadence should emerge by about age 3; persistent toe walking signals calf/Achilles tightness and is associated with cerebral palsy and children on the spectrum, per the professor's lecture (Transcript 2).

options.label: C
options.text: Isolated vitamin D deficiency rickets
options.rationale: Rickets produces bowing and widened physes, not isolated toe walking; nothing in the vignette suggests it.

options.label: D
options.text: Benign positional foot preference that resolves by age 5
options.rationale: Positional preference resolves as the heel-toe gait matures by age 3; persistence is pathologic until proven otherwise.

questions.sourceMapping: Transcript 2 (persistent toe walking after age 3; tight calves/Achilles; spectrum association)

stem: A parent reports that her 10-month-old always reaches with the right hand and never uses the left. Examination shows decreased spontaneous movement of the left arm. What does fixed hand preference before 18 months most suggest?

options.label: A
options.text: Normal establishment of handedness
options.rationale: True handedness does not normally fixate before 18 months; symmetric bimanual reach is expected in infancy.

options.label: B
options.text: Weakness or impaired motor function of the non-preferred side
options.rationale: Fixed hand preference before 18 months is a listed red flag because infants normally use both hands symmetrically; early fixation suggests weakness of the non-preferred limb (hemiparesis, brachial plexus injury), and the professor paired this with the 4-month two-hand reach test (Part 2, Slide 10; Transcript 2).

options.label: C
options.text: Advanced cognitive development
options.rationale: Hand preference at 10 months reflects motor asymmetry, not cognition.

options.label: D
options.text: Typical proximodistal maturation
options.rationale: Proximodistal maturation describes trunk-to-fingers control, not lateralized hand use.

questions.sourceMapping: Growth & Development Part 2, Slide 10; Transcript 2 (fixed hand preference before 18 months; 4-month object test)

stem: A PNP reviews five parent-reported fine motor observations from different infants in clinic today. Select all findings that should trigger further developmental evaluation.

options.label: A
options.text: Raking grasp to obtain a cube at 7 months of age
options.rationale: Raking precedes pincer and is expected around 6-8 months, so a 7-month raking grasp is on pattern.

options.label: B
options.text: Absent pincer grasp at 15 months of age
options.rationale: An abnormal or absent pincer grasp by 15 months is a listed red flag; pincer normally matures across 9-12 months.

options.label: C
options.text: Bringing both hands to midline to grasp a rattle at 4 months of age
options.rationale: A two-hand midline reach at 4 months is exactly the expected response the professor uses as her office screen for symmetry.

options.label: D
options.text: Hands held in persistent fists at 4 months of age
options.rationale: Persistently fisted hands beyond 3 months is a listed abnormal fine motor sign suggesting neurologic dysfunction; at 4 months hands should be open and reaching (Part 2, Slide 16; Transcript 2).

options.label: E
options.text: No hand-to-hand transfer of objects by 12 months of age
options.rationale: Failure to transfer an object from hand to hand by 1 year is a listed fine motor red flag.

questions.sourceMapping: Growth & Development Part 2, Slides 12, 16; Transcript 2 (fisted at 3 months; transfer by 1 year; pincer by 15 months; two-hand screen) | Parallel Form B (options re-randomized)

stem: A 6-month-old is brought in for a well visit. While reviewing the reflex chart shown, the PNP elicits one reflex that should no longer be present at this age. Which finding is most concerning?

images.alt: Figure 2: Milestone Combined Documents, page 1 reference asset - newborn reflex chart with stimulation, response, and expected disappearance.
images.caption: Figure 2: Milestone Combined Documents, page 1 reference asset - newborn reflex chart with stimulation, response, and expected disappearance.

options.label: A
options.text: Asymmetric tonic neck (fencer) posture when supine
options.rationale: The tonic neck reflex disappears by about 2 months; its persistence at 6 months indicates failure of primitive reflex integration and possible neurologic pathology, exactly the concept the professor flagged as frequently tested (chart; Slides 37-39; Transcript 3).

options.label: B
options.text: Blinking in response to a flash of light
options.rationale: The blink reflex is permanent and should persist throughout life.

options.label: C
options.text: Babinski response with fanning of the toes
options.rationale: A Babinski with toe fanning is normal in infancy and disappears between 9 months and 1 year.

options.label: D
options.text: Grasping an examiner's finger placed in the palm
options.rationale: The palmar grasp weakens after 3 months but may persist to about 1 year; a weak grasp at 6 months is not by itself abnormal, whereas a persistent tonic neck is.

questions.sourceMapping: Milestone Documents p1 reflex chart; Newborn/Infant deck Slides 37-39; Transcript 3 (reflex timing is exam material; persistent primitive reflex = neurologic concern) | Parallel Form B (options re-randomized)

stem: A 5-month-old still demonstrates a strong Moro response with arm extension and adduction on head-drop testing. What is the best interpretation?

options.label: A
options.text: Expected in formerly premature infants regardless of corrected age
options.rationale: Corrected age adjusts milestone expectations in the first years, but a blanket exemption for ex-preemies is incorrect; reflex timing should be interpreted against corrected age, and the vignette gives no prematurity history.

options.label: B
options.text: Abnormal only if the response is symmetric
options.rationale: Asymmetry of the Moro suggests focal injury (e.g., clavicle fracture, brachial plexus palsy); symmetric persistence is itself the abnormality at this age.

options.label: C
options.text: Expected; the Moro reflex normally persists to 8 months
options.rationale: An 8-month Moro is not normal; the integration window closes at 3-4 months.

options.label: D
options.text: Abnormal; Moro should disappear by 3-4 months and persistence warrants neurologic assessment
options.rationale: The Moro reflex disappears at 3-4 months (chart and Slides 38-39); persistence at 5 months (even before correcting for prematurity in most cases) is a primitive reflex that has outlived its window and requires assessment, consistent with the professor's warning about retained reflexes (Transcript 3).

questions.sourceMapping: Milestone Documents p1; Newborn/Infant deck Slides 38-39; Transcript 3 | Parallel Form B (options re-randomized)

stem: A 24-month-old speaks in two-word phrases, but only family members understand her speech. Using course standards, how should the PNP classify her expressive language?

options.label: A
options.text: Delayed; speech should be 75% intelligible to strangers by 2 years
options.rationale: Seventy-five percent intelligibility is the 3-year standard, not the 2-year standard.

options.label: B
options.text: Normal; about 50% intelligibility to an outside listener is expected at 2 years
options.rationale: At 2 years the expected profile is two-word sentences, roughly 50 words, and about 50% intelligibility to strangers; family-only understanding at this level is within expectations (Part 2, Slides 19-20; Transcript 2; WCC chart).

options.label: C
options.text: Delayed; two-word sentences belong to the 18-month repertoire
options.rationale: Two-word combinations emerge 18-24 months and remain appropriate at 24 months.

options.label: D
options.text: Normal only if receptive language is equally limited
options.rationale: Receptive language normally exceeds expressive language; equal limitation would in fact be more concerning, since receptive deficits imply cognitive or hearing pathology.

questions.sourceMapping: Growth & Development Part 2, Slides 19-22; Transcript 2 (50% legible at 2 years); WCC chart

stem: A 30-month-old from a Spanish-English bilingual home has age-appropriate receptive language, normal hearing screening, and social engagement, but expresses fewer words per language than monolingual peers. What is the most appropriate action?

options.label: A
options.text: Reassure; bilingual exposure can slow expressive language temporarily, with catch-up expected
options.rationale: The professor specifically taught that bilingual children may show a temporary expressive lag while receptive skills and social communication remain intact, and they catch up; total vocabulary across both languages should be considered (Transcript 2).

options.label: B
options.text: Refer for immediate autism evaluation
options.rationale: Intact receptive language, joint attention, and social engagement argue against autism; referral on bilingual expressive lag alone is inappropriate.

options.label: C
options.text: Diagnose expressive language disorder and start speech therapy
options.rationale: Labeling a transient bilingual expressive lag as a disorder over-medicalizes a normal variant.

options.label: D
options.text: Order brainstem auditory evoked response testing today
options.rationale: Hearing was screened and is normal; ABR is reserved for failed screens or suspected hearing loss.

questions.sourceMapping: Transcript 2 (bilingual expressive delay catches up; check hearing first) | Parallel Form B (options re-randomized)

stem: Which language milestone, if absent at the stated age, is the strongest indicator of a receptive-language or cognitive problem rather than a mechanical speech difficulty?

options.label: A
options.text: No cooing at 3 months
options.rationale: Absent cooing at 3 months is an early expressive/social cue but less specific than comprehension failure.

options.label: B
options.text: No babbling at 6 months
options.rationale: Absent babbling at 6 months is a red flag, but it primarily prompts hearing evaluation before cognitive inference.

options.label: C
options.text: Failure to follow simple verbal directions at 18 months despite normal hearing
options.rationale: Receptive language (Wernicke-mediated comprehension) deficits are more concerning than expressive delays because they imply cognitive processing problems; failure to understand verbal directions with normal hearing localizes the deficit to comprehension (Part 2, Slide 18; Transcript 2).

options.label: D
options.text: Illegible words at 20 months
options.rationale: Illegible words at 18-24 months is an expressive articulation concern, often mechanical or maturational.

questions.sourceMapping: Growth & Development Part 2, Slides 18, 22; Transcript 2 (receptive deficits more concerning; Broca vs Wernicke)

stem: At a 2-month well visit, the PNP notes the infant does not smile back when smiled to and does not respond to the parent's voice, though startle to sound is present. Which domain should be evaluated first?

options.label: A
options.text: Gross motor development
options.rationale: Motor domains are unrelated to social smiling and voice response.

options.label: B
options.text: Social-emotional engagement and hearing
options.rationale: The social smile appears by about 6 weeks and responsiveness to the parent's voice is an early social-communication milestone; absent social smile plus poor voice response mandates hearing re-evaluation and social engagement assessment (participation, eye contact), as these are early autism-spectrum and hearing signals (Part 2, Slides 23, 25; Transcript 2).

options.label: C
options.text: Fine motor eye-hand coordination
options.rationale: Fixation and following are fine motor/vision precursors but not the primary deficit described.

options.label: D
options.text: Feeding and growth pattern
options.rationale: Growth is important but does not explain absent social responsiveness.

questions.sourceMapping: Growth & Development Part 2, Slides 23, 25; Transcript 2 (social smile 6 weeks; not engaging = delay)

stem: A parent of a 7-month-old is worried because the infant cries when handed to relatives although previously easygoing. Which response by the PNP is most accurate?

options.label: A
options.text: This suggests insecure attachment and requires parenting intervention
options.rationale: Onset of stranger anxiety in the second half of year one is normative, not insecure attachment.

options.label: B
options.text: Stranger anxiety at 6-12 months reflects object permanence and a secure primary attachment
options.rationale: Stranger anxiety emerges around 6-8 months alongside object permanence (peekaboo age) and indicates the infant has formed a specific attachment; the lecture notes lack of stranger anxiety is the worrisome finding because it can indicate no consistent caregiver (Slides 58-60; Transcript 3; WCC chart).

options.label: C
options.text: Stranger anxiety should not appear before 18 months
options.rationale: Stranger anxiety appears in the 6-12 month window, not after 18 months; its disappearance by about 2 years is the expected course.

options.label: D
options.text: This is an early sign of autism spectrum disorder
options.rationale: Isolated stranger anxiety with otherwise normal social communication is developmental, not autistic.

questions.sourceMapping: Newborn/Infant deck Slides 58-60; Transcript 3; WCC chart (separation anxiety at 8 months)

stem: During a 24-month well visit, two children sit side by side playing with trucks, occasionally watching but not coordinating with each other. How should the PNP document this play pattern?

options.label: A
options.text: Cooperative play, expected at this age
options.rationale: Cooperative play with shared goals is a preschool (about 4-year) skill.

options.label: B
options.text: Parallel play, expected at this age
options.rationale: Two-year-olds characteristically engage in parallel play (playing next to, not with, peers); cooperative and imaginative play emerge around age 4 (Transcript 2).

options.label: C
options.text: Solitary play, concerning after age 3
options.rationale: Solitary play that persists beyond age 3 with poor engagement is the red flag; side-by-side play with mutual watching is parallel, not solitary.

options.label: D
options.text: Imaginative play, expected after age 4
options.rationale: Pretend/imaginative play belongs to the 4-year repertoire.

questions.sourceMapping: Transcript 2 (parallel play at 2 years; cooperative play at 4 years)

stem: The photograph shows the first erupted primary teeth in a 7-month-old. Based on the eruption pattern taught in this course, which statement is correct?

images.alt: Figure 3: Growth & Development Part 2, Slide 44 reference asset - primary dentition eruption beginning with the lower central incisors.
images.caption: Figure 3: Growth & Development Part 2, Slide 44 reference asset - primary dentition eruption beginning with the lower central incisors.

options.label: A
options.text: Lower central incisors erupt first, typically around 6 months of age
options.rationale: Primary eruption begins with the lower central incisors at about 6 months; the course also directs a first dental visit by 1-2 years (Part 2, Slides 44-45; Transcript 2; WCC chart dentist at 1).

options.label: B
options.text: Upper central incisors erupt first, typically around 4 months of age
options.rationale: Upper incisors follow the lower centrals; 4 months is earlier than the typical window.

options.label: C
options.text: First molars erupt first, typically around 6 months of age
options.rationale: Molars erupt after the incisors and first molars appear in the second year.

options.label: D
options.text: Teeth erupt in a fixed order that allows accurate age estimation
options.rationale: The professor explicitly cautioned that eruption timing varies too much to age a child by teeth.

stem: A parent asks whether she should let her 6-week-old cry without responding so the baby will not become spoiled. Which response reflects the course teaching on attachment?

options.label: A
options.text: Withhold response until the infant self-soothes to build independence
options.rationale: Deliberate non-response undermines the trust-vs-mistrust task of the first year.

options.label: B
options.text: Respond promptly; infants cannot be spoiled in the first months and responsiveness builds secure attachment
options.rationale: The deck states babies cannot be spoiled, need to feel secure, and are happier and more predictable when parents respond quickly; the professor added that cause-and-effect recognition begins around 3 months, so early responsiveness builds trust (Erikson trust vs mistrust) without overindulgence (Slides 47; Transcript 3).

options.label: C
options.text: Respond only to crying that lasts longer than 20 minutes
options.rationale: Arbitrary time thresholds have no basis in the attachment teaching.

options.label: D
options.text: Use scheduled feeding and ignoring to establish routine by 2 months
options.rationale: Rigid scheduling with ignoring conflicts with on-demand feeding and responsive parenting guidance for young infants.

stem: According to Erikson, which psychosocial conflict and virtue pair correctly describes the toddler period (1-3 years)?

options.label: A
options.text: Initiative vs guilt; purpose
options.rationale: Initiative vs guilt with purpose is the preschool (3-6 years) stage.

options.label: B
options.text: Autonomy vs shame and doubt; will
options.rationale: Toddlerhood (1-3 years) is autonomy vs shame and doubt with the virtue of will, centered on toilet training and doing things independently (Part 1, Slides 17-18).

options.label: C
options.text: Industry vs inferiority; competence
options.rationale: Industry vs inferiority with competence is the school-age (6-11 years) stage.

options.label: D
options.text: Trust vs mistrust; hope
options.rationale: Trust vs mistrust with hope is the infancy (birth-1 year) stage.

stem: A 5-year-old proudly shows the PNP a drawing of the family and insists on buttoning his own coat before kindergarten. Failure to successfully negotiate this stage, per Erikson, most likely results in which outcome?

options.label: A
options.text: Guilt and suppressed initiative
options.rationale: Guilt follows unsuccessful negotiation of the preschool initiative-vs-guilt stage, which precedes this child's current task.

options.label: B
options.text: Role confusion
options.rationale: Role confusion is the adolescent identity crisis outcome.

options.label: C
options.text: Mistrust of caregivers
options.rationale: Mistrust results from unresolved infancy (trust vs mistrust).

options.label: D
options.text: Feelings of inferiority and low self-esteem
options.rationale: School-age children (6-11 years, with the kindergarten transition marking entry) face industry vs inferiority; failure to cope with academic and social demands produces inferiority and diminished self-esteem (Part 1, Slide 19; Transcript 1).

stem: A PNP pours equal juice from a short wide glass into a tall narrow glass in front of a 5-year-old, who insists the tall glass now holds more. According to Piaget, the inability to understand conservation places this child in which stage?

options.label: A
options.text: Sensorimotor
options.rationale: Sensorimotor (0-2 years) is defined by sensory-motor exploration and object permanence, not conservation tasks.

options.label: B
options.text: Preoperational
options.rationale: Lack of conservation with egocentric, magical thinking is characteristic of the preoperational stage (about 2-7 years); the professor walked through exactly this beaker experiment as the discriminator for concrete operations, which this child has not yet reached (Part 1, Slides 25-30; Transcript 1; WCC chart).

options.label: C
options.text: Concrete operational
options.rationale: A concrete operational child (about 7-11 years) understands conservation and reversibility and would answer correctly.

options.label: D
options.text: Formal operational
options.rationale: Formal operations involve abstract and hypothetical reasoning in adolescence.

questions.sourceMapping: Growth & Development Part 1, Slides 25-30; Transcript 1 (conservation beaker demonstration); WCC chart

stem: An 8-month-old searches for a toy hidden under a blanket rather than acting as though it no longer exists. This behavior demonstrates which Piagetian achievement?

options.label: A
options.text: Conservation
options.rationale: Conservation is a concrete operational skill.

options.label: B
options.text: Object permanence within the sensorimotor stage
options.rationale: Searching for a hidden object reflects object permanence, the landmark sensorimotor (0-2 years) achievement the course ties to peekaboo play at 6-12 months (Part 1, Slides 26-27; Transcript 1; WCC chart).

options.label: C
options.text: Abstract reasoning
options.rationale: Abstract reasoning is formal operational (adolescence).

options.label: D
options.text: Centration
options.rationale: Centration (focusing on one feature) is a preoperational limitation, not demonstrated here.

questions.sourceMapping: Growth & Development Part 1, Slides 26-27; Transcript 1; WCC chart (peekaboo 6-12 months; object permanence at 8 months)

stem: Which theorist's framework would best support a parenting plan built on praising desired behaviors immediately and ignoring minor misbehavior, with no reference to internal thoughts or feelings?

options.label: A
options.text: Piaget's cognitive-developmental theory
options.rationale: Piaget addresses internal thought structures, which this plan explicitly ignores.

options.label: B
options.text: Skinner's operant conditioning within behaviorism
options.rationale: Behaviorism considers only observable behavior shaped by rewards, punishment, and reinforcement; Skinner's operant conditioning with immediate rewards is the basis, and the professor linked it to modern positive-parenting practice (Part 1, Slides 22-24; Transcript 1).

options.label: C
options.text: Bowlby's attachment theory
options.rationale: Bowlby centers on the caregiver-infant bond, not reinforcement schedules.

options.label: D
options.text: Erikson's psychosocial theory
options.rationale: Erikson describes stage-based psychosocial conflicts, not contingent reinforcement.

stem: A foster parent worries that an infant placed in her home at 3 weeks of age cannot form a healthy attachment because she is not the biological mother. Which response is most accurate?

options.label: A
options.text: Attachment requires a biological parent in the first year of life
options.rationale: Biology is not required; consistency is.

options.label: B
options.text: Attachment forms with any adult who responds consistently, regardless of biological relation
options.rationale: The professor emphasized that the attachment figure does not need to be a biological parent; any adult who is consistently present and responsive becomes the attachment figure (Transcript 1; Bowlby).

options.label: C
options.text: Attachment is fixed at birth and cannot develop after the neonatal period
options.rationale: Attachment develops across the first year (trust vs mistrust), not at birth.

options.label: D
options.text: Attachment forms only with the person who feeds the infant
options.rationale: Feeding is one context of responsive care, but attachment is built through consistent responsiveness, not feeding alone.

stem: A woman planning pregnancy asks about substance use. Which pairing of prenatal exposure and fetal consequence reflects the course teaching?

options.label: A
options.text: Nicotine/vaping - low birth weight and increased ADHD risk
options.rationale: The professor cited multiple studies linking nicotine (including vaping) to low birth weight and later ADHD, alcohol to fetal alcohol syndrome, and cannabis to cognitive impairment and prematurity (Transcript 1; Part 1, Slide 11).

options.label: B
options.text: Alcohol - isolated macrosomia without neurobehavioral effects
options.rationale: Alcohol causes fetal alcohol syndrome with neurobehavioral impairment, not isolated macrosomia.

options.label: C
options.text: Cannabis - post-term gestation and accelerated cognition
options.rationale: Cannabis is associated with cognitive impairment and premature birth, the opposite of the option.

options.label: D
options.text: Nicotine/vaping - neural tube defects
options.rationale: Neural tube defects are linked to folate deficiency and certain teratogens, not nicotine per the course content.

stem: A quality-improvement committee reviews pediatric outcomes by social determinants of health. Which association was taught in this course?

options.label: A
options.text: Infant mortality increases as maternal education level decreases
options.rationale: The SDOH slide states infant mortality increases as the mother's education decreases, and children from impoverished families are twice as likely to have psychosocial problems (Slides 3, 5; Transcript 3).

options.label: B
options.text: Children from low-socioeconomic families are more likely to be immunized by age 4
options.rationale: Low-SES children are less likely to be immunized at 4 years and less likely to receive dental care.

options.label: C
options.text: Children with public insurance report excellent health more often than those with private insurance
options.rationale: Children with public insurance are less likely to be in excellent health than those with private insurance.

options.label: D
options.text: Income level has no measurable association with psychosocial problems
options.rationale: Impoverished children are twice as likely to have psychosocial problems, a direct income association.

stem: A 6-month-old was born at 32 weeks' gestation. The infant pulls to a seated position with trunk support, reaches and transfers objects, and babbles. Using corrected age, how should the PNP interpret these skills?

options.label: A
options.text: Appropriate; corrected age is about 4 months, matching the observed skills
options.rationale: Corrected age = chronological age minus weeks of prematurity: 6 months minus 8 weeks (2 months) = 4 months; reaching, transferring, and babbling with supported sitting fit a 4-month corrected profile, and the professor insisted preemies be tracked by corrected age (Part 2, Slides 26-29; Transcript 2).

options.label: B
options.text: Indeterminate; corrected age cannot be calculated without birth weight
options.rationale: Corrected age requires gestational age or weeks premature, not birth weight.

options.label: C
options.text: Advanced; these are 9-month skills
options.rationale: These are 4-6 month skills, not 9-month skills.

options.label: D
options.text: Delayed; a 6-month-old should sit independently regardless of gestational age at birth
options.rationale: Independent sitting is a 6-9 month uncorrected expectation; applying it without correction misjudges the ex-preemie.

questions.sourceMapping: Growth & Development Part 2, Slides 26-29; Transcript 2 (corrected age calculation example) | Parallel Form B (options re-randomized)

stem: Until what age should corrected age generally be applied when assessing a former 30-week gestation infant (10 weeks premature), using the course's weeks-times-ten rule?

options.label: A
options.text: Until 6 months of chronological age
options.rationale: Six months is far earlier than either rule allows.

options.label: B
options.text: Until about 100 weeks (roughly 25 months), consistent with catch-up by 2-2.5 years
options.rationale: The course teaches catch-up by 2-2.5 years or weeks premature times 10 (10 weeks x 10 = 100 weeks about 25 months), after which the child should equal non-premature peers (Part 2, Slide 29; Transcript 2).

options.label: C
options.text: Until 12 months of chronological age always
options.rationale: A fixed 12-month cutoff ignores the degree of prematurity and the 2-2.5 year catch-up window.

options.label: D
options.text: Until 5 years of age
options.rationale: By 5 years correction is unnecessary; catch-up is complete by 2-2.5 years.

stem: A parent reports that her 20-month-old previously used 15 words and two-word phrases but now speaks only a few unintelligible sounds. What is the most appropriate action?

options.label: A
options.text: Reassure; language regression is common between 18 and 24 months
options.rationale: Regression is never a normal variant to be reassured away.

options.label: B
options.text: Schedule prompt developmental evaluation; loss of an achieved milestone is always significant
options.rationale: The professor's key point, stated twice and marked 'most important' on the slide: any milestone met and then lost prompts immediate further evaluation, and caregiver concern must be investigated (Part 2, Slides 2, 30; Transcript 2).

options.label: C
options.text: Repeat screening at the 24-month visit
options.rationale: Waiting delays evaluation of a red-flag regression (e.g., hearing loss, seizure disorder, autism spectrum, neurodegenerative disease).

options.label: D
options.text: Obtain a chromosomal microarray as the first step
options.rationale: Microarray may be part of a regression workup but follows, not replaces, prompt developmental and medical evaluation.

questions.sourceMapping: Growth & Development Part 2, Slides 2, 30; Transcript 2 (milestone lost = evaluate; listen to parents)

stem: A mother states she is sure something is wrong with her 12-month-old's development, though the PNP's screening tool scores within normal limits. What is the most appropriate response?

options.label: A
options.text: Reassure the mother that validated tools outweigh parental impression
options.rationale: Screening tools have imperfect sensitivity; parental concern independently warrants evaluation.

options.label: B
options.text: Investigate the concern further; caregiver suspicion of a sensory or motor difference must be taken seriously
options.rationale: The course's 'Most Important' slide: caregiver suspicion that the child is not seeing, hearing, moving, or taking notice like peers must be taken very seriously and investigated appropriately; listen to parents (Part 2, Slide 2; Transcript 2).

options.label: C
options.text: Repeat the same screening tool at the next visit
options.rationale: Repeating an insensitive tool delays the workup the course mandates.

options.label: D
options.text: Refer directly to psychiatry for maternal anxiety
options.rationale: Attributing concern to maternal anxiety without evaluation dismisses the flagged red flag.

questions.sourceMapping: Growth & Development Part 2, Slide 2; Transcript 2

stem: A 14-month-old with a congenital cardiac defect feeds vigorously yet remains below the 5th percentile for weight with preserved length and head circumference. Which mechanism best explains this pattern?

options.label: A
options.text: Inadequate caloric intake from poor feeding technique alone
options.rationale: The vignette describes vigorous feeding, pointing to demand, not intake technique.

options.label: B
options.text: Increased metabolic demand from the cardiac condition outstripping intake
options.rationale: The professor taught that feeding is exercise for infants: cardiac (or endocrine) disease raises caloric demand so weight gain falters despite good intake, and weight is the first parameter to fall in caloric deficit (Part 2, Slides 21, 43; Transcript 2).

options.label: C
options.text: Normal constitutional growth variant
options.rationale: A falling weight percentile with a cardiac lesion is pathologic, not constitutional.

options.label: D
options.text: Measurement error from an uncalibrated scale
options.rationale: Rechecking discrepant measurements is good practice, but the pattern plus cardiac history makes increased demand the mechanism.

questions.sourceMapping: Growth & Development Part 2, Slides 21, 43; Transcript 2 (feeding as exercise; cardiac caloric demand)

stem: In an infant with prolonged inadequate caloric intake, in what order do the growth parameters typically fall?

options.label: A
options.text: Head circumference, then length, then weight
options.rationale: Head circumference is the most protected parameter and falls last, not first.

options.label: B
options.text: Weight, then length, then head circumference
options.rationale: With caloric insufficiency the weight percentile falls first, then height/length, and head circumference last; the professor repeated this sequence as an exam-worthy concept and noted all three falling signals a global problem (Newborn/Infant deck Slide 21; Transcripts 2 and 4).

options.label: C
options.text: Length, then weight, then head circumference
options.rationale: Length is spared relative to weight early in undernutrition.

options.label: D
options.text: All three fall simultaneously
options.rationale: Simultaneous decline suggests a global or syndromic process rather than simple caloric insufficiency.

questions.sourceMapping: Newborn/Infant deck Slide 21; Transcript 2; Transcript 4 (weight, then length, then head)

stem: A 4-month-old's head circumference has crossed from the 50th to the 97th percentile over two visits. Length and weight track at the 50th. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.text: Reassure; head circumference variability is common in the first year
options.rationale: A two-line upward crossing is not normal variability.

options.label: B
options.text: Re-measure to confirm, then evaluate for macrocephaly causes such as hydrocephalus
options.rationale: Abnormal head growth is defined as more than 2 SD (about crossing two major percentile lines) above or below the expected trajectory; rapid upward crossing requires re-measurement for technique and then evaluation for macrocephaly (hydrocephalus, familial, masses), with fontanelle and suture assessment (Slides 23, 33; Transcripts 2, 3).

options.label: C
options.text: Order routine skull radiographs as first-line testing
options.rationale: Imaging begins with ultrasound through the open fontanelle or MRI as indicated, not routine radiographs.

options.label: D
options.text: Defer evaluation until the anterior fontanelle closes
options.rationale: Waiting forfeits the window in which the open fontanelle both signals and permits evaluation of raised intracranial pressure.

questions.sourceMapping: Newborn/Infant deck Slides 23, 33; Growth & Development Part 2, Slide 42; Transcripts 2-3

stem: Which fontanelle closure pairing is correct according to the course tables?

options.label: A
options.text: Posterior fontanelle closes by 2 months of age
options.rationale: The closure table: posterior 2 months, sphenoid (anterolateral) 3 months, mastoid (posterolateral) 1 year, anterior 12-18 months; the professor required knowing these (Slide 24; Transcript 3).

options.label: B
options.text: Anterior fontanelle closes by 3 months of age
options.rationale: The anterior fontanelle closes at 12-18 months, not 3 months.

options.label: C
options.text: Mastoid (posterolateral) fontanelle closes by 2 months of age
options.rationale: The mastoid fontanelle closes around 1 year.

options.label: D
options.text: Sphenoid (anterolateral) fontanelle closes at 12-18 months
options.rationale: The sphenoid fontanelle closes around 3 months.

questions.sourceMapping: Newborn/Infant deck Slide 24; Growth & Development Part 2, Slide 40; Transcript 3

stem: During a well visit for a 7-month-old with 3 days of vomiting and poor intake, the anterior fontanelle feels sunken and mucous membranes are dry. What does the fontanelle finding indicate?

options.label: A
options.text: Craniosynostosis
options.rationale: Craniosynostosis is identified by ridged, prematurely fused sutures and head shape, not fontanelle depression.

options.label: B
options.text: Normal age-related fontanelle change
options.rationale: A sunken fontanelle is never a normal variant.

options.label: C
options.text: Increased intracranial pressure
options.rationale: Raised intracranial pressure produces a bulging, tense fontanelle.

options.label: D
options.text: Dehydration
options.rationale: A sunken fontanelle signals dehydration (or shock), while a bulging fontanelle signals excess fluid or raised intracranial pressure; the professor tied fontanelle assessment directly to acute hydration status (Transcript 3; Slide 90).

questions.sourceMapping: Transcript 3 (fontanelles assess hydration); Newborn/Infant deck Slide 90 | Parallel Form B (options re-randomized)

stem: A term infant's weight, length, and head circumference all track just below the 5th percentile along parallel curves since birth. Parents are both under 5 feet 4 inches and 5 feet 7 inches. Development is normal. Which interpretation is most appropriate?

options.label: A
options.text: Endocrine growth failure requires immediate growth hormone testing
options.rationale: Endocrine failure shows declining or discrepant patterns; stable familial tracking does not warrant immediate GH testing.

options.label: B
options.text: Caloric insufficiency is the leading diagnosis
options.rationale: Caloric insufficiency produces declining or discrepant percentiles (weight first), not stable parallel tracking.

options.label: C
options.text: This pattern indicates an intrauterine insult requiring genetic testing today
options.rationale: Intrauterine insult or genetic abnormality is considered when growth is symmetrically low but discordant with parental pattern or accompanied by dysmorphism; parental heights here explain the curve.

options.label: D
options.text: Constitutional or familial short stature is likely; confirm with midparental height assessment
options.rationale: When all three parameters track together on the same low percentile with normal development and short statured parents, familial/constitutional short stature is likely; the growth-pattern table directs midparental height evaluation first (Part 2, Slide 43; Transcript 2).

questions.sourceMapping: Growth & Development Part 2, Slide 43; Transcript 2 (all three tracking same percentile may be their pattern) | Parallel Form B (options re-randomized)

stem: A 9-month-old's chart shows weight at the 5th percentile, length at the 10th, and head circumference at the 75th, with weight crossing down two percentile lines since the 4-month visit. Which category from the course growth-pattern table applies?

options.label: A
options.text: Familial short stature
options.rationale: Familial short stature shows all parameters low and parallel, not head-sparing discrepancy.

options.label: B
options.text: Catch-down growth of a large-for-gestational-age infant
options.rationale: LGA catch-down occurs 6-18 months without exceeding 2 SD and with normal development; a head-sparing weight drop is not catch-down.

options.label: C
options.text: Discrepant and declining percentiles suggesting caloric insufficiency or endocrine growth failure
options.rationale: Discrepancy between weight/length and a preserved head percentile plus declining weight percentiles matches the table's caloric insufficiency/endocrine growth failure row, prompting dietary and social history and further workup (Part 2, Slide 43; Transcript 2).

options.label: D
options.text: Normal variant requiring no action
options.rationale: A two-line downward weight cross is a red flag, not a normal variant.

questions.sourceMapping: Growth & Development Part 2, Slide 43; Newborn/Infant deck Slide 21; Transcript 2 | Parallel Form B (options re-randomized)

stem: A large-for-gestational-age infant of a diabetic mother shows weight dropping from the 90th to the 60th percentile between 6 and 12 months while length and head circumference track normally and development is appropriate. What is the best interpretation?

options.label: A
options.text: Pathologic failure to thrive requiring admission
options.rationale: A controlled, development-normal catch-down within 2 SD is not failure to thrive.

options.label: B
options.text: Expected catch-down growth until the curve matches genetic programming
options.rationale: LGA infants typically catch down in weight between 6-18 months until matching genetic potential, provided the drop does not exceed 2 SD and development is normal (Newborn/Infant deck Slide 21; Transcript 2).

options.label: C
options.text: Onset of growth hormone deficiency
options.rationale: GH deficiency would show declining length/height and often hypoglycemia, not isolated appropriate catch-down.

options.label: D
options.text: Misplotting; LGA infants should remain above the 90th percentile
options.rationale: LGA infants are not expected to stay above the 90th percentile; recalibration to parental size is normal.

questions.sourceMapping: Newborn/Infant deck Slide 21; Transcript 2 (LGA catch-down 6-18 months)

stem: Which statement about catch-up growth in premature and small-for-gestational-age infants reflects the course teaching?

options.label: A
options.text: Catch-up growth typically begins around 6 months and may require higher caloric intake
options.rationale: The deck states premature and SGA infants show catch-up growth around 6 months, feed on demand, and may need higher caloric intake, while remaining at risk for later obesity (Slide 21; Transcript 2).

options.label: B
options.text: Catch-up growth is complete by 3 months of age in all preterm infants
options.rationale: Catch-up timing varies with degree of prematurity and extends into the second year.

options.label: C
options.text: SGA infants should never receive supplemental calories
options.rationale: Higher caloric density is often needed during catch-up.

options.label: D
options.text: Catch-up growth is signaled by head circumference falling first
options.rationale: Head circumference is protected and rises appropriately during catch-up; it does not fall first.

stem: Which growth-chart selection is correct for a 15-month-old born at term in the United States?

options.label: A
options.text: CDC charts for all parameters
options.rationale: CDC charts apply from 2 years onward, not at 15 months.

options.label: B
options.text: WHO charts for weight, length, and head circumference
options.rationale: CDC recommends WHO growth charts for children 0-2 years and CDC charts from age 2; term infants use sex-specific WHO charts (Slides 20; Transcripts 2-3; Milestone documents include WHO 0-36 month charts).

options.label: C
options.text: CDC charts for weight and WHO charts for length
options.rationale: Chart systems are not mixed by parameter.

options.label: D

stem: A parent asks what anticipatory guidance means. Which definition matches the course?

options.label: A
options.text: Treatment of developmental disorders after they are diagnosed
options.rationale: Anticipatory guidance is preventive counseling, not treatment.

options.label: B
options.text: Age-specific provider guidance based on expected developmental and physical events to assist caregivers
options.rationale: Anticipatory guidance is provider-delivered, age-specific counseling built on expected developmental and physical events so caregivers know what to expect, what to watch for, and when to call (Part 1, Slide 32; Transcript 1).

options.label: C
options.text: Standardized developmental testing performed at every well visit
options.rationale: Screening tools (e.g., ASQ) supplement but are not the definition of anticipatory guidance.

options.label: D
options.text: Counseling provided only when parents raise a concern
options.rationale: Guidance is proactively delivered at each visit, not only reactively.

questions.sourceMapping: Growth & Development Part 1, Slide 32; Transcript 1 (anticipatory guidance at each well visit)

stem: Which recommendation about infant positioning best supports both motor development and skull shape?

options.label: A
options.text: Supine sleep and supervised prone play (tummy time) while awake
options.rationale: The professor emphasized tummy time while awake to build core and head control and to offload the occiput (preventing positional plagiocephaly), while sleep must remain supine for SIDS prevention (Transcripts 2, 3; Slide 50).

options.label: B
options.text: Prone sleep to strengthen neck muscles
options.rationale: Prone sleep increases SIDS risk and is never recommended.

options.label: C
options.text: Continuous supine positioning including play time
options.rationale: Exclusive supine positioning without awake prone time contributes to positional flattening and delays motor milestones.

options.label: D
options.text: Side-lying sleep with a positioning wedge
options.rationale: Side-lying and wedges are unsafe sleep practices.

questions.sourceMapping: Transcript 2 (tummy time importance); Newborn/Infant deck Slide 50 (safe sleep)

stem: A 17-month-old has not yet received any developmental services despite documented expressive language delay. The family has limited income. Which resource should the PNP prioritize?

options.label: A
options.text: Private speech therapy referral with self-pay
options.rationale: Self-pay therapy ignores the free entitlement the course emphasizes.

options.label: B
options.text: State early intervention program (Birth to Three/Early Intervention), which provides free in-home assessment and services
options.rationale: The professor highlighted Birth to Three/Early Intervention as a free home-based evaluation and service program, stressing referral before age 3 because families must pay after 3; early intervention reduces long-term impact of delays (Transcript 2).

options.label: C
options.text: Wait until age 3 when school district services begin
options.rationale: After age 3 families pay; delaying forfeits free services and critical intervention time.

options.label: D
options.text: Observation with re-screening in 6 months
options.rationale: Documented delay at 17 months warrants action now, not observation.

stem: At which well visit does the course specify administration of a standardized developmental questionnaire (ASQ) as part of surveillance?

options.label: A
options.text: 2-month visit

options.text: 12-month visit
options.rationale: The 12-month visit emphasizes walking and language emergence; the named ASQ point is 9 months.

questions.sourceMapping: Newborn/Infant deck Slide 62; Transcript 3 (ASQ at 9 months)

stem: A PNP observes a 4-month-old during a well visit. Which cluster of findings is expected at this age?

options.label: A
options.text: Sits unassisted, pincer grasp, waves bye-bye
options.rationale: Those are 9-12 month skills.

options.label: B
options.text: Holds head at midline prone, lifts head and chest, rolls front to back, reaches with both hands, laughs
options.rationale: The 4-month profile: head midline in prone with head/chest lift, front-to-back rolling, purposeful two-hand reach, open hands, laughing and vowel sounds (Slides 56-57; WCC chart; Transcript 2).

options.label: C
options.text: Cruises along furniture, says mama/dada specifically, feeds self with fingers
options.rationale: Cruising, specific parent names, and finger feeding are 9-12 month skills.

options.label: D
options.text: Walks alone, stacks two blocks, uses three-word sentences
options.rationale: Walking, block stacking, and three-word sentences belong to 12-36 months.

questions.sourceMapping: Newborn/Infant deck Slides 56-57; WCC chart; Transcript 2

stem: Select all social-emotional findings that warrant further evaluation in the infant described.

options.label: A
options.text: A 7-month-old who plays alone, rarely looks at people, and seems to stare off despite documented normal hearing
options.rationale: Not engaging socially, poor eye contact, and staring off with normal hearing are listed abnormal social signs requiring evaluation; parents often first suspect hearing (Part 2, Slides 23, 25; Transcript 2).

options.label: B
options.text: A 3-month-old who has never smiled back when smiled to
options.rationale: The social smile should appear by about 6 weeks and certainly by 2 months; its absence is an early social-emotional red flag.

options.label: C
options.text: A 20-month-old who lost previously used words and no longer responds to his name
options.rationale: Loss of achieved language and social response is milestone regression, which the course flags for immediate evaluation.

options.label: D
options.text: A 7-month-old who cries when handed to unfamiliar relatives after previously being easygoing
options.rationale: New-onset stranger anxiety in the second half of year one reflects object permanence and secure attachment; it is reassuring.

options.label: E
options.text: An 8-month-old who delights in peekaboo and turns to mother when distressed
options.rationale: Peekaboo delight and turning to the caregiver when distressed demonstrate object permanence and healthy attachment.

questions.sourceMapping: Growth & Development Part 2, Slides 2, 23, 25; Transcript 2; Newborn/Infant deck Slides 58-60

stem: A 15-month-old cannot demonstrate a pincer grasp and rakes at small objects with the whole hand. Which additional finding, if present, most strengthens the case for prompt referral?

options.label: A
options.text: Walking independently since 13 months
options.rationale: Independent walking at 13 months is normal gross motor and does not add concern.

options.label: B
options.text: Persistent fisting of the hands until 5 months of age
options.rationale: Abnormal pincer by 15 months plus a history of persistently fisted hands beyond 3 months stacks two listed fine motor red flags, indicating a neurologic or motor disorder needing referral (Part 2, Slide 16; Transcript 2).

options.label: C
options.text: Saying four words
options.rationale: Four words at 15 months is within the 4-10 word expectation.

options.label: D
options.text: Feeding self with a spoon messily
options.rationale: Messy spoon self-feeding is an age-appropriate adaptive skill.

questions.sourceMapping: Growth & Development Part 2, Slide 16; Transcript 2 (pincer by 15 months; fisted at 3 months)

stem: The professor described an office technique to screen for unilateral weakness at the 4-month visit. What is it?

options.label: A
options.text: Placing the infant in vertical suspension and watching shoulder strength
options.rationale: Vertical suspension assesses global tone, not unilateral weakness, in the newborn period.

options.label: B
options.text: Presenting an object at midline and observing whether both hands come to it
options.rationale: At 4 months the PNP places an object in front of the face and expects both hands to come to it; bringing only one hand suggests weakness on the other side (Transcript 2).

options.label: C
options.text: Eliciting the Moro reflex and comparing arm excursion
options.rationale: Asymmetric Moro suggests clavicle fracture or brachial plexus injury in the newborn, not the 4-month office screen described.

options.label: D
options.text: Measuring grip strength with a dynamometer
options.rationale: Dynamometry is not an infant office technique.

questions.sourceMapping: Transcript 2 (4-month two-hand object screen) | Parallel Form B (options re-randomized)

stem: A 3-year-old is brought in for a kindergarten-readiness concern. Per the professor's office practice, which fine motor tasks would she expect to assess at the 5-year pre-kindergarten examination?

options.label: A
options.text: Pincer grasp of a raisin and hand-to-hand transfer
options.rationale: Those are infant (9-12 month) fine motor tasks.

options.label: B
options.text: Writing name, letter formation, pencil grip, and drawing a person with about five parts
options.rationale: The professor described her 5-year pre-kindergarten exam: can the child write name, form letters, show a mature pencil grip, and draw a person with roughly five body parts (head, body, two arms, two legs) (Transcript 2).

options.label: C
options.text: Copying a triangle and cutting with scissors exclusively
options.rationale: Triangle copying and scissors are later preschool skills and were not the described screen.

options.label: D
options.text: Stacking nine cubes and threading beads
options.rationale: Nine-cube towers belong to about 3-4 years, not the described 5-year screen.

questions.sourceMapping: Transcript 2 (5-year pre-K writing, pencil grip, draw-a-person)

stem: A 6-hour-old term newborn rests with a respiratory rate of 68 breaths per minute, heart rate 150, and temperature 98.2 F. Using the normal newborn ranges taught in this course, how should the PNP interpret the respiratory rate?

options.label: A
options.text: Normal; newborn respiratory rates range up to 80 at rest
options.rationale: The taught range ends at 60; 68 at rest is abnormal.

options.label: B
options.text: Tachypneic; above 60 requires evaluation for respiratory distress and transition problems
options.rationale: Normal newborn respiratory rate is 40-60; the professor stressed that a rate above 60 signals possible cardiopulmonary pathology and mandates assessment for distress (grunting, flaring, retractions, cyanosis) and transition problems such as TTN or RDS (Slide 17; Transcript 3; AAFP Part I).

options.label: C
options.text: Normal if the infant was delivered by cesarean
options.rationale: Cesarean delivery raises TTN risk but does not normalize tachypnea; it raises the index of suspicion.

options.label: D
options.text: Concerning only if accompanied by fever
options.rationale: Newborns with serious respiratory or cardiac disease are typically afebrile; fever is not required for concern.

questions.sourceMapping: Newborn/Infant deck Slide 17; Transcript 3; AAFP Part I (respiratory distress signs)

stem: On auscultation of a 4-hour-old newborn, breath sounds are markedly decreased on the left with asymmetric chest movement. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.text: Reassure and re-auscultate at the 2-week visit
options.rationale: Asymmetric breath sounds are never a watch-and-wait finding in the first hours of life.

options.label: B
options.text: Obtain chest imaging to evaluate for pneumothorax or congenital lung lesion
options.rationale: Unequal breath sounds may indicate pneumothorax, congenital pulmonary malformation, or diaphragmatic hernia and should prompt imaging per AAFP Part II; chest movement should be symmetric (AAFP Part II, chest section).

options.label: C
options.text: Start empiric antibiotics for pneumonia
options.rationale: Early-onset sepsis presents with respiratory distress and temperature instability, not isolated unilateral decreased breath sounds; imaging comes first.

options.label: D
options.text: Order an echocardiogram for congenital heart disease
options.rationale: Echocardiography evaluates cardiac disease; the finding here is pulmonary asymmetry.

questions.sourceMapping: AAFP Part II (chest symmetry, pneumothorax, cystic malformation, diaphragmatic hernia)

stem: A term newborn delivered by repeat cesarean develops tachypnea at 2 hours of age with mild retractions. Chest radiograph shows retained fluid and hyperinflation. The infant otherwise appears well. Which diagnosis and management pair is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: Respiratory distress syndrome; administer surfactant
options.rationale: RDS results from surfactant deficiency, typically in preterm infants or infants of diabetic mothers, with a ground-glass pattern, not retained fluid in a well-appearing term cesarean newborn.

options.label: B
options.text: Transient tachypnea of the newborn; supportive respiratory care with expected resolution within 48 hours
options.rationale: TTN predominates after cesarean or precipitous delivery from retained fetal lung fluid, causes alveolar hypoventilation, and resolves within about 48 hours with supportive care (AAFP Part I).

options.label: C
options.text: Meconium aspiration syndrome; initiate mechanical ventilation
options.rationale: Meconium aspiration follows meconium-stained deliveries with patchy infiltrates and often severe distress.

options.label: D
options.text: Congenital diaphragmatic hernia; emergent surgical consultation
options.rationale: Diaphragmatic hernia presents with scaphoid abdomen, severe distress, and bowel sounds in the chest prenatally or at birth.

questions.sourceMapping: AAFP Part I (TTN vs RDS; precipitous/cesarean association; 48-hour resolution)

stem: Which assessment tool combines physical and neuromuscular characteristics to establish gestational age in a newborn with uncertain dates?

options.label: A
options.text: Apgar scoring at 1 and 5 minutes
options.rationale: Apgar scores evaluate transition and need for resuscitation, not gestational age.

options.label: B
options.text: The Ortolani maneuver
options.rationale: Ortolani tests hip reducibility.

options.label: C
options.text: The New Ballard Score
options.rationale: The New Ballard Score assesses gestational age through physical characteristics and neuromuscular maturity, per AAFP Part I (AAFP Part I, general assessment).

options.label: D
options.text: The Brazelton Neonatal Behavioral Assessment Scale
options.rationale: Brazelton assesses behavioral responses, not gestational dating.

questions.sourceMapping: AAFP Part I (Ballard score) | Parallel Form B (options re-randomized)

stem: Select all newborn populations for which the AAP recommends scheduled glucose screening.

options.label: A
options.text: Newborns of mothers with diabetes mellitus
options.rationale: Infants of diabetic mothers experience hyperinsulinism-driven hypoglycemia and are screened.

options.label: B
options.text: Appropriate-for-gestational-age term newborns born by cesarean
options.rationale: Cesarean delivery alone in an AGA term newborn is not an indication for scheduled glucose screening.

options.label: C
options.text: Late preterm newborns (34 0/7 to 36 6/7 weeks)
options.rationale: Late preterm infants (34-36 6/7 weeks) have immature feeding and stores and are screened.

options.label: D
options.text: Small for gestational age newborns
options.rationale: SGA infants (below the 10th percentile) have limited glycogen stores and are screened.

options.label: E
options.text: Large for gestational age newborns
options.rationale: LGA infants (above the 90th percentile, often from maternal diabetes) are at increased hypoglycemia risk and require scheduled screening (AAFP Part I, SORT C).

questions.sourceMapping: AAFP Part I SORT recommendations (hypoglycemia screening populations) | Parallel Form B (options re-randomized)

stem: A newborn is SGA with birth weight below the 10th percentile. Head circumference is preserved near the 50th percentile while weight and length are both below the 10th. Which etiology does this asymmetric pattern suggest?

options.label: A
options.text: A congenital TORCH infection early in gestation
options.rationale: Early congenital infection typically causes symmetric growth restriction with dysmorphic or systemic features.

options.label: B
options.text: Late-gestation uteroplacental insufficiency with brain-sparing
options.rationale: When the insult occurs later in pregnancy (uteroplacental insufficiency), head circumference is preserved relative to weight and length (brain-sparing, asymmetric IUGR); early chronic insults (smoking, TORCH, chromosomal) produce symmetric reduction (AAFP Part I).

options.label: C
options.text: A chromosomal trisomy
options.rationale: Trisomies generally cause symmetric restriction with dysmorphism.

options.label: D
options.text: Constitutional smallness of a healthy small parent
options.rationale: Constitutional smallness tracks all parameters proportionally along a parental pattern, not head-sparing asymmetry.

questions.sourceMapping: AAFP Part I (symmetric vs asymmetric IUGR; head-sparing)

stem: Using the labeled newborn skull diagram, which structure is normally no larger than 1 to 1.5 cm in diameter at birth?

images.alt: Figure 1: AAFP Part I, Figure 1A reference asset - top-down view of the normal newborn skull with sutures and fontanelles labeled.
images.caption: Figure 1: AAFP Part I, Figure 1A reference asset - top-down view of the normal newborn skull with sutures and fontanelles labeled.

options.label: A
options.text: Sagittal suture
options.rationale: Sutures are linear joints, not measured as fontanelle diameters.

options.label: B
options.text: Posterior fontanelle
options.rationale: The posterior fontanelle measures no more than 1-1.5 cm at birth, while the anterior fontanelle averages 3-6 cm; the diagram's posterior triangle at the lambdoid-metopic junction is that structure (AAFP Part I).

options.label: C
options.text: Coronal suture
options.rationale: The coronal suture is a linear joint between frontal and parietal bones.

options.label: D
options.text: Anterior fontanelle
options.rationale: The anterior fontanelle is the large 3-6 cm diamond at the coronal-sagittal-metopic junction.

questions.sourceMapping: AAFP Part I (fontanelle sizes); Newborn/Infant deck Slide 24 | Parallel Form B (options re-randomized)

stem: A newborn's anterior fontanelle measures 7 cm and feels widely open. Which condition belongs in the differential diagnosis for an abnormally large anterior fontanelle?

options.label: A
options.text: Congenital hypothyroidism
options.rationale: A large anterior fontanelle may indicate increased intracranial pressure, Down syndrome, hypophosphatemia, trisomies, or congenital hypothyroidism (AAFP Part I).

options.label: B
options.text: Craniosynostosis of the sagittal suture
options.rationale: Craniosynostosis involves premature suture fusion with ridging and head-shape change, not a large open fontanelle.

options.label: C
options.text: Isolated familial macrocephaly
options.rationale: Familial macrocephaly enlarges head circumference without necessarily enlarging the fontanelle.

options.label: D
options.text: Caput succedaneum
options.rationale: Caput is scalp edema overlying the skull, unrelated to fontanelle size.

questions.sourceMapping: AAFP Part I (large anterior fontanelle differential)

stem: A 3-week-old has an elongated, narrow skull with a palpable ridge along the midline top of the head. Compensatory growth has occurred along the long axis. Which suture is prematurely fused?

options.label: A
options.text: Metopic
options.rationale: Metopic fusion causes trigonocephaly (triangular forehead).

options.label: B
options.text: Sagittal
options.rationale: Sagittal synostosis produces scaphocephaly (elongated head), the most common craniosynostosis; compensatory growth proceeds parallel to the fused suture, and a ridged suture distinguishes synostosis from positional molding (Slides 25-27; AAFP Part I).

options.label: C
options.text: Unicoronal
options.rationale: Unicoronal fusion causes anterior plagiocephaly with forehead flattening on the fused side.

options.label: D
options.text: Lambdoid
options.rationale: Lambdoid fusion causes posterior plagiocephaly, not midline elongation.

questions.sourceMapping: Newborn/Infant deck Slides 25-27; AAFP Part I (craniosynostosis patterns)

stem: The diagram contrasts three scalp lesions. A newborn has soft, boggy, pitting scalp edema present immediately at birth that crosses the midline and suture lines. Which lesion and expectation pair is correct?

images.alt: Figure 2: Newborn/Infant deck Slide 31 reference asset - cross-section and comparison of caput succedaneum, cephalohematoma, and subgaleal hemorrhage.
images.caption: Figure 2: Newborn/Infant deck Slide 31 reference asset - cross-section and comparison of caput succedaneum, cephalohematoma, and subgaleal hemorrhage.

options.label: A
options.text: Cephalohematoma; will enlarge over 1-3 days and cause jaundice
options.rationale: Cephalohematoma is subperiosteal, does NOT cross sutures, appears hours after birth, and is firm rather than pitting.

options.label: B
options.text: Caput succedaneum; should resolve within about 24-72 hours without complication
options.rationale: Caput succedaneum is edema above the periosteum that crosses suture lines, is present at birth, pits on pressure, and resolves in 24-72 (up to 48) hours (Slide 31; AAFP Part I; Transcript 3).

options.label: C
options.text: Subgaleal hemorrhage; requires immediate emergency evaluation
options.rationale: Subgaleal hemorrhage is a fluctuant shifting collection crossing sutures with risk of shock; the described pitting edema present at birth fits caput.

options.label: D
options.text: Depressed skull fracture; requires computed tomography
options.rationale: Fracture is suggested by a depressed, focal bony defect or neurologic signs, not diffuse pitting edema.

questions.sourceMapping: Newborn/Infant deck Slide 31; AAFP Part I Figure 2; Transcript 3

stem: A 2-day-old vacuum-assisted newborn develops a firm, fluctuant swelling limited to the right parietal bone that has enlarged since birth. Which complication should the PNP monitor for?

options.label: A
options.text: Hyperbilirubinemia and anemia from blood breakdown
options.rationale: Cephalohematoma (subperiosteal, suture-limited, instrument-associated, enlarging over 1-3 days) carries risk of jaundice from resorbing blood and anemia; it may take 3-4 months to fully resorb (Slide 31; AAFP Part I).

options.label: B
options.text: Immediate hypovolemic shock within minutes of birth
options.rationale: Rapid shock characterizes subgaleal hemorrhage, not cephalohematoma.

options.label: C
options.text: Bacterial meningitis within 24 hours
options.rationale: Meningitis is not a typical complication; the hemorrhage is extravascular and sterile.

options.label: D
options.text: Permanent suture fusion
options.rationale: Cephalohematoma does not fuse sutures; calcified rims resolve over months.

questions.sourceMapping: Newborn/Infant deck Slide 31; AAFP Part I (cephalohematoma complications)

stem: During the newborn examination, palpation of a soft, fluctuant scalp mass that shifts forward when pressure is applied to the occiput and freely crosses suture lines is noted. The infant is pale with a heart rate of 180. What is the most appropriate action?

options.label: A
options.text: Document and recheck at the 2-week visit
options.rationale: Delay risks decompensation from ongoing bleeding.

options.label: B
options.text: Immediate emergency evaluation for subgaleal hemorrhage with monitoring for hypotension and shock
options.rationale: A fluctuant, shifting collection crossing sutures indicates subgaleal hemorrhage; the blood volume lost into this space can cause hypotension and shock, so the course demands immediate ED evaluation (Slide 32; Transcript 3).

options.label: C
options.text: Apply a pressure dressing and discharge home
options.rationale: Pressure dressings do not address ongoing subgaleal bleeding and discharge is unsafe.

options.label: D
options.text: Order serum bilirubin and follow up in 48 hours
options.rationale: Bilirubin follow-up addresses cephalohematoma jaundice, not acute hemorrhagic shock risk.

questions.sourceMapping: Newborn/Infant deck Slide 32; Transcript 3 (subgaleal = high acuity, immediate ED eval)

stem: Row C of the illustration shows a normal red reflex in the right eye and no reflex in the left eye. What does an absent red reflex indicate?

images.alt: Figure 3: AAFP Part I, Figure 3 reference asset - interpretation of red reflex results: A symmetric normal, B diminished left reflex, C absent left reflex.
images.caption: Figure 3: AAFP Part I, Figure 3 reference asset - interpretation of red reflex results: A symmetric normal, B diminished left reflex, C absent left reflex.

options.label: A
options.text: Normal variation in fundus pigmentation
options.rationale: Pigmentation alters reflex color but should never abolish it; a white or absent reflex is never normal.

options.label: B
options.text: Blockage of the reflection by an opacity such as a cataract, warranting urgent ophthalmology referral
options.rationale: An absent reflex occurs when the reflection is blocked by an opacity such as a cataract (or other leukokoria cause); any abnormal red reflex warrants urgent ophthalmology referral (AAFP Part I, Figure 3 and text).

options.label: C
options.text: Transient finding of the first month that resolves spontaneously
options.rationale: An absent red reflex never resolves on observation; retinoblastoma and cataract are time-critical.

options.label: D
options.text: A refractive error between the eyes requiring routine glasses
options.rationale: A diminished (not absent) reflex, row B, most commonly reflects refractive difference; absence implies opacity.

questions.sourceMapping: AAFP Part I (red reflex technique and Figure 3; leukokoria differential) | Parallel Form B (options re-randomized)

stem: Which cause of leukokoria is the most common intraocular tumor of childhood and must be excluded in any newborn with a white pupillary reflex?

options.label: A
options.text: Chorioretinitis
options.rationale: Chorioretinitis reflects intrauterine infection (CMV, toxoplasmosis).

options.label: B
options.text: Coats disease
options.rationale: Coats disease is a congenital vascular disorder, not the most common tumor.

options.label: C
options.text: Retinoblastoma
options.rationale: Retinoblastoma is the most common intraocular tumor in children and tops the leukokoria differential; family history of retinoblastoma, cataracts, glaucoma, or retinal abnormalities mandates referral regardless of reflex findings (AAFP Part I, Table 2 and SORT).

options.label: D
options.text: Persistent fetal vasculature
options.rationale: Persistent fetal vasculature results from failed hyaloid involution.

questions.sourceMapping: AAFP Part I Table 2 and SORT recommendation (ophthalmology referral) | Parallel Form B (options re-randomized)

stem: A 10-day-old has sticky yellow discharge matting the lashes of the right eye; the conjunctiva is white and non-injected. Which diagnosis is most likely?

options.label: A
options.text: Gonococcal ophthalmia neonatorum
options.rationale: Gonococcal infection (days 2-7) causes bilateral purulent conjunctivitis with marked injection.

options.label: B
options.text: Chlamydial conjunctivitis
options.rationale: Chlamydia (days 5-14) causes hyperemia to diffuse swelling and chemosis.

options.label: C
options.text: Dacryostenosis (nasolacrimal duct obstruction)
options.rationale: Dacryostenosis produces accumulated sticky yellow secretions with an otherwise normal-appearing eye, distinguishing it from ophthalmia neonatorum, which shows conjunctival injection and edema (AAFP Part I, Table 3).

options.label: D
options.text: Herpes simplex keratoconjunctivitis
options.rationale: HSV (days 6-14) causes keratoconjunctivitis with vesicles and systemic risk.

questions.sourceMapping: AAFP Part I Table 3 (dacryostenosis vs ophthalmia neonatorum timing)

stem: A newborn's ear helix meets the cranium below a horizontal plane through the inner canthi. Which action is most appropriate?

options.label: A
options.text: Reassure; this is a normal positional variant
options.rationale: Defined low-set positioning is a dysmorphic marker, not a positional variant.

options.label: B
