options.text: Evaluate for genetic conditions such as Down, Turner, or trisomy 18 syndromes
options.rationale: Low-set ears are a marker for genetic conditions (Down, Turner, trisomy 18); the finding should prompt dysmorphology evaluation (AAFP Part I, Figure 4).

options.label: C
options.text: Order renal ultrasonography immediately as an isolated response
options.rationale: Renal ultrasound is reserved for ear anomalies accompanied by other malformations, teratogenic exposures, family history of deafness, or maternal gestational diabetes; isolated pits/cup ears no longer trigger routine imaging.

options.label: D
options.text: Refer for audiology testing because low-set ears cause deafness
options.rationale: Low-set ears themselves do not cause hearing loss; preauricular tags/pits are the hearing-impairment association.

questions.sourceMapping: AAFP Part I (ear position, Figure 4; renal ultrasound criteria SORT)

stem: A newborn exhibits cyclic cyanosis that worsens during quiet feeding and sleeping and improves with crying. Which diagnosis does this pattern suggest?

options.label: A
options.text: Bilateral choanal atresia
options.rationale: Newborns are obligate nasal breathers; bilateral choanal atresia causes cyanosis relieved by crying (when the mouth opens), classically worsening with quiet sleep or feeding; patency can be tested by passing a small catheter (AAFP Part I, nose).

options.label: B
options.text: Tetralogy of Fallot spell
options.rationale: Tetralogy spells cause cyanotic episodes with hyperpnea and are not relieved by crying.

options.label: C
options.text: Methemoglobinemia
options.rationale: Methemoglobinemia causes persistent cyanosis unresponsive to oxygen or crying.

options.label: D
options.text: Persistent pulmonary hypertension
options.rationale: PPHN causes persistent hypoxemia with distress, not crying-relieved cycling.

questions.sourceMapping: AAFP Part I (choanal atresia; cyanosis relieved by crying)

stem: During the oral examination, the PNP notes 1-3 mm white cystic vesicles along the median palatal raphe. Which statement is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: These are Epstein pearls, the oral counterpart of milia, and resolve spontaneously
options.rationale: Epstein pearls are white cystic vesicles on the median palatal raphe, the oral counterpart of milia, resolving spontaneously (AAFP Part I, Table 4).

options.label: B
options.text: These are natal teeth requiring removal for aspiration risk
options.rationale: Natal teeth are actual teeth on the lower gum, removed only if loose.

options.label: C
options.text: These are ranulas requiring surgical removal
options.rationale: Ranulas are mucus retention cysts on the floor of the mouth.

options.label: D
options.text: These represent oral thrush requiring nystatin
options.rationale: Thrush presents as adherent white plaques on buccal mucosa and tongue, not discrete midline cysts.

questions.sourceMapping: AAFP Part I Table 4 (oral cavity findings)

stem: A breastfeeding mother reports painful latch and poor transfer; examination shows a short frenulum tethering the tongue tip to the floor of the mouth with limited elevation. What is the most appropriate management?

options.label: A
options.text: Immediate frenotomy in all cases regardless of symptoms
options.rationale: Routine frenotomy without functional impact is not supported.

options.label: B
options.text: Consider frenotomy because ankyloglossia may interfere with breastfeeding, recognizing the procedure is controversial
options.rationale: Ankyloglossia may interfere with breastfeeding or articulation; frenotomy may be considered when feeding is impacted, but the intervention remains controversial per AAFP (SORT/text).

options.label: C
options.text: Reassure that ankyloglossia never affects feeding or speech
options.rationale: Ankyloglossia can impair latch and, in some cases, articulation.

options.label: D
options.text: Prescribe a proton pump inhibitor for the infant
options.rationale: Acid suppression does not address a mechanical latch problem.

questions.sourceMapping: AAFP Part I (ankyloglossia and frenotomy controversy)

stem: A newborn is noted to have a bifid uvula on examination. Which associated condition should the PNP specifically assess for?

options.label: A
options.text: Submucosal cleft palate
options.rationale: A bifid uvula is often associated with a submucosal cleft, which can affect feeding and later speech and is easily missed without palpation (AAFP Part I, mouth).

options.label: B
options.text: Choanal atresia
options.rationale: Choanal atresia is assessed by nasal patency, not uvular morphology.

options.label: C
options.text: Ankyloglossia
options.rationale: Ankyloglossia is a frenulum finding, unrelated to the uvula.

options.label: D
options.text: Pierre Robin sequence
options.rationale: Pierre Robin sequence features micrognathia, glossoptosis, and airway obstruction; micrognathia is its oral marker.

questions.sourceMapping: AAFP Part I (bifid uvula and submucosal cleft)

stem: A 3-week-old holds his head tilted to the right with a firm swelling palpable in the right sternocleidomastoid muscle and limited passive neck rotation. Without correction, this condition most likely leads to which complications?

options.label: A
options.text: Plagiocephaly and ear misalignment
options.rationale: Congenital muscular torticollis from SCM birth trauma/hematoma is treated with physical therapy; uncorrected torticollis leads to positional plagiocephaly and ear misalignment (AAFP Part I, neck; Transcript 3).

options.label: B
options.text: Craniosynostosis of the lambdoid suture
options.rationale: Craniosynostosis is suture fusion, not a consequence of torticollis; positional flattening lacks suture ridging.

options.label: C
options.text: Brachial plexus palsy
options.rationale: Brachial plexus palsy results from traction injury at delivery, not from torticollis.

options.label: D
options.text: Atlantoaxial instability
options.rationale: Atlantoaxial instability is associated with Down syndrome and trauma, not infant torticollis.

questions.sourceMapping: AAFP Part I (torticollis complications); Transcript 3 (torticollis causes plagiocephaly)

stem: A midline neck mass in a newborn moves upward with tongue protrusion. Which diagnosis is most likely?

options.label: A
options.text: Cystic hygroma
options.rationale: Cystic hygroma is a congenital lymphatic malformation, typically soft and transilluminating, not tongue-tethered.

options.label: B
options.text: Thyroglossal duct cyst
options.rationale: A midline neck lesion that shifts with tongue movement is classic for a thyroglossal duct cyst (AAFP Part I, neck).

options.label: C
options.text: Branchial cleft cyst
options.rationale: Branchial cleft cysts are lateral, not midline.

options.label: D
options.text: Sternocleidomastoid tumor
options.rationale: SCM tumor presents with torticollis and a firm muscle mass, not tongue-linked movement.

questions.sourceMapping: AAFP Part I (neck masses)

stem: After a difficult shoulder delivery, a newborn's Moro reflex is asymmetric with decreased movement of the left arm. Which additional assessment is most important?

options.label: A
options.text: Palpate the clavicles for fracture and confirm with radiograph if suspected
options.rationale: A nondisplaced clavicular fracture may manifest only as an asymmetric Moro; suspected fractures are confirmed radiographically and treated with analgesia (AAFP Part I, neck).

options.label: B
options.text: Order immediate brachial plexus MRI
options.rationale: MRI is not first-line; examination distinguishes clavicle fracture from brachial plexus palsy (Erb posture).

options.label: C
options.text: Reassure; asymmetric Moro is normal in the first week
options.rationale: Asymmetric Moro is never normal; it localizes injury.

options.label: D
options.text: Test for hypoglycemia as the cause of focal weakness
options.rationale: Hypoglycemia causes jitteriness or seizures, not unilateral arm hypomobility.

questions.sourceMapping: AAFP Part I (clavicle fracture and asymmetric Moro)

stem: In the illustrated maneuvers, panel A adducts the thigh while applying posterior pressure, and panel B abducts the thigh while lifting the femoral head anteriorly with a palpable clunk. Which pairing is correct?

images.alt: Figure 4: AAFP Part II, Figure 3 reference asset - hip examination maneuvers: panel A adducts the hip with posterior pressure; panel B abducts the hip with anterior lift.
images.caption: Figure 4: AAFP Part II, Figure 3 reference asset - hip examination maneuvers: panel A adducts the hip with posterior pressure; panel B abducts the hip with anterior lift.

options.label: A
options.text: A = Barlow (dislocation test); B = Ortolani (reduction test)
options.rationale: Barlow adducts the hip with posterior pressure to discover a dislocatable hip; Ortolani flexes and abducts while lifting the femoral head anteriorly, producing a clunk of reduction - exactly the panels shown (Slides 44-46; AAFP Part II Figure 3).

options.label: B
options.text: A = Ortolani (dislocation test); B = Barlow (reduction test)
options.rationale: The tests are reversed in this option.

options.label: C
options.text: A = Barlow (reduction test); B = Galeazzi test
options.rationale: Barlow is a dislocation (provocative) test, and panel B is Ortolani, not Galeazzi.

options.label: D
options.text: A = Galeazzi test; B = Trendelenburg test
options.rationale: Galeazzi compares knee heights with hips flexed; Trendelenburg assesses abductor function at walking age.

questions.sourceMapping: Newborn/Infant deck Slides 44-46; AAFP Part II Figure 3; Transcript 3 (clunk you do not miss) | Parallel Form B (options re-randomized)

stem: A female newborn was breech at 38 weeks. Family history is negative for hip dysplasia. Per AAP guidance cited in this course, what is the most appropriate hip surveillance plan?

options.label: A
options.text: No imaging; clinical examination alone at each visit
options.rationale: Clinical examination alone misses late-presenting dysplasia in this high-risk group.

options.label: B
options.text: Hip imaging: ultrasonography at about 6 weeks of age (or radiography at about 4 months)
options.rationale: Breech girls carry a dysplasia risk of about 120 per 1,000 and should receive imaging - ultrasound at 6 weeks or radiography at 4 months; the professor also taught ultrasound around the 2-3 month mark for high-risk infants (AAFP Part II SORT; Slide 44; Transcript 3).

options.label: C
options.text: Immediate pelvic radiography in the first week of life
options.rationale: Radiography in the first week is insensitive because the femoral head is unossified; ultrasound is the modality of choice early.

options.label: D
options.text: Prophylactic Pavlik harness without imaging
options.rationale: Treatment follows documented instability or imaging findings, not prophylaxis.

questions.sourceMapping: AAFP Part II SORT (breech girls imaging); Newborn/Infant deck Slide 44; Transcript 3 (hip ultrasound 2-3 months for high risk)

stem: At a 2-week well visit, the PNP hears a soft click with mild asymmetry of hip motion but no Ortolani or Barlow sign. What is the recommended management?

options.label: A
options.text: Immediate orthopedic referral
options.rationale: Referral is reserved for positive Ortolani/Barlow or persistent findings.

options.label: B
options.text: Follow-up hip examination by the physician in 2 weeks
options.rationale: Equivocally positive newborn hip findings (soft click, mild asymmetry without Ortolani/Barlow) warrant a repeat examination in 2 weeks by the child's physician (AAFP Part II).

options.label: C
options.text: Hip ultrasonography today
options.rationale: Immediate ultrasound is indicated for positive maneuvers or high-risk screening protocols, not an equivocal click alone at 2 weeks.

options.label: D
options.text: Reassurance with no follow-up until 12 months
options.rationale: Deferring a year risks missing treatable dysplasia.

questions.sourceMapping: AAFP Part II (equivocal hip exam follow-up)

stem: Which cluster of findings suggests developmental dysplasia of the hip in a 5-month-old, an age at which Ortolani and Barlow become less reliable?

options.label: A
options.text: Limited hip abduction, thigh-length discrepancy, and asymmetric thigh skin folds
options.rationale: Beyond 3 months, DDH presents with limited abduction, Galeazzi (uneven knee heights), thigh-length discrepancy, and asymmetric gluteal/thigh folds; at walking age a Trendelenburg gait appears (Slide 44; AAFP Part II).

options.label: B
options.text: Hip clicking with full symmetric abduction
options.rationale: Full symmetric abduction with a click is reassuring; restricted abduction is the concern.

options.label: C
options.text: Frog-leg resting posture with symmetric gluteal folds
options.rationale: Frog-leg posture and symmetric folds are normal infant findings.

options.label: D
options.text: Toeing-in during supported standing
options.rationale: Toeing-in relates to torsional variants, not hip instability.

questions.sourceMapping: Newborn/Infant deck Slide 44 (>3 months findings; Galeazzi; Trendelenburg)

stem: A term male newborn has a urethral opening on the ventral midshaft. The parents request circumcision before discharge. What is the correct action?

options.label: A
options.text: Proceed with circumcision using the Gomco clamp
options.rationale: Circumcision would discard tissue needed by the surgeon.

options.label: B
options.text: Defer circumcision; the foreskin may be needed for surgical repair, and refer to urology
options.rationale: Newborns with hypospadias should not be circumcised because the foreskin may be required for repair; chordee and buried penis are additional contraindications (AAFP Part II SORT and text; Slides 42-43).

options.label: C
options.text: Circumcise after applying topical steroid to the prepuce
options.rationale: Steroid therapy has no role and does not change the contraindication.

options.label: D
options.text: Perform circumcision and schedule repair at puberty
options.rationale: Repair is performed in early childhood, not at puberty.

questions.sourceMapping: AAFP Part II SORT (hypospadias and circumcision); Newborn/Infant deck Slides 42-43

stem: A 3-month-old former 30-week preterm male has bilateral undescended testes that cannot be milked into the scrotum. What is the appropriate next step per the course?

options.label: A
options.text: Continue observation until age 2 years
options.rationale: Observation beyond 6 months risks germ-cell damage and torsion.

options.label: B
options.text: Arrange evaluation by a pediatric urologist; undescended testes warrant evaluation by 6 months of age
options.rationale: Cryptorchidism occurs in about 3% of term and 30% of preterm infants; patients with undescended testes should be evaluated by a pediatric urologist by 6 months of age (Slide 41).

options.label: C
options.text: Order testosterone therapy today
options.rationale: Hormonal therapy is not the first-line office action described.

options.label: D
options.text: Reassure that cryptorchidism never occurs in preterm infants
options.rationale: Preterm infants have a tenfold higher rate than term infants.

questions.sourceMapping: Newborn/Infant deck Slide 41 (cryptorchidism rates and urology evaluation by 6 months)

stem: A newborn's left scrotum is enlarged, soft, and transilluminates with light; the swelling is non-tender and reducible only slowly. Which statement is most accurate?

options.label: A
options.text: This is an inguinal hernia requiring prompt surgical repair
options.rationale: Inguinal hernias contain bowel (bulge may extend to scrotum, bowel sounds, reducible with pressure) and are repaired surgically because of incarceration risk; transillumination favors hydrocele.

options.label: B
options.text: This is a hydrocele, which usually resolves within the first 1-2 years of life
options.rationale: A hydrocele results from patent processus vaginalis admitting only fluid, transilluminates, and typically resolves within 1-2 years (AAFP Part II, Figure 1).

options.label: C
options.text: This is testicular torsion requiring emergent surgery
options.rationale: Torsion presents with an acute, tender, discolored scrotum and a distressed infant.

options.label: D
options.text: This is a varicocele requiring urology referral
options.rationale: Varicoceles are venous, typically left-sided, and appear later in childhood/adolescence.

questions.sourceMapping: AAFP Part II (hydrocele vs inguinal hernia, Figure 1)

stem: Select all newborn genital findings that should prompt urgent investigation for a disorder of sex development, with deferral of sex assignment until evaluation is complete.

options.label: A
options.text: Clitoromegaly with fused labia in a phenotypic female
options.rationale: Clitoromegaly and labial fusion are signs of ambiguous genitalia requiring endocrine, genetic, and urologic consultation (AAFP Part II SORT).

options.label: B
options.text: Bilateral nonpalpable testes in a phenotypic male
options.rationale: Bilateral undescended testes may represent ambiguous genitalia and require investigation.

options.label: C
options.text: Micropenis (stretched penile length 1.5 cm in a term male)
options.rationale: Micropenis (term normal 2.5-3.5 cm) is a listed ambiguous-genitalia trigger.

options.label: D
options.text: Bifid scrotum
options.rationale: A bifid scrotum is a listed ambiguous-genitalia trigger.

options.label: E
options.text: A unilateral retractile testis that milks down into the scrotum
options.rationale: A retractile testis that can be milked into the scrotum is a normal variant requiring no intervention.

questions.sourceMapping: AAFP Part II SORT and genitourinary text (ambiguous genitalia workup)

stem: A newborn has failed to pass meconium, and examination reveals an imperforate anus. Which association should guide the workup?

options.label: A
options.text: VACTERL association and trisomies 18 and 21
options.rationale: An imperforate anus may be isolated or syndromic; VACTERL (vertebral/vascular, anorectal, cardiac, tracheoesophageal, radial/renal, limb) and trisomies 18/21 are the taught associations (AAFP Part II).

options.label: B
options.text: Isolated finding requiring no further evaluation
options.rationale: Associated anomalies are common and must be screened.

options.label: C
options.text: Cystic fibrosis as the sole association
options.rationale: CF causes meconium ileus, not imperforate anus, and is not the sole association.

options.label: D
options.text: Hirschsprung disease as the only consideration
options.rationale: Hirschsprung causes functional obstruction with a patent anus; it is not the only consideration.

questions.sourceMapping: AAFP Part II (imperforate anus; VACTERL)

stem: The umbilical cord of a newborn contains a single umbilical artery. There are no other anomalies on examination. Which counseling is most accurate?

options.label: A
options.text: Routine renal ultrasonography is required in all cases of single umbilical artery
options.rationale: Routine imaging for isolated SUA is explicitly not recommended.

options.label: B
options.text: Single umbilical artery is associated with renal anomalies, IUGR, and prematurity, but routine renal imaging in isolated cases has not proven beneficial
options.rationale: The cord normally has 2 arteries and 1 vein; a single umbilical artery is associated with congenital (especially renal) anomalies, IUGR, and prematurity, yet routine renal ultrasound in isolated cases is not beneficial per AAFP SORT (Slides 11, 41; AAFP Part II).

options.label: C
options.text: Single umbilical artery is a normal variant with no associations
options.rationale: Associations exist; careful examination is required.

options.label: D
options.text: Immediate voiding cystourethrogram is indicated
options.rationale: VCUG evaluates reflux/obstruction symptoms, not isolated SUA.

questions.sourceMapping: Newborn/Infant deck Slide 11; AAFP Part II SORT (isolated single umbilical artery)

stem: During abdominal palpation of a newborn, a firm mass is appreciated in the left flank. Which origin is statistically most likely?

options.label: A
options.text: Renal (e.g., multicystic dysplastic kidney or hydronephrosis)
options.rationale: About half of newborn abdominal masses are renal in origin (multicystic dysplastic kidney, Wilms tumor, hydronephrosis, renal vein thrombosis, UPJ obstruction); the liver edge 1-2 cm below the costal margin is normal (AAFP Part II).

options.label: B
options.text: Hepatic
options.rationale: Hepatic masses are rare in newborns; a palpable liver edge is normal.

options.label: C
options.text: Splenic
options.rationale: Splenic masses are uncommon and usually accompanied by hematologic disease.

options.label: D
options.text: Ovarian
options.rationale: Ovarian cysts occur but are far less common than renal masses.

questions.sourceMapping: AAFP Part II (abdominal masses; normal liver edge)

stem: Select all skin findings in a well-appearing newborn that require reassurance and documentation only, without treatment or referral.

options.label: A
options.text: Erythema toxicum neonatorum with flesh-colored papules on an erythematous base
options.rationale: Erythema toxicum contains eosinophils, appears in the first days, and resolves within the first week without treatment (AAFP Part II Table 1).

options.label: B
options.text: Milia over the nose
options.rationale: Milia are keratin epidermal cysts that rupture and resolve in the first weeks; squeezing is discouraged.

options.label: C
options.text: Dermal melanocytosis (blue-gray macules) over the sacrum
options.rationale: Dermal melanocytosis is benign and fades by about 4 years but must be documented because it can be mistaken for bruising or abuse.

options.label: D
options.text: Salmon patch (nevus simplex) on the nape
options.rationale: Salmon patches (stork bites) fade over time, typically by 1-2 years, and need reassurance only.

options.label: E
options.text: Port-wine stain over the trigeminal distribution
options.rationale: A port-wine stain in the trigeminal distribution raises concern for Sturge-Weber syndrome (seizures, glaucoma) and requires ophthalmology and further evaluation; it does not fade.

questions.sourceMapping: AAFP Part II Table 1; Newborn/Infant deck Slides 73-84; Transcript 4 (reassurance and documentation)

stem: A 2-day-old has yellow-white papules and pustules on an erythematous base over the trunk; a Wright stain of a pustule shows eosinophils. What is the diagnosis?

options.label: A
options.text: Erythema toxicum neonatorum
options.rationale: Erythema toxicum features flesh-colored papules/pustules on an erythematous base containing eosinophils and resolves in the first week (AAFP Part II Table 1).

options.label: B
options.text: Neonatal herpes simplex
options.rationale: HSV produces grouped vesicles on an erythematous base with systemic illness; it does not resolve spontaneously.

options.label: C
options.text: Transient neonatal pustular melanosis
options.rationale: TNPM shows pustules WITHOUT erythema containing neutrophils, leaving hyperpigmented macules.

options.label: D
options.text: Staphylococcal pustulosis
options.rationale: Staphylococcal pustulosis would show bacteria and neutrophils with surrounding cellulitis or a ill infant.

questions.sourceMapping: AAFP Part II Table 1 (erythema toxicum vs TNPM cytology) | Parallel Form B (options re-randomized)

stem: A Black newborn has pustules without surrounding erythema at birth that rupture and leave hyperpigmented macules on the soles and trunk. The infant is well-appearing. Which diagnosis fits?

options.label: A
options.text: Erythema toxicum neonatorum
options.rationale: Erythema toxicum appears after birth with an erythematous base and eosinophils.

options.label: B
options.text: Transient neonatal pustular melanosis
options.rationale: TNPM presents at birth (more common in Black infants, about 4-5%) with neutrophilic pustules lacking erythema that rupture and leave hyperpigmented macules persisting for months; the infant is well (AAFP Table 1; Slide 81-82).

options.label: C
options.text: Candidal diaper dermatitis
options.rationale: Candidal dermatitis involves the diaper area with beefy erythema and satellite lesions.

options.label: D
options.text: Miliaria crystallina
options.rationale: Miliaria presents as clear or red vesicles in sweat-prone areas from duct obstruction.

questions.sourceMapping: AAFP Part II Table 1; Newborn/Infant deck Slides 81-82 | Parallel Form B (options re-randomized)

stem: Why must dermal melanocytosis (Mongolian spots) be explicitly documented in the newborn record?

options.label: A
options.text: Because they predict future neurofibromatosis
options.rationale: Neurofibromatosis is associated with multiple cafe-au-lait macules, not dermal melanocytosis.

options.label: B
options.text: Because they can be confused with bruising and raise false concerns for abuse
options.rationale: The AAFP article stresses that dermal melanocytosis can be confused with abuse and should be documented; lesions usually fade by about 4 years (AAFP Part II Table 1).

options.label: C
options.text: Because they require laser treatment in infancy
options.rationale: No treatment is indicated; lesions fade.

options.label: D
options.text: Because they indicate congenital dermal infection
options.rationale: They are benign melanocyte collections, not infection.

questions.sourceMapping: AAFP Part II Table 1 (documentation to avoid abuse misinterpretation) | Parallel Form B (options re-randomized)

stem: A newborn has a flat, dark purple-red patch over the left forehead and upper eyelid that has not faded by the 2-month visit. Which complication warrants proactive referral?

options.label: A
options.text: Seizures and glaucoma from Sturge-Weber syndrome; ophthalmology evaluation
options.rationale: Port-wine stains (nevus flammeus) persist and darken; lesions over the trigeminal distribution associate with Sturge-Weber syndrome (seizures, glaucoma), and any lesion near the eye requires ophthalmology referral (AAFP Table 1; Slide 77; Transcript 4).

options.label: B
options.text: Spontaneous resolution by 12 months expected
options.rationale: Port-wine stains do not fade; salmon patches do.

options.label: C
options.text: Progression to hemangioma with ulceration
options.rationale: Port-wine stains are capillary malformations, not proliferative hemangiomas.

options.label: D
options.text: Anemia from chronic blood loss within the lesion
options.rationale: These malformations do not cause chronic blood-loss anemia.

questions.sourceMapping: AAFP Part II Table 1; Newborn/Infant deck Slide 77; Transcript 4

stem: At the 4-month visit, an infant has six cafe-au-lait macules, the largest 2.5 cm, plus two more noted today. What is the most appropriate action?

options.label: A
options.text: Reassure; cafe-au-lait macules are always benign
options.rationale: Solitary macules are usually benign, but counts above six are a NF1 criterion trigger.

options.label: B
options.text: Measure, document, and evaluate for neurofibromatosis given more than six macules
options.rationale: More than six cafe-au-lait macules (especially large ones) raise concern for neurofibromatosis; the course directs measuring and documenting at well exams and monitoring or referring for further evaluation (Slide 12/83; Transcript 4; AAFP Table 1).

options.label: C
options.text: Biopsy the largest macule today
options.rationale: Diagnosis is clinical; biopsy is not indicated.

options.label: D
options.text: Order serum cortisol for McCune-Albright syndrome only
options.rationale: McCune-Albright is considered (precocious puberty, fibrous dysplasia), but the immediate course-taught action is NF-oriented evaluation with measurement and documentation.

questions.sourceMapping: Newborn/Infant deck Slides 12, 83; Transcript 4 (>6 cafe-au-lait = neurofibromatosis concern)

stem: A newborn has a sixth digit arising from the ulnar side of the left little finger, composed of a small pedunculated skin tag without bone. What is the appropriate management?

options.label: A
options.text: Observation only; supernumerary digits never require removal
options.rationale: Removal is typically performed for cosmetic and functional reasons.

options.label: B
options.text: Surgical reconstruction by a plastic surgeon in the newborn period
options.rationale: Plastic surgical repair is reserved for digits with bone/cartilage involvement.

options.label: C
options.text: Immediate amputation at the bedside without examination for other anomalies
options.rationale: Bedside removal without evaluating for associated anomalies misses syndromic clues.

options.label: D
options.text: Tie-off ligation at the base is usually sufficient for digits without bone involvement, with examination for associated anomalies
options.rationale: Supernumerary digits without bone involvement can be tied off at the base; those with bone require skilled surgical removal; polydactyly also warrants a careful exam for genetic abnormalities (AAFP Part II, extremities).

questions.sourceMapping: AAFP Part II (polydactyly management) | Parallel Form B (options re-randomized)

stem: A newborn is noted to have a single transverse palmar crease on the right hand only. Which counseling is most accurate?

options.label: A
options.text: This finding confirms trisomy 21
options.rationale: No single soft sign confirms a trisomy; karyotype and pattern of features do.

options.label: B
options.text: A single palmar crease may accompany trisomy 21 but also occurs in 3-10% of persons without the syndrome
options.rationale: The single palmar crease is a soft sign: associated with trisomy 21 yet present in 3-10% of the general population, so it modifies, not determines, dysmorphology assessment (AAFP Part II).

options.label: C
options.text: A single palmar crease indicates fetal alcohol syndrome
options.rationale: FAS has distinct facial and growth features; the crease is nonspecific.

options.label: D
options.text: This finding requires immediate chromosomal microarray
options.rationale: Microarray is not triggered by an isolated soft sign without other findings.

questions.sourceMapping: AAFP Part II (single palmar crease prevalence)

stem: After a shoulder-dystocia delivery of a 4,600 g newborn, the infant holds the right arm adducted and internally rotated at the side with the forearm pronated (waiter's tip). Which injury and nerve roots are implicated?

options.label: A
options.text: Erb palsy; C5-C7 traction injury
options.rationale: Erb palsy from C5-C7 traction produces the waiter's-tip posture (arm medially rotated, pronated hand) and is most common in LGA infants with shoulder dystocia or prolonged delivery; physical therapy may be needed (AAFP Part II).

options.label: B
options.text: Klumpke palsy; C8-T1 injury
options.rationale: Klumpke palsy (C8-T1) causes paralysis of the entire arm with absent reflexes or a claw-hand variant.

options.label: C
options.text: Clavicle fracture; no nerve involvement
options.rationale: Clavicle fracture causes pseudoparalysis with asymmetric Moro but not the classic waiter's-tip posture.

options.label: D
options.text: Posterior shoulder dislocation
options.rationale: Neonatal shoulder dislocation is rare and presents with deformity and pain on movement, not this posture.

questions.sourceMapping: AAFP Part II (brachial plexus palsies)

stem: A newborn's forefoot is inverted and adducted, but the examiner easily corrects the position to neutral with gentle manipulation. What is the correct interpretation?

options.label: A
options.text: True talipes equinovarus requiring orthopedic casting
options.rationale: True talipes equinovarus is not passively correctable to neutral.

options.label: B
options.text: Positional deformity that is easily corrected with manipulation and requires no further management
options.rationale: The examiner must first distinguish a flexible positional deformity (correctable with manipulation, no management) from true clubfoot (rigid inversion/adduction with limited ankle extension, requiring orthopedic consultation and casting) (AAFP Part II).

options.label: C
options.text: Metatarsus adductus requiring serial casting regardless of flexibility
options.rationale: Flexible metatarsus adductus typically resolves; casting is reserved for rigid cases.

options.label: D
options.text: Neurologic disorder requiring MRI
options.rationale: Isolated flexible foot positioning is not a neurologic sign.

questions.sourceMapping: AAFP Part II (clubfoot vs positional deformity)

stem: Bilateral pitting edema of a female newborn's feet is noted. Which associated condition should be considered?

options.label: A
options.text: Turner syndrome
options.rationale: Pedal (and hand) lymphedema in a newborn female is a classic Turner syndrome clue, alongside webbed neck and widely spaced nipples (AAFP Part II; Part I neck/chest).

options.label: B
options.text: Congenital nephrotic syndrome as the only cause
options.rationale: Nephrotic syndrome is exceedingly rare in newborns and not the taught association.

options.label: C
options.text: Dependent edema from supine positioning
options.rationale: Positional dependent edema does not produce pitting pedal lymphedema at birth.

options.label: D
options.text: Vitamin K deficiency
options.rationale: Vitamin K deficiency causes bleeding, not edema.

questions.sourceMapping: AAFP Part II (pedal edema and Turner syndrome)

stem: When suspending a newborn vertically under the arms, the infant slips downward through the examiner's hands because of shoulder-girdle weakness. What does this indicate?

options.label: A
options.text: Normal newborn tone
options.rationale: Normal tone resists slipping.

options.label: B
options.text: Hypotonia requiring evaluation
options.rationale: In vertical suspension, a hypotonic newborn slips through the examiner's hands from shoulder-girdle and leg weakness; normal infants hold themselves between the examiner's hands (AAFP Part II, neurologic).

options.label: C
options.text: Hypertonia requiring evaluation
options.rationale: Hypertonia presents with rigidity and extended posturing, not slipping.

options.label: D
options.text: Normal finding in infants of diabetic mothers only
options.rationale: IDM infants may be hypotonic, but the finding is abnormal in any newborn and warrants evaluation.

questions.sourceMapping: AAFP Part II (vertical suspension and tone)

stem: Which sequence reflects the recommended approach to ordering the newborn physical examination?

options.label: A
options.text: Head-to-toe in fixed order regardless of infant state
options.rationale: Rigid head-to-toe ordering guarantees a crying infant during auscultation.

options.label: B
options.text: Least invasive first while the infant is quiet (auscultation, palpation), saving ears and mouth for last
options.rationale: The professor taught performing the least invasive maneuvers first while the infant is quiet - heart, lungs, abdomen, joints - and leaving provocative exams (ears, mouth) for last, with the infant in the parent's arms when possible (Transcript 3; Slide 54).

options.label: C
options.text: Ears and mouth first while the infant is still drowsy
options.rationale: Starting with provocative exams forfeits the quiet window.

options.label: D
options.text: Genital examination first, then head
options.rationale: Genital examination is delegated to diaper change timing, not first.

questions.sourceMapping: Transcript 3 (exam sequencing; least invasive first); Newborn/Infant deck Slide 54

stem: Select all interventions and screenings that should be completed before or around hospital discharge for a term newborn, per this course.

options.label: A
options.text: Critical congenital heart disease pulse oximetry screening at 24 hours of life or later
options.rationale: CCHD pulse oximetry screening is recommended before discharge at 24 hours or later, with echocardiography if positive (AAFP SORT).

options.label: B
options.text: Routine chest radiography
options.rationale: Routine chest radiography is not a discharge screening test.

options.label: C
options.text: Hepatitis B vaccine
options.rationale: The birth-dose hepatitis B vaccine is a standard newborn intervention (Slide 12).

options.label: D
options.text: Hearing screening by otoacoustic emissions or auditory brainstem response
options.rationale: Hearing should be evaluated before 1 month, preferably before discharge, using ABR or OAE (AAFP SORT).

options.label: E
options.text: Intramuscular vitamin K
options.rationale: Vitamin K prevents hemorrhagic disease of the newborn (Slide 12).

options.label: F
options.text: Erythromycin ophthalmic prophylaxis
options.rationale: Eye prophylaxis prevents gonococcal ophthalmia and is a listed birth intervention (Slide 12).

questions.sourceMapping: Newborn/Infant deck Slide 12; AAFP Part I SORT (hearing, CCHD screening) | Parallel Form B (options re-randomized)

stem: A CCHD pulse oximetry screen at 26 hours of life shows preductal 96% and postductal 92%, failing the protocol. What is the next step?

options.label: A
options.text: Repeat the screen in 24 hours and discharge if normal
options.rationale: A failed screen is not cleared by repeat testing alone when the protocol is failed.

options.label: B
options.text: Perform diagnostic echocardiography
options.rationale: A positive CCHD screen mandates diagnostic echocardiography per the cited recommendation (AAFP Part I SORT and Table 6).

options.label: C
options.text: Start prostaglandin infusion before any imaging
options.rationale: Prostaglandin is started for ductal-dependent lesions identified clinically or echo-confirmed with instability, not as a blind first step.

options.label: D
options.text: Reassure; a 4-point difference is normal
options.rationale: A pre-post difference of this magnitude fails screening and is not normal.

questions.sourceMapping: AAFP Part I SORT and Tables 5-6 (positive screen = echocardiography)

stem: A forceps-delivered newborn cannot close the left eye, has loss of the left nasolabial fold, and droops at the left mouth corner when crying. What is the expected course?

options.label: A
options.text: Peripheral facial nerve palsy from birth trauma, usually resolving within the first few weeks
options.rationale: Forceps or difficult delivery can cause peripheral facial palsy (inability to close the eye, lost nasolabial fold, asymmetric crying face) that usually resolves in the first weeks; persistence warrants further evaluation (AAFP Part I; CN VII exam Slide 40).

options.label: B
options.text: Central stroke requiring neuroimaging today
options.rationale: Neonatal stroke is rare and would show central patterns and other deficits.

options.label: C
options.text: Permanent deficit requiring surgical repair
options.rationale: Most birth-related peripheral palsies recover spontaneously.

options.label: D
options.text: Moebius syndrome requiring genetic testing today
options.rationale: Moebius involves bilateral congenital facial and abducens palsies, not unilateral post-traumatic palsy.

questions.sourceMapping: AAFP Part I (facial nerve palsy); Newborn/Infant deck Slide 40 (CN VII crying face) | Parallel Form B (options re-randomized)

stem: A mother calls on day 1 of life (18 hours old) to report that her breastfed term newborn looks yellow from the face to the chest. What is the most appropriate interpretation and action?

options.label: A
options.text: Physiologic jaundice; reassure and repeat visual check at the 2-week visit
options.rationale: Physiologic jaundice appears AFTER 24 hours and peaks days 3-5; day-1 jaundice never qualifies.

options.label: B
options.text: Jaundice before 24 hours is pathologic until proven otherwise; obtain a bilirubin level and evaluate for hemolysis today
options.rationale: The course's high-yield rule, stated by the professor and on the slide: jaundice within the first 24 hours is abnormal and warrants prompt TcB/TSB measurement and hemolysis evaluation (Slides 65, 67-68; Transcript 4).

options.label: C
options.text: Breast milk jaundice; continue breastfeeding and recheck in one week
options.rationale: Breast milk jaundice arises after the first week in a thriving infant.

options.label: D
options.text: Normal finding if the infant is otherwise feeding well
options.rationale: Feeding well does not normalize early-onset jaundice; hemolysis and sepsis must be excluded.

questions.sourceMapping: Newborn/Infant deck Slides 65, 67-68; Transcript 4 (jaundice <24 hours = problem)

stem: Which profile best fits physiologic neonatal jaundice?

options.label: A
options.text: Onset after 24 hours, peak at days 3-5, unconjugated bilirubin, infant otherwise well
options.rationale: Physiologic jaundice follows immature hepatic conjugation: appears after 24 hours, peaks days 3-5, unconjugated, in a well infant, and resolves without treatment (Slide 67 comparison table).

options.label: B
options.text: Onset before 24 hours with a rise of 0.4 mg/dL per hour
options.rationale: Early onset with a rapid rise indicates hemolysis (pathologic).

options.label: C
options.text: Onset at day 10 with conjugated hyperbilirubinemia
options.rationale: Conjugated hyperbilirubinemia at any age is never physiologic and suggests cholestasis.

options.label: D
options.text: Onset at days 2-5 with 12% weight loss and decreased stooling
options.rationale: That profile is suboptimal-intake (breastfeeding) jaundice with dehydration.

questions.sourceMapping: Newborn/Infant deck Slide 67 (quick comparison table)

stem: A 4-day-old exclusively breastfed newborn is jaundiced to the abdomen. Weight is down 11% from birth, there have been three stools in 48 hours, and latch is painful with short feeds. Which etiology is most likely?

options.label: A
options.text: Breast milk jaundice
options.rationale: Breast milk jaundice occurs after the first week in a well-fed, gaining infant.

options.label: B
options.text: Suboptimal intake (breastfeeding) jaundice with increased enterohepatic circulation
options.rationale: Inadequate intake reduces stooling, increases enterohepatic bilirubin circulation, and accompanies excess weight loss and dehydration in the first week - the classic breastfeeding (suboptimal intake) pattern; management centers on feeding assessment and lactation support (Slide 67; Transcript 4).

options.label: C
options.text: Rh alloimmunization
options.rationale: Rh disease causes jaundice within the first 24 hours with anemia and a positive DAT.

options.label: D
options.text: Biliary atresia
options.rationale: Biliary atresia causes conjugated jaundice with acholic stools, typically after 2 weeks.

questions.sourceMapping: Newborn/Infant deck Slide 67; Transcript 4 (suboptimal intake hyperbilirubinemia)

stem: A 3-week-old exclusively breastfed infant has mild scleral and facial icterus, total bilirubin 12 mg/dL with indirect predominance, weight gain appropriate, stools yellow and frequent, and a normal examination. What is the most appropriate management?

options.label: A
options.text: Stop breastfeeding for 48 hours to confirm the diagnosis
options.rationale: Interruption of breastfeeding is not recommended; the slide directs continuing breastfeeding.

options.label: B
options.text: Continue breastfeeding while evaluating and monitoring persistent jaundice; breast milk jaundice is usually benign
options.rationale: Breast milk jaundice presents after the first week in a thriving, well-feeding infant and may persist for weeks; the taught action is to continue breastfeeding while evaluating persistent jaundice (Slide 67; Transcript 4).

options.label: C
options.text: Start exchange transfusion
options.rationale: Exchange transfusion thresholds apply to severe, rapidly rising unconjugated bilirubin with toxicity risk, not a thriving 3-week-old at 12 mg/dL.

options.label: D
options.text: Order abdominal ultrasound for biliary atresia as the first test
options.rationale: Conjugated (direct) hyperbilirubinemia or acholic stools would trigger the biliary atresia pathway; this infant is indirect-predominant and well.

questions.sourceMapping: Newborn/Infant deck Slide 67 (breast milk jaundice row); Transcript 4

stem: A 3-week-old has persistent jaundice, pale acholic stools, dark urine, and hepatomegaly. Bilirubin shows a direct fraction of 2.8 mg/dL. What is the most appropriate action?

options.label: A
options.text: Reassure; prolonged jaundice in a breastfed infant is benign
options.rationale: Benign prolonged jaundice is unconjugated; direct elevation is pathologic by definition.

options.label: B
options.text: Urgent evaluation and referral for cholestasis, including biliary atresia
options.rationale: Conjugated/direct hyperbilirubinemia is NEVER physiologic; pale stools, dark urine, and hepatomegaly point to cholestasis/biliary atresia, which the slide flags as always abnormal with prompt evaluation/referral (Slides 66-67; Transcript 4).

options.label: C
options.text: Trial of extensively hydrolyzed formula for 2 weeks
options.rationale: Formula change addresses cow's milk protein allergy, not cholestasis.

options.label: D
options.text: Phototherapy at home and recheck in one week
options.rationale: Phototherapy treats unconjugated bilirubin; direct elevation requires anatomic/hepatic workup.

questions.sourceMapping: Newborn/Infant deck Slides 66-67 (direct never physiologic; biliary atresia row); Transcript 4

stem: A 30-hour-old newborn's total serum bilirubin has risen from 6 to 10 mg/dL over 12 hours. Which interpretation does the course teach?

options.label: A
options.text: An expected physiologic rise of about 0.33 mg/dL per hour requiring no workup
options.rationale: That rate exceeds physiologic expectations and is the defined hemolysis threshold, not a benign rise.

options.label: B
options.text: A rise of 0.3 mg/dL per hour or more in the first 24 hours (or 0.2 thereafter) suggests hemolysis and warrants evaluation
options.rationale: The slide defines a rapid rise suggesting hemolysis as >=0.3 mg/dL/hr in the first 24 hours or >=0.2 mg/dL/hr thereafter; this infant's ~0.33/hr rate triggers hemolysis evaluation (Slide 65).

options.label: C
options.text: A normal rise confirming adequate feeding
options.rationale: Rapid rises are not evidence of adequate feeding; suboptimal intake also raises bilirubin but more slowly with weight loss.

options.label: D
options.text: An artifact of transcutaneous measurement
options.rationale: TSB (not TcB) is the definitive value; the rise is real until proven otherwise.

questions.sourceMapping: Newborn/Infant deck Slide 65 (rate of rise thresholds)

stem: Select all neurotoxicity risk factors that lower the treatment threshold for neonatal hyperbilirubinemia per the AAP-based slide content.

options.label: A
options.text: Gestational age less than 38 weeks
options.rationale: GA <38 weeks is a listed neurotoxicity risk factor used with hour-specific thresholds.

options.label: B
options.text: Hemolysis or G6PD deficiency
options.rationale: Hemolysis, including G6PD deficiency, is a listed risk factor.

options.label: C
options.text: Sepsis
options.rationale: Sepsis is a listed risk factor.

options.label: D
options.text: Serum albumin less than 3 g/dL
options.rationale: Albumin <3 g/dL reduces bilirubin binding and is a listed risk factor.

options.label: E
options.text: Birth weight above the 90th percentile in an infant of a diabetic mother
options.rationale: LGA/IDM status is a hypoglycemia-screening indication, not a listed bilirubin neurotoxicity risk factor.

questions.sourceMapping: Newborn/Infant deck Slide 65 (neurotoxicity risk factors)

stem: Which statement about bilirubin measurement in the newborn is correct per the course?

options.label: A
options.text: Transcutaneous bilirubin is the definitive value for phototherapy decisions
options.rationale: TcB is a screening tool; TSB confirms and drives treatment.

options.label: B
options.text: Visual assessment in daylight reliably estimates bilirubin concentration
options.rationale: Visual appearance alone cannot reliably estimate bilirubin concentration.

options.label: C
options.text: Total serum bilirubin is the definitive value for phototherapy and escalation decisions, interpreted by age in hours and gestational age
options.rationale: The slide pearl is SEE jaundice, MEASURE bilirubin, INTERPRET by age in hours plus gestational age plus risk factors, with TSB as the definitive value for treatment decisions (Slide 65).

options.label: D
options.text: Bilirubin need only be measured if jaundice is visible at discharge
options.rationale: All newborns >=35 weeks should have at least one TcB or TSB at 24-48 hours or before discharge, regardless of visible jaundice.

questions.sourceMapping: Newborn/Infant deck Slide 65 (assessment protocol and pearl)

stem: A jaundiced 5-day-old becomes lethargic with hypotonia and a high-pitched cry. Which complication is the PNP most concerned about?

options.label: A
options.text: Acute bilirubin encephalopathy progressing to kernicterus
options.rationale: Lethargy, hypotonia, and high-pitched cry in a jaundiced neonate signal acute bilirubin encephalopathy; unconjugated bilirubin crosses the immature blood-brain barrier causing kernicterus - the professor's stated reason we watch bilirubin so closely (Slides 65, 69-70; Transcript 4; AAFP Part II).

options.label: B
options.text: Physiologic jaundice peak
options.rationale: Physiologic peaks do not produce neurologic signs.

options.label: C
options.text: Breast milk jaundice
options.rationale: Breast milk jaundice infants are well-appearing by definition.

options.label: D
options.text: Congenital hypothyroidism
options.rationale: Hypothyroidism causes prolonged jaundice with other features (large fontanelle, constipation), not acute encephalopathic signs.

questions.sourceMapping: Newborn/Infant deck Slides 65, 69-70; Transcript 4 (neurotoxicity, blood-brain barrier); AAFP Part II

stem: A type O mother delivers a type A newborn who is jaundiced at 16 hours with a reticulocytosis and a weakly positive direct antiglobulin test. Which statement is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: This is Rh alloimmunization and will worsen in future pregnancies without prophylaxis
options.rationale: Rh disease requires an Rh-negative mother and usually affects subsequent sensitized pregnancies.

options.label: B
options.text: This is ABO incompatibility, which can affect the first pregnancy and is typically milder than Rh disease
options.rationale: ABO incompatibility (mother O, infant A or B) results from maternal anti-A/B IgG crossing the placenta, can affect the FIRST pregnancy, is typically milder than Rh disease, and may show a weak or even negative DAT (Slide 68).

options.label: C
options.text: ABO incompatibility occurs only in mothers with type AB blood
options.rationale: The classic pairing is mother O with infant A or B.

options.label: D
options.text: The negative-strong DAT excludes immune hemolysis
options.rationale: DAT may be weak or negative in ABO hemolysis; a weak positive supports, not excludes, the diagnosis.

questions.sourceMapping: Newborn/Infant deck Slide 68 (ABO incompatibility)

stem: An Rh-negative mother with no prior Rh immune globulin prophylaxis delivers her third child, an Rh-positive newborn with severe anemia, hydrops, and marked hyperbilirubinemia within hours. Which mechanism explains why the first pregnancy was unaffected?

options.label: A
options.text: Maternal IgM antibodies cannot sensitize the fetus at any time
options.rationale: IgM is irrelevant to the explanation; the key is timing of sensitization and IgG placental transfer.

options.label: B
options.text: Sensitization typically occurs at the first exposure, so disease manifests in a subsequent Rh-positive pregnancy after maternal IgG is formed
options.rationale: Rh(D) alloimmunization requires maternal sensitization (usually at first delivery or exposure); once IgG anti-D exists, subsequent Rh-positive fetuses are at risk for hemolysis, hydrops, and severe hyperbilirubinemia - the professor's 'first time is not a problem, second time is' teaching (Slide 68; Transcript 4).

options.label: C
options.text: Rh disease is autosomal recessive and requires two affected alleles
options.rationale: Rh disease is immune-mediated, not Mendelian.

options.label: D
options.text: Fetal hemoglobin resists anti-D antibodies in first pregnancies
options.rationale: Fetal hemoglobin does not protect against anti-D hemolysis.

questions.sourceMapping: Newborn/Infant deck Slide 68; Transcript 4 (Rh: first pregnancy fine, second affected; RhoGAM prevention)

stem: Which intervention largely prevents Rh(D) alloimmunization and its fetal consequences?

options.label: A
options.text: Intravenous immunoglobulin to the newborn at birth
options.rationale: IVIG treats, not prevents, alloimmune hemolysis in affected neonates.

options.label: B
options.text: Appropriate Rh(D) immune globulin prophylaxis to the Rh-negative mother
options.rationale: Rh(D) immune globulin prophylaxis prevents maternal sensitization and is largely protective, per the slide (Slide 68).

options.label: C
options.text: Early phototherapy to the firstborn
options.rationale: Phototherapy manages bilirubin but does not prevent maternal antibody formation.

options.label: D
options.text: Maternal plasma exchange during every pregnancy
options.rationale: Plasma exchange is not standard prophylaxis.

questions.sourceMapping: Newborn/Infant deck Slide 68 (prevention with Rh(D) immune globulin) | Parallel Form B (options re-randomized)

stem: A 4-day-old with a large vacuum-associated cephalohematoma is jaundiced with an unconjugated predominance. Why does this lesion raise bilirubin?

options.label: A
options.text: The hematoma obstructs biliary flow
options.rationale: Biliary obstruction produces conjugated bilirubinemia and is not caused by scalp hematomas.

options.label: B
options.text: Breakdown of extravasated red cells increases the bilirubin load during resorption
options.rationale: Resorbing blood from a cephalohematoma or bruising adds a heme load, increasing unconjugated bilirubin; such infants need close bilirubin monitoring (Slides 31, 67; AAFP Part I).

options.label: C
options.text: The hematoma causes hepatic immaturity
options.rationale: Hepatic conjugation maturity is independent of the hematoma.

options.label: D
options.text: Cephalohematomas cause conjugated hyperbilirubinemia
options.rationale: The load is unconjugated (pre-hepatic), not conjugated.

questions.sourceMapping: Newborn/Infant deck Slides 31, 67 (cephalohematoma/bruising row); AAFP Part I

stem: Which management bundle reflects the course's jaundice treatment slide for an infant approaching phototherapy thresholds?

options.label: A
options.text: Phototherapy per AAP nomograms, continue breastfeeding with supplementation if intake is inadequate or weight loss is excessive, serial total bilirubin, and consider re-admission if trending upward
options.rationale: The treatment slide lists phototherapy per AAP guidelines/nomograms, continued breastfeeding with formula supplementation when intake is inadequate or weight loss excessive, serial total bilirubin monitoring, and re-admission consideration for upward trends (Slides 69-70).

options.label: B
options.text: Immediate exchange transfusion for any bilirubin above 15 mg/dL
options.rationale: Exchange transfusion is reserved for severe thresholds or encephalopathy signs, not a fixed 15 mg/dL.

options.label: C
options.text: Stop breastfeeding, start clear fluids, and recheck in 3 days
options.rationale: Stopping breastfeeding and giving water contradicts the slide and worsens enterohepatic circulation.

options.label: D
options.text: Sunlight exposure through a window as definitive therapy
options.rationale: Sunlight is not definitive therapy; phototherapy uses controlled irradiance.

questions.sourceMapping: Newborn/Infant deck Slides 69-70 (treatment slide)

stem: A nursing student asks why the PNP measures bilirubin rather than judging jaundice by eye in a darker-skinned newborn. Which response is most accurate?

options.label: A
options.text: Visual assessment is reliable if performed in warm fluorescent light
options.rationale: Lighting improves detection but never replaces measurement.

options.label: B
options.text: Visual appearance alone cannot reliably estimate bilirubin; jaundice is best seen in natural daylight and in the sclera, but measurement is required
options.rationale: The slide states visual appearance alone cannot reliably estimate bilirubin concentration and recommends assessment in daylight with scleral inspection, followed by measurement (Slide 69 presentation column).

options.label: C
options.text: Darker skin prevents jaundice from ever developing
options.rationale: Jaundice occurs in all skin tones; detection is harder, not absent.

options.label: D
options.text: Transcutaneous bilirubin is invalid in darker skin, so only clinical judgment may be used
options.rationale: TcB and TSB remain the standard; clinical judgment alone is insufficient.

questions.sourceMapping: Newborn/Infant deck Slide 69 (presentation and assessment)

stem: A discharge summary notes a 30-hour TcB of 6.2 mg/dL plotted in the low-risk zone. What responsibility does the course assign the primary care provider?

options.label: A
options.text: Treat all discharge values above 5 mg/dL with phototherapy
options.rationale: Treatment follows hour-specific, gestational-age-adjusted thresholds, not a flat cutoff.

options.label: B
options.text: Track the plotted value on the hour-specific nomogram and assess the infant serially to ensure the trend is falling, not rising
options.rationale: The professor described receiving the discharge bilirubin, plotting it on the hour-based graph, and following the child to ensure the value trends down - with readmission when it climbs into moderate/high-risk zones (Transcript 4; Slides 69-70).

options.label: C
options.text: Repeat TcB daily for 14 days in all newborns
options.rationale: Routine daily TcB for two weeks is not the protocol; risk-stratified follow-up is.

options.label: D
options.text: None; the hospital completes all bilirubin follow-up
options.rationale: Continuity of bilirubin follow-up is a primary care responsibility.

questions.sourceMapping: Transcript 4 (plotting discharge bilirubin and tracking); Newborn/Infant deck Slides 69-70 | Parallel Form B (options re-randomized)

stem: A 3-week-old presents with a moist, shiny, pink-red nodule at the umbilical base that appeared after cord separation, with scant serous drainage on the diaper. The infant is afebrile, feeding well, and the periumbilical skin is soft and non-tender. What is the most appropriate management?

options.label: A
options.text: Emergency department referral for intravenous antibiotics
options.rationale: IV antibiotics treat omphalitis, which requires erythema, tenderness, purulence, or systemic signs.

options.label: B
options.text: Office application of silver nitrate to cauterize the granulation tissue, with follow-up
options.rationale: The image and vignette show an umbilical granuloma: a small, moist, pink-red granulation nodule after cord separation, painless, without surrounding erythema, in a well infant; the taught treatment is silver nitrate cauterization (Slides 71-72; Transcript 4).

options.label: C
options.text: Oral cephalexin and warm compresses
options.rationale: Oral antibiotics are not indicated for a benign granuloma.

options.label: D
options.text: Surgical excision in the operating room today
options.rationale: Excision is unnecessary; silver nitrate (or suture ligation) is first-line office therapy. Figure 1: Newborn/Infant deck Slide 71 (second-half PPTX slide 8) reference asset - moist, shiny red-pink nodule at the umbilical base without significant surrounding erythema.

questions.sourceMapping: Newborn/Infant deck Slides 71-72; Transcript 4 (granuloma = silver nitrate; professor emphasis)

stem: A 10-day-old presents with periumbilical erythema extending 3 cm onto the abdominal wall, edema, purulent foul-smelling drainage, and tenderness with crying on palpation. Temperature is 38.1 C and feeding is poor. What is the most appropriate action?

options.label: A
options.text: Office silver nitrate application and recheck in 3 days
options.rationale: Silver nitrate treats granuloma; applying it here would delay limb- and life-threatening infection control.

options.label: B
options.text: Urgent hospital evaluation for omphalitis with intravenous broad-spectrum antibiotics
options.rationale: The image and findings depict omphalitis - erythema spreading outward, purulent foul drainage, tenderness, and systemic signs - a potential medical emergency that can progress rapidly to sepsis and requires hospital evaluation and IV broad-spectrum antibiotics (Slides 71-72; Transcript 4, professor's flagged confusion point).

options.label: C
options.text: Topical mupirocin and oral antipyretics
options.rationale: Topical therapy is inadequate for invasive umbilical infection with systemic signs.

options.label: D
options.text: Observation; cord-site drainage is normal at 10 days
options.rationale: Foul purulent drainage with erythema and fever is never normal cord separation. Figure 2: Newborn/Infant deck Slide 71 reference asset - umbilicus with surrounding erythema, edema, and purulent-appearing discharge (figure caption: erythema and tenderness around the umbilicus).

questions.sourceMapping: Newborn/Infant deck Slides 71-72; Transcript 4 (omphalitis = ED, medical emergency)

stem: Select all features that favor omphalitis over umbilical granuloma in a newborn with umbilical drainage.

options.label: A
options.text: Surrounding erythema that may spread outward from the umbilicus
options.rationale: Peri-umbilical erythema is absent in granuloma and present (often spreading) in omphalitis.

options.label: B
options.text: Purulent or foul-smelling drainage
options.rationale: Granuloma drainage is scant, clear-to-yellow serous; purulence and odor indicate infection.

options.label: C
options.text: Tenderness and warmth on palpation
options.rationale: Granulomas are painless; tenderness and warmth indicate infection - the professor's key discriminator.

options.label: D
options.text: Fever, lethargy, or poor feeding
options.rationale: Systemic signs mark the transition from local to systemic infection and mandate urgent care.

options.label: E
options.text: A small moist pink nodule first noticed after cord separation in a well-appearing infant
options.rationale: That description is the granuloma itself, not omphalitis.

questions.sourceMapping: Newborn/Infant deck Slide 72 comparison table; Transcript 4 (tender/red = omphalitis)

stem: After silver nitrate treatment of an umbilical granuloma, the lesion recurs and now appears different, with increasing moisture and a redder base. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.text: Repeat silver nitrate without further assessment
options.rationale: Blind repetition risks masking progressive infection.

options.label: B
options.text: Discharge with routine 2-month follow-up
options.rationale: Deferral ignores the flagged reassessment trigger.

options.label: C
options.text: Apply a topical steroid to reduce inflammation
options.rationale: Steroids have no role and may worsen infection.

options.label: D
options.text: Reassess for an underlying omphalitis or alternative diagnosis beneath the granulation tissue
options.rationale: The professor warned that a granuloma that returns looking different requires reassessment for missed omphalitis or another cause of persistent drainage (Transcript 4; Slide 72 note that persistent drainage warrants evaluation).

questions.sourceMapping: Transcript 4 (recurrent granuloma = reassess for omphalitis); Newborn/Infant deck Slide 72 | Parallel Form B (options re-randomized)

stem: At what age does the umbilical cord stump typically separate, per the course?

options.label: A
options.text: 4-6 weeks
options.rationale: Separation beyond 3 weeks raises concern for immune or anatomic disorders, but typical separation is 1-2 weeks.

options.label: B
options.text: 1-2 weeks
options.rationale: The cord stump usually falls off in 1-2 weeks; granulation tissue then closes the wound, and overgrowth produces granuloma (Slides 71; Transcript 4).

options.label: C
options.text: 3-4 months
options.rationale: 3-4 months corresponds to cephalohematoma resorption, not cord separation.

options.label: D
options.text: 24-48 hours
options.rationale: 24-48 hours is the meconium passage window, not cord separation.

questions.sourceMapping: Newborn/Infant deck Slide 71; Transcript 4 (cord falls off in 1-2 weeks) | Parallel Form B (options re-randomized)

stem: A 6-week-old has a soft, skin-covered bulge at the umbilicus that enlarges with crying and reduces easily. The parents ask about strangulation risk. Which counseling is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: Umbilical hernias frequently strangulate and require repair in infancy
options.rationale: Inguinal, not umbilical, hernias carry the incarceration urgency in infants.

options.label: B
options.text: Umbilical hernias rarely incarcerate or strangulate, and most resolve by about 3 years of age
options.rationale: AAFP teaches umbilical hernias are common, rarely incarcerate or strangulate, and most resolve by age 3 (AAFP Part II, abdomen).

options.label: C
options.text: Umbilical hernias indicate an underlying immunodeficiency
options.rationale: No immune association exists; delayed cord separation does.

options.label: D
options.text: Taping a coin over the hernia accelerates closure and is recommended
options.rationale: Coin taping is an ineffective folk practice with skin-risk and no benefit.

questions.sourceMapping: AAFP Part II (umbilical hernia natural history)

stem: The professor repeatedly contrasted inflammation with infection using the bug-bite example. Which principle should guide assessment of a red, swollen umbilical area?

options.label: A
options.text: Inflammation and infection are synonymous in newborns
options.rationale: The course explicitly separates the two concepts.

options.label: B
options.text: Inflammation may be sterile; systemic signs such as fever, warmth, and toxicity shift suspicion toward infection
options.rationale: Inflammation (swelling, redness) can arise from sterile processes; fever, warmth, induration, and systemic illness indicate infection - the professor's framework for separating granuloma from omphalitis and local from systemic disease (Transcript 4).

options.label: C
options.text: Any redness in a newborn is infection until cultured negative
options.rationale: Over-attribution leads to unnecessary antibiotics; discrimination is the taught skill.

options.label: D
options.text: Infection never occurs without visible pus
options.rationale: Early infection may lack visible pus while showing erythema and tenderness.

questions.sourceMapping: Transcript 4 (inflammation vs infection; local vs systemic)

stem: When documenting periumbilical erythema suspected to be early omphalitis, which documentation practice did the professor require?

options.label: A
options.text: Photograph only, without measurements
options.rationale: Photos supplement but do not replace measured documentation.

options.label: B
options.text: Record as present or absent without dimensions
options.rationale: Binary documentation forfeits trending capability.

options.label: C
options.text: Describe color only (pink vs red)
options.rationale: Color alone cannot track spread.

options.label: D
options.text: Measure and document the width of erythema and induration in centimeters for trending
options.rationale: The professor insisted on measuring and charting the extent of erythema and induration in centimeters so progression or resolution can be tracked objectively (Transcript 4).

questions.sourceMapping: Transcript 4 (document erythema in centimeters) | Parallel Form B (options re-randomized)

stem: A 6-hour-old term newborn cries vigorously with blue-purple hands and feet while the trunk and mouth remain pink. The finding has been present since birth. What is the most appropriate interpretation?

options.label: A
options.text: Central cyanosis requiring immediate echocardiography
options.rationale: Central cyanosis involves the mouth and tongue; this infant's mucosa is pink.

options.label: B
options.text: Acrocyanosis, a benign finding of immature peripheral vasculature that typically resolves in 24-48 hours
options.rationale: The photograph shows acrocyanosis: peripheral, persistent cyanosis of hands and feet (sometimes face) in the first hours, from immature vessels shunting blood to core organs; it resolves in 24-48 hours and needs reassurance (Slide 73; Transcript 4).

options.label: C
options.text: Methemoglobinemia requiring methylene blue
options.rationale: Methemoglobinemia causes gray-blue central cyanosis unrelieved by crying or warming.

options.label: D
options.text: Early sepsis requiring a full sepsis evaluation
options.rationale: A vigorous, feeding newborn with isolated peripheral cyanosis lacks sepsis signs; temperature instability and lethargy would change the picture. Figure 3: Newborn/Infant deck Slide 73 reference asset - blue-purple discoloration of the hands and feet in a crying newborn with a pink trunk.

questions.sourceMapping: Newborn/Infant deck Slide 73; Transcript 4 (acrocyanosis benign; worry about central cyanosis)

stem: Which finding converts a cyanotic-appearing newborn from reassurance to urgent cardiopulmonary evaluation?

options.label: A
options.text: Cyanosis limited to the hands and feet in the first 24 hours
options.rationale: Hand-foot cyanosis in the first day is acrocyanosis.

options.label: B
options.text: Cyanosis of the tongue and oral mucosa (central cyanosis)
options.rationale: The professor contrasted benign acrocyanosis with central cyanosis - the mouth and tongue are the discriminating sites that demand evaluation for cardiac or pulmonary disease (Transcript 4; AAFP Part I).

options.label: C
options.text: Transient bluish feet during a cool room exposure that pink with warming
options.rationale: Cold-induced mottling or acrocyanosis that warms is peripheral and benign.

options.label: D
options.text: Bluish discoloration that resolves with crying
options.rationale: Cyanosis relieved by crying suggests choanal atresia, a different airway issue; central cyanosis is not relieved by crying.

questions.sourceMapping: Transcript 4 (central vs peripheral cyanosis); AAFP Part I (acrocyanosis vs cyanotic heart disease)

stem: Using the comparison table shown, a 2-day-old well-appearing newborn has 1-4 mm non-erythematous pustules with milky fluid on the face and trunk that rupture easily, leaving collarettes of scale and hyperpigmented macules. Which conclusion is correct?

images.alt: Figure 4: Newborn/Infant deck Slide 82 reference asset - comparison table distinguishing transient neonatal pustular melanosis from neonatal herpes simplex infection.
images.caption: Figure 4: Newborn/Infant deck Slide 82 reference asset - comparison table distinguishing transient neonatal pustular melanosis from neonatal herpes simplex infection.

options.label: A
options.text: Neonatal HSV; start IV acyclovir immediately
options.rationale: HSV shows vesicles on an erythematous base with a rosy-petal dewdrop look, onset 5-14 days, grouped lesions, and systemic illness - none present here.

options.label: B
options.text: TNPM; benign and self-limited, requiring reassurance only
options.rationale: The table's TNPM column matches exactly: onset 1-3 days, non-erythematous pustules with milky fluid, easy rupture with scale collarettes and hyperpigmented macules, well-appearing infant, benign course resolving in 1-2 weeks with no lab testing needed (Slides 81-82; Transcript 4).

options.label: C
options.text: Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome; admit for IV antibiotics
options.rationale: SSSS produces diffuse tender erythema with desquamation and toxicity.

options.label: D
options.text: Candidiasis; start oral fluconazole
options.rationale: Candidiasis favors intertriginous and diaper areas with satellite pustules and erythema.

questions.sourceMapping: Newborn/Infant deck Slides 81-82; Transcript 4 (TNPM vs herpes discrimination)

stem: A 10-day-old presents with grouped vesicles on an erythematous base over the scalp and periorbital area, poor feeding, lethargy, and temperature instability. What is the most appropriate action?

options.label: A
options.text: Start oral acyclovir and discharge with close follow-up
options.rationale: Oral therapy is inadequate for neonatal HSV, which can disseminate.

options.label: B
options.text: Confirm with HSV PCR from a lesion swab, consider blood and CSF testing, and start urgent IV acyclovir with subspecialty consultation
options.rationale: The table and lecture define neonatal HSV as vesicles on an erythematous base, onset 5-14 days, possible mucous membrane and CNS involvement, and systemic illness; management is urgent evaluation, PCR confirmation, and IV acyclovir (Slide 82; Transcript 4).

options.label: C
options.text: Apply topical antibiotics and recheck in 48 hours
options.rationale: Topical antibiotics do not treat HSV and delay life-saving antivirals.

options.label: D
options.text: Reassure; the eruption matches transient neonatal pustular melanosis
options.rationale: TNPM infants are well-appearing with non-erythematous pustules; this infant is systemically ill.

questions.sourceMapping: Newborn/Infant deck Slide 82; Transcript 4 (neonatal herpes severity) | Parallel Form B (options re-randomized)

stem: The photograph shows a shallow midline sacral dimple at the top of the gluteal cleft, less than 0.5 cm, with a visible base and no hair tuft, tag, mass, or discoloration. What is the most appropriate management?

options.label: A
options.text: Spinal ultrasonography before 3 months of age
options.rationale: Ultrasound is reserved for high-risk dimples (base not seen, >2.5 cm above the anus, or associated cutaneous stigmata).

options.label: B
options.text: MRI of the spine under sedation
options.rationale: MRI is a second-line study for abnormal ultrasound or neurologic signs.

options.label: C
options.text: Routine care with documentation; the dimple meets simple-dimple criteria and needs no imaging
options.rationale: A simple sacral dimple (<0.5 cm, within 2.5 cm of the anal verge, base visible, no cutaneous markers) carries low risk for occult spinal dysraphism and requires no imaging; the professor stressed that not every dimple gets an ultrasound (Slides 74; AAFP Part II SORT; Transcript 4).

options.label: D
options.text: Neurosurgery referral for tethered cord release
options.rationale: There is no evidence of tethered cord in a simple dimple. Figure 5: Newborn/Infant deck Slide 74 reference asset - photograph of the sacral region showing a shallow midline dimple at the apex of the gluteal cleft.

questions.sourceMapping: Newborn/Infant deck Slide 74; AAFP Part II SORT; Transcript 4 (dimple criteria; not every dimple gets ultrasound)

stem: Select all sacral dimple features that classify the dimple as high risk for occult spinal dysraphism and warrant ultrasonography.

options.label: A
options.text: The dimple measures 3 mm with a visible base at the gluteal cleft apex
options.rationale: A small dimple with visible base near the gluteal cleft is simple and low risk.

options.label: B
options.text: The dimple is located more than 2.5 cm above the anus
options.rationale: Location >2.5 cm above the anus is a listed high-risk criterion.

options.label: C
options.text: The dimple is associated with a midline mass or skin discoloration
options.rationale: Midline masses, discoloration, or hemangiomas accompanying a dimple raise risk.

options.label: D
options.text: The base of the dimple cannot be visualized
options.rationale: An unseen base is a listed high-risk criterion (ACR-based slide).

options.label: E
options.text: The dimple is accompanied by a hair tuft or midline skin tag
options.rationale: Hair tufts and skin tags are cutaneous markers of occult dysraphism.

questions.sourceMapping: Newborn/Infant deck Slides 74 (high-risk criteria); AAFP Part II (simple vs complex dimple) | Parallel Form B (options re-randomized)

stem: A 2-month-old has a bright red raised plaque over the lateral forehead that was absent at birth, appeared at 3 weeks, and has enlarged steadily. The parents are distressed. Which counseling is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: This is a port-wine stain that will darken permanently
options.rationale: Port-wine stains are present at birth as flat patches and do not proliferate then involute.

options.label: B
options.text: This is an infantile hemangioma: expect growth through the first year followed by involution over several years
options.rationale: Hemangiomas are vascular tumors that typically appear in the first weeks, grow rapidly during the first year, then involute over years; anticipatory guidance about the growth phase prevents parental alarm (Slide 78; Transcript 4; AAFP Table 1).

options.label: C
options.text: This is a salmon patch that will fade by 12 months
options.rationale: Salmon patches are flat, present at birth, and fade; they do not grow as raised plaques.

options.label: D
options.text: This is dermal melanocytosis that will fade by age 4
options.rationale: Dermal melanocytosis is blue-gray and macular, typically sacral.

questions.sourceMapping: Newborn/Infant deck Slide 78; Transcript 4 (hemangioma course); AAFP Part II Table 1

stem: Which hemangioma location mandates early referral for treatment rather than observation?

options.label: A
options.text: A hemangioma near the eye or other critical structures (airway), because of risk to vision or function
options.rationale: The course and slide direct early dermatology (and ophthalmology) referral for hemangiomas near the eye, airway, or other critical structures because growth can impair vision or function; the professor singled out periocular lesions (Slide 78; Transcript 4).

options.label: B
options.text: A hemangioma on the thigh
options.rationale: Extremity hemangiomas away from function are observed unless ulcerating or segmental-large.

options.label: C
options.text: A hemangioma on the heel
options.rationale: Heel lesions are observed unless ulcerated.

options.label: D
options.text: A 2-cm hemangioma on the upper back
options.rationale: Trunk hemangiomas without complications are observed.

questions.sourceMapping: Newborn/Infant deck Slide 78; Transcript 4 (hemangiomas near eyes get treated) | Parallel Form B (options re-randomized)

stem: A newborn has a flat pink-salmon patch on the upper eyelids and glabella plus a similar patch on the nape. The parent asks if treatment is needed. Which statement is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: These are salmon patches (nevus simplex) that usually fade by 1-2 years of age
options.rationale: Salmon patches (stork bites/angel kisses) are flat pink-salmon capillary patches on eyelids, glabella, or nape, present at birth and typically fading by 1-2 years; reassurance is the management (Slide 77; AAFP Table 1).

options.label: B
options.text: These are port-wine stains requiring pulsed-dye laser in infancy
