options.rationale: Port-wine stains are darker, persist, and darken; they do not fade.

options.label: C
options.text: These are hemangiomas that will proliferate over the first year
options.rationale: Hemangiomas are raised vascular tumors with a proliferative phase.

options.label: D
options.text: These patches indicate Sturge-Weber syndrome regardless of distribution
options.rationale: Sturge-Weber concern applies to port-wine stains in trigeminal distribution, not fading salmon patches.

questions.sourceMapping: Newborn/Infant deck Slide 77; AAFP Part II Table 1

stem: A 6-week-old has thick yellow-white greasy scales over the scalp that parents find distressing. Hair growth beneath is unaffected so far. What is the most appropriate management?

options.label: A
options.text: Oral antifungal therapy for tinea capitis
options.rationale: Tinea capitis causes alopecia and inflammation, not greasy adherent scale in a young infant.

options.label: B
options.text: Gentle removal with a soft brush or comb after emollient or oil, with reassurance that seborrheic dermatitis is benign and self-limiting
options.rationale: Cradle cap (seborrheic dermatitis) results from sebaceous gland overproduction; the course teaches gentle scale removal (soft brush/toothbrush with oil) and reassurance, noting it is usually not itchy and self-limiting (Slide 75; Transcript 4).

options.label: C
options.text: Topical corticosteroids to the scalp daily for 3 months
options.rationale: Prolonged potent steroids on an infant scalp are inappropriate for a self-limited condition.

options.label: D
options.text: Selenium sulfide shampoo contraindicated in infancy
options.rationale: Medicated shampoos are not categorically contraindicated; conservative care is simply first-line.

questions.sourceMapping: Newborn/Infant deck Slide 75; Transcript 4 (cradle cap care)

stem: A 3-week-old develops inflammatory papules and pustules on the cheeks without comedones. The infant is otherwise well. Which statement is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: Atopic dermatitis requiring topical immunosuppressants
options.rationale: Atopic dermatitis is pruritic, dry, and eczematous, not pustular on the cheeks at 3 weeks.

options.label: B
options.text: Neonatal acne, stimulated by maternal and endogenous androgens, typically appearing after 2 weeks and resolving spontaneously
options.rationale: Neonatal acne affects up to 20% of infants, appears after about 2 weeks from sebaceous stimulation by maternal/endogenous androgens, lacks comedones, and resolves in weeks to months without treatment (Slide 76; Transcript 4).

options.label: C
options.text: Herpes simplex, requiring PCR testing
options.rationale: HSV produces grouped vesicles with systemic features.

options.label: D
options.text: Erythema toxicum, which appears at this age with eosinophils
options.rationale: Erythema toxicum arises in the first days on an erythematous base and resolves within the first week.

questions.sourceMapping: Newborn/Infant deck Slide 76; Transcript 4 (neonatal acne self-limited) | Parallel Form B (options re-randomized)

stem: A 2-month-old bundled in heavy clothing develops clusters of tiny clear and red bumps under the neck folds and axillae during a heat wave. Which counseling point carries the greatest safety significance?

options.label: A
options.text: Apply topical antibiotics to prevent secondary infection
options.rationale: Miliaria is sterile; antibiotics are unnecessary.

options.label: B
options.text: Keep the infant cool and dry with lightweight clothing; overheating is also a modifiable SIDS risk factor
options.rationale: Miliaria results from sweat-duct obstruction with heat and humidity; management is cooling and lightweight clothing, and the professor linked overheating directly to SIDS risk counseling (Slide 80; Transcript 4).

options.label: C
options.text: Expose the infant to direct sunlight to dry the lesions
options.rationale: Sun exposure risks burns and overheating.

options.label: D
options.text: Restrict fluids to reduce sweating
options.rationale: Fluid restriction is dangerous in infancy.

questions.sourceMapping: Newborn/Infant deck Slide 80; Transcript 4 (prickly heat and overheating/SIDS link)

stem: During a cool examination room assessment, a newborn's lower limbs show a lacy, reticular mottled pattern that disappears when the infant is warmed. What is the diagnosis?

options.label: A
options.text: Cutis marmorata, a benign vascular response to cold
options.rationale: Cutis marmorata is reticular mottling from vascular response to cold that resolves with warming, typically on the limbs (AAFP Part II Table 1).

options.label: B
options.text: Purpura fulminans
options.rationale: Purpura fulminans shows non-blanching purpuric necrosis with toxicity.

options.label: C
options.text: Necrotizing fasciitis
options.rationale: Necrotizing infection shows erythema, edema, and systemic illness.

options.label: D
options.text: Congenital dermal melanocytosis
options.rationale: Dermal melanocytosis is a fixed blue-gray macule, not temperature-dependent mottling.

questions.sourceMapping: AAFP Part II Table 1 (cutis marmorata)

stem: A vigorous newborn delivered after a difficult delivery shows localized bruising and a few petechiae on the face. Coagulation studies are normal and the infant is well. Which counseling is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: These findings indicate hemophilia until factor levels return
options.rationale: Hemophilia presents with deep bleeding; isolated traumatic petechiae with normal studies do not diagnose it.

options.label: B
options.text: Bruising at birth is a confirmed marker of non-accidental trauma
options.rationale: Birth trauma explains the distribution; documentation (including dermal melanocytosis distinctions) prevents misattribution later.

options.label: C
options.text: Bruising and petechiae from delivery trauma are common and typically resolve over time
options.rationale: AAFP notes bruising and petechiae are common birth-related findings that typically resolve over time in a well infant with normal studies (AAFP Part II, skin).

options.label: D
options.text: Petechiae in any newborn mandate immediate platelet transfusion
options.rationale: Transfusion follows thrombocytopenia or bleeding, not isolated traumatic petechiae.

questions.sourceMapping: AAFP Part II (bruising/petechiae resolve) | Parallel Form B (options re-randomized)

stem: Select all findings in a jaundiced newborn that constitute red flags requiring urgent evaluation rather than routine follow-up.

options.label: A
options.text: Jaundice appearing within the first 24 hours of life
options.rationale: Jaundice <24 hours is pathologic until proven otherwise.

options.label: B
options.text: Direct (conjugated) hyperbilirubinemia at any age
options.rationale: Conjugated hyperbilirubinemia is never physiologic and suggests cholestasis/biliary atresia.

options.label: C
options.text: Lethargy, poor feeding, or a high-pitched cry in a jaundiced infant
options.rationale: Neurologic or systemic signs suggest acute bilirubin encephalopathy or sepsis.

options.label: D
options.text: Acholic stools with dark urine and jaundice beyond 2 weeks
options.rationale: That cluster indicates biliary obstruction requiring prompt referral.

options.label: E
options.text: Mild facial jaundice on day 4 in a well-feeding term infant with bilirubin in the low-risk zone
options.rationale: Day-4 mild jaundice in a well infant within the low-risk zone is the expected physiologic pattern with routine follow-up.

questions.sourceMapping: Newborn/Infant deck Slides 65, 67-68 (high-yield row); Transcript 4

stem: Which pairing of newborn skin finding and characteristic is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: Milia - white keratin cysts on the nose that resolve spontaneously in the first weeks
options.rationale: Milia are white epidermal keratin cysts, most often on the nose, rupturing and resolving in the first weeks (AAFP Table 1; Slide 79).

options.label: B
options.text: Erythema toxicum - pustules without erythema containing neutrophils
options.rationale: That description belongs to TNPM; erythema toxicum has an erythematous base with eosinophils.

options.label: C
options.text: Transient neonatal pustular melanosis - papules on an erythematous base with eosinophils
options.rationale: Reversed: TNPM has neutrophils without erythema; erythema toxicum has eosinophils on red bases.

options.label: D
options.text: Salmon patch - persists and darkens with age
options.rationale: Salmon patches fade; port-wine stains persist and darken.

questions.sourceMapping: AAFP Part II Table 1; Newborn/Infant deck Slides 77-81

stem: What mechanism is proposed for breast milk jaundice in a thriving breastfed infant?

options.label: A
options.text: A factor in some breast milks interferes with hepatic conjugation of bilirubin, delaying excretion
options.rationale: The professor described the theory that something in some breast milks interferes with the liver's breakdown (conjugation) of heme, so bilirubin remains in the bloodstream - in a well, feeding, gaining infant (Transcript 4; Slide 67).

options.label: B
options.text: Breast milk contains bilirubin that is absorbed intact
options.rationale: Bilirubin is not absorbed intact from milk.

options.label: C
options.text: Breastfeeding causes hemolysis through anti-Rh antibodies
options.rationale: ABO/Rh hemolysis is immune and independent of feeding type.

options.label: D
options.text: Lactose in breast milk blocks bilirubin excretion in the kidney
options.rationale: Bilirubin is excreted via the gut after conjugation, not renally via lactose mechanisms.

questions.sourceMapping: Transcript 4 (breast milk jaundice theory); Newborn/Infant deck Slide 67

stem: How often should newborns be visually assessed for jaundice until discharge, per the slide protocol?

options.label: A
options.text: Once daily
options.rationale: Daily assessment misses rapid risers.

options.label: B
options.text: At least every 12 hours
options.rationale: The assessment column directs visual jaundice assessment at least every 12 hours until discharge (Slide 65).

options.label: C
options.text: Only at admission and discharge
options.rationale: Interval assessment is explicitly required.

options.label: D
options.text: Every 48 hours
options.rationale: 48-hour intervals are inadequate for early detection.

questions.sourceMapping: Newborn/Infant deck Slide 65 (assessment frequency)

stem: A jaundiced 2-day-old of Mediterranean descent shows a rapid bilirubin rise, anemia, and reticulocytosis with a negative DAT. Coombs-negative hemolysis in this context should prompt evaluation for which condition?

options.label: A
options.text: Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency
options.rationale: G6PD deficiency is a listed cause of hemolytic jaundice and neurotoxicity risk; DAT-negative hemolysis with risk-background ancestry fits G6PD (Slides 65, 67-68).

options.label: B
options.text: ABO incompatibility
options.rationale: ABO incompatibility typically shows a positive (sometimes weak) DAT and mother O/infant A-B pairing.

options.label: C
options.text: Rh alloimmunization
options.rationale: Rh disease shows positive DAT and maternal sensitization history.

options.label: D
options.text: Physiologic jaundice
options.rationale: Rapid rise with anemia and reticulocytosis is not physiologic.

questions.sourceMapping: Newborn/Infant deck Slides 65, 67-68 (G6PD in hemolytic jaundice)

stem: A septic-appearing 6-day-old has jaundice with both conjugated and unconjugated elevation, temperature instability, and poor feeding. Which row of the comparison table does this presentation match?

options.label: A
options.text: Physiologic jaundice
options.rationale: Physiologic jaundice occurs in well infants after 24 hours.

options.label: B
options.text: Suboptimal intake jaundice
options.rationale: Intake jaundice shows dehydration and weight loss without toxicity.

options.label: C
options.text: Breast milk jaundice
options.rationale: Breast milk jaundice infants are thriving and afebrile.

options.label: D
options.text: Infection/sepsis, which may produce unconjugated or conjugated hyperbilirubinemia and requires urgent evaluation
options.rationale: The table lists infection/sepsis with variable timing and either unconjugated or conjugated bilirubin, accompanied by poor feeding, lethargy, or temperature instability, mandating urgent evaluation (Slide 67).

questions.sourceMapping: Newborn/Infant deck Slide 67 (infection/sepsis row) | Parallel Form B (options re-randomized)

stem: The professor asked the class why unconjugated bilirubin is dangerous to the newborn brain. Which answer reflects the taught mechanism?

options.label: A
options.text: Bilirubin binds irreversibly to skull sutures, raising intracranial pressure
options.rationale: Suture binding is not a mechanism.

options.label: B
options.text: Unconjugated bilirubin is water-soluble and floods cerebrospinal fluid
options.rationale: Unconjugated bilirubin is water-INSOLUBLE; conjugated is water-soluble.

options.label: C
options.text: Unconjugated bilirubin crosses the immature blood-brain barrier, causing neurotoxicity and kernicterus
options.rationale: The professor tied neurotoxicity to the blood-brain barrier concept in pediatrics: unconjugated (lipid-soluble, albumin-bound) bilirubin can cross the immature barrier and damage developing brain tissue - kernicterus (Transcript 4; Slide 69 key point; AAFP Part II).

options.label: D
options.text: Bilirubin causes cerebral vasospasm through renal metabolites
options.rationale: Vasospasm is not the mechanism of bilirubin neurotoxicity.

questions.sourceMapping: Transcript 4 (blood-brain barrier discussion); Newborn/Infant deck Slide 69 key point | Parallel Form B (options re-randomized)

stem: An ill-appearing 12-day-old presents with umbilical drainage and a moist pink nodule at the base, but today also has fever and a 2-cm blanching erythema ring. How should the PNP reconcile these overlapping findings?

options.label: A
options.text: Treat as granuloma with silver nitrate and recheck tomorrow
options.rationale: Silver nitrate in a febrile infant with spreading erythema delays critical treatment.

options.label: B
options.text: Treat as omphalitis until proven otherwise; systemic signs override the granuloma-like nodule and mandate urgent evaluation
options.rationale: When local granuloma-like findings coexist with erythema and systemic signs, the safety-first synthesis is omphalitis until excluded; the professor warned that a returning or changing granuloma-like lesion may hide omphalitis, and omphalitis can progress rapidly to sepsis (Slides 71-72; Transcript 4).

options.label: C
options.text: Observe; mixed findings are common during cord healing
options.rationale: Fever is never an expected cord-healing finding.

options.label: D
options.text: Order outpatient ultrasound of the umbilicus and wait for results
options.rationale: Imaging must not delay urgent antibiotic therapy in suspected omphalitis.

questions.sourceMapping: Newborn/Infant deck Slides 71-72; Transcript 4 (local vs systemic; reassess changing lesions)

stem: Select all appropriate components of management for an infant with unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia approaching the phototherapy threshold due to suboptimal breastfeeding intake.

options.label: A
options.text: Assess feeding technique and provide lactation support
options.rationale: Feeding assessment and lactation support address the root cause of intake jaundice.

options.label: B
options.text: Supplement with formula if intake is inadequate or weight loss is excessive
options.rationale: Supplementation is indicated when intake is inadequate or weight loss excessive (treatment slide).

options.label: C
options.text: Continue breastfeeding rather than stopping it
options.rationale: Continuing breastfeeding maintains stooling and enterohepatic clearance; stopping worsens jaundice.

options.label: D
options.text: Arrange serial total serum bilirubin monitoring with a defined follow-up interval
options.rationale: Serial TSB with planned follow-up detects upward trends requiring readmission.

options.label: E
options.text: Give plain water between feeds to flush bilirubin
options.rationale: Plain water is contraindicated in young infants and does not enhance bilirubin excretion.

questions.sourceMapping: Newborn/Infant deck Slides 67, 69-70 (treatment slide); Transcript 4

stem: According to the slide protocol, which universal bilirubin screening applies to newborns of 35 weeks' gestation or more?

options.label: A
options.text: At least one transcutaneous or total serum bilirubin at 24-48 hours of age or before discharge if earlier
options.rationale: All newborns >=35 weeks should have at least one TcB or TSB at 24-48 hours or before discharge if earlier, providing the plotted discharge value the primary care provider then tracks (Slide 65; Transcript 4).

options.label: B
options.text: Bilirubin testing only if jaundice is observed by nursing staff
options.rationale: Universal screening is required regardless of visible jaundice, which appears later.

options.label: C
options.text: Routine conjugated bilirubin fraction at 72 hours for all newborns
options.rationale: Fractionation is indicated during evaluation of jaundice, not as universal screening.

options.label: D
options.text: Cord blood bilirubin as the sole required measurement
options.rationale: Cord bilirubin does not replace the 24-48 hour or pre-discharge measurement.

questions.sourceMapping: Newborn/Infant deck Slide 65 (universal screening protocol)

stem: A 4-day-old's jaundice has progressed from the face to the abdomen and now is visible on the lower legs and palms. Using the taught cephalocaudal progression concept, what does this pattern imply?

options.label: A
options.text: The bilirubin is falling and the jaundice is resolving from the head downward
options.rationale: Resolution fades in reverse order but the clinical task is unchanged: measure, do not infer.

options.label: B
options.text: Cephalocaudal progression to the extremities suggests a higher bilirubin burden; measure TSB promptly rather than estimating visually
options.rationale: Jaundice appears first on the face/sclera and progresses head-to-toe as levels rise; visibility at the legs and palms signals a higher burden, and the slide pearl demands measurement and hour-specific interpretation instead of visual estimation (Slides 65, 69; Transcript 4).

options.label: C
options.text: The pattern confirms physiologic jaundice requiring no measurement
options.rationale: Extent of progression raises concern and mandates TSB.

options.label: D
options.text: Distal jaundice indicates conjugated hyperbilirubinemia specifically
options.rationale: Progression pattern reflects total burden, not the conjugated fraction.

questions.sourceMapping: Newborn/Infant deck Slides 65, 69 (cephalocaudal progression; SEE-MEASURE-INTERPRET)

stem: In class the professor asked whether a baby born before 37 weeks is at lower or higher risk for jaundice. Which rationale supports the correct answer?

options.label: A
options.text: Lower risk, because preterm infants have fewer red cells to break down
options.rationale: Preterm infants have relatively higher red cell turnover, not lower.

options.label: B
options.text: Higher risk, because hepatic conjugation and feeding maturity are still developing
options.rationale: Preterm infants are at higher risk for hyperbilirubinemia because conjugation capacity, feeding, and elimination are immature; GA <38 weeks is also a neurotoxicity risk factor that lowers treatment thresholds (Transcript 4; Slide 65).

options.label: C
options.text: Equal risk, because gestational age does not affect bilirubin metabolism
options.rationale: Gestational age directly shapes both bilirubin production-conjugation balance and treatment thresholds.

options.label: D
options.text: Lower risk, because preterm infants are monitored more closely
options.rationale: Monitoring intensity does not change biologic risk.

questions.sourceMapping: Transcript 4 (Socratic: prematurity = higher jaundice risk); Newborn/Infant deck Slide 65

stem: Using the gastric capacity graphic, a parent of a 3-day-old asks how much the stomach can hold per feed. Which volume range should the PNP cite?

images.alt: Figure 1: Newborn/Infant deck Slide 14 reference asset - newborn gastric capacity from day 1 (cherry) through 1 month (large egg).
images.caption: Figure 1: Newborn/Infant deck Slide 14 reference asset - newborn gastric capacity from day 1 (cherry) through 1 month (large egg).

options.label: A
options.text: 5-7 mL per feed
options.rationale: 5-7 mL is day-1 capacity.

options.label: B
options.text: 22-27 mL per feed
options.rationale: Day 3 gastric capacity equals a walnut: 22-27 mL (0.75-1 oz); day 1 is 5-7 mL, one week 45-60 mL, and one month 80-150 mL - the graphic's taught values that explain small, frequent newborn feeds (Slide 14; Transcript 3).

options.label: C
options.text: 45-60 mL per feed
options.rationale: 45-60 mL corresponds to one week of age.

options.label: D
options.text: 80-150 mL per feed
options.rationale: 80-150 mL corresponds to one month of age.

questions.sourceMapping: Newborn/Infant deck Slide 14; Transcript 3 (stomach size visual)

stem: Which feeding interval rule applies to a 2-week-old newborn?

options.label: A
options.text: Feed on demand every 1-3 hours and do not let the neonate go more than 3 hours without eating in the first month
options.rationale: Newborns feed on demand every 1-3 hours initially (every 1-2 hours the first week, then every 2-2.5 hours), and the neonate must not exceed 3 hours without feeding in the first month of life (Slides 13, 48; Transcript 3).

options.label: B
options.text: Schedule feeds every 4 hours to establish routine
options.rationale: Four-hour scheduling starves a neonate with a cherry-to-walnut stomach.

options.label: C
options.text: Feed every 6 hours overnight to protect maternal sleep
options.rationale: Overnight gaps beyond 3 hours risk dehydration and weight-loss exceedance.

options.label: D
options.text: Feed only when the infant cries, regardless of interval
options.rationale: Crying is a late hunger cue; feeding cues precede crying, and hibernating infants may not cry at all.

questions.sourceMapping: Newborn/Infant deck Slides 13, 48; Transcript 3 (never >3 hours without eating first month)

stem: A mother reports her 10-day-old is 'so good - he sleeps through everything' and rarely wakes to feed. Weight is down 12% from birth. Which concept must guide the PNP's response?

options.label: A
options.text: The infant is temperamentally easy; encourage continued sleep consolidation
options.rationale: Labeling underfeeding as easy temperament is the exact trap the professor warned about.

options.label: B
options.text: Infants who do not get enough calories hibernate rather than cry; excessive sleepiness with excess weight loss signals inadequate intake and requires feeding evaluation today
options.rationale: The professor's 'very, very, very important concept': underfed newborns hibernate - they sleep instead of crying - and a too-quiet, too-sleepy infant is a red flag; loss beyond 10% of birth weight is a concern requiring immediate feeding assessment (Transcripts 3, 4; Slide 19).

options.label: C
options.text: Sleeping through feeds is protective against SIDS and should be encouraged
options.rationale: Safe sleep requires supine positioning, not skipped feeds; waking to feed every 2-3 hours is mandated.

options.label: D
options.text: Weight loss of 12% is within the expected 5-10% range
options.rationale: Expected loss is 5-10%; 12% exceeds it and, with no return toward birth weight by day 10, is pathologic.

questions.sourceMapping: Transcript 3 (hibernation concept); Transcript 4 (too quiet = red flag); Newborn/Infant deck Slide 19

stem: A breastfeeding mother cannot tell how much milk the infant transfers. Which office technique quantifies transfer?

options.label: A
options.text: Estimate from diaper weight alone
options.rationale: Diaper counts assess hydration trends, not per-feed transfer.

options.label: B
options.text: Weigh the infant, have the mother breastfeed, then re-weigh to calculate intake (test/weighted feeding)
options.rationale: The course describes weighted (test) feeds: weigh, breastfeed, re-weigh to determine grams transferred, because breastfed intake cannot otherwise be measured (Transcript 3).

options.label: C
options.text: Measure milk volume by manual expression after feeds
options.rationale: Expression volume does not equal infant transfer efficiency.

options.label: D
options.text: Rely on maternal report of breast fullness
options.rationale: Breast fullness is subjective and unreliable.

questions.sourceMapping: Transcript 3 (weigh-feed-weigh method)

stem: A 5-day-old breastfed newborn has lost 8% of birth weight; at the 2-week visit the infant remains 4% below birth weight. How should each finding be interpreted?

options.label: A
options.text: The 8% loss at day 5 is within the expected 5-10% range, but failure to regain birth weight by the 2-week visit is a problem requiring feeding intervention
options.rationale: Loss of 5-10% in the first days is normal and return to birth weight occurs by 7-10 days; not being back at birth weight by the 2-week visit is explicitly 'a problem' requiring action (Slides 19; Transcripts 2, 3 - professor: these questions appear on exams).

options.label: B
options.text: Both findings mandate hospital admission
options.rationale: Admission follows severe dehydration or failure of outpatient management, not an isolated 4% deficit with otherwise stable status.

options.label: C
options.text: Both findings are normal
options.rationale: The 2-week deficit is not normal.

options.label: D
options.text: The 8% loss is abnormal, while the 2-week deficit is acceptable
options.rationale: The interpretation is reversed.

questions.sourceMapping: Newborn/Infant deck Slide 19; Transcript 2 (not back to BW at 2 weeks = problem); Transcript 3 (exam cue) | Parallel Form B (options re-randomized)

stem: Which cluster of weight milestones is correct per the course?

options.label: A
options.text: Double birth weight by 4-5 months, triple by 1 year, with about 25-40 g/day gain in the first 3-4 months
options.rationale: The deck teaches doubling by 4-5 months, tripling by 1 year, daily gain of 25-40 g (about 1 lb per 2 weeks) for the first 3-4 months, then 15-20 g/day (5-7 oz weekly) for the rest of the year (Slide 19).

options.label: B
options.text: Double birth weight by 6-7 months, triple by 2 years
options.rationale: Doubling by 6-7 months understates it; tripling occurs at 1 year, not 2.

options.label: C
options.text: Double birth weight by 2 months, triple by 6 months
options.rationale: Doubling by 2 months overstates early gain.

options.label: D
options.text: Gain 50 g/day throughout the first year
options.rationale: 50 g/day exceeds the taught ranges.

questions.sourceMapping: Newborn/Infant deck Slide 19; Growth & Development Part 2, Slide 34 | Parallel Form B (options re-randomized)

stem: Using the feeding guide shown, a parent of a 5-month-old asks when solids may begin. Which combination of guidance is correct?

images.alt: Figure 2: Newborn/Infant deck Slide 49 reference asset - infant feeding guide by age band with volumes, food groups, hunger/fullness cues, and developmental eating skills.
images.caption: Figure 2: Newborn/Infant deck Slide 49 reference asset - infant feeding guide by age band with volumes, food groups, hunger/fullness cues, and developmental eating skills.

options.label: A
options.text: Solids at 4–6 months when sitting independently and drinking from a cup.
options.rationale: Independent sitting and straw drinking are later skills (6-8 and 10-12 months); readiness at 6 months includes sitting with support.

options.label: B
options.text: Solids around 6 months when developmentally ready, alongside breast milk or formula.
options.rationale: Complementary foods generally around 6 months, guided by developmental readiness (sits with help, pushes up on arms, tongue movements), with breast milk or formula remaining primary: The guide places first complementary foods in the 6-8 month column (with readiness cues developing across 4-8 months: sitting with help then independently), and the course teaches introduction of solids around 6 months with breast milk/formula continuing as the nutritional foundation (Slides 49, 59-60; AAP exclusive BF 6 months).

options.label: C
options.text: Solids from 3 months when showing hunger cues and sleeping for longer periods.
options.rationale: Solids from 3 months to improve sleep: Early cereal for sleep is an outdated myth with no evidence and aspiration risk.

options.label: D
options.text: Cow’s milk with cereal from 6 months when ready for thicker food textures.
options.rationale: Whole cow's milk with cereal beginning at 6 months: Whole cow's milk is deferred until after 12 months.

questions.sourceMapping: Newborn/Infant deck Slides 49, 59-60; Milestone documents feeding guide; Transcript 3 (solids at 6 months)

stem: Which sequence for introducing complementary foods reflects the course teaching?

options.label: A
options.text: Iron-fortified rice cereal first, one new food at a time every 3-4 days, then vegetables before fruits
options.rationale: The course sequence: iron-fortified rice cereal (least allergenic) first, single-ingredient introductions every 3-4 days (or weekly) to identify reactions, then vegetables before fruits because sweets are easier to learn to like; combination dinners are avoided early (Slides 59-61).

options.label: B
options.text: Mixed meat-and-vegetable dinners first for protein
options.rationale: Combination dinners obscure allergy attribution and provide little meat.

options.label: C
options.text: Egg white as the first food to induce tolerance
options.rationale: Egg yolk may come around 6 months with whites delayed per the slide; neither is the first food.

options.label: D
options.text: Fruits first because they are most palatable, then cereal
options.rationale: Starting with sweet fruits biases later vegetable acceptance; the slide explicitly reverses this.

questions.sourceMapping: Newborn/Infant deck Slides 59-61 (cereal first, one food 3-4 days, vegetables before fruits) | Parallel Form B (options re-randomized)

stem: A parent reports the 7-month-old becomes constipated after starting solids. Using the course's food-effect teaching, which adjustment is most appropriate?

options.label: A
options.text: Increase bananas and applesauce
options.rationale: Bananas and applesauce worsen constipation.

options.label: B
options.text: Offer pears, peaches, or prunes, which soften stool, and reduce constipating bananas/applesauce
options.rationale: The slide categorizes bananas and applesauce as constipating and pears, peaches, and prunes as bowel-softening - a direct dietary lever for infant constipation after solids (Slide 61).

options.label: C
options.text: Add honey to warm water for softening
options.rationale: Honey is contraindicated in the first year due to infant botulism.

options.label: D
options.text: Switch to whole cow's milk immediately
options.rationale: Cow's milk before 12 months risks intestinal blood loss and iron deficiency.

questions.sourceMapping: Newborn/Infant deck Slide 61 (constipating vs softening fruits)

stem: Select all foods the course directs avoiding during the first year of life.

options.label: A
options.text: Honey
options.rationale: Honey carries infant botulism risk and is avoided until after 12 months.

options.label: B
options.text: Hot dogs
options.rationale: Hot dogs are a classic choking hazard of the first year.

options.label: C
options.text: Popcorn
options.rationale: Popcorn is a listed choking hazard.

options.label: D
options.text: Whole nuts and dollops of peanut butter
options.rationale: Nuts and sticky peanut butter are listed first-year choking hazards in the course slide (distinct from age-appropriate thin peanut-containing products introduced per allergy guidance).

options.label: E
options.text: Iron-fortified rice cereal
options.rationale: Iron-fortified rice cereal is the recommended FIRST food, not an avoided one.

questions.sourceMapping: Newborn/Infant deck Slide 60 (avoid peanut butter, honey, hot dogs, popcorn, nuts first year)

stem: At the 9-month visit, a parent offers the infant apple juice in a bottle at bedtime. Which counseling is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: Juice is appropriate after 6 months in unlimited amounts
options.rationale: Juice is not recommended in infancy per the course.

options.label: B
options.text: No juice and no supplemental water are recommended at this age; introduce a cup with meals and avoid bottles at bedtime
options.rationale: The 9-month guidance slide directs no juice or supplemental water, cup introduction, and the course warns against bottles at bedtime (dental caries, ear positioning); AAP juice restriction aligns (Slides 60, 63; Transcript 3).

options.label: C
options.text: Juice should replace one formula feeding daily
options.rationale: Juice displaces iron-containing formula or breast milk.

options.label: D
options.text: Bedtime bottles of juice protect against hypoglycemia
options.rationale: Bedtime juice promotes caries; healthy 9-month-olds do not need nocturnal calories.

questions.sourceMapping: Newborn/Infant deck Slides 60, 63; Transcript 3 (no juice; cup at 9 months)

stem: Which statement about milk transition in the first year is correct per the course?

options.label: A
options.text: Whole cow's milk may replace formula at 9 months if weight gain is good
options.rationale: Cow's milk before 12 months is associated with intestinal blood loss and iron deficiency.

options.label: B
options.text: Breast milk or formula remain the milk source through 12 months, with whole milk introduced after 1 year alongside solids
options.rationale: The course sequence: exclusive breastfeeding (or formula) for about 6 months, continued milk feeds with solids thereafter, and transition to whole milk after 12 months (Transcript 3; Slides 59-60).

options.label: C
options.text: Skim milk is preferred from 6 months to prevent obesity
options.rationale: Skim milk lacks the fat required for brain growth in the second year.

options.label: D
options.text: Soy milk is an equivalent default substitute at 6 months
options.rationale: Soy formula has specific indications; soy milk is not an infant default.

questions.sourceMapping: Transcript 3 (whole milk after a year); Newborn/Infant deck Slides 59-60

stem: Which supplementation is routinely addressed for the exclusively breastfed infant at well visits per course and AAP practice?

options.label: A
options.text: Vitamin D (400 IU daily) beginning in the first weeks of life
options.rationale: Breastfed infants require vitamin D supplementation (400 IU/day) from the first weeks; the course ties vitamin and fluoride decisions to office protocol and breastfeeding status, with fluoride typically beginning later where water is deficient (Slides 59-60; Transcript 3).

options.label: B
options.text: Vitamin C drops
options.rationale: Vitamin C is unnecessary in breastfed infants.

options.label: C
options.text: Routine fluoride from birth
options.rationale: Fluoride supplementation begins after 6 months per local water fluoridation, not at birth.

options.label: D
options.text: Iron drops from birth for all breastfed infants
options.rationale: Iron needs are met by breast milk bioavailability and timely iron-fortified solids; routine drops from birth are not standard.

questions.sourceMapping: Newborn/Infant deck Slides 59-60 (vitamins and fluoride per protocol); Transcript 3 (vitamin D with breastfeeding)

stem: Why does the 6-month well visit include a hemoglobin or hematocrit check?

options.label: A
options.text: To screen for anemia as fetal iron stores wane and solids begin
options.rationale: The 6-month visit slide directs checking hemoglobin for anemia, coinciding with depletion of fetal iron stores and introduction of iron-fortified cereal (Slide 59-60).

options.label: B
options.text: To detect polycythemia from dehydration
options.rationale: Polycythemia screening is a newborn concern, not a 6-month routine.

options.label: C
options.text: To monitor response to phototherapy
options.rationale: Phototherapy follow-up uses bilirubin, not hemoglobin.

options.label: D
options.text: To screen for leukemia per AAP protocol
options.rationale: Leukemia screening is not a well-visit component.

questions.sourceMapping: Newborn/Infant deck Slides 59-60 (check hgb for anemia at 6 months)

stem: A 6-week-old exclusively breastfed infant presents with blood-streaked, mucusy stools, mild eczema, and good weight gain; the infant is well-appearing and afebrile. Using the slide shown, what is the most appropriate next step?

images.alt: Figure 3: Newborn/Infant deck Slide 92 reference asset - cow's milk protein sensitivity (non-IgE mediated): hematoc hezia/hemoccult-positive stools, maternal elimination response in 72-96 hours, eHF in about 7%, amino-acid formula in about 5%.
images.caption: Figure 3: Newborn/Infant deck Slide 92 reference asset - cow's milk protein sensitivity (non-IgE mediated): hematoc hezia/hemoccult-positive stools, maternal elimination response in 72-96 hours, eHF in about 7%, amino-acid formula in about 5%.

options.label: A
options.text: Start empiric intravenous antibiotics for bacterial enteritis
options.rationale: A well-appearing afebrile infant with blood-streaked stools and eczema fits CMPA, not invasive bacterial enteritis.

options.label: B
options.text: Maternal elimination of cow's milk protein with expectation that rectal bleeding resolves within about 72-96 hours
options.rationale: Non-IgE cow's milk protein sensitivity presents in the first 1-6 months with hematochezia (visible or occult) in a well infant; maternal cow's milk elimination typically resolves rectal bleeding within 72-96 hours, with extensively hydrolyzed formula needed in about 7% and amino-acid formula in about 5% (Slide 92; Transcript 4).

options.label: C
options.text: Immediate colonoscopy
options.rationale: Endoscopy is reserved for atypical, severe, or refractory cases via GI.

options.label: D
options.text: Switch to soy formula and recheck in 1 month
options.rationale: Soy formula cross-reacts in a proportion of CMPA infants and is not the taught first move for a breastfed dyad.

questions.sourceMapping: Newborn/Infant deck Slide 92; Transcript 4 (cow's milk protein sensitivity; often outgrown)

stem: Which feature most strongly favors cow's milk protein allergy over acute viral gastroenteritis in an infant with loose stools?

options.label: A
options.text: Blood and mucus in stool with eczema, in an afebrile well-appearing infant
options.rationale: Blood/mucus with eczema in a well infant points to food-protein-induced (allergic) colitis; the differential slide assigns vomiting plus watery diarrhea with exposures to viral gastroenteritis (Slides 88-89, 92).

options.label: B
options.text: Vomiting plus watery diarrhea with sick-contact exposure
options.rationale: That pattern favors viral gastroenteritis.

options.label: C
options.text: Diarrhea beginning 48 hours after a single antibiotic dose
options.rationale: Antibiotic timing suggests medication-associated diarrhea.

options.label: D
options.text: Diarrhea resolving within 5 days
options.rationale: Short duration defines acute infectious-type diarrhea.

questions.sourceMapping: Newborn/Infant deck Slides 88-89, 92 (clues that narrow the differential) | Parallel Form B (options re-randomized)

stem: The professor stated an absolute rule about stool content in infants. Which is it?

options.label: A
options.text: Mucus in stool is normal in breastfed infants
options.rationale: Mucus is also abnormal per the course and suggests colonic inflammation.

options.label: B
options.text: Blood should never be present in stool; any blood requires investigation
options.rationale: 'There should never be blood in stool; if there's blood, there's a reason and we must investigate' - stated in both the slide and transcript as a never-miss rule (Slide 15; Transcripts 3, 4).

options.label: C
options.text: Black meconium after day 10 is normal
options.rationale: Meconium transitions by 24-48 hours to transitional then milk stools; persistent black stool later suggests blood.

options.label: D
options.text: Green stool always indicates infection
options.rationale: Green and mustard hues are normal breastfed stool colors.

questions.sourceMapping: Newborn/Infant deck Slide 15; Transcript 3; Transcript 4 (blood never normal)

stem: Which stool pattern description is correct for a healthy exclusively breastfed 3-week-old?

options.label: A
options.text: Formed, brown, once daily like peanut butter
options.rationale: Peanut-butter consistency describes formula-fed stools.

options.label: B
options.text: Soft to watery, yellow-mustard or green seedy stools, possibly after each feeding
options.rationale: Breastfed stools transition from meconium (24-48 hours) to green seedy then mustard-yellow, very soft or watery, and may follow each feeding; formula-fed stools are tan-brown and peanut-butter thick (Slide 15; Transcript 3).

options.label: C
options.text: Pale, acholic, foul-smelling stools
options.rationale: Acholic stools indicate cholestasis.

options.label: D
options.text: Hard pellets every 3 days
options.rationale: Hard pellets indicate constipation, not normal breastfed pattern.

questions.sourceMapping: Newborn/Infant deck Slide 15; Transcript 3 (stool colors)

stem: A 3-month-old spits up small volumes after most feeds, is cheerful between feeds, and tracks along the 60th percentile for weight. Using the slide shown, what is the most appropriate management?

images.alt: Figure 4: Second-half PPTX slide 24 reference asset - gastroesophageal reflux (spitting up): common, worst at 2-4 months, driven by air ingestion and overfeeding, improved by burping.
images.caption: Figure 4: Second-half PPTX slide 24 reference asset - gastroesophageal reflux (spitting up): common, worst at 2-4 months, driven by air ingestion and overfeeding, improved by burping.

options.label: A
options.text: Order an upper GI series today
options.rationale: Upper GI does not diagnose GERD and is reserved for suspected anatomic disease.

options.label: B
options.text: Start a proton pump inhibitor trial
options.rationale: Acid suppression is not routine first-line and is reserved for established acid-mediated disease.

options.label: C
options.text: Reassure: this is uncomplicated reflux ('happy spitter') with normal growth; counsel on burping and avoiding overfeeding
options.rationale: The clinical pearl is explicit: happy spitter plus normal growth equals reassurance; reflux peaks at 2-4 months, relates to air ingestion/overfeeding and an immature lower esophageal sphincter, and improves with frequent burping and paced volumes (Slides 86-87; Transcript 4).

options.label: D
options.text: Stop all feeds for 12 hours to rest the gut
options.rationale: Feed interruption harms nutrition and hydration.

questions.sourceMapping: Second-half PPTX slides 24-25; Newborn/Infant deck Slide 87 pearl; Transcript 4 | Parallel Form B (options re-randomized)

stem: Which feature converts uncomplicated infant reflux into GERD per the course definition?

options.label: A
options.text: Spitting up that resolves by 6 months
options.rationale: Self-resolution is characteristic of simple reflux.

options.label: B
options.text: Arching during feeds in an infant gaining normally
options.rationale: Arching without growth impact or feeding refusal is nonspecific and does not define disease.

options.label: C
options.text: Visible regurgitation three times daily in a thriving infant
options.rationale: Frequency alone in a thriving infant remains uncomplicated reflux.

options.label: D
options.text: Reflux causing troublesome symptoms or complications such as poor weight gain, feeding refusal, or pain with feeds
options.rationale: GERD is defined as reflux causing troublesome symptoms and/or complications - poor weight gain or weight loss, feeding refusal/difficulty; crying/arching alone is nonspecific (Slide 87; Transcript 4).

questions.sourceMapping: Newborn/Infant deck Slide 87; Transcript 4 (reflux vs GERD distinction) | Parallel Form B (options re-randomized)

stem: Which first-line management bundle is correct for an infant with GERD confirmed by poor weight gain and feeding refusal?

options.label: A
options.text: Continue breastfeeding and avoid overfeeding; consider thickened feeds; if symptoms persist, a 2-4 week trial of extensively hydrolyzed or amino-acid formula (or maternal cow's-milk elimination if breastfed), then reassess growth
options.rationale: The NASPGHAN-based slide sequence: continue breastfeeding, avoid overfeeding, thickened feeds for troublesome regurgitation, then a 2-4 week cow's-milk-protein trial with reassessment of response and growth (Slide 87; Transcript 4).

options.label: B
options.text: Begin high-dose PPI immediately and continue for 12 months
options.rationale: Acid suppression is not routine first-line; when used it is a short monitored course with weaning at 4-8 weeks.

options.label: C
options.text: Switch to soy formula and add rice cereal to every bottle including nighttime
options.rationale: Soy is not the taught trial formula, and supine sleep safety overrides positional reflux management.

options.label: D
options.text: Place the infant prone for sleep to reduce regurgitation
options.rationale: Prone sleep increases SIDS risk and is never prescribed for reflux in infants.

questions.sourceMapping: Newborn/Infant deck Slide 87 (first-line management); Transcript 4

stem: An infant with acid-mediated erosive esophagitis documented by GI is started on a short course of acid suppression. What follow-up does the course specify?

options.label: A
options.text: Switch to prokinetic therapy at 1 week
options.rationale: Prokinetics are not the taught next step.

options.label: B
options.text: Continue indefinitely without review
options.rationale: Indefinite therapy contradicts the wean directive.

options.label: C
options.text: Double the dose at 2 weeks routinely
options.rationale: Dose doubling is not protocol.

options.label: D
options.text: Reassess after 4-8 weeks and attempt to wean
options.rationale: When acid suppression is used, the slide directs reassessment after 4-8 weeks with an attempt to wean, avoiding automatic long-term escalation (Slide 87).

questions.sourceMapping: Newborn/Infant deck Slide 87 (acid suppression reassess/wean) | Parallel Form B (options re-randomized)

stem: Select all alarm (red flag) features in a spitting-up infant that require evaluation for diagnoses other than GERD.

options.label: A
options.text: Bilious vomiting
options.rationale: Bilious emesis suggests obstruction (e.g., malrotation) and is an alarm feature.

options.label: B
options.text: Forceful or projectile vomiting
options.rationale: Forceful/projectile vomiting raises pyloric stenosis and obstruction concerns - the professor's mimic list.

options.label: C
options.text: Gastrointestinal bleeding
options.rationale: GI bleeding indicates mucosal injury or allergy/other pathology.

options.label: D
options.text: Lethargy or systemic illness
options.rationale: Lethargy or systemic illness never fits uncomplicated GERD.

options.label: E
options.text: Abdominal distention
options.rationale: Abdominal distention is a listed red flag prompting surgical/obstructive evaluation.

options.label: F
options.text: Non-forceful spit-up with normal growth trajectory
options.rationale: Non-forceful spit-up with normal growth is the reassuring happy-spitter pattern.

questions.sourceMapping: Newborn/Infant deck Slides 87-88; Transcript 4 (red flags: projectile vomiting, GI bleeding, lethargy, distention)

stem: A 5-week-old presents with progressively forceful, non-bilious projectile vomiting after feeds, persistent hunger after vomiting, and a firm olive-shaped epigastric mass palpable after emptying the stomach. Which diagnosis must be excluded before labeling this GERD?

options.label: A
options.text: Pyloric stenosis
options.rationale: The course names pyloric stenosis as the classic GERD mimic - 'these kids don't just spit up, they puke' - with projectile non-bilious emesis; the vignette adds the olive mass, making exclusion mandatory (Transcript 4; Slide 87 alarm features).

options.label: B
options.text: Hiatal hernia
options.rationale: Hiatal hernia is associated with GERD but does not produce the olive mass or classic projectile pattern alone.

options.label: C
options.text: Cow's milk protein allergy
options.rationale: CMPA presents with blood/mucus and eczema rather than projectile emesis with an olive mass.

options.label: D
options.text: Transient lactose intolerance
options.rationale: Lactose intolerance causes watery diarrhea and gas, not projectile vomiting.

questions.sourceMapping: Transcript 4 (pyloric stenosis mimic); Newborn/Infant deck Slide 87 (alarm features)

stem: Which statement about diagnostic testing in infant GERD is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: Upper GI series confirms GERD in most infants
options.rationale: Upper GI cannot diagnose GERD.

options.label: B
options.text: Uncomplicated infant reflux usually requires no laboratory or imaging studies; upper GI is used when anatomic disease is suspected
options.rationale: Diagnosis begins with history, feeding assessment, growth trajectory, and examination; uncomplicated reflux needs no tests, and upper GI does not diagnose GERD - it evaluates anatomy; persistent/severe/atypical cases go to GI for targeted endoscopy or pH-impedance (Slide 87; Transcript 4: swallow study 'theoretically, in practice no').

options.label: C
options.text: Empiric pH-impedance testing is first-line in primary care
options.rationale: pH-impedance is a GI-level targeted test for atypical or refractory disease.

options.label: D
options.text: Gastric emptying scans are routine before any feeding change
options.rationale: Emptying studies are not routine first-line.

questions.sourceMapping: Newborn/Infant deck Slide 87 (diagnosis column); Transcript 4 (swallow study discussion)

stem: An infant evaluated for GERD is also noted to have a hiatal hernia on imaging obtained for other reasons. How does this affect the GERD assessment?

options.label: A
options.text: Hiatal hernia excludes GERD
options.rationale: It increases, not excludes, reflux risk.

options.label: B
options.text: Hiatal hernia is a predisposing condition for GERD because of pressure on the stomach, so it belongs in the differential and script
options.rationale: The professor taught that babies with hiatal hernias are at risk for GERD from gastric pressure and crying, so thinking GERD includes assessing for hiatal hernia (Transcript 4; Slide 87 predisposing conditions).

options.label: C
options.text: Hiatal hernia guarantees need for fundoplication
options.rationale: Most cases are managed medically/positionally first; surgery is not automatic.

options.label: D
options.text: Hiatal hernia causes only bilious vomiting
options.rationale: Bilious vomiting suggests obstruction elsewhere, not hiatal hernia per se.

questions.sourceMapping: Transcript 4 (hiatal hernia and GERD); Newborn/Infant deck Slide 87

stem: A parent describes the 8-month-old's stools as 'diarrhea' because they are loose and occur four times daily since starting pureed pears. The infant is well and gaining. What is the first analytic step per the diarrhea slide?

options.label: A
options.text: Order stool culture and C. difficile toxin
options.rationale: Testing is selective; uncomplicated changes without red flags need none, and C. difficile is avoided under 12 months.

options.label: B
options.text: Determine whether the pattern is a true change from the infant's baseline, recognizing loose frequent stools can be normal
options.rationale: The slide opens by instructing clinicians to first determine whether stooling represents a true change from baseline; loose, frequent stools can be normal in breastfed and young infants, and dietary changes shift stool character (Slide 88).

options.label: C
options.text: Start oral rehydration solution immediately
options.rationale: ORS is for dehydration, which is absent here.

options.label: D
options.text: Prescribe an antidiarrheal agent
options.rationale: Antidiarrheals are inappropriate in infants.

questions.sourceMapping: Newborn/Infant deck Slide 88 (define the pattern first)

stem: Match the duration categories taught for infant diarrhea: which pairing is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: Acute less than 7 days; prolonged 7-13 days; persistent 14-29 days; chronic 30 days or more
options.rationale: The slide defines acute <7 days, prolonged 7-13 days, persistent 14-29 days, and chronic >=30 days - categories that drive the differential toward malabsorption, allergy, or congenital diarrheal disorders as duration lengthens (Slide 88).

options.label: B
options.text: Acute less than 3 days; persistent 4-10 days; chronic 11 days or more
options.rationale: These thresholds do not match the taught categories.

options.label: C
options.text: Acute less than 14 days; chronic 15 days or more
options.rationale: This two-category scheme omits prolonged and persistent windows.

options.label: D
options.text: Prolonged less than 7 days; persistent 7-30 days; chronic over 30 days
options.rationale: Prolonged begins at 7 days, not under 7.

questions.sourceMapping: Newborn/Infant deck Slide 88 (duration definitions)

stem: Select all red flags the course lists for infant diarrhea that mandate urgent evaluation or workup.

options.label: A
options.text: Signs of dehydration or a toxic/lethargic appearance
options.rationale: Dehydration and toxic appearance drive urgent resuscitation pathways.

options.label: B
options.text: Bilious or forceful vomiting
options.rationale: Bilious or forceful vomiting signals obstruction or surgical pathology.

options.label: C
options.text: Blood in stool
options.rationale: Blood in stool is a never-normal red flag.

options.label: D
options.text: Fever in a young infant
options.rationale: Fever in a young infant raises sepsis concern and lowers the evaluation threshold.

options.label: E
options.text: Three soft breastfed stools per day in a well infant
options.rationale: Three soft stools daily in a well breastfed infant is within normal baseline.

options.label: F
options.text: Abdominal distention or tenderness
options.rationale: Distention/tenderness suggests invasive disease or obstruction.

questions.sourceMapping: Newborn/Infant deck Slide 88 (RED FLAGS row) | Parallel Form B (options re-randomized)

stem: Which clue-to-differential pairing is correct per the diarrhea differential slide?

options.label: A
options.text: Blood and mucus in stool suggest invasive bacterial disease or food-protein-induced disease
options.rationale: The slide's narrowing clues assign blood/mucus to invasive bacterial or food-protein-induced disease (Slide 89).

options.label: B
options.text: Vomiting with watery diarrhea suggests biliary atresia
options.rationale: Vomiting plus watery diarrhea points to viral gastroenteritis, not biliary atresia.

options.label: C
options.text: Poor growth with chronic diarrhea suggests simple viral gastroenteritis
options.rationale: Poor growth with chronic symptoms broadens to malabsorption, allergy, or congenital disease - not simple viral illness.

options.label: D
options.text: Pure mucus without blood suggests Giardia as the leading cause in a 6-week-old
options.rationale: Giardia is exposure-driven and uncommon at 6 weeks; mucus alone first suggests colonic inflammation including CMPA.

questions.sourceMapping: Newborn/Infant deck Slide 89 (clues that narrow the differential)

stem: Which stool-testing approach is correct for infants per the course?

options.label: A
options.text: Routine stool culture for every episode of acute watery diarrhea
options.rationale: Universal culturing is explicitly discouraged.

options.label: B
options.text: Routine C. difficile testing in any infant under 12 months with diarrhea
options.rationale: C. difficile testing is avoided under 12 months because asymptomatic colonization is common.

options.label: C
options.text: Selective testing reserved for bloody diarrhea, severe illness, outbreak or exposure concerns, immunocompromise, or persistent symptoms
options.rationale: Most uncomplicated acute watery diarrhea requires no stool testing; testing is selective for bloody diarrhea, severe illness, outbreaks/exposures, immunocompromise, or persistence (Slide 89).

options.label: D
options.text: Ova and parasite screening on all diarrheal infants regardless of exposure
options.rationale: Parasitic testing follows exposure or history suggesting it.

questions.sourceMapping: Newborn/Infant deck Slide 89 (testing: be selective)

stem: A 14-month-old with 4 days of viral gastroenteritis now has improved vomiting but transient loose stools after milk feeds. Which mechanism is most likely?

options.label: A
options.text: Transient lactose/carbohydrate malabsorption following gastroenteritis
options.rationale: Post-gastroenteritis transient lactose/carbohydrate malabsorption is a listed differential entry explaining temporary osmotic diarrhea after mucosal injury (Slide 89).

options.label: B
options.text: Secondary bacterial superinfection
options.rationale: Superinfection would show toxicity or blood.

options.label: C
options.text: New-onset cow's milk protein allergy
options.rationale: CMPA onset is typically in the first 1-6 months with blood/mucus and eczema.

options.label: D
options.text: Inflammatory bowel disease
options.rationale: IBD is exceedingly rare at this age and presents with growth failure and blood.

questions.sourceMapping: Newborn/Infant deck Slide 89 (postinfectious malabsorption) | Parallel Form B (options re-randomized)

stem: Which chronic-diarrhea association should prompt evaluation for cystic fibrosis or other malabsorption?

options.label: A
options.text: One episode of watery stools after a new fruit
options.rationale: Single dietary episodes are osmotic and self-limited.

options.label: B
options.text: Persistent diarrhea with poor growth, greasy stools, or failure to thrive from early life
options.rationale: The persistent/chronic column lists malabsorption or pancreatic insufficiency (including cystic fibrosis), protein-losing or inflammatory enteropathy, and congenital diarrheal disorders, to consider when severe from early life, persistent, or associated with failure to thrive (Slide 89).

options.label: C
options.text: Diarrhea resolving within 72 hours of ORT
options.rationale: Rapid resolution fits acute self-limited illness.

options.label: D
options.text: Loose stools limited to a teething week
options.rationale: Teething-related loose stools are transient and non-pathologic.

questions.sourceMapping: Newborn/Infant deck Slide 89 (persistent/chronic column) | Parallel Form B (options re-randomized)

stem: On examination of a dehydrated 9-month-old, which finding indicates the dehydration has become severe and ominous?

options.label: A
options.text: Hypotension
options.rationale: Hypotension is a LATE, ominous sign of decompensated shock in infants; tachycardia, sunken fontanelle, and absent tears precede it and should trigger action earlier (Slide 90).

options.label: B
options.text: Absent tears
options.rationale: Absent tears appear before circulatory collapse.

options.label: C
options.text: Tachycardia with delayed capillary refill
options.rationale: Tachycardia with prolonged refill indicates significant but still compensated dehydration.

options.label: D
options.text: Sunken anterior fontanelle
options.rationale: A sunken fontanelle is an earlier moderate-to-severe sign.

questions.sourceMapping: Newborn/Infant deck Slide 90 (hypotension is late and ominous) | Parallel Form B (options re-randomized)

stem: A parent reports the 5-week-old has had only one wet diaper in the past 24 hours during a diarrheal illness. How should this be interpreted?

options.label: A
options.text: Normal; urine output varies widely in infancy
options.rationale: One wet diaper is far below the expected minimum.

options.label: B
options.text: Severe dehydration pattern; urination only 1-2 times per day warrants prompt urgent evaluation
options.rationale: After day 4-5 of life a well-hydrated infant produces >=5-6 wet diapers per 24 hours; fewer than 6 suggests dehydration and 1-2 per day indicates severe dehydration requiring prompt evaluation (Slide 90; Transcript 4).

options.label: C
options.text: Mild dehydration manageable with juice at home
options.rationale: Juice is contraindicated for rehydration and severe dehydration needs emergency care.

options.label: D
options.text: Expected if the infant is breastfeeding exclusively
options.rationale: Breastfeeding does not reduce expected urine output when intake is adequate.

questions.sourceMapping: Newborn/Infant deck Slide 90; Transcript 4 (wet diaper counts; >6-8 hours without urine concerning)

stem: An 11-month-old with gastroenteritis is lethargic, difficult to arouse, has mottled cool extremities, a sunken fontanelle, and a heart rate of 190 with hypotension. What is the most appropriate action?

options.label: A
options.text: Begin oral rehydration with 5 mL aliquots and reassess in 2 hours
options.rationale: ORT is contraindicated as sole therapy in shock or altered mental status.

options.label: B
options.text: Emergency evaluation with IV/IO fluid resuscitation
options.rationale: Severe dehydration with altered mental status and poor perfusion/shock mandates emergency evaluation and IV/IO resuscitation per the slide's URGENT row; oral therapy is for mild-moderate cases in alert infants (Slide 90).

options.label: C
options.text: Send stool studies and schedule follow-up tomorrow
options.rationale: Delay risks cardiovascular collapse.

options.label: D
options.text: Prescribe an antiemetic and clear liquids
options.rationale: Antiemetics and clear liquids do not restore circulatory volume.

questions.sourceMapping: Newborn/Infant deck Slide 90 (URGENT row)

stem: For a 8-kg infant with mild-to-moderate dehydration from diarrhea, which ORS volume plan is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: 50-100 mL/kg of commercial ORS over 2-4 hours, then replace ongoing losses at about 10 mL/kg per watery stool
options.rationale: The ORT slide specifies 50-100 mL/kg ORS over 2-4 hours for mild-moderate dehydration with ongoing loss replacement of ~10 mL/kg per watery stool (or 60-120 mL per stool for infants <10 kg) (Slide 91).

options.label: B
options.text: 10 mL/kg of half-strength ORS over 30 minutes
options.rationale: Half-strength ORS and 30-minute volumes contradict the protocol.

options.label: C
options.text: Undiluted sports drinks ad libitum
options.rationale: Sports drinks have inappropriate sodium/glucose ratios and are listed to avoid.

options.label: D
options.text: 20 mL/kg of plain water hourly
options.rationale: Plain water is explicitly avoided and causes hyponatremia.

questions.sourceMapping: Newborn/Infant deck Slide 91 (ORT volumes) | Parallel Form B (options re-randomized)

stem: Which administration technique maximizes ORT success in a vomiting infant?

options.label: A
options.text: Give a full bottle of ORS at once to finish rehydration quickly
options.rationale: Large volumes provoke emesis - the explicit anti-pearl.

options.label: B
options.text: Start with 5 mL (1 teaspoon) by syringe every 1-5 minutes, increasing as tolerated; vomiting does not automatically mean ORT failure
options.rationale: The teaching pearl: ORT works best given SMALL amounts FREQUENTLY - 5 mL every 1-5 minutes, escalating as tolerated; continued vomiting is not automatic failure (Slide 91; Transcript 4 syringe every 15 minutes discussion).

options.label: C
options.text: Withhold all fluids for 6 hours to stop vomiting
options.rationale: Withholding fluids worsens dehydration.

options.label: D
options.text: Dilute the commercial ORS by half to reduce osmolarity
options.rationale: Commercial ORS should not be diluted unless the product requires mixing.

questions.sourceMapping: Newborn/Infant deck Slide 91; Transcript 4 (start small, syringe technique)

stem: Select all fluids the course directs avoiding for infant rehydration.

options.label: A
options.text: Soda
options.rationale: Soda's sugar load worsens osmotic diarrhea.

options.label: B
options.text: Commercial oral rehydration solution (e.g., Pedialyte)
options.rationale: Commercial ORS is the recommended rehydration fluid, not an avoided one.

options.label: C
options.text: Plain water
options.rationale: Plain water lacks electrolytes and risks hyponatremia.

options.label: D
options.text: Undiluted juice
options.rationale: Undiluted juice is hyperosmolar and aggravates stool losses.

options.label: E
options.text: Sports drinks
options.rationale: Sports drinks have inappropriate sodium content for infant rehydration.

questions.sourceMapping: Newborn/Infant deck Slide 91 (avoid/escalate column) | Parallel Form B (options re-randomized)

stem: During ORT for a breastfed 7-month-old with moderate dehydration, what should happen to breastfeeding?

options.label: A
options.text: Stop breastfeeding until diarrhea fully resolves
options.rationale: Stopping breastfeeding removes immunologic and nutritional benefits unnecessarily.

options.label: B
options.text: Continue breastfeeding throughout rehydration and resume usual feeding once rehydrated and vomiting improves
options.rationale: The slide directs continuing breastfeeding during ORT and resuming usual formula/age-appropriate feeding once rehydrated and vomiting improves (Slide 91).

options.label: C
options.text: Replace breastfeeding with ORS exclusively for 72 hours
options.rationale: ORS supplements but does not replace milk feeds beyond the rehydration window.

options.label: D
options.text: Switch to lactose-free formula permanently
options.rationale: Routine permanent lactose-free conversion is not indicated.

questions.sourceMapping: Newborn/Infant deck Slide 91 (continue breastfeeding)

stem: Using the colic slide shown, a 6-week-old cries 3-4 hours daily, predominantly in the early evening, is consolable with holding and pacing, and is gaining 30 g per day. Which diagnosis and counseling pair is correct?

images.alt: Figure 5: Newborn/Infant deck Slide 85 reference asset - colic: inconsolable crying in an otherwise healthy infant starting at 2 weeks, rule of 3s, evening peak, improving by about 3 months.
images.caption: Figure 5: Newborn/Infant deck Slide 85 reference asset - colic: inconsolable crying in an otherwise healthy infant starting at 2 weeks, rule of 3s, evening peak, improving by about 3 months.

options.label: A
options.text: Colic; reassure that crying peaks in late afternoon/evening, begins around 2 weeks, and improves by about 3 months, while screening caregiver coping
options.rationale: The slide defines colic as inconsolable-appearing crying in an otherwise healthy infant starting at 2 weeks with the rule of 3s (3 hours/day, 3 days/week, more than 3 weeks), an evening peak, and improvement by about 3 months; growth is normal and counseling includes caregiver support and shaken-baby prevention (Slide 85; Transcript 4).

options.label: B
options.text: GERD; start acid suppression today
options.rationale: GERD requires troublesome symptoms or complications such as poor growth; a thriving 30 g/day gainer with consolable crying does not meet criteria.

options.label: C
options.text: Intussusception; send to the emergency department now
options.rationale: Intussusception causes paroxysmal pain with vomiting and currant-jelly stools, not predictable evening crying in a well grower.

options.label: D
options.text: Sepsis; obtain blood cultures today
options.rationale: A febrile or toxic appearance would drive sepsis evaluation; this infant is afebrile and gaining well.

questions.sourceMapping: Newborn/Infant deck Slide 85; Transcript 4 (rule of 3s; consolable = reassuring)

stem: When a parent reports that the infant 'cries all the time,' which single question best separates reassurance from red flag per the professor?

options.label: A
options.text: Is the crying louder at night?
options.rationale: Evening predominance fits colic but does not assess severity or consolability.

options.label: B
options.text: Is the infant consolable - can crying be stopped by holding, rocking, feeding, or a pacifier?
options.rationale: The professor's key question: consolability. Consolable crying is reassuring; unconsolable crying is a red flag that 'the baby is telling you something' and triggers a search for pathology (Transcript 4).

options.label: C
options.text: Does the crying occur after formula feeds only?
options.rationale: Feed timing narrows GI causes but misses the global red-flag screen.

options.label: D
options.text: How many diapers are wet per day?
options.rationale: Wet diapers assess hydration, an important but separate domain.

questions.sourceMapping: Transcript 4 (consolable vs unconsolable crying)

stem: A mother describes her 3-week-old as 'perfect - he never cries and sleeps all day,' but the infant is difficult to rouse for feeds and has regained only to birth weight. How should the PNP interpret this quietness?

options.label: A
options.text: An easy temperament requiring no action
options.rationale: Labeling lethargy as temperament delays recognition of sepsis or dehydration.

options.label: B
options.text: A possible red flag: infants who are underfed or ill may become quiet and lethargic instead of crying, warranting full assessment today
options.rationale: The professor warned that sick or underfed newborns go in the opposite direction - quiet, sleepy, lethargic - and a parent's delight at a 'good baby' can mask deterioration; the 9-month slide likewise flags the too-good, dull baby (Transcript 4; Slide 62).

options.label: C
options.text: Evidence of secure attachment
options.rationale: Attachment is assessed by interaction quality, not absence of crying.

options.label: D
options.text: Normal newborn sleep consolidation
options.rationale: Newborns should wake to feed every 2-3 hours; sleeping through feeds is abnormal.

questions.sourceMapping: Transcript 4 (too quiet = red flag); Newborn/Infant deck Slide 62 (too good of a baby)

stem: Which resource and message did the course pair with colic counseling to prevent abusive head trauma?

options.label: A
options.text: The Period of PURPLE Crying (dontshake.org/purple-crying), normalizing developmental crying and teaching safe coping instead of shaking
options.rationale: The slide references the PURPLE Crying website under Don't Shake the Baby; the professor tied colic counseling to shaken-baby prevention because these infants are at highest risk when caregivers reach their wits' end (Slide 85; Transcript 4).

options.label: B
options.text: A sleep-training website recommending cry-it-out from 2 weeks
options.rationale: Cry-it-out from 2 weeks contradicts responsive parenting and does not address safety.

options.label: C
options.text: A teething gel recommendation for evening fussing
options.rationale: Teething begins later and gel use is not the taught intervention.

options.label: D
options.text: A herbal remedy website for gripe water
options.rationale: Gripe water lacks evidence and is not the course resource.

questions.sourceMapping: Newborn/Infant deck Slide 85 (PURPLE crying link); Transcript 4 (shaken baby risk)

options.label: A
options.text: An umbilical granuloma is a moist pink nodule without surrounding erythema treated with silver nitrate, while omphalitis with erythema and tenderness is an emergency needing IV antibiotics.

options.text: After day 4 to 5 of life a well-hydrated infant has at least 5 to 6 wet diapers per day; fewer than 6 suggests dehydration and 1 to 2 per day or no urine for over 8 hours is severe.
options.rationale: Accurate for JAUNDICE, not JAUNDICE.

options.label: C

options.label: E
options.text: Jaundice appearing within the first 24 hours of life is pathologic until proven otherwise and requires prompt bilirubin measurement and hemolysis evaluation.

options.label: F

stem: At what age does the umbilical cord stump typically separate, per the course?

options.label: A
options.text: 4-6 weeks
options.rationale: Separation beyond 3 weeks raises concern for immune or anatomic disorders, but typical separation is 1-2 weeks.

options.label: B
options.text: 1-2 weeks
options.rationale: The cord stump usually falls off in 1-2 weeks; granulation tissue then closes the wound, and overgrowth produces granuloma (Slides 71; Transcript 4).

options.label: C
options.text: 3-4 months
options.rationale: 3-4 months corresponds to cephalohematoma resorption, not cord separation.

options.label: D
options.text: 24-48 hours
options.rationale: 24-48 hours is the meconium passage window, not cord separation.
