stem: Why must dermal melanocytosis (Mongolian spots) be explicitly documented in the newborn record?

options.label: A
options.text: Because they predict future neurofibromatosis
options.rationale: Neurofibromatosis is associated with multiple cafe-au-lait macules, not dermal melanocytosis.

options.label: B
options.text: Because they can be confused with bruising and raise false concerns for abuse
options.rationale: The AAFP article stresses that dermal melanocytosis can be confused with abuse and should be documented; lesions usually fade by about 4 years (AAFP Part II Table 1).

options.label: C
options.text: Because they require laser treatment in infancy
options.rationale: No treatment is indicated; lesions fade.

options.label: D
options.text: Because they indicate congenital dermal infection
options.rationale: They are benign melanocyte collections, not infection.

questions.sourceMapping: AAFP Part II Table 1 (documentation to avoid abuse misinterpretation) | Parallel Form B (options re-randomized)

stem: Which sequence for introducing complementary foods reflects the course teaching?

options.label: A
options.text: Iron-fortified rice cereal first, one new food at a time every 3-4 days, then vegetables before fruits
options.rationale: The course sequence: iron-fortified rice cereal (least allergenic) first, single-ingredient introductions every 3-4 days (or weekly) to identify reactions, then vegetables before fruits because sweets are easier to learn to like; combination dinners are avoided early (Slides 59-61).

options.label: B
options.text: Mixed meat-and-vegetable dinners first for protein
options.rationale: Combination dinners obscure allergy attribution and provide little meat.

options.label: C
options.text: Egg white as the first food to induce tolerance
options.rationale: Egg yolk may come around 6 months with whites delayed per the slide; neither is the first food.

options.label: D
options.text: Fruits first because they are most palatable, then cereal
options.rationale: Starting with sweet fruits biases later vegetable acceptance; the slide explicitly reverses this.

questions.sourceMapping: Newborn/Infant deck Slides 59-61 (cereal first, one food 3-4 days, vegetables before fruits) | Parallel Form B (options re-randomized)

stem: A 9-month-old's chart shows weight at the 5th percentile, length at the 10th, and head circumference at the 75th, with weight crossing down two percentile lines since the 4-month visit. Which category from the course growth-pattern table applies?

options.label: A
options.text: Familial short stature
options.rationale: Familial short stature shows all parameters low and parallel, not head-sparing discrepancy.

options.label: B
options.text: Catch-down growth of a large-for-gestational-age infant
options.rationale: LGA catch-down occurs 6-18 months without exceeding 2 SD and with normal development; a head-sparing weight drop is not catch-down.

options.label: C
options.text: Discrepant and declining percentiles suggesting caloric insufficiency or endocrine growth failure
options.rationale: Discrepancy between weight/length and a preserved head percentile plus declining weight percentiles matches the table's caloric insufficiency/endocrine growth failure row, prompting dietary and social history and further workup (Part 2, Slide 43; Transcript 2).

options.label: D
options.text: Normal variant requiring no action
options.rationale: A two-line downward weight cross is a red flag, not a normal variant.

questions.sourceMapping: Growth & Development Part 2, Slide 43; Newborn/Infant deck Slide 21; Transcript 2 | Parallel Form B (options re-randomized)

stem: During a well visit for a 7-month-old with 3 days of vomiting and poor intake, the anterior fontanelle feels sunken and mucous membranes are dry. What does the fontanelle finding indicate?

options.label: A
options.text: Craniosynostosis
options.rationale: Craniosynostosis is identified by ridged, prematurely fused sutures and head shape, not fontanelle depression.

options.label: B
options.text: Normal age-related fontanelle change
options.rationale: A sunken fontanelle is never a normal variant.

options.label: C
options.text: Increased intracranial pressure
options.rationale: Raised intracranial pressure produces a bulging, tense fontanelle.

options.label: D
options.text: Dehydration
options.rationale: A sunken fontanelle signals dehydration (or shock), while a bulging fontanelle signals excess fluid or raised intracranial pressure; the professor tied fontanelle assessment directly to acute hydration status (Transcript 3; Slide 90).

questions.sourceMapping: Transcript 3 (fontanelles assess hydration); Newborn/Infant deck Slide 90 | Parallel Form B (options re-randomized)

stem: A vigorous newborn delivered after a difficult delivery shows localized bruising and a few petechiae on the face. Coagulation studies are normal and the infant is well. Which counseling is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: These findings indicate hemophilia until factor levels return
options.rationale: Hemophilia presents with deep bleeding; isolated traumatic petechiae with normal studies do not diagnose it.

options.label: B
options.text: Bruising at birth is a confirmed marker of non-accidental trauma
options.rationale: Birth trauma explains the distribution; documentation (including dermal melanocytosis distinctions) prevents misattribution later.

options.label: C
options.text: Bruising and petechiae from delivery trauma are common and typically resolve over time
options.rationale: AAFP notes bruising and petechiae are common birth-related findings that typically resolve over time in a well infant with normal studies (AAFP Part II, skin).

options.label: D
options.text: Petechiae in any newborn mandate immediate platelet transfusion
options.rationale: Transfusion follows thrombocytopenia or bleeding, not isolated traumatic petechiae.

questions.sourceMapping: AAFP Part II (bruising/petechiae resolve) | Parallel Form B (options re-randomized)

stem: Which feature converts uncomplicated infant reflux into GERD per the course definition?

options.label: A
options.text: Spitting up that resolves by 6 months
options.rationale: Self-resolution is characteristic of simple reflux.

options.label: B
options.text: Arching during feeds in an infant gaining normally
options.rationale: Arching without growth impact or feeding refusal is nonspecific and does not define disease.

options.label: C
options.text: Visible regurgitation three times daily in a thriving infant
options.rationale: Frequency alone in a thriving infant remains uncomplicated reflux.

options.label: D
options.text: Reflux causing troublesome symptoms or complications such as poor weight gain, feeding refusal, or pain with feeds
options.rationale: GERD is defined as reflux causing troublesome symptoms and/or complications - poor weight gain or weight loss, feeding refusal/difficulty; crying/arching alone is nonspecific (Slide 87; Transcript 4).

questions.sourceMapping: Newborn/Infant deck Slide 87; Transcript 4 (reflux vs GERD distinction) | Parallel Form B (options re-randomized)

stem: After silver nitrate treatment of an umbilical granuloma, the lesion recurs and now appears different, with increasing moisture and a redder base. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.text: Repeat silver nitrate without further assessment
options.rationale: Blind repetition risks masking progressive infection.

options.label: B
options.text: Discharge with routine 2-month follow-up
options.rationale: Deferral ignores the flagged reassessment trigger.

options.label: C
options.text: Apply a topical steroid to reduce inflammation
options.rationale: Steroids have no role and may worsen infection.

options.label: D
options.text: Reassess for an underlying omphalitis or alternative diagnosis beneath the granulation tissue
options.rationale: The professor warned that a granuloma that returns looking different requires reassessment for missed omphalitis or another cause of persistent drainage (Transcript 4; Slide 72 note that persistent drainage warrants evaluation).

questions.sourceMapping: Transcript 4 (recurrent granuloma = reassess for omphalitis); Newborn/Infant deck Slide 72 | Parallel Form B (options re-randomized)

stem: According to Erikson, which psychosocial conflict and virtue pair correctly describes the toddler period (1-3 years)?

options.label: A
options.text: Initiative vs guilt; purpose
options.rationale: Initiative vs guilt with purpose is the preschool (3-6 years) stage.

options.label: B
options.text: Autonomy vs shame and doubt; will
options.rationale: Toddlerhood (1-3 years) is autonomy vs shame and doubt with the virtue of will, centered on toilet training and doing things independently (Part 1, Slides 17-18).

options.label: C
options.text: Industry vs inferiority; competence
options.rationale: Industry vs inferiority with competence is the school-age (6-11 years) stage.

options.label: D
options.text: Trust vs mistrust; hope
options.rationale: Trust vs mistrust with hope is the infancy (birth-1 year) stage.

questions.sourceMapping: Growth & Development Part 1, Slides 17-19 | Parallel Form B (options re-randomized)

stem: Row C of the illustration shows a normal red reflex in the right eye and no reflex in the left eye. What does an absent red reflex indicate?

images.alt: Figure 3: AAFP Part I, Figure 3 reference asset - interpretation of red reflex results: A symmetric normal, B diminished left reflex, C absent left reflex.
images.caption: Figure 3: AAFP Part I, Figure 3 reference asset - interpretation of red reflex results: A symmetric normal, B diminished left reflex, C absent left reflex.

options.label: A
options.text: Normal variation in fundus pigmentation
options.rationale: Pigmentation alters reflex color but should never abolish it; a white or absent reflex is never normal.

options.label: B
options.text: Blockage of the reflection by an opacity such as a cataract, warranting urgent ophthalmology referral
options.rationale: An absent reflex occurs when the reflection is blocked by an opacity such as a cataract (or other leukokoria cause); any abnormal red reflex warrants urgent ophthalmology referral (AAFP Part I, Figure 3 and text).

options.label: C
options.text: Transient finding of the first month that resolves spontaneously
options.rationale: An absent red reflex never resolves on observation; retinoblastoma and cataract are time-critical.

options.label: D
options.text: A refractive error between the eyes requiring routine glasses
options.rationale: A diminished (not absent) reflex, row B, most commonly reflects refractive difference; absence implies opacity.

questions.sourceMapping: AAFP Part I (red reflex technique and Figure 3; leukokoria differential) | Parallel Form B (options re-randomized)

stem: A PNP reviews five parent-reported fine motor observations from different infants in clinic today. Select all findings that should trigger further developmental evaluation.

options.label: A
options.text: Raking grasp to obtain a cube at 7 months of age
options.rationale: Raking precedes pincer and is expected around 6-8 months, so a 7-month raking grasp is on pattern.

options.label: B
options.text: Absent pincer grasp at 15 months of age
options.rationale: An abnormal or absent pincer grasp by 15 months is a listed red flag; pincer normally matures across 9-12 months.

options.label: C
options.text: Bringing both hands to midline to grasp a rattle at 4 months of age
options.rationale: A two-hand midline reach at 4 months is exactly the expected response the professor uses as her office screen for symmetry.

options.label: D
options.text: Hands held in persistent fists at 4 months of age
options.rationale: Persistently fisted hands beyond 3 months is a listed abnormal fine motor sign suggesting neurologic dysfunction; at 4 months hands should be open and reaching (Part 2, Slide 16; Transcript 2).

options.label: E
options.text: No hand-to-hand transfer of objects by 12 months of age
options.rationale: Failure to transfer an object from hand to hand by 1 year is a listed fine motor red flag.

questions.sourceMapping: Growth & Development Part 2, Slides 12, 16; Transcript 2 (fisted at 3 months; transfer by 1 year; pincer by 15 months; two-hand screen) | Parallel Form B (options re-randomized)

stem: Select all red flags the course lists for infant diarrhea that mandate urgent evaluation or workup.

options.label: A
options.text: Signs of dehydration or a toxic/lethargic appearance
options.rationale: Dehydration and toxic appearance drive urgent resuscitation pathways.

options.label: B
options.text: Bilious or forceful vomiting
options.rationale: Bilious or forceful vomiting signals obstruction or surgical pathology.

options.label: C
options.text: Blood in stool
options.rationale: Blood in stool is a never-normal red flag.

options.label: D
options.text: Fever in a young infant
options.rationale: Fever in a young infant raises sepsis concern and lowers the evaluation threshold.

options.label: E
options.text: Three soft breastfed stools per day in a well infant
options.rationale: Three soft stools daily in a well breastfed infant is within normal baseline.

options.label: F
options.text: Abdominal distention or tenderness
options.rationale: Distention/tenderness suggests invasive disease or obstruction.

questions.sourceMapping: Newborn/Infant deck Slide 88 (RED FLAGS row) | Parallel Form B (options re-randomized)

stem: A 2-day-old has yellow-white papules and pustules on an erythematous base over the trunk; a Wright stain of a pustule shows eosinophils. What is the diagnosis?

options.label: A
options.text: Erythema toxicum neonatorum
options.rationale: Erythema toxicum features flesh-colored papules/pustules on an erythematous base containing eosinophils and resolves in the first week (AAFP Part II Table 1).

options.label: B
options.text: Neonatal herpes simplex
options.rationale: HSV produces grouped vesicles on an erythematous base with systemic illness; it does not resolve spontaneously.

options.label: C
options.text: Transient neonatal pustular melanosis
options.rationale: TNPM shows pustules WITHOUT erythema containing neutrophils, leaving hyperpigmented macules.

options.label: D
options.text: Staphylococcal pustulosis
options.rationale: Staphylococcal pustulosis would show bacteria and neutrophils with surrounding cellulitis or a ill infant.

questions.sourceMapping: AAFP Part II Table 1 (erythema toxicum vs TNPM cytology) | Parallel Form B (options re-randomized)

stem: A 10-day-old presents with grouped vesicles on an erythematous base over the scalp and periorbital area, poor feeding, lethargy, and temperature instability. What is the most appropriate action?

options.label: A
options.text: Start oral acyclovir and discharge with close follow-up
options.rationale: Oral therapy is inadequate for neonatal HSV, which can disseminate.

options.label: B
options.text: Confirm with HSV PCR from a lesion swab, consider blood and CSF testing, and start urgent IV acyclovir with subspecialty consultation
options.rationale: The table and lecture define neonatal HSV as vesicles on an erythematous base, onset 5-14 days, possible mucous membrane and CNS involvement, and systemic illness; management is urgent evaluation, PCR confirmation, and IV acyclovir (Slide 82; Transcript 4).

options.label: C
options.text: Apply topical antibiotics and recheck in 48 hours
options.rationale: Topical antibiotics do not treat HSV and delay life-saving antivirals.

options.label: D
options.text: Reassure; the eruption matches transient neonatal pustular melanosis
options.rationale: TNPM infants are well-appearing with non-erythematous pustules; this infant is systemically ill.

questions.sourceMapping: Newborn/Infant deck Slide 82; Transcript 4 (neonatal herpes severity) | Parallel Form B (options re-randomized)

stem: When documenting periumbilical erythema suspected to be early omphalitis, which documentation practice did the professor require?

options.label: A
options.text: Photograph only, without measurements
options.rationale: Photos supplement but do not replace measured documentation.

options.label: B
options.text: Record as present or absent without dimensions
options.rationale: Binary documentation forfeits trending capability.

options.label: C
options.text: Describe color only (pink vs red)
options.rationale: Color alone cannot track spread.

options.label: D
options.text: Measure and document the width of erythema and induration in centimeters for trending
options.rationale: The professor insisted on measuring and charting the extent of erythema and induration in centimeters so progression or resolution can be tracked objectively (Transcript 4).

questions.sourceMapping: Transcript 4 (document erythema in centimeters) | Parallel Form B (options re-randomized)

stem: Which hemangioma location mandates early referral for treatment rather than observation?

options.label: A
options.text: A hemangioma near the eye or other critical structures (airway), because of risk to vision or function
options.rationale: The course and slide direct early dermatology (and ophthalmology) referral for hemangiomas near the eye, airway, or other critical structures because growth can impair vision or function; the professor singled out periocular lesions (Slide 78; Transcript 4).

options.label: B
options.text: A hemangioma on the thigh
options.rationale: Extremity hemangiomas away from function are observed unless ulcerating or segmental-large.

options.label: C
options.text: A hemangioma on the heel
options.rationale: Heel lesions are observed unless ulcerated.

options.label: D
options.text: A 2-cm hemangioma on the upper back
options.rationale: Trunk hemangiomas without complications are observed.

questions.sourceMapping: Newborn/Infant deck Slide 78; Transcript 4 (hemangiomas near eyes get treated) | Parallel Form B (options re-randomized)

stem: A parent brings a 9-month-old for a well visit. The infant sits only in a tripod position and cannot sit unassisted, but rolls both ways and bears weight on the legs when held. Which conclusion is most appropriate?

options.label: A
options.text: Observation at the 12-month visit is sufficient before acting
options.rationale: Deferring evaluation to 12 months delays identification of hypotonia or motor disorder and contradicts the course directive to evaluate missed milestones at the visit where they are identified.

options.label: B
options.text: Development is normal because tripod sitting is expected through 12 months
options.rationale: Tripod sitting is expected at about 6 months, not through 12 months; by 9 months independent sitting is the standard.

options.label: C
options.text: Unassisted sitting should be achieved by 9 months; delay warrants evaluation for tone and motor disorder
options.rationale: Tripod sitting is a 6-month skill and unassisted sitting is expected by 9 months; failure to sit alone at 9 months is a listed red flag (possible hypotonia) requiring evaluation, and the professor stated parents' concerns and missed milestones must be investigated, not watched (Part 2, Slides 6, 10; Transcript 2).

options.label: D
options.text: The infant meets criteria for isolated fine motor delay
options.rationale: The deficit described is gross motor (trunk control), not fine motor eye-hand coordination.

questions.sourceMapping: Growth & Development Part 2, Slides 6, 10; Transcript 2 (sit by 9 months; low tone discussion) | Parallel Form B (options re-randomized)

stem: A 30-month-old from a Spanish-English bilingual home has age-appropriate receptive language, normal hearing screening, and social engagement, but expresses fewer words per language than monolingual peers. What is the most appropriate action?

options.label: A
options.text: Reassure; bilingual exposure can slow expressive language temporarily, with catch-up expected
options.rationale: The professor specifically taught that bilingual children may show a temporary expressive lag while receptive skills and social communication remain intact, and they catch up; total vocabulary across both languages should be considered (Transcript 2).

options.label: B
options.text: Refer for immediate autism evaluation
options.rationale: Intact receptive language, joint attention, and social engagement argue against autism; referral on bilingual expressive lag alone is inappropriate.

options.label: C
options.text: Diagnose expressive language disorder and start speech therapy
options.rationale: Labeling a transient bilingual expressive lag as a disorder over-medicalizes a normal variant.

options.label: D
options.text: Order brainstem auditory evoked response testing today
options.rationale: Hearing was screened and is normal; ABR is reserved for failed screens or suspected hearing loss.

questions.sourceMapping: Transcript 2 (bilingual expressive delay catches up; check hearing first) | Parallel Form B (options re-randomized)

stem: Using the labeled newborn skull diagram, which structure is normally no larger than 1 to 1.5 cm in diameter at birth?

images.alt: Figure 1: AAFP Part I, Figure 1A reference asset - top-down view of the normal newborn skull with sutures and fontanelles labeled.
images.caption: Figure 1: AAFP Part I, Figure 1A reference asset - top-down view of the normal newborn skull with sutures and fontanelles labeled.

options.label: A
options.text: Sagittal suture
options.rationale: Sutures are linear joints, not measured as fontanelle diameters.

options.label: B
options.text: Posterior fontanelle
options.rationale: The posterior fontanelle measures no more than 1-1.5 cm at birth, while the anterior fontanelle averages 3-6 cm; the diagram's posterior triangle at the lambdoid-metopic junction is that structure (AAFP Part I).

options.label: C
options.text: Coronal suture
options.rationale: The coronal suture is a linear joint between frontal and parietal bones.

options.label: D
options.text: Anterior fontanelle
options.rationale: The anterior fontanelle is the large 3-6 cm diamond at the coronal-sagittal-metopic junction.

questions.sourceMapping: AAFP Part I (fontanelle sizes); Newborn/Infant deck Slide 24 | Parallel Form B (options re-randomized)

stem: A septic-appearing 6-day-old has jaundice with both conjugated and unconjugated elevation, temperature instability, and poor feeding. Which row of the comparison table does this presentation match?

options.label: A
options.text: Physiologic jaundice
options.rationale: Physiologic jaundice occurs in well infants after 24 hours.

options.label: B
options.text: Suboptimal intake jaundice
options.rationale: Intake jaundice shows dehydration and weight loss without toxicity.

options.label: C
options.text: Breast milk jaundice
options.rationale: Breast milk jaundice infants are thriving and afebrile.

options.label: D
options.text: Infection/sepsis, which may produce unconjugated or conjugated hyperbilirubinemia and requires urgent evaluation
options.rationale: The table lists infection/sepsis with variable timing and either unconjugated or conjugated bilirubin, accompanied by poor feeding, lethargy, or temperature instability, mandating urgent evaluation (Slide 67).

questions.sourceMapping: Newborn/Infant deck Slide 67 (infection/sepsis row) | Parallel Form B (options re-randomized)

stem: A Black newborn has pustules without surrounding erythema at birth that rupture and leave hyperpigmented macules on the soles and trunk. The infant is well-appearing. Which diagnosis fits?

options.label: A
options.text: Erythema toxicum neonatorum
options.rationale: Erythema toxicum appears after birth with an erythematous base and eosinophils.

options.label: B
options.text: Transient neonatal pustular melanosis
options.rationale: TNPM presents at birth (more common in Black infants, about 4-5%) with neutrophilic pustules lacking erythema that rupture and leave hyperpigmented macules persisting for months; the infant is well (AAFP Table 1; Slide 81-82).

options.label: C
options.text: Candidal diaper dermatitis
options.rationale: Candidal dermatitis involves the diaper area with beefy erythema and satellite lesions.

options.label: D
options.text: Miliaria crystallina
options.rationale: Miliaria presents as clear or red vesicles in sweat-prone areas from duct obstruction.

questions.sourceMapping: AAFP Part II Table 1; Newborn/Infant deck Slides 81-82 | Parallel Form B (options re-randomized)

stem: A forceps-delivered newborn cannot close the left eye, has loss of the left nasolabial fold, and droops at the left mouth corner when crying. What is the expected course?

options.label: A
options.text: Peripheral facial nerve palsy from birth trauma, usually resolving within the first few weeks
options.rationale: Forceps or difficult delivery can cause peripheral facial palsy (inability to close the eye, lost nasolabial fold, asymmetric crying face) that usually resolves in the first weeks; persistence warrants further evaluation (AAFP Part I; CN VII exam Slide 40).

options.label: B
options.text: Central stroke requiring neuroimaging today
options.rationale: Neonatal stroke is rare and would show central patterns and other deficits.

options.label: C
options.text: Permanent deficit requiring surgical repair
options.rationale: Most birth-related peripheral palsies recover spontaneously.

options.label: D
options.text: Moebius syndrome requiring genetic testing today
options.rationale: Moebius involves bilateral congenital facial and abducens palsies, not unilateral post-traumatic palsy.

questions.sourceMapping: AAFP Part I (facial nerve palsy); Newborn/Infant deck Slide 40 (CN VII crying face) | Parallel Form B (options re-randomized)

stem: Which cluster of weight milestones is correct per the course?

options.label: A
options.text: Double birth weight by 4-5 months, triple by 1 year, with about 25-40 g/day gain in the first 3-4 months
options.rationale: The deck teaches doubling by 4-5 months, tripling by 1 year, daily gain of 25-40 g (about 1 lb per 2 weeks) for the first 3-4 months, then 15-20 g/day (5-7 oz weekly) for the rest of the year (Slide 19).

options.label: B
options.text: Double birth weight by 6-7 months, triple by 2 years
options.rationale: Doubling by 6-7 months understates it; tripling occurs at 1 year, not 2.

options.label: C
options.text: Double birth weight by 2 months, triple by 6 months
options.rationale: Doubling by 2 months overstates early gain.

options.label: D
options.text: Gain 50 g/day throughout the first year
options.rationale: 50 g/day exceeds the taught ranges.

questions.sourceMapping: Newborn/Infant deck Slide 19; Growth & Development Part 2, Slide 34 | Parallel Form B (options re-randomized)

stem: Select all fluids the course directs avoiding for infant rehydration.

options.label: A
options.text: Soda
options.rationale: Soda's sugar load worsens osmotic diarrhea.

options.label: B
options.text: Commercial oral rehydration solution (e.g., Pedialyte)
options.rationale: Commercial ORS is the recommended rehydration fluid, not an avoided one.

options.label: C
options.text: Plain water
options.rationale: Plain water lacks electrolytes and risks hyponatremia.

options.label: D
options.text: Undiluted juice
options.rationale: Undiluted juice is hyperosmolar and aggravates stool losses.

options.label: E
options.text: Sports drinks
options.rationale: Sports drinks have inappropriate sodium content for infant rehydration.

questions.sourceMapping: Newborn/Infant deck Slide 91 (avoid/escalate column) | Parallel Form B (options re-randomized)

stem: A discharge summary notes a 30-hour TcB of 6.2 mg/dL plotted in the low-risk zone. What responsibility does the course assign the primary care provider?

options.label: A
options.text: Treat all discharge values above 5 mg/dL with phototherapy
options.rationale: Treatment follows hour-specific, gestational-age-adjusted thresholds, not a flat cutoff.

options.label: B
options.text: Track the plotted value on the hour-specific nomogram and assess the infant serially to ensure the trend is falling, not rising
options.rationale: The professor described receiving the discharge bilirubin, plotting it on the hour-based graph, and following the child to ensure the value trends down - with readmission when it climbs into moderate/high-risk zones (Transcript 4; Slides 69-70).

options.label: C
options.text: Repeat TcB daily for 14 days in all newborns
options.rationale: Routine daily TcB for two weeks is not the protocol; risk-stratified follow-up is.

options.label: D
options.text: None; the hospital completes all bilirubin follow-up
options.rationale: Continuity of bilirubin follow-up is a primary care responsibility.

questions.sourceMapping: Transcript 4 (plotting discharge bilirubin and tracking); Newborn/Infant deck Slides 69-70 | Parallel Form B (options re-randomized)

stem: Which cause of leukokoria is the most common intraocular tumor of childhood and must be excluded in any newborn with a white pupillary reflex?

options.label: A
options.text: Chorioretinitis
options.rationale: Chorioretinitis reflects intrauterine infection (CMV, toxoplasmosis).

options.label: B
options.text: Coats disease
options.rationale: Coats disease is a congenital vascular disorder, not the most common tumor.

options.label: C
options.text: Retinoblastoma
options.rationale: Retinoblastoma is the most common intraocular tumor in children and tops the leukokoria differential; family history of retinoblastoma, cataracts, glaucoma, or retinal abnormalities mandates referral regardless of reflex findings (AAFP Part I, Table 2 and SORT).

options.label: D
options.text: Persistent fetal vasculature
options.rationale: Persistent fetal vasculature results from failed hyaloid involution.

questions.sourceMapping: AAFP Part I Table 2 and SORT recommendation (ophthalmology referral) | Parallel Form B (options re-randomized)

stem: A term infant's weight, length, and head circumference all track just below the 5th percentile along parallel curves since birth. Parents are both under 5 feet 4 inches and 5 feet 7 inches. Development is normal. Which interpretation is most appropriate?

options.label: A
options.text: Endocrine growth failure requires immediate growth hormone testing
options.rationale: Endocrine failure shows declining or discrepant patterns; stable familial tracking does not warrant immediate GH testing.

options.label: B
options.text: Caloric insufficiency is the leading diagnosis
options.rationale: Caloric insufficiency produces declining or discrepant percentiles (weight first), not stable parallel tracking.

options.label: C
options.text: This pattern indicates an intrauterine insult requiring genetic testing today
options.rationale: Intrauterine insult or genetic abnormality is considered when growth is symmetrically low but discordant with parental pattern or accompanied by dysmorphism; parental heights here explain the curve.

options.label: D
options.text: Constitutional or familial short stature is likely; confirm with midparental height assessment
options.rationale: When all three parameters track together on the same low percentile with normal development and short statured parents, familial/constitutional short stature is likely; the growth-pattern table directs midparental height evaluation first (Part 2, Slide 43; Transcript 2).

questions.sourceMapping: Growth & Development Part 2, Slide 43; Transcript 2 (all three tracking same percentile may be their pattern) | Parallel Form B (options re-randomized)

stem: An infant with acid-mediated erosive esophagitis documented by GI is started on a short course of acid suppression. What follow-up does the course specify?

options.label: A
options.text: Switch to prokinetic therapy at 1 week
options.rationale: Prokinetics are not the taught next step.

options.label: B
options.text: Continue indefinitely without review
options.rationale: Indefinite therapy contradicts the wean directive.

options.label: C
options.text: Double the dose at 2 weeks routinely
options.rationale: Dose doubling is not protocol.

options.label: D
options.text: Reassess after 4-8 weeks and attempt to wean
options.rationale: When acid suppression is used, the slide directs reassessment after 4-8 weeks with an attempt to wean, avoiding automatic long-term escalation (Slide 87).

questions.sourceMapping: Newborn/Infant deck Slide 87 (acid suppression reassess/wean) | Parallel Form B (options re-randomized)

stem: Which feature most strongly favors cow's milk protein allergy over acute viral gastroenteritis in an infant with loose stools?

options.label: A
options.text: Blood and mucus in stool with eczema, in an afebrile well-appearing infant
options.rationale: Blood/mucus with eczema in a well infant points to food-protein-induced (allergic) colitis; the differential slide assigns vomiting plus watery diarrhea with exposures to viral gastroenteritis (Slides 88-89, 92).

options.label: B
options.text: Vomiting plus watery diarrhea with sick-contact exposure
options.rationale: That pattern favors viral gastroenteritis.

options.label: C
options.text: Diarrhea beginning 48 hours after a single antibiotic dose
options.rationale: Antibiotic timing suggests medication-associated diarrhea.

options.label: D
options.text: Diarrhea resolving within 5 days
options.rationale: Short duration defines acute infectious-type diarrhea.

questions.sourceMapping: Newborn/Infant deck Slides 88-89, 92 (clues that narrow the differential) | Parallel Form B (options re-randomized)

stem: For a 8-kg infant with mild-to-moderate dehydration from diarrhea, which ORS volume plan is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: 50-100 mL/kg of commercial ORS over 2-4 hours, then replace ongoing losses at about 10 mL/kg per watery stool
options.rationale: The ORT slide specifies 50-100 mL/kg ORS over 2-4 hours for mild-moderate dehydration with ongoing loss replacement of ~10 mL/kg per watery stool (or 60-120 mL per stool for infants <10 kg) (Slide 91).

options.label: B
options.text: 10 mL/kg of half-strength ORS over 30 minutes
options.rationale: Half-strength ORS and 30-minute volumes contradict the protocol.

options.label: C
options.text: Undiluted sports drinks ad libitum
options.rationale: Sports drinks have inappropriate sodium/glucose ratios and are listed to avoid.

options.label: D
options.text: 20 mL/kg of plain water hourly
options.rationale: Plain water is explicitly avoided and causes hyponatremia.

questions.sourceMapping: Newborn/Infant deck Slide 91 (ORT volumes) | Parallel Form B (options re-randomized)

stem: A newborn has a sixth digit arising from the ulnar side of the left little finger, composed of a small pedunculated skin tag without bone. What is the appropriate management?

options.label: A
options.text: Observation only; supernumerary digits never require removal
options.rationale: Removal is typically performed for cosmetic and functional reasons.

options.label: B
options.text: Surgical reconstruction by a plastic surgeon in the newborn period
options.rationale: Plastic surgical repair is reserved for digits with bone/cartilage involvement.

options.label: C
options.text: Immediate amputation at the bedside without examination for other anomalies
options.rationale: Bedside removal without evaluating for associated anomalies misses syndromic clues.

options.label: D
options.text: Tie-off ligation at the base is usually sufficient for digits without bone involvement, with examination for associated anomalies
options.rationale: Supernumerary digits without bone involvement can be tied off at the base; those with bone require skilled surgical removal; polydactyly also warrants a careful exam for genetic abnormalities (AAFP Part II, extremities).

questions.sourceMapping: AAFP Part II (polydactyly management) | Parallel Form B (options re-randomized)

stem: In the illustrated maneuvers, panel A adducts the thigh while applying posterior pressure, and panel B abducts the thigh while lifting the femoral head anteriorly with a palpable clunk. Which pairing is correct?

images.alt: Figure 4: AAFP Part II, Figure 3 reference asset - hip examination maneuvers: panel A adducts the hip with posterior pressure; panel B abducts the hip with anterior lift.
images.caption: Figure 4: AAFP Part II, Figure 3 reference asset - hip examination maneuvers: panel A adducts the hip with posterior pressure; panel B abducts the hip with anterior lift.

options.label: A
options.text: A = Barlow (dislocation test); B = Ortolani (reduction test)
options.rationale: Barlow adducts the hip with posterior pressure to discover a dislocatable hip; Ortolani flexes and abducts while lifting the femoral head anteriorly, producing a clunk of reduction - exactly the panels shown (Slides 44-46; AAFP Part II Figure 3).

options.label: B
options.text: A = Ortolani (dislocation test); B = Barlow (reduction test)
options.rationale: The tests are reversed in this option.

options.label: C
options.text: A = Barlow (reduction test); B = Galeazzi test
options.rationale: Barlow is a dislocation (provocative) test, and panel B is Ortolani, not Galeazzi.

options.label: D
options.text: A = Galeazzi test; B = Trendelenburg test
options.rationale: Galeazzi compares knee heights with hips flexed; Trendelenburg assesses abductor function at walking age.

stem: A 5-month-old still demonstrates a strong Moro response with arm extension and adduction on head-drop testing. What is the best interpretation?

options.label: A
options.text: Expected in formerly premature infants regardless of corrected age
options.rationale: Corrected age adjusts milestone expectations in the first years, but a blanket exemption for ex-preemies is incorrect; reflex timing should be interpreted against corrected age, and the vignette gives no prematurity history.

options.label: B
options.text: Abnormal only if the response is symmetric
options.rationale: Asymmetry of the Moro suggests focal injury (e.g., clavicle fracture, brachial plexus palsy); symmetric persistence is itself the abnormality at this age.

options.label: C
options.text: Expected; the Moro reflex normally persists to 8 months
options.rationale: An 8-month Moro is not normal; the integration window closes at 3-4 months.

options.label: D
options.text: Abnormal; Moro should disappear by 3-4 months and persistence warrants neurologic assessment
options.rationale: The Moro reflex disappears at 3-4 months (chart and Slides 38-39); persistence at 5 months (even before correcting for prematurity in most cases) is a primitive reflex that has outlived its window and requires assessment, consistent with the professor's warning about retained reflexes (Transcript 3).

stem: On examination of a dehydrated 9-month-old, which finding indicates the dehydration has become severe and ominous?

options.label: A
options.text: Hypotension
options.rationale: Hypotension is a LATE, ominous sign of decompensated shock in infants; tachycardia, sunken fontanelle, and absent tears precede it and should trigger action earlier (Slide 90).

options.label: B
options.text: Absent tears
options.rationale: Absent tears appear before circulatory collapse.

options.label: C
options.text: Tachycardia with delayed capillary refill
options.rationale: Tachycardia with prolonged refill indicates significant but still compensated dehydration.

options.label: D
options.text: Sunken anterior fontanelle
options.rationale: A sunken fontanelle is an earlier moderate-to-severe sign.

stem: Select all sacral dimple features that classify the dimple as high risk for occult spinal dysraphism and warrant ultrasonography.

options.label: A
options.text: The dimple measures 3 mm with a visible base at the gluteal cleft apex
options.rationale: A small dimple with visible base near the gluteal cleft is simple and low risk.

options.label: B
options.text: The dimple is located more than 2.5 cm above the anus
options.rationale: Location >2.5 cm above the anus is a listed high-risk criterion.

options.label: C
options.text: The dimple is associated with a midline mass or skin discoloration
options.rationale: Midline masses, discoloration, or hemangiomas accompanying a dimple raise risk.

options.label: D
options.text: The base of the dimple cannot be visualized
options.rationale: An unseen base is a listed high-risk criterion (ACR-based slide).

options.label: E
options.text: The dimple is accompanied by a hair tuft or midline skin tag
options.rationale: Hair tufts and skin tags are cutaneous markers of occult dysraphism.

stem: A 3-month-old spits up small volumes after most feeds, is cheerful between feeds, and tracks along the 60th percentile for weight. Look at this baby 👶. What is the most appropriate management?

images.alt: Figure 4: Second-half PPTX slide 24 reference asset - gastroesophageal reflux (spitting up): common, worst at 2-4 months, driven by air ingestion and overfeeding, improved by burping.
images.caption: Figure 4: Second-half PPTX slide 24 reference asset - gastroesophageal reflux (spitting up): common, worst at 2-4 months, driven by air ingestion and overfeeding, improved by burping.

options.label: A
options.text: Order an upper GI series today
options.rationale: Upper GI does not diagnose GERD and is reserved for suspected anatomic disease.

options.label: B
options.text: Start a proton pump inhibitor trial
options.rationale: Acid suppression is not routine first-line and is reserved for established acid-mediated disease.

options.label: C
options.text: Reassure: this is uncomplicated reflux ('happy spitter') with normal growth; counsel on burping and avoiding overfeeding
options.rationale: The clinical pearl is explicit: happy spitter plus normal growth equals reassurance; reflux peaks at 2-4 months, relates to air ingestion/overfeeding and an immature lower esophageal sphincter, and improves with frequent burping and paced volumes (Slides 86-87; Transcript 4).

options.label: D
options.text: Stop all feeds for 12 hours to rest the gut
options.rationale: Feed interruption harms nutrition and hydration.

stem: Which assessment tool combines physical and neuromuscular characteristics to establish gestational age in a newborn with uncertain dates?

options.label: A
options.text: Apgar scoring at 1 and 5 minutes
options.rationale: Apgar scores evaluate transition and need for resuscitation, not gestational age.

options.label: B
options.text: The Ortolani maneuver
options.rationale: Ortolani tests hip reducibility.

options.label: C
options.text: The New Ballard Score
options.rationale: The New Ballard Score assesses gestational age through physical characteristics and neuromuscular maturity, per AAFP Part I (AAFP Part I, general assessment).

options.label: D
options.text: The Brazelton Neonatal Behavioral Assessment Scale
options.rationale: Brazelton assesses behavioral responses, not gestational dating.

stem: A 5-day-old breastfed newborn has lost 8% of birth weight; at the 2-week visit the infant remains 4% below birth weight. How should each finding be interpreted?

options.label: A
options.text: The 8% loss at day 5 is within the expected 5-10% range, but failure to regain birth weight by the 2-week visit is a problem requiring feeding intervention
options.rationale: Loss of 5-10% in the first days is normal and return to birth weight occurs by 7-10 days; not being back at birth weight by the 2-week visit is explicitly 'a problem' requiring action (Slides 19; Transcripts 2, 3 - professor: these questions appear on exams).

options.label: B
options.text: Both findings mandate hospital admission
options.rationale: Admission follows severe dehydration or failure of outpatient management, not an isolated 4% deficit with otherwise stable status.

options.label: C
options.text: Both findings are normal
options.rationale: The 2-week deficit is not normal.

options.label: D
options.text: The 8% loss is abnormal, while the 2-week deficit is acceptable
options.rationale: The interpretation is reversed.

stem: Select all newborn populations for which the AAP recommends scheduled glucose screening.

options.label: A
options.text: Newborns of mothers with diabetes mellitus
options.rationale: Infants of diabetic mothers experience hyperinsulinism-driven hypoglycemia and are screened.

options.label: B
options.text: Appropriate-for-gestational-age term newborns born by cesarean
options.rationale: Cesarean delivery alone in an AGA term newborn is not an indication for scheduled glucose screening.

options.label: C
options.text: Late preterm newborns (34 0/7 to 36 6/7 weeks)
options.rationale: Late preterm infants (34-36 6/7 weeks) have immature feeding and stores and are screened.

options.label: D
options.text: Small for gestational age newborns
options.rationale: SGA infants (below the 10th percentile) have limited glycogen stores and are screened.

options.label: E
options.text: Large for gestational age newborns
options.rationale: LGA infants (above the 90th percentile, often from maternal diabetes) are at increased hypoglycemia risk and require scheduled screening (AAFP Part I, SORT C).

stem: Which statement about jaundice is correct per this course?

options.label: A
options.text: An umbilical granuloma is a moist pink nodule without surrounding erythema treated with silver nitrate, while omphalitis with erythema and tenderness is an emergency needing IV antibiotics.

options.label: B
options.text: After day 4 to 5 of life a well-hydrated infant has at least 5 to 6 wet diapers per day; fewer than 6 suggests dehydration and 1 to 2 per day or no urine for over 8 hours is severe.
options.rationale: Accurate for JAUNDICE, not JAUNDICE.

options.label: C
options.text: Newborns should not go more than 3 hours without feeding in the first month, and weight loss greater than 10 percent of birth weight or failure to regain birth weight by 2 weeks is a problem.

options.label: D
options.text: Supine sleep on a firm bare surface with room-sharing but not bed-sharing for at least 6 months reduces SIDS risk by as much as 50 percent; pacifier use for the first 6 months is recommended.
options.rationale: Accurate for SIDS, not JAUNDICE.

options.label: E
options.text: Jaundice appearing within the first 24 hours of life is pathologic until proven otherwise and requires prompt bilirubin measurement and hemolysis evaluation.
options.rationale: Core course fact for JAUNDICE: Jaundice appearing within the first 24 hours of life is pathologic until proven otherwise and requires prompt bilirubin measurement and hemolysis evaluation.

options.label: F
options.text: Colic follows the rule of 3s (3 hours per day, 3 days per week, for more than 3 weeks), peaks in the early evening, begins around 2 weeks, and improves by about 3 months in a thriving infant.
options.rationale: Accurate for FEEDING, not JAUNDICE.

stem: Which intervention largely prevents Rh(D) alloimmunization and its fetal consequences?

options.label: A
options.text: Intravenous immunoglobulin to the newborn at birth
options.rationale: IVIG treats, not prevents, alloimmune hemolysis in affected neonates.

options.label: B
options.text: Appropriate Rh(D) immune globulin prophylaxis to the Rh-negative mother
options.rationale: Rh(D) immune globulin prophylaxis prevents maternal sensitization and is largely protective, per the slide (Slide 68).

options.label: C
options.text: Early phototherapy to the firstborn
options.rationale: Phototherapy manages bilirubin but does not prevent maternal antibody formation.

options.label: D
options.text: Maternal plasma exchange during every pregnancy
options.rationale: Plasma exchange is not standard prophylaxis.

stem: A 6-month-old was born at 32 weeks' gestation. The infant pulls to a seated position with trunk support, reaches and transfers objects, and babbles. Using corrected age, how should the PNP interpret these skills?

options.label: A
options.text: Appropriate; corrected age is about 4 months, matching the observed skills
options.rationale: Corrected age = chronological age minus weeks of prematurity: 6 months minus 8 weeks (2 months) = 4 months; reaching, transferring, and babbling with supported sitting fit a 4-month corrected profile, and the professor insisted preemies be tracked by corrected age (Part 2, Slides 26-29; Transcript 2).

options.label: B
options.text: Indeterminate; corrected age cannot be calculated without birth weight
options.rationale: Corrected age requires gestational age or weeks premature, not birth weight.

options.label: C
options.text: Advanced; these are 9-month skills
options.rationale: These are 4-6 month skills, not 9-month skills.

options.label: D
options.text: Delayed; a 6-month-old should sit independently regardless of gestational age at birth
options.rationale: Independent sitting is a 6-9 month uncorrected expectation; applying it without correction misjudges the ex-preemie.

questions.sourceMapping: Growth & Development Part 2, Slides 26-29; Transcript 2 (corrected age calculation example) | Parallel Form B (options re-randomized)

stem: A 14-month-old with 4 days of viral gastroenteritis now has improved vomiting but transient loose stools after milk feeds. Which mechanism is most likely?

options.label: A
options.text: Transient lactose/carbohydrate malabsorption following gastroenteritis
options.rationale: Post-gastroenteritis transient lactose/carbohydrate malabsorption is a listed differential entry explaining temporary osmotic diarrhea after mucosal injury (Slide 89).

options.label: B
options.text: Secondary bacterial superinfection
options.rationale: Superinfection would show toxicity or blood.

options.label: C
options.text: New-onset cow's milk protein allergy
options.rationale: CMPA onset is typically in the first 1-6 months with blood/mucus and eczema.

options.label: D
options.text: Inflammatory bowel disease
options.rationale: IBD is exceedingly rare at this age and presents with growth failure and blood.

questions.sourceMapping: Newborn/Infant deck Slide 89 (postinfectious malabsorption) | Parallel Form B (options re-randomized)

stem: A 6-month-old is brought in for a well visit. While reviewing the reflex chart shown, the PNP elicits one reflex that should no longer be present at this age. Which finding is most concerning?

images.alt: Figure 2: Milestone Combined Documents, page 1 reference asset - newborn reflex chart with stimulation, response, and expected disappearance.
images.caption: Figure 2: Milestone Combined Documents, page 1 reference asset - newborn reflex chart with stimulation, response, and expected disappearance.

options.label: A
options.text: Asymmetric tonic neck (fencer) posture when supine
options.rationale: The tonic neck reflex disappears by about 2 months; its persistence at 6 months indicates failure of primitive reflex integration and possible neurologic pathology, exactly the concept the professor flagged as frequently tested (chart; Slides 37-39; Transcript 3).

options.label: B
options.text: Blinking in response to a flash of light
options.rationale: The blink reflex is permanent and should persist throughout life.

options.label: C
options.text: Babinski response with fanning of the toes
options.rationale: A Babinski with toe fanning is normal in infancy and disappears between 9 months and 1 year.

options.label: D
options.text: Grasping an examiner's finger placed in the palm
options.rationale: The palmar grasp weakens after 3 months but may persist to about 1 year; a weak grasp at 6 months is not by itself abnormal, whereas a persistent tonic neck is.

questions.sourceMapping: Milestone Documents p1 reflex chart; Newborn/Infant deck Slides 37-39; Transcript 3 (reflex timing is exam material; persistent primitive reflex = neurologic concern) | Parallel Form B (options re-randomized)

stem: Which chronic-diarrhea association should prompt evaluation for cystic fibrosis or other malabsorption?

options.label: A
options.text: One episode of watery stools after a new fruit
options.rationale: Single dietary episodes are osmotic and self-limited.

options.label: B
options.text: Persistent diarrhea with poor growth, greasy stools, or failure to thrive from early life
options.rationale: The persistent/chronic column lists malabsorption or pancreatic insufficiency (including cystic fibrosis), protein-losing or inflammatory enteropathy, and congenital diarrheal disorders, to consider when severe from early life, persistent, or associated with failure to thrive (Slide 89).

options.label: C
options.text: Diarrhea resolving within 72 hours of ORT
options.rationale: Rapid resolution fits acute self-limited illness.

options.label: D
options.text: Loose stools limited to a teething week
options.rationale: Teething-related loose stools are transient and non-pathologic.

questions.sourceMapping: Newborn/Infant deck Slide 89 (persistent/chronic column) | Parallel Form B (options re-randomized)

stem: The professor asked the class why unconjugated bilirubin is dangerous to the newborn brain. Which answer reflects the taught mechanism?

options.label: A
options.text: Bilirubin binds irreversibly to skull sutures, raising intracranial pressure
options.rationale: Suture binding is not a mechanism.

options.label: B
options.text: Unconjugated bilirubin is water-soluble and floods cerebrospinal fluid
options.rationale: Unconjugated bilirubin is water-INSOLUBLE; conjugated is water-soluble.

options.label: C
options.text: Unconjugated bilirubin crosses the immature blood-brain barrier, causing neurotoxicity and kernicterus
options.rationale: The professor tied neurotoxicity to the blood-brain barrier concept in pediatrics: unconjugated (lipid-soluble, albumin-bound) bilirubin can cross the immature barrier and damage developing brain tissue - kernicterus (Transcript 4; Slide 69 key point; AAFP Part II).

options.label: D
options.text: Bilirubin causes cerebral vasospasm through renal metabolites
options.rationale: Vasospasm is not the mechanism of bilirubin neurotoxicity.

questions.sourceMapping: Transcript 4 (blood-brain barrier discussion); Newborn/Infant deck Slide 69 key point | Parallel Form B (options re-randomized)

stem: A 5-year-old proudly shows the PNP a drawing of the family and insists on buttoning his own coat before kindergarten. Failure to successfully negotiate this stage, per Erikson, most likely results in which outcome?

options.label: A
options.text: Guilt and suppressed initiative
options.rationale: Guilt follows unsuccessful negotiation of the preschool initiative-vs-guilt stage, which precedes this child's current task.

options.label: B
options.text: Role confusion
options.rationale: Role confusion is the adolescent identity crisis outcome.

options.label: C
options.text: Mistrust of caregivers
options.rationale: Mistrust results from unresolved infancy (trust vs mistrust).

options.label: D
options.text: Feelings of inferiority and low self-esteem
options.rationale: School-age children (6-11 years, with the kindergarten transition marking entry) face industry vs inferiority; failure to cope with academic and social demands produces inferiority and diminished self-esteem (Part 1, Slide 19; Transcript 1).

questions.sourceMapping: Growth & Development Part 1, Slides 17, 19; Transcript 1 | Parallel Form B (options re-randomized)

stem: Select all interventions and screenings that should be completed before or around hospital discharge for a term newborn, per this course.

options.label: A
options.text: Critical congenital heart disease pulse oximetry screening at 24 hours of life or later
options.rationale: CCHD pulse oximetry screening is recommended before discharge at 24 hours or later, with echocardiography if positive (AAFP SORT).

options.label: B
options.text: Routine chest radiography
options.rationale: Routine chest radiography is not a discharge screening test.

options.label: C
options.text: Hepatitis B vaccine
options.rationale: The birth-dose hepatitis B vaccine is a standard newborn intervention (Slide 12).

options.label: D
options.text: Hearing screening by otoacoustic emissions or auditory brainstem response
options.rationale: Hearing should be evaluated before 1 month, preferably before discharge, using ABR or OAE (AAFP SORT).

options.label: E
options.text: Intramuscular vitamin K
options.rationale: Vitamin K prevents hemorrhagic disease of the newborn (Slide 12).

options.label: F
options.text: Erythromycin ophthalmic prophylaxis
options.rationale: Eye prophylaxis prevents gonococcal ophthalmia and is a listed birth intervention (Slide 12).

questions.sourceMapping: Newborn/Infant deck Slide 12; AAFP Part I SORT (hearing, CCHD screening) | Parallel Form B (options re-randomized)

stem: The professor described an office technique to screen for unilateral weakness at the 4-month visit. What is it?

options.label: A
options.text: Placing the infant in vertical suspension and watching shoulder strength
options.rationale: Vertical suspension assesses global tone, not unilateral weakness, in the newborn period.

options.label: B
options.text: Presenting an object at midline and observing whether both hands come to it
options.rationale: At 4 months the PNP places an object in front of the face and expects both hands to come to it; bringing only one hand suggests weakness on the other side (Transcript 2).

options.label: C
options.text: Eliciting the Moro reflex and comparing arm excursion
options.rationale: Asymmetric Moro suggests clavicle fracture or brachial plexus injury in the newborn, not the 4-month office screen described.

options.label: D
options.text: Measuring grip strength with a dynamometer
options.rationale: Dynamometry is not an infant office technique.

stem: A 3-week-old develops inflammatory papules and pustules on the cheeks without comedones. The infant is otherwise well. Which statement is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: Atopic dermatitis requiring topical immunosuppressants
options.rationale: Atopic dermatitis is pruritic, dry, and eczematous, not pustular on the cheeks at 3 weeks.

options.label: B
options.text: Neonatal acne, stimulated by maternal and endogenous androgens, typically appearing after 2 weeks and resolving spontaneously
options.rationale: Neonatal acne affects up to 20% of infants, appears after about 2 weeks from sebaceous stimulation by maternal/endogenous androgens, lacks comedones, and resolves in weeks to months without treatment (Slide 76; Transcript 4).

options.label: C
options.text: Herpes simplex, requiring PCR testing
options.rationale: HSV produces grouped vesicles with systemic features.

options.label: D
options.text: Erythema toxicum, which appears at this age with eosinophils
options.rationale: Erythema toxicum arises in the first days on an erythematous base and resolves within the first week.

questions.sourceMapping: Newborn/Infant deck Slide 76; Transcript 4 (neonatal acne self-limited) | Parallel Form B (options re-randomized)

stem: The cropped photograph shows thick yellow-white greasy scales adherent to an infant's scalp without significant erythema or discomfort. Which management is most appropriate?

options.label: A
options.text: Gentle scale removal with a soft brush or comb after emollient or oil, with reassurance
options.rationale: The morphology is cradle cap (seborrheic dermatitis): greasy yellow scale over scalp and skin-fold-rich areas, non-pruritic in infants, benign and self-limiting; conservative care with soft brushing and emollient is the taught management (Slide 75; Transcript 4).

options.label: B
options.text: Oral griseofulvin for tinea capitis
options.rationale: Tinea capitis shows alopecia, black dots, and inflammation, absent here.

options.label: C
options.text: Mid-potency topical steroid twice daily for 8 weeks
options.rationale: Prolonged potent steroids are inappropriate for a self-limited eruption.

options.label: D
options.text: Selenium sulfide shampoo daily with occlusive dressing
options.rationale: Aggressive medicated shampooing with occlusion is unnecessary and irritating. Figure 1: Cropped clinical photograph from Newborn/Infant deck Slide 75 (seborrheic dermatitis slide) - image only, slide text removed.

questions.sourceMapping: Newborn/Infant deck Slide 75; Transcript 4 (cradle cap care)

stem: A 3-week-old shows the facial inflammatory papules and pustules pictured, without comedones, on an otherwise well infant. Which statement is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: This is neonatal acne, a self-limited variant stimulated by maternal and endogenous androgens
options.rationale: Neonatal acne appears after about 2 weeks of age as inflammatory papulopustules on face and cheeks without comedones, affects up to 20% of infants, and resolves spontaneously; reassurance is the management (Slide 76; Transcript 4).

options.label: B
options.text: This is erythema toxicum and will resolve within 24 hours
options.rationale: Erythema toxicum presents in the first days as papules on erythematous bases and resolves within the first week, not at 3 weeks.

options.label: C
options.text: This is neonatal herpes requiring immediate PCR testing
options.rationale: HSV produces grouped vesicles on an erythematous base with systemic illness.

options.label: D
options.text: This is atopic dermatitis requiring topical calcineurin inhibitor
options.rationale: Atopic dermatitis is eczematous and pruritic, not pustular at 3 weeks. Figure 2: Cropped clinical photograph from Newborn/Infant deck Slide 76 (neonatal acne slide) - image only, slide text removed.

stem: The cropped image shows a flat pink-to-red patch over the forehead and upper eyelid present since birth with sharp midline respect. Which counseling is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: It will fade spontaneously by 1-2 years of age like a salmon patch
options.rationale: Fading by 1-2 years describes salmon patches, not port-wine stains.

options.label: B
options.text: It represents a capillary malformation (port-wine stain) that persists and may darken; trigeminal distribution warrants evaluation for Sturge-Weber syndrome and ophthalmology referral
options.rationale: Port-wine stain (nevus flammeus) is a flat capillary malformation present at birth that persists and darkens; lesions over the trigeminal region associate with seizures and glaucoma (Sturge-Weber) and any periocular lesion needs ophthalmology input (Slide 77; AAFP Table 1; Transcript 4).

options.label: C
options.text: It is an infantile hemangioma that will involute by school age
options.rationale: Hemangiomas are raised proliferative tumors, not flat birth patches.

options.label: D
options.text: It is dermal melanocytosis that will fade by age 4
options.rationale: Dermal melanocytosis is blue-gray and typically sacral. Figure 3: Cropped clinical photograph from Newborn/Infant deck Slide 77 (vascular lesions slide) - flat pink-red facial patch, image only.

questions.sourceMapping: Newborn/Infant deck Slide 77; AAFP Part II Table 1; Transcript 4

stem: The cropped photograph shows a flat pink-salmon macular patch on the nape of a newborn's neck. Which statement is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: Salmon patch (nevus simplex, stork bite); usually fades by 1-2 years of age
options.rationale: Salmon patches (stork bites) are flat pink capillary patches on nape, eyelids, or glabella, present at birth and typically fading by 1-2 years; reassurance is appropriate (Slide 77; AAFP Table 1).

options.label: B
options.text: Port-wine stain (nevus flammeus); requires pulsed-dye laser before 6 months
options.rationale: Port-wine stains are darker, persist, and do not fade; laser is not indicated for fading salmon patches.

options.label: C
options.text: Hemangioma; will proliferate over the first year. Monitor closely for progression into a painful rash.
options.rationale: Hemangiomas are raised and proliferative.

options.label: D
options.text: Cutis marmorata; resolves only with anticoagulation
options.rationale: Cutis marmorata is transient reticulated mottling from cold, resolving with warming. Figure 4: Cropped clinical photograph from Newborn/Infant deck Slide 77 (vascular lesions slide) - pink macular patch on the nape, image only.

questions.sourceMapping: Newborn/Infant deck Slide 77; AAFP Part II Table 1

stem: A 10-week-old presents with the bright red raised plaque on the hand shown, first noted at 2 weeks and enlarging since. Which counseling is most accurate?

options.label: A
options.text: Expect rapid growth during the first year followed by involution over several years; observe uncomplicated extremity lesions
options.rationale: Infantile hemangiomas proliferate during the first year then involute over years; observation suits uncomplicated extremity lesions, with treatment reserved for critical-site or complicated lesions (Slide 78; Transcript 4; AAFP Table 1).

options.label: B
options.text: Immediate surgical excision is required to prevent further growth
options.rationale: Excision is not first-line for a proliferating hemangioma.

options.label: C
options.text: The lesion is a port-wine stain and will never change
options.rationale: Port-wine stains are flat and present at birth; this lesion appeared at 2 weeks and is raised.

options.label: D
options.text: Systemic corticosteroids are first-line for all extremity hemangiomas
options.rationale: Systemic therapy (e.g., beta-blockers) is reserved for high-risk lesions, not all extremity hemangiomas. Figure 5: Cropped clinical photograph from Newborn/Infant deck Slide 78 (hemangioma slide) - vascular lesion on hand, image only.

questions.sourceMapping: Newborn/Infant deck Slide 78; Transcript 4; AAFP Part II Table 1

stem: The cropped photograph shows a small red vascular tumor immediately adjacent to the upper eyelid of a 6-week-old. What is the most appropriate action?

options.label: A
options.text: Reassure and observe like any extremity hemangioma
options.rationale: Observation applies to uncomplicated non-critical-site lesions.

options.label: B
options.text: Early referral for treatment because periocular hemangiomas can affect vision
options.rationale: Hemangiomas near the eye (or airway and other critical structures) warrant early dermatology/ophthalmology referral and treatment because proliferation can impair vision - the professor's explicit exception to observation (Slide 78; Transcript 4).

options.label: C
options.text: Apply topical antibiotic ointment
options.rationale: Antibiotics have no role in a vascular tumor.

options.label: D
options.text: Schedule routine reassessment at the 12-month visit only
options.rationale: Deferring a year risks amblyopia during the proliferative phase.

questions.sourceMapping: Newborn/Infant deck Slide 78; Transcript 4 (hemangiomas near eyes get treated)

stem: The cropped image shows tiny white papules over a newborn's nose and cheeks. Which statement is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: They are milia and will resolve spontaneously
options.rationale: They are milia - keratin-filled epidermal cysts that resolve spontaneously; advise against squeezing: Milia are white keratin cysts of the pilosebaceous unit, most often on nose and cheeks, benign and self-limited within the first weeks; squeezing or picking is discouraged (Slide 79; AAFP Table 1).

options.label: B
options.text: They are neonatal herpes vesicles requiring acyclovir
options.rationale: HSV vesicles are fluid-filled on erythematous bases with systemic features.

options.label: C
options.text: They are candidal pustules requiring oral fluconazole
options.rationale: Candidal pustules occur with erythema in intertriginous areas.

options.label: D
options.text: They are Epstein pearls located on the nasal skin
options.rationale: Epstein pearls are the oral counterpart on the palatal raphe, not nasal skin.

questions.sourceMapping: Newborn/Infant deck Slide 79; AAFP Part II Table 1

stem: The cropped photograph shows clustered tiny red papulovesicles on an infant's skin during a heat wave, in an area prone to sweating. Beyond skin care, which counseling point carries the greatest safety weight?

options.label: A
options.text: Keep the infant cool with lightweight clothing and avoid overbundling
options.rationale: Miliaria rubra signals overheating; the course links overheating directly to SIDS risk counseling, making cooling and light clothing the safety-critical message (Slide 80; Transcript 4).

options.label: B
options.text: Apply occlusive petrolatum thickly to protect the skin
options.rationale: Occlusion worsens sweat-duct obstruction.

options.label: C
options.text: Restrict fluids to reduce excessive sweating
options.rationale: Fluid restriction is dangerous in infancy.

options.label: D
options.text: Expose the rash to sunlight daily to dry out vesicles
options.rationale: Sun exposure adds heat and burn risk.

questions.sourceMapping: Newborn/Infant deck Slide 80; Transcript 4 (overheating and SIDS)

stem: The cropped image shows clear, thin-walled superficial vesicles without surrounding erythema on a bundled newborn's trunk. Which diagnosis fits?

options.label: A
options.text: Miliaria crystallina from sweat-duct obstruction
options.rationale: Miliaria crystallina presents as clear superficial vesicles without erythema from sweat retention; management is cooling and lightweight clothing with spontaneous resolution (Slide 80).

options.label: B
options.text: Transient neonatal pustular melanosis
options.rationale: TNPM shows pustules that rupture leaving hyperpigmented macules, typically at birth.

options.label: C
options.text: Staphylococcal bullous impetigo
options.rationale: Bullous impetigo produces larger flaccid bullae with erosion and requires antibiotics.

options.label: D
options.text: Herpes Simplex virus infection requiring urgent treatment with IV Acyclovir
options.rationale: Incontinentia pigmenti: Incontinentia pigmenti follows Blaschko lines with vesicular then verrucous stages.

questions.sourceMapping: Newborn/Infant deck Slide 80 (miliaria crystallina)

stem: A well-appearing 1-day-old shows the scattered thin-walled pustules on the trunk pictured, without surrounding erythema. A smear would most likely show which cellular content?

options.label: A
options.text: Neutrophils, consistent with transient neonatal pustular melanosis
options.rationale: TNPM pustules contain neutrophils, lack an erythematous base, and occur in well infants (more common in Black infants); lesions rupture leaving scale and hyperpigmented macules (Slides 81-82; AAFP Table 1).

options.label: B
options.text: Eosinophils, consistent with erythema toxicum
options.rationale: Eosinophils characterize erythema toxicum, which has red bases and appears after birth.

options.label: C
options.text: Multinucleated giant cells, consistent with herpes simplex
options.rationale: Giant cells indicate HSV, which shows grouped vesicles on erythematous bases with illness.

options.label: D
options.text: Hyphae, consistent with candidiasis
options.rationale: Candidiasis shows yeast and pseudohyphae with intertriginous erythema.

questions.sourceMapping: Newborn/Infant deck Slides 81-82; AAFP Part II Table 1

stem: The cropped photograph shows pustules and resolving hyperpigmented macules on a newborn's sole. How does this distribution help discriminate TNPM from neonatal HSV?

options.label: A
options.text: TNPM characteristically involves face, neck, extremities, palms, and soles while sparing mucous membranes, in a well infant; HSV clusters vesicles on erythematous bases with systemic illness
options.rationale: The comparison table lists TNPM distribution across face, neck, extremities, lower back, shins, palms, and soles with mucous membrane sparing and a well-appearing infant, versus HSV's grouped vesicles on erythematous bases, possible mucous membrane/CNS involvement, and systemic signs (Slide 82).

options.label: B
options.text: TNPM spares the palms and soles, whereas HSV favors them
options.rationale: The opposite is true: palm/sole involvement supports TNPM here.

options.label: C
options.text: HSV lesions never occur on the face
options.rationale: HSV commonly involves face, scalp, and perioral areas.

options.label: D
options.text: TNPM always involves mucous membranes
options.rationale: TNPM spares mucous membranes by definition.

questions.sourceMapping: Newborn/Infant deck Slide 82 (TNPM vs HSV table)

stem: For the eruption pictured on this newborn's foot, what course and counseling should the PNP give?

options.label: A
options.text: Benign and self-limited, resolving within about 1-2 weeks with transient hyperpigmentation; reassurance only
options.rationale: TNPM resolves within 3-14 days (1-2 weeks) without sequelae beyond transient hyperpigmented macules; no laboratory testing or treatment is needed (Slides 81-82).

options.label: B
options.text: Progressive without treatment, requiring IV acyclovir
options.rationale: Progression and acyclovir describe untreated HSV, not TNPM.

options.label: C
options.text: A marker of immunodeficiency requiring immunology referral
options.rationale: No immunodeficiency association exists.

options.label: D
options.text: Contagious, requiring isolation from other newborns
options.rationale: TNPM is not infectious or contagious.

questions.sourceMapping: Newborn/Infant deck Slides 81-82

stem: The cropped photograph shows light-brown hyperpigmented macules on an infant's back. Which office action does the course require?

options.label: A
options.text: Measure and document number and size at well exam
options.rationale: s; more than six macules raises concern for neurofibromatosis and warrants further evaluation: Cafe-au-lait macules are common benign hyperpigmentation, but counts above six (especially large lesions) trigger neurofibromatosis concern; the course directs measuring, documenting, and monitoring at well exams (Slides 12, 83; Transcript 4).

options.label: B
options.text: Reassure that all cafe-au-lait macules disappear by puberty
options.rationale: They typically persist rather than disappear.

options.label: C
options.text: Biopsy the largest lesion today
options.rationale: Diagnosis is clinical; biopsy adds nothing.

options.label: D
options.text: Order serum uric acid as the first screening test
options.rationale: Uric acid is not a screening test for NF1.

questions.sourceMapping: Newborn/Infant deck Slides 12, 83; Transcript 4

stem: The cropped photograph shows a crying newborn with blue-purple hands and forearms while the trunk remains pink in the first hours of life. Which interpretation is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: Acrocyanosis from immature peripheral vasculature
options.rationale: , typically resolving within 24-48 hours: Acrocyanosis is benign peripheral cyanosis of hands and feet (sometimes face) in the first hours, reflecting immature vessels shunting flow centrally; it resolves in 24-48 hours (Slide 73; Transcript 4).

options.label: B
options.text: Central cyanosis requiring prostaglandin infusion
options.rationale: Central cyanosis involves mouth and tongue; the trunk and mucosa here are pink.

options.label: C
options.text: Methemoglobinemia requiring methylene blue
options.rationale: Methemoglobinemia causes gray-blue central cyanosis unresponsive to warming or crying.

options.label: D
options.text: Cold-induced injury requiring rewarming in a water bath
options.rationale: This is physiologic peripheral discoloration, not cold injury.

questions.sourceMapping: Newborn/Infant deck Slide 73; Transcript 4

stem: While examining the feet shown, which additional site must the PNP inspect to exclude pathologic cyanosis?

options.label: A
options.text: The tongue and oral mucosa
options.rationale: , because central cyanosis is defined by mucosal involvement: The professor taught that central cyanosis - the worrisome finding - is identified at the mouth and tongue; peripheral acrocyanosis with pink mucosa is benign (Transcript 4; AAFP Part I).

options.label: B
options.text: The scalp, because cephalic cyanosis precedes acrocyanosis
options.rationale: Scalp color does not define central cyanosis.

options.label: C
options.text: The palmar creases, because palmar blanching indicates anemia
options.rationale: Palmar blanching assesses perfusion/anemia, not cyanosis classification.

options.label: D
options.text: The sacrum, because sacral cyanosis indicates spinal dysraphism
options.rationale: Sacral color has no such association.

questions.sourceMapping: Transcript 4 (central vs peripheral cyanosis); AAFP Part I

stem: The cropped photograph shows a moist, shiny, red-pink nodule protruding from a healed umbilical base with scant serous drainage and no surrounding erythema in a well 3-week-old. What is the treatment of choice?

options.label: A
options.text: Office silver nitrate and recheck in 72 hours
options.rationale: Silver nitrate cauterization in the office: Umbilical granuloma - a moist pink-red granulation nodule after cord separation, painless and without erythema - is treated with silver nitrate cauterization (or suture ligation), per slide and professor (Slides 71-72; Transcript 4).

options.label: B
options.text: Urgent hospital evaluation for omphalitis with intravenous broad-spectrum antibiotics
options.rationale: Intravenous broad-spectrum antibiotics: IV antibiotics treat omphalitis, which shows erythema, tenderness, purulence, or systemic signs.

options.label: C
options.text: Topical hydrocortisone
options.rationale: Steroids do not ablate granulation tissue here.

options.label: D
options.text: Surgical excision under anesthesia
options.rationale: Excision is unnecessary for a benign granuloma.

questions.sourceMapping: Newborn/Infant deck Slides 71-72; Transcript 4

stem: The cropped photograph shows an umbilicus with surrounding erythema, edema, and purulent-appearing drainage in a 9-day-old who feeds poorly. Which disposition is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: Urgent hospital evaluation for omphalitis with intravenous broad-spectrum antibiotics
options.rationale: Periumbilical erythema with purulent drainage and poor feeding is omphalitis, a potential emergency that can progress rapidly to sepsis; hospital evaluation and IV antibiotics are indicated (Slides 71-72; Transcript 4).

options.label: B
options.text: Office silver nitrate and recheck in 72 hours
options.rationale: Silver nitrate addresses granuloma and would delay life-threatening infection care.

options.label: C
options.text: Topical antifungal cream and recheck in 1 week
options.rationale: Antifungals have no role in bacterial umbilical infection.

options.label: D
options.text: Reassurance; this is normal cord separation
options.rationale: Normal cord separation lacks erythema, purulence, and feeding change.

questions.sourceMapping: Newborn/Infant deck Slides 71-72; Transcript 4
