stem: A 5-month-old (20 weeks) has received no rotavirus vaccine due to repeated illness deferrals. The parents request starting the series today. What is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: Start the series today; there is no upper age limit for the first dose
options.rationale: Upper age limits exist because of intussusception risk considerations.

options.label: B
options.text: Do not start the series; the first dose must be given by 15 weeks of age and the series completed by 8 months
options.rationale: The schedule's age limits prohibit initiating rotavirus vaccine after 15 weeks (first dose) and require series completion by 8 months; a 20-week-old cannot start the series (Milestone documents pp4-6, CDC 2025 schedule footnotes).

options.label: C
options.text: Give a single dose today and complete the series at 12 months
options.rationale: No single-dose catch-up exists beyond the age limits.

options.label: D
options.text: Substitute an inactivated injectable rotavirus vaccine
options.rationale: No inactivated injectable rotavirus vaccine is in the schedule.

stem: At the 6-month well visit, which immunization addition is correct per the course and schedule?

options.label: A
options.text: Influenza vaccine becomes eligible from 6 months of age, and the hepatitis B third dose may be given within its 6-18 month window
options.rationale: The 6-month visit slide adds influenza when seasonally appropriate and lists hepatitis B dose 3 within its 6-18 month window, alongside DTaP/Hib/PCV/IPV/rotavirus continuations (Slide 60; Milestone documents pp4-6).

options.label: B
options.text: MMR may be given at 6 months during influenza season
options.rationale: MMR is a 12-month vaccine except in special circumstances not described here.

options.label: C
options.text: Varicella vaccine is due at 6 months
options.rationale: Varicella begins at 12 months.

options.label: D
options.text: Hepatitis A series begins at 6 months
options.rationale: Hepatitis A begins at 12 months.

options.label: A
options.text: MMR

options.label: B
options.text: Varicella
options.rationale: Varicella is given from 12 months.

options.label: C
options.text: Hepatitis A
options.rationale: Hepatitis A series begins at 12 months.

options.label: D
options.text: Hib and PCV boosters
options.rationale: Hib and PCV booster doses fall in the 12-15 month window.

stem: Parents ask to space out vaccines one at a time to reduce risk. Which response reflects the professor's taught counseling?

options.label: A
options.text: Spacing reduces total antigen exposure and is preferred when parents request it
options.rationale: Spacing does not reduce risk and fragments protection.

options.label: B
options.text: Spacing increases painful visits and local reactions, confounds side-effect attribution, and combination vaccines are formulated with fewer unnecessary preservatives; the evidence supports the bundled schedule
options.rationale: The professor listed spacing downsides - more visits and discomfort, repeated local reactions, confused adverse-event assessment - and noted modern combination formulations contain fewer unnecessary preservatives, supporting the bundled schedule within shared decision making (Transcript 3).

options.label: C
options.text: Spacing is acceptable because combination vaccines contain more mercury than single vaccines
options.rationale: The opposite is true per the lecture.

options.label: D
options.text: Spacing has no downsides but is logistically inconvenient
options.rationale: Downsides are clinical and immunologic, not merely logistical.

questions.sourceMapping: Transcript 3 (spacing immunizations counseling)

stem: Which scenario is a true contraindication (not a precaution) to administering DTaP today?

options.label: A
options.text: Anaphylaxis to a prior DTaP dose
options.rationale: Severe allergic reaction (anaphylaxis) to a prior dose or component is a contraindication per general best-practice immunization guidance cited in the milestone documents (p7).

options.label: B
options.text: Moderate acute illness with fever
options.rationale: Moderate or severe acute illness is a precaution - defer, but not a contraindication.

options.label: C
options.text: Mild upper respiratory infection without fever
options.rationale: Mild illness without fever is not a reason to delay.

options.label: D
options.text: Current oral antibiotic therapy
options.rationale: Antibiotic therapy does not contraindicate inactivated or routine infant vaccines.

questions.sourceMapping: Milestone Combined Documents p7 (ACIP general best practice: contraindications and precautions)

stem: Which vaccine in the infant series is administered orally rather than by injection?

options.label: A
options.text: Rotavirus
options.rationale: The professor emphasized rotavirus as the only oral vaccine in the infant sets; the others are intramuscular injections (Transcript 3; Slide 54).

options.label: B
options.text: IPV
options.rationale: IPV is injected.

options.label: C
options.text: Hib
options.rationale: Hib is injected.

options.label: D
options.text: PCV
options.rationale: PCV is injected.

questions.sourceMapping: Transcript 3 (rotavirus oral); Newborn/Infant deck Slide 54

stem: A 10-month-old adopted internationally has no immunization records. What is the correct approach per schedule guidance?

options.label: A
options.text: Restart all series from dose 1
options.rationale: Restarting wastes opportunities and delays protection.

options.label: B
options.text: Use the catch-up schedule: valid prior doses need not be repeated; interval-based catch-up rows guide completion
options.rationale: The schedule includes catch-up ranges precisely for incomplete or undocumented histories; doses are not restarted, and catch-up intervals complete the series (Milestone documents pp5-6).

options.label: C
options.text: Give only live vaccines to avoid overload
options.rationale: Live vaccine selection is age- and indication-based, not a default.

options.label: D
options.text: Wait until 12 months to begin any vaccine
options.rationale: Deferring to 12 months leaves the infant unprotected.

stem: The milestone reference chart flags a specific autism-spectrum screening tool at a specific age. Which pairing is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: M-CHAT at 18 months
options.rationale: The WCC chart notes M-CHAT at 18 months; the course also uses ASQ at 9 months and Edinburgh postpartum depression screening at each visit for the first 6 months (WCC chart; Slides 54, 62).

options.label: B
options.text: ASQ at 2 months
options.rationale: ASQ is the 9-month developmental tool in this course.

options.label: C
options.text: Edinburgh at 12 months
options.rationale: Edinburgh screens maternal depression from the early visits through 6 months.

options.label: D
options.text: Pediavision at 18 months
options.rationale: Pediavision is instrument-based vision screening noted around 6 months.

stem: According to the reference chart's breastfeeding summary, breastfeeding is associated with reductions in which cluster of infant problems?

options.label: A
options.text: Illness from transferred antibodies, GERD, diarrhea, and allergies/atopic dermatitis
options.rationale: The WCC chart's side note lists breastfeeding benefits: decreased illness via maternal antibodies, decreased GERD, decreased diarrhea, improved digestion, decreased allergies/atopic dermatitis, possible analgesia, and lower later overweight risk (WCC chart; Transcript 3).

options.label: B
options.text: Neural tube defects and congenital heart disease
options.rationale: Structural anomalies are not prevented by breastfeeding.

options.label: C
options.text: Physiologic weight loss in the first week
options.rationale: Early weight loss is physiologic regardless of feeding type.

options.label: D
options.text: Craniosynostosis and positional plagiocephaly
options.rationale: Skull shape conditions relate to sutures and positioning.

stem: Select all conditions included on the newborn screening list provided in the course milestone documents.

options.label: A
options.text: Phenylketonuria and other amino acid metabolism disorders
options.rationale: Amino acid and organic acid metabolism disorders (including PKU) are on the panel.

options.label: B

options.label: C

options.rationale: Hemoglobinopathies including Hb SS, S/beta-thalassemia, and S,C disease are screened.

options.label: D

options.rationale: Biotinidase deficiency and CCHD (pulse oximetry) are listed, alongside hearing screening.

options.label: E

stem: The course's sample baby card records birth weight 8 lb 10 oz and discharge weight 8 lb 5 oz. How should the PNP interpret the discharge weight loss?

options.label: A
options.text: About 3-4 percent loss, within the expected 5-10 percent window; continue routine feeding follow-up
options.rationale: 5 oz lost from 138 oz birth weight is roughly 3.6 percent, comfortably within the expected 5-10 percent physiologic loss range (here even below it), so routine feeding surveillance and the 2-week weight check apply (Baby card pp42-43; Slide 19).

options.label: B
options.text: About 10 percent loss, requiring admission
options.rationale: Ten percent would be about 14 oz, far more than recorded.

options.label: C
options.text: About 1 percent loss, indicating overfeeding
options.rationale: One percent understates the recorded difference.

options.label: D
options.text: Weight loss cannot be calculated from these values
options.rationale: Both weights are provided precisely to compute percentage loss.

stem: Using the reference chart's infant caloric requirement of about 100 kcal/kg/day, what daily intake does a 5.0-kg 4-month-old require?

options.label: A
options.text: About 250 kcal/day

options.label: B

options.label: C

options.rationale: 750 kcal exceeds infant needs at this weight.

options.label: D

stem: A newborn has a small mandible with posterior displacement of the tongue and upper airway obstruction noted at birth. Which syndrome does the AAFP article associate with micrognathia?

options.label: A
options.text: Pierre Robin sequence
options.rationale: Micrognathia occurs with Pierre Robin sequence (micrognathia, glossoptosis, airway obstruction, often cleft palate) per AAFP Part I (AAFP Part I, mouth).

options.label: B
options.text: Turner syndrome
options.rationale: Turner features include webbed neck, pedal edema, and low-set ears.

options.label: C
options.text: Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome
options.rationale: Beckwith-Wiedemann causes macrosomia and macroglossia, not micrognathia.

options.label: D
options.text: CHARGE syndrome
options.rationale: CHARGE includes coloboma, heart defects, choanal atresia, ear anomalies.

stem: A newborn's eye examination reveals a full-thickness iris coloboma. Which syndromic association and action does the AAFP article direct?

options.label: A
options.text: CHARGE association; formal ophthalmology evaluation
options.rationale: Colobomas may occur with many syndromes including CHARGE (coloboma, heart defects, choanal atresia, growth retardation, genital/urinary anomalies, ear anomalies/deafness), and infants with colobomas need formal ophthalmology evaluation (AAFP Part I, eyes).

options.label: B
options.text: Down syndrome; chromosomal microarray only
options.rationale: Down syndrome eye clues are epicanthal folds and upslanting fissures; microarray alone misses CHARGE workup.

options.label: C
options.text: Marfan syndrome; echocardiography only
options.rationale: Marfan presents with lens dislocation, not coloboma.

options.label: D
options.text: No association; document and discharge
options.rationale: Coloboma always warrants ophthalmology and syndromic evaluation.

questions.sourceMapping: AAFP Part I (coloboma and CHARGE)

stem: At birth, a newborn is noted to have intestines protruding through the abdominal wall to the RIGHT of the umbilicus without a covering sac. Which diagnosis and action pair is correct?

options.text: Gastroschisis; emergent surgical consultation
options.rationale: Gastroschisis is evisceration without a sac, usually right of the umbilicus, and warrants emergent surgical consultation; omphalocele protrudes within a midline sac (AAFP Part II, abdomen).

options.label: B
options.text: Omphalocele; elective repair after 6 months
options.rationale: Omphalocele is midline with a sac and also requires prompt surgical care, not elective delay.

options.label: C
options.text: Umbilical hernia; observe until age 3
options.rationale: Umbilical hernia is skin-covered and reducible.

options.label: D
options.text: Diastasis recti; reassure
options.rationale: Diastasis recti is a midline fascial gap without evisceration.

stem: You palpate the scalp of a newborn delivered vertex after a prolonged labor and note a soft, diffuse area of scalp swelling over the presenting part. The swelling crosses suture lines. The infant is otherwise well appearing.
What is your interpretation of this finding? What management is indicated?

answerBlock.text: Answer source: Faculty Answer Key, Card 1.
Expected diagnosis: Caput succedaneum
Category: BENIGN/EXPECTED
Key reasoning
Soft, diffuse scalp edema.
Crosses suture lines.
Related to pressure on the presenting part during delivery.
Usually resolves spontaneously within several days.
Expected student response
Recognizes the finding as caput succedaneum.
Provides reassurance.
No diagnostic testing is generally required in a well-appearing newborn.
Documents location and appearance and monitors for resolution.

metadata.headingSuffix: Card 1 - Scalp Examination (question stem inferred from the answer key)

questions.title: Card 2 - Scalp Finding
stem: You palpate a well-defined, fluctuant swelling over the right parietal bone that does not cross the suture lines.
The remainder of the examination is normal.
What is your interpretation of this finding? What complication should you monitor for?

answerBlock.text: Answer source: Faculty Answer Key, Card 2.
Expected diagnosis: Cephalohematoma
Category: REQUIRES FOLLOW-UP
Key reasoning
Subperiosteal collection of blood.
Does not cross suture lines.
May take weeks to resolve.
Increased bilirubin load can contribute to neonatal hyperbilirubinemia.
Expected student response
Differentiates cephalohematoma from caput.
Assesses jaundice risk and follows bilirubin as clinically indicated.
Provides reassurance regarding gradual resolution.
Avoids aspiration.

questions.title: Card 3 - Scalp Swelling With Vital-Sign Changes (question stem inferred from the answer key)
stem: Hours after a difficult operative vaginal delivery, you note an increasingly boggy, diffuse scalp swelling that feels fluctuant, appears to shift with pressure, and crosses suture lines. The infant appears pale and is tachycardic.
How do you interpret this finding? What should you do next?

answerBlock.text: Answer source: Faculty Answer Key, Card 3.
Expected diagnosis: Subgaleal hemorrhage
Category: URGENT/EMERGENT
Key reasoning
Blood accumulates in the potential space beneath the scalp aponeurosis.
Swelling may be diffuse and cross suture lines.
Significant blood loss can occur.
Pallor and tachycardia suggest hemodynamic compromise.
Expected student response
Immediately recognizes this as potentially life-threatening.
Initiates urgent/emergency evaluation.
Assesses vital signs and perfusion.
Escalates care rather than arranging routine outpatient follow-up.
Critical safety item.

metadata.headingSuffix: Card 3 - Scalp Swelling With Vital-Sign Changes (question stem inferred from the answer key)

questions.title: Card 4 - Eye Examination
stem: You perform the red reflex examination.
The right red reflex is present and symmetric. The left red reflex is absent.
How do you interpret this finding? What should you do next?

answerBlock.text: Answer source: Faculty Answer Key, Card 4.
Potential concerns: Cataract, retinoblastoma, other ocular abnormality
Category: URGENT/PROMPT SPECIALTY EVALUATION
Key reasoning
Red reflex should be present and symmetric.
An absent or markedly abnormal reflex requires prompt ophthalmologic evaluation.
Expected student response
Recognizes this as abnormal.
Does not reassure the family that this is a normal newborn variation.
Arranges prompt ophthalmology evaluation.
Critical safety item.

questions.title: Card 5 - Oral Examination
stem: During the oral examination, you note that the lingual frenulum appears short and restricts elevation and extension of the tongue.
The parent reports nipple pain during breastfeeding, and the newborn has difficulty maintaining a latch.
What additional assessment is needed? What management would you consider?

answerBlock.text: Answer source: Faculty Answer Key, Card 5.
Expected diagnosis: Symptomatic ankyloglossia
Category: REQUIRES FOLLOW-UP
Expected student response
Assesses breastfeeding effectiveness rather than relying solely on appearance of the frenulum.
Assesses latch, maternal pain, milk transfer, weight and hydration.
Considers lactation support.
Referral/evaluation for frenotomy may be appropriate when significant functional feeding problems persist.

questions.title: Card 6 - Cardiac Examination
stem: You hear a grade II/VI systolic murmur.
The infant is pink and comfortable. Femoral pulses are palpable and symmetric. Feeding is reported as normal.
What additional information or assessment do you need before deciding whether this is an innocent transitional finding or requires further evaluation?

answerBlock.text: Answer source: Faculty Answer Key, Card 6.
Category: REQUIRES FURTHER ASSESSMENT
Expected student assessment
Color/cyanosis.
Respiratory status.
Feeding tolerance.
Precordial activity.
Heart rate/rhythm.
Murmur characteristics.
Brachial and femoral pulses.
Perfusion.
Pulse oximetry/newborn critical congenital heart disease screening results.
Clinical reasoning

A murmur in a newborn should not automatically be labeled innocent. The student should determine whether other findings suggest congenital heart disease and recognize when further cardiac evaluation is indicated.

questions.title: Card 7 - Respiratory Examination
stem: The newborn's respiratory rate is 72 breaths/minute. You observe nasal flaring and intercostal retractions.
How do you interpret these findings? What should you do next?

answerBlock.text: Answer source: Faculty Answer Key, Card 7.
Finding: Neonatal respiratory distress
Category: URGENT
Expected student response
Recognizes tachypnea and increased work of breathing.
Assesses oxygenation, color, temperature, perfusion and feeding.
Recognizes the need for immediate evaluation rather than routine outpatient observation.
Considers a broad differential rather than assuming a single diagnosis.
Critical safety item.

questions.title: Card 8 - Umbilical Examination
stem: The umbilical cord has separated. You observe a small, moist, pink-red area of tissue at the base of the umbilicus with a small amount of clear drainage.
The surrounding skin is not erythematous.
What is the likely explanation? What management may be indicated?

answerBlock.text: Answer source: Faculty Answer Key, Card 8.
Expected diagnosis: Umbilical granuloma
Category: REQUIRES ROUTINE FOLLOW-UP/TREATMENT
Key reasoning
Small amount of moist granulation tissue after cord separation.
Absence of surrounding erythema/systemic symptoms makes omphalitis less likely.
Expected student response
Identifies likely granuloma.
Evaluates for drainage, surrounding infection or anatomic abnormalities.
Discusses appropriate treatment/follow-up.

questions.title: Card 9 - Hip Examination
stem: During the Ortolani maneuver, you appreciate a distinct palpable "clunk" as the left hip is abducted.
How do you interpret this finding? What is the appropriate next step?

answerBlock.text: Answer source: Faculty Answer Key, Card 9.
Concern: Developmental dysplasia of the hip
Category: REQUIRES PROMPT FOLLOW-UP/REFERRAL
Expected student response
Recognizes a true palpable clunk as abnormal.
Does not repeatedly perform provocative maneuvers.
Arranges appropriate orthopedic evaluation and age-appropriate imaging based on clinical guidance.
Critical safety item.

questions.title: Card 10 - Male Genital Examination
stem: You are unable to palpate the right testicle within the scrotum. The left testicle is palpable.
The newborn is otherwise well appearing.
What is your assessment? What follow-up is needed?

answerBlock.text: Answer source: Faculty Answer Key, Card 10.
Expected diagnosis: Cryptorchidism
Category: REQUIRES FOLLOW-UP
Expected student response
Documents whether testis is palpable and its location.
Reassesses during subsequent examinations.
Recognizes need for referral if spontaneous descent does not occur within the expected timeframe.
Does not order routine imaging before referral solely to locate a nonpalpable testis.

questions.title: Card 11 - Male Genital Examination
stem: You note that the urethral opening is located on the ventral surface of the penis rather than at the tip of the glans.
What is your interpretation? What important anticipatory guidance should you provide before the infant leaves your care?

Expected diagnosis: Hypospadias
Category: REQUIRES FOLLOW-UP/REFERRAL
Expected student response
Identifies abnormal urethral location.
Assesses genital anatomy.
Does not recommend circumcision, because foreskin may be needed for surgical repair.
Refers appropriately to pediatric urology.
Critical safety item: circumcision should be deferred.

questions.title: Card 12 - Spine/Sacral Examination
stem: You identify a deep sacral dimple located above the gluteal crease. The base of the dimple cannot be visualized.
Is this an expected newborn finding? What additional evaluation should be considered?

answerBlock.text: Answer source: Faculty Answer Key, Card 12.
Concern: Possible occult spinal dysraphism
Category: REQUIRES FOLLOW-UP/EVALUATION
Concerning features
High location.
Deep lesion.
Base cannot be visualized.
Other concerning cutaneous findings would further increase concern.
Expected student response
Distinguishes this from a simple low sacral dimple.
Recognizes need for further evaluation/imaging based on age and clinical findings.

questions.title: Card 13 - Musculoskeletal Examination
stem: You note that the newborn moves the left arm less than the right. The infant cries when you palpate the left clavicle, and you appreciate crepitus over the area.
What is the most likely explanation? What additional assessment is important?

answerBlock.text: Answer source: Faculty Answer Key, Card 13.
Expected diagnosis: Birth-related clavicular fracture
Category: REQUIRES FOLLOW-UP
Expected student response
Recognizes likely clavicular fracture.
Assesses upper-extremity movement, perfusion and neurologic function.
Considers brachial plexus injury in the differential.
Provides appropriate supportive management and follow-up.

questions.title: Card 14 - Skin Examination (febrile newborn with vesicles)
stem: 2 week old baby with multiple vesicles on erythematous base along with erythematous papules over the trunk and extremities.
The newborn is febrile, and fussy.
What is the likely explanation? Is treatment necessary?

answerBlock.text: Answer source: NOT in the provided Faculty Answer Key - faculty-level answer prepared for this study document.
Note: Numbering mismatch: Faculty Key Card 14 (erythema toxicum neonatorum) does not match this stem, so a faculty-level answer is provided here instead.
Expected diagnosis: Neonatal herpes simplex virus (HSV) infection (skin-eye-mouth disease, with potential for dissemination and CNS involvement) until proven otherwise.
Category: URGENT/EMERGENT
Key reasoning
Vesicles on an erythematous base in a neonate are HSV until excluded; fever and fussiness indicate possible systemic involvement.

The benign mimic, erythema toxicum neonatorum (Faculty Key Card 14), occurs in WELL, afebrile infants as erythematous macules/papules with central pustules - not vesicles with fever. That key card matches Scenario 5 in Part III of this document, not this stem.
Onset at 1-2 weeks of life fits peripartum HSV acquisition.
Expected student response
Recognizes the eruption as non-benign and does not reassure the family.
Initiates urgent evaluation: sepsis-style workup with HSV PCR of blood, CSF and surface swabs; liver enzymes and coagulation studies; assesses eyes and CNS.
Starts empiric IV acyclovir immediately, without waiting for test results.
Institutes contact isolation precautions, involves infectious diseases, and obtains ophthalmology evaluation for keratoconjunctivitis.
Critical safety item.

answerBlock.text: Answer source: Faculty Answer Key, Card 15.
Category: REQUIRES ASSESSMENT
Expected student assessment
Age in hours/days.
Gestational age.
Timing of onset.
Feeding frequency and effectiveness.
Weight change from birth.
Urine/stool output.
Maternal and infant blood type when relevant.
Bruising/cephalohematoma.
Family history and other risk factors.
Bilirubin measurement when indicated.
Expected reasoning
The student should recognize that visual assessment alone is insufficient to determine bilirubin severity and that bilirubin interpretation is based on the infant’s age and clinical risk factors.

Category: GENERALLY BENIGN

Category: URGENT/EMERGENT

questions.title: Picture Case - Feet, Photo A (rigid)
stem: Handwritten note on the card: "foot is rigid can not be moved."
Describe the finding in medical terminology and state your assessment and plan.

images.alt: Photo A: newborn feet - the deformity cannot be passively corrected.
images.caption: Photo A: newborn feet - the deformity cannot be passively corrected.

answerBlock.text: Answer source: NOT in the provided Faculty Answer Key - faculty-level answer prepared for this study document.
Note: The key has no standalone clubfoot card; Card 26 contrasts rigid structural deformity with flexible positional deformity, and a faculty-level answer is provided here.
Expected diagnosis: Congenital talipes equinovarus (clubfoot) - a rigid structural deformity.
Category: REQUIRES PROMPT FOLLOW-UP/REFERRAL
Key reasoning

The foot is held in equinus, hindfoot varus and forefoot adduction/supination and CANNOT be passively brought to neutral - the feature that distinguishes it from a flexible positional deformity (compare Faculty Key Card 26 and Photo B of this station).
May be isolated or associated with neuromuscular conditions or syndromes (e.g., spina bifida, myotonic dystrophy); examine the spine, hips and neurologic status.
Expected student response
Describes the deformity in medical terms and documents that it is rigid/non-correctable.
Does not force correction during the examination.
Refers early to pediatric orthopedics - treatment (Ponseti serial casting, usually with bracing and often percutaneous tenotomy) works best when started in the first weeks of life.
Considers spinal/hip evaluation for associated anomalies and provides parent education about excellent outcomes with early treatment.

questions.title: Picture Case - Feet, Photo B (flexible)
stem: Handwritten note on the card: "foot can be brought to neutral with passive movement."
Describe the finding in medical terminology and state your assessment and plan.

images.alt: Photo B: plantar view - the foot can be brought to neutral with passive movement.
images.caption: Photo B: plantar view - the foot can be brought to neutral with passive movement.

answerBlock.text: Answer source: Faculty Answer Key, Card 26.
Finding: Foot appears turned inward but can be gently brought into a normal position.
Likely finding: Flexible positional deformity
Category: FOLLOW-UP/OBSERVATION
Expected response: Assesses flexibility and distinguishes a flexible positional finding from a rigid structural deformity such as clubfoot.

questions.title: Picture Case - Scalp Swellings, Photos A-D (one station, two infants)
stem: Four photographs from a single examination station. Photos A and B are two views of the same infant; photos C and D are two views of a second infant.
Handwritten notes on the cards read: A - "fluid moves when pressure applied"; C - "palpation leave..." (the remainder of note C is cut off at the edge of the photograph).
Identify each pattern of scalp swelling, explain how you would distinguish them on examination, and give your management for each.
Photo A (infant 1, lateral view) - note: "fluid moves when pressure applied."
Photo B (infant 1, frontal view).
Photo C (infant 2, lateral view) - note begins "palpation leave..." (truncated in original photo).
Photo D (infant 2, vertex view).

answerBlock.text: Answer source: Faculty Answer Key, Cards 1-3 (all three scalp cards apply to this station).
This station covers the three neonatal scalp swellings of the Faculty Answer Key (Cards 1-3). The full key text for all three follows; match each photograph to the pattern described.
Card 1 - Diffuse Scalp Swelling
Expected diagnosis: Caput succedaneum
Category: BENIGN/EXPECTED
Soft, diffuse scalp edema.
Crosses suture lines.
Related to pressure on the presenting part during delivery.
Usually resolves spontaneously within several days.
Student: recognizes caput succedaneum, provides reassurance, no diagnostic testing generally required in a well-appearing newborn, documents location/appearance and monitors for resolution.
Card 2 - Localized Scalp Swelling
Expected diagnosis: Cephalohematoma
Category: REQUIRES FOLLOW-UP
Subperiosteal collection of blood.
Does not cross suture lines.
May take weeks to resolve.
Increased bilirubin load can contribute to neonatal hyperbilirubinemia.
Student: differentiates cephalohematoma from caput, assesses jaundice risk and follows bilirubin as clinically indicated, reassures regarding gradual resolution, avoids aspiration.
Card 3 - Increasing Boggy Scalp Swelling + Pallor/Tachycardia
Expected diagnosis: Subgaleal hemorrhage
Category: URGENT/EMERGENT
Blood accumulates in the potential space beneath the scalp aponeurosis.
Swelling may be diffuse and cross suture lines.
Significant blood loss can occur.
Pallor and tachycardia suggest hemodynamic compromise.

Student: immediately recognizes this as potentially life-threatening, initiates urgent/emergency evaluation, assesses vital signs and perfusion, escalates care rather than arranging routine outpatient follow-up. Critical safety item.
Applying the photographs
Diffuse, soft/pitting edema of the presenting part that crosses suture lines (fluid shifts/pits with pressure) = caput succedaneum - reassure, no testing in a well infant.
A discrete, firm-to-fluctuant collection confined to one bone that does NOT cross suture lines (best seen on the vertex view, Photo D) = cephalohematoma - follow bilirubin; do not aspirate.
A boggy, fluctuant swelling that shifts/ballots with pressure and expands - especially with pallor or tachycardia = subgaleal hemorrhage - emergency escalation.

questions.title: Picture Case - Face / Medial Canthi
stem: Printed question on the card (partially obscured by equipment in the photograph): "Describe what you see using medical terminology ... medial canthi of both ... to identify."
Examine the photograph and identify the finding.
Printed card photo: newborn face - note the blue-gray discoloration at the medial canthus/infraorbital region.

answerBlock.text: Answer source: Faculty Answer Key, Card 17.

Note: Key Card 17 describes the typical sacral/buttock location; periorbital/facial involvement (including the medial canthi, as photographed) is a recognized variant. The key teaching - document it and distinguish it from bruising - applies unchanged.
Finding: Flat blue-gray patch over the sacral/buttock region.
Diagnosis: Congenital dermal melanocytosis
Category: BENIGN
Expected response: Recognizes benign birthmark. Documents location, size and appearance to distinguish it from bruising in future examinations. Reassures family.

questions.title: Picture Case - Eyes, Photo 1 (red reflex)
stem: Printed question on the card: "Describe what you see using medical terminology. List two potential diagnoses."
Printed card photo: red reflex view - compare the two eyes.

answerBlock.text: Answer source: Faculty Answer Key, Card 4.
Potential concerns: Cataract, retinoblastoma, other ocular abnormality
Category: URGENT/PROMPT SPECIALTY EVALUATION
Key reasoning
Red reflex should be present and symmetric.
An absent or markedly abnormal reflex requires prompt ophthalmologic evaluation.
Expected student response
Recognizes this as abnormal.
Does not reassure the family that this is a normal newborn variation.
Arranges prompt ophthalmology evaluation.
Critical safety item.

questions.title: Picture Case - Eyes, Photo 2 (lid swelling and discharge)
stem: Printed question on the card: "Describe what you see using medical terminology? List 3 differentials indicating the most likely."
Printed card photo: newborn eyes with lid swelling and discharge at the canthi.

answerBlock.text: Answer source: NOT in the provided Faculty Answer Key - faculty-level answer prepared for this study document.

Expected diagnosis: Neonatal conjunctivitis (ophthalmia neonatorum). Most likely/important cause until excluded: Neisseria gonorrhoeae. Differentials: Chlamydia trachomatis conjunctivitis; other bacterial conjunctivitis or dacryocystitis; (within the first 24-48 h) chemical conjunctivitis.
Category: URGENT/EMERGENT
Key reasoning
Marked lid edema with purulent discharge in a newborn is gonococcal conjunctivitis until proven otherwise; it can perforate the cornea within days.
Timing helps: chemical <48 h; gonococcal 2-5 days and purulent; chlamydial 5-14 days, watery progressing to purulent, often with lid swelling.
This is NOT nasolacrimal duct obstruction (Faculty Key Card 27), which causes recurrent tearing/mucoid discharge WITHOUT significant conjunctival erythema or lid edema.
Expected student response
Obtains urgent conjunctival Gram stain, culture and NAAT (gonorrhea/chlamydia); considers HSV if vesicles or corneal involvement.

Starts prompt systemic therapy per suspicion (gonococcal: systemic third-generation cephalosporin plus frequent saline irrigation; chlamydial: systemic macrolide, with counseling about pyloric stenosis risk) - topical therapy alone is insufficient.
Examines the cornea, monitors for systemic involvement/sepsis, addresses maternal and partner treatment per public-health guidance, and isolates per policy.
Critical safety item.

metadata.headingSuffix: Picture Case - Eyes, Photo 2 (lid swelling and discharge)

questions.title: Picture Case - Eyes, Photo 3 ("what is the cause of this finding?")
stem: Printed question on the card: "Describe what you see? What is the cause of this finding?"
Printed card photo: both eyes, standard (non-coaxial) photograph.

answerBlock.text: Answer source: NOT in the provided Faculty Answer Key - faculty-level answer prepared for this study document.
Description

Both eyes show dark pupils, each with a single small, bright, symmetric pinpoint light reflection; there is no white pupil (leukocoria), and no red reflex is demonstrated because this is a standard (non-coaxial) photograph. Lids, conjunctivae and ocular alignment appear unremarkable.
Cause of the finding

The small white dots are normal specular (corneal) light reflections of the light source - not a red reflex and not leukocoria. The red reflex can only be judged with coaxial illumination (direct ophthalmoscope, dimmed room, about 15 cm): light reflecting off the retina through clear media produces the normal bright red-orange glow.
Expected student response
Does not mistake the corneal light reflection for a red reflex, and does not mistake a dark pupil on a standard photograph for leukocoria.
Performs and interprets a true red reflex examination on both eyes.
Any absent, white, dull or asymmetric reflex is referred urgently to ophthalmology (same principle as Faculty Key Card 4).

metadata.headingSuffix: Picture Case - Eyes, Photo 3 ("what is the cause of this finding?")

questions.title: Picture Case - Eyes, Photo 4 ("do you see a light reflex?")
stem: Printed question on the card: "Describe what you see in medical terms? Do you see a light reflex?"
Printed card photo: eye with lids gently held open by gloved fingers.

answerBlock.text: Answer source: NOT in the provided Faculty Answer Key - faculty-level answer prepared for this study document (management principles mirror Faculty Key Card 4).
Description
With the lids gently held open, the pupil/media return a dull gray-white glow instead of a bright, symmetric red reflex - an absent/abnormal red reflex (leukocoria) of this eye.
Do you see a light reflex?
No normal red reflex is seen. Only surface (specular) reflections from the lids and cornea are present; the reflex through the pupil is dull/white-gray.
Key reasoning / differential
Cataract, retinoblastoma, corneal opacity, persistent fetal vasculature, vitreous hemorrhage or severe retinal disease.
Expected student response
Recognizes the reflex as abnormal, does not reassure the family, and arranges prompt ophthalmology evaluation (same principle as Faculty Key Card 4).
Critical safety item.

questions.title: Scenario 1 - Jaundice, 5 days old
stem: A parent brings in a 5-day-old because the baby's skin and eyes look increasingly yellow. The infant is exclusively breastfed and seems sleepier during feeds. The parent reports 4 wet diapers in the past 24 hours.
What would you do? What additional history and examination would you obtain? What testing, if any, is indicated? What determines the urgency of your management?

answerBlock.text: Answer source: Faculty Answer Key, Card 15.

Note: Key Card 15 is written for day-4 jaundice; the identical assessment framework applies to this day-5 scenario (suboptimal intake - 4 wet diapers, sleepiness - makes breastfeeding/before (suboptimal intake) jaundice with dehydration the leading concern, and a measured bilirubin plotted on hour-specific nomogram is mandatory).
Category: REQUIRES ASSESSMENT
Expected student assessment
Age in hours/days.
Gestational age.
Timing of onset.
Feeding frequency and effectiveness.
Weight change from birth.
Urine/stool output.
Maternal and infant blood type when relevant.
Bruising/cephalohematoma.
Family history and other risk factors.
Bilirubin measurement when indicated.
Expected reasoning
The student should recognize that visual assessment alone is insufficient to determine bilirubin severity and that bilirubin interpretation is based on the infant’s age and clinical risk factors.

questions.title: Scenario 2 - Bloody Stool, 6 weeks old
stem: A parent reports seeing several streaks of bright red blood and mucus in the infant’s stool. The infant is exclusively breastfed, feeding well, gaining weight, and has no fever, vomiting, or abdominal distention.
What would you do? What are your differential diagnoses? What additional examination is important? What would you recommend to the parent?

answerBlock.text: Answer source: NOT in the provided Faculty Answer Key - faculty-level answer prepared for this study document.
Most likely diagnosis: Food protein-induced allergic proctocolitis (FPIAP, typically cow’s milk protein transferred through breast milk).
Category: REQUIRES OUTPATIENT ASSESSMENT/FOLLOW-UP (well-appearing, thriving infant).
Differential considerations
Anal fissure (most common cause of streaky bright red blood; inspect the anus).
Food protein-induced allergic proctocolitis.
Infectious colitis (usually with diarrhea, fever, or ill appearance).
Swallowed maternal blood (Apt test applies in the neonatal period, not at 6 weeks).
Rare/surgical causes if NOT well appearing: intussusception, volvulus/malrotation, necrotizing enterocolitis, coagulopathy/vitamin K deficiency.
Expected student response
Completes a focused examination: growth parameters, hydration, abdominal exam, and perianal inspection for fissure.
Reviews feeding, stool pattern, recent travel or antibiotic exposures, and family history of allergy or inflammatory bowel disease.

For FPIAP in a breastfed infant: maternal elimination of cow’s milk protein (usually also soy) for 2-4 weeks with expected resolution of bleeding, then guided rechallenge; if formula-fed, switch to extensively hydrolyzed formula.
Reassures that the condition is benign and self-limited in a thriving infant and that breastfeeding can usually continue.
Gives return precautions: increased blood, bilious vomiting, distention, fever, lethargy, poor weight gain.
Avoids unnecessary antibiotics, hospitalization or extensive stool testing in the well infant; limited tests (e.g., CBC, stool culture) only if atypical features.
Critical teaching point: a WELL, thriving infant with streaky hematochezia is managed very differently from an ill infant with bloody stool (Faculty Key Card 37 - emergent).

questions.title: Scenario 3 - Fever, 6 weeks old
stem: A parent calls because the infant felt warm and has a rectal temperature of 100.6°F (38.1°C). The baby is slightly sleepier than usual but is still taking bottles. There are no obvious respiratory or gastrointestinal symptoms.
What would you do? Does the infant’s appearance change your management? What should you tell the parent?

answerBlock.text: Answer source: Faculty Answer Key, Card 32.

Note: Key Card 32 is written for a 12-day-old; the same urgent principle governs any febrile infant ≤8 weeks (rectal ≥38.0°C = full sepsis evaluation and empiric antibiotics/HSV consideration per age-based protocol, in person today - never "watch and wait"). Appearance does NOT reliably exclude serious bacterial infection, though ill appearance raises urgency further.
Finding: A 12-day-old infant has a rectal temperature of 38.1°C (100.6°F).
Category: URGENT
Expected response: Recognizes fever in a neonate as requiring immediate medical evaluation for possible serious bacterial infection rather than routine outpatient observation.
Critical safety item.

questions.title: Scenario 4 - Prolonged Crying, 7 weeks old
stem: Parents report that their infant cries for 3-4 hours most evenings, usually beginning around 6 PM. The infant draws the legs toward the abdomen, becomes red in the face, and is difficult to console. Between episodes, the infant feeds normally and appears happy. Growth is appropriate.
What would you do? What diagnoses would you consider? What findings would you specifically look for before reassuring the parents? What anticipatory guidance would you provide?

answerBlock.text: Answer source: NOT in the provided Faculty Answer Key - faculty-level answer prepared for this study document.
Most likely diagnosis: Colic (excessive crying of infancy; a behavioral/developmental pattern, diagnosis of exclusion in a thriving infant).
Category: BENIGN/REASSURANCE WITH FOLLOW-UP.
Differential / exclusions before reassuring

Corneal abrasion, hair tourniquet (digit/penis), otitis media, hernia (incarcerated), anal fissure, gastroesophageal reflux with esophagitis, cow’s milk protein allergy, urinary tract infection, supraventricular tachycardia/other pain sources.
Expected student response
Takes a structured crying/feeding/sleep history (onset, duration, consolability, stooling, parental coping) and confirms normal growth.
Performs a complete examination including eyes (fluorescein if suspected), hair tourniquet check of digits/genitalia, ears, hernia orifices, anus, abdomen, and neurologic status.
Reassures that colic typically peaks around 6 weeks and resolves by 3-4 months; the infant is not in pain from a dangerous cause.

Offers soothing strategies: swaddling, side-held shushing, swinging, sucking, white noise, paced feeding with burping, avoiding overfeeding; avoids unproven or unsafe remedies (dicyclomine, alcohol-containing gripe water).
Screens for parental exhaustion, safety of shaking (never shake), and postpartum depression; arranges follow-up and respite plans.
Critical safety item: shaken-baby prevention counseling.

questions.title: Scenario 5 - Rash, 3 weeks old
stem: A parent is concerned about a rash that appeared several days ago. Examination reveals numerous small erythematous papules and pustules over the cheeks and forehead. The infant is afebrile, feeding normally, and appears well.
What would you do? How would you describe the rash? What are your differentials? Would you treat it, observe it, or obtain additional testing?

answerBlock.text: Answer source: Faculty Answer Key, Card 14.
Note: This is the scenario that matches Faculty Key Card 14. (The febrile, vesicular Card 14 stem in Part I is a different - and urgent - entity; see Question 14.)
Expected diagnosis: Erythema toxicum neonatorum
Category: BENIGN/EXPECTED
Expected student response
Recognizes classic benign newborn eruption.
Notes infant is otherwise well.
Provides reassurance.
No treatment is required.

questions.title: Scenario 6 - Crying With Feeding, 2 months old
stem: A parent reports that the infant has recently started crying during feeds. The infant begins feeding eagerly but then pulls away from the bottle, cries, and tries to feed again. There is also increased drooling. There is no fever or vomiting.
What would you do? What areas would you examine carefully? What diagnoses are on your differential? What additional questions would help determine the cause?

answerBlock.text: Answer source: NOT in the provided Faculty Answer Key - faculty-level answer prepared for this study document.
Differential considerations
Oral lesions: Candida thrush, herpetic gingivostomatitis/enteroviral ulcers (painful vesicles/ulcers), teething (possible but early at 2 months).
Otitis media (sucking/swallowing changes middle-ear pressure).
Nasal obstruction/congestion preventing breathe-while-feeding.
Gastroesophageal reflux with esophagitis.
Pharyngitis/tonsillitis; corneal abrasion or other pain as always in a crying infant.
Expected student response
Examines carefully: oral cavity (buccal mucosa, palate, gums, tongue, posterior pharynx), ears, eyes, neck, skin including hands/feet, and growth/hydration.
Asks about fever, sick contacts, daycare/siblings, stooling, urine output, maternal nipple pain (thrush), feeding volume and technique, drooling/voicing changes, and immunization status.

Manages per finding: e.g., nystatin for thrush with attention to feeding equipment and maternal nipples; supportive care (and acyclovir consideration if disseminated/herpetic with systemic signs); antibiotics for acute otitis media meeting criteria; reflux measures if esophagitis suspected.
Provides return precautions for poor intake, dehydration, fever, or respiratory symptoms and schedules weight/follow-up check.

questions.title: Scenario 7 - Abnormal Head Shape / Absent Anterior Fontanelle, 2 months old
stem: During a well-child examination, you notice an unusual elongated and asymmetric head shape. You are unable to palpate an open anterior fontanelle, and the parent reports that the head has "looked a little different" since birth. Head circumference is tracking along its previous percentile.
What would you do next? What conditions are you concerned about? What aspects of the skull examination are particularly important, and does this infant require referral?

answerBlock.text: Answer source: NOT in the provided Faculty Answer Key - faculty-level answer prepared for this study document.
Primary concern: Craniosynostosis (premature fusion of one or more cranial sutures; sagittal scaphocephaly most common), with a closed/absent anterior fontanelle.
Category: REQUIRES PROMPT REFERRAL (pediatric neurosurgery/craniofacial team).
Differential considerations
Positional/deformational plagiocephaly (fontanelle open, no suture ridging; flattens with positioning).
Microcephaly or primary brain growth failure (small HC, open sutures).
Syndromic craniosynostosis (e.g., Crouzon, Apert - look for dysmorphic features, midface hypoplasia, proptosis).
Expected student response

Performs a detailed skull examination: palpation for ridged/fused sutures, fontanelle status, head-shape pattern (scapho-, plagio-, brachy-, trigonocephaly), and serial head circumferences on the growth curve.
Recognizes that a normal head-circumference trajectory does NOT exclude synostosis early, and that a closed anterior fontanelle at 2 months is abnormal.
Reviews development and searches for dysmorphic/associated anomalies (hips, hands, palate).
Refers promptly to pediatric neurosurgery/craniofacial surgery (corrective surgery typically in the first year); imaging (e.g., 3D CT) per specialist rather than as a gatekeeping requirement.
Counsels parents that the condition is treatable and that early referral improves outcomes; does not prescribe repositioning therapy as treatment for true synostosis.
