questions.title: Scenario 8 - Persistent Jaundice, 4 weeks old
stem: A 4-week-old remains visibly jaundiced. The infant is gaining weight and breastfeeding well. When you ask about elimination, the parent says the baby’s stools have recently become very pale or "almost white."

What would you do? How does this information change your differential diagnosis? What additional questions, examination, and laboratory evaluation are needed? How quickly should this infant be evaluated?

answerBlock.text: Answer source: NOT in the provided Faculty Answer Key - faculty-level answer prepared for this study document.
Primary concern: Cholestatic (conjugated) hyperbilirubinemia - biliary atresia until proven otherwise.
Category: URGENT, TIME-SENSITIVE EVALUATION (surgical outcomes best when Kasai portoenterostomy is performed early, ideally before 6-8 weeks of age).
Differential considerations
Biliary atresia.
Neonatal hepatitis/idiopathic giant-cell hepatitis; viral (CMV, etc.).
Alagille syndrome; choledochal cyst; inspissated bile/mucus plug.
Metabolic/endocrine: galactosemia, hypothyroidism, tyrosinemia; TPN- or sepsis-associated cholestasis.
Expected student response
Recognizes that jaundice beyond 2 weeks of age PLUS acholic (pale/white) stools mandates a FRACTIONATED (direct/conjugated) bilirubin now - not reassurance, not a breastfeeding-jaundice label.

Orders: total and direct bilirubin, liver enzymes/GGT, alkaline phosphatase, albumin, PT/INR, TSH, glucose; considers blood/urine culture, CMV testing, metabolic workup, and sweat/alpha-1 antitrypsin as guided.
Asks about stool color over time (stool-color card), urine color (dark), bleeding/bruising (fat-soluble vitamin deficiency), pruritus, family history, and galactosemia screening result.
Examines for hepatosplenomegaly, growth, and signs of fat-soluble vitamin deficiency; gives vitamin K if coagulopathic.
Arranges urgent (days, not weeks) pediatric hepatology/surgery referral with abdominal ultrasound (e.g., triangular cord sign) per specialist.
Critical safety item: missing biliary atresia delays curative-intent surgery.

stem: A 26-month-old is brought for a well-child visit. The child insists on putting on shoes independently, becomes frustrated when helped, and protests loudly when a parent completes the task for them. According to Erikson's framework, mastery of this developmental task yields which virtue?

options.label: A
options.text: Will, through successful resolution of autonomy versus shame and doubt
options.rationale: The toddler stage (1-3 years) is defined by autonomy versus shame and doubt, with the virtue of will; insisting on self-dressing and wanting control over the environment is the hallmark struggle of this stage, and the professor stressed that failure at this stage produces shame and doubt.

options.label: B
options.text: Competence, through successful resolution of industry versus inferiority
options.rationale: Industry versus inferiority (virtue: competence) describes school-age children (5-11 years).

options.label: C
options.text: Purpose, through successful resolution of initiative versus guilt
options.rationale: Initiative versus guilt (virtue: purpose) describes the preschool period (3-5 years), not a 26-month-old.

options.label: D
options.text: Hope, through successful resolution of trust versus mistrust
options.rationale: Trust versus mistrust (virtue: hope) is the infancy crisis of the first year of life.

questions.sourceMapping: Slide 3 (Developmental Theories - Toddler); Slide 18; Week 3 transcript, developmental theory discussion

stem: A 4-year-old spends a well visit narrating an elaborate story about a dragon living in the exam room, assigns the clinician a role in the story, and assumes the clinician sees the room exactly as he does. These behaviors are best explained by which cognitive stage?

options.label: A
options.text: Concrete operational stage, characterized by logical reasoning and conservation
options.rationale: Concrete operational (school age) adds logical thought, sequencing, and conservation, which are not the behaviors described.

options.label: B
options.text: Sensorimotor stage, dominated by object permanence and sensory coordination
options.rationale: Sensorimotor (0-2 years) centers on coordinating senses and acquiring object permanence, not symbolic storytelling.

options.label: C
options.text: Formal operational stage, characterized by abstract and hypothetical reasoning
options.rationale: Formal operational reasoning emerges in adolescence and is not described in this course's age span.

options.label: D
options.text: Preoperational stage, characterized by symbolic thought, imaginative play, and egocentrism
options.rationale: Piaget's preoperational stage (roughly 2-7 years) features symbolic and imaginative play, thinking beyond the present, and egocentrism - exactly the pretend narrative and perspective limitation described.

questions.sourceMapping: Slide 18 (Developmental Theories - Preschool, Piaget preoperational); Week 3 transcript, preschool discussion

stem: A 15-month-old presents for a health maintenance visit. The parent reports the child gestures, walks independently, and feeds themselves finger foods. which additional finding would mandate further evaluation?

options.label: A
options.text: No words at all in the child's current expressive vocabulary
options.rationale: The table lists 'no words' among the 15-month warning signs; absence of any expressive words at this age is a red flag requiring audiologic and developmental evaluation. The professor emphasized this table is organized as 'if they are NOT doing this, it is a problem.'

options.label: B
options.text: Self-feeding with fingers during most family meals
options.rationale: Self-feeding is an expected 15-month skill; its absence ('no self-feeding') is the listed red flag.

options.label: C
options.text: Consistent use of pointing to request desired objects
options.rationale: Pointing to request objects is expected by 12 months and is reassuring, not concerning.

options.label: D
options.text: Independent walking achieved at 13 months of age
options.rationale: Walking by 13 months is within normal limits; the table flags 'no attempts at walking' at 15 months.

questions.sourceMapping: Slide 15 (developmental warning signs table, 12-15 months); Week 3 transcript, 'this table is telling you if they're not doing this, it's a problem'

stem: A 12-month-old with no vaccine contraindications presents for the first birthday visit. Immunization review shows completion of the 6-month primary series only. Select all vaccines that should be administered at this visit.

options.label: A
options.text: Hepatitis A dose 2
options.rationale: follows dose 1 (offered at the 18-month visit in this schedule if not already given); it is not due at 12 months.

options.label: B
options.text: Pneumococcal conjugate (PCV) dose 4
options.rationale: PCV #4 completes the series at the 12-15 month visit.

options.label: C
options.text: DTaP dose 5
options.rationale: DTaP #5 belongs to the 4-6 year school-entry boosters, not the first birthday.

options.label: D
options.text: Varicella dose 1
options.rationale: Varicella #1 is due at the 12-15 month visit per the course schedule.

options.label: E
options.text: Measles-mumps-rubella (MMR) dose 1
options.rationale: MMR #1 is due at the 12-15 month visit per the course schedule.

questions.sourceMapping: Slide 5 (12-15 month anticipatory guidance/immunizations); Slide 24; AFP HCM Part I (Riley 2019), immunization section

stem: A 20-month-old consumes 30 ounces of whole milk daily, eats few solids, and appears pale. Laboratory studies confirm microcytic anemia. Which mechanism best explains the association between excessive cow's milk intake and this anemia?

options.label: A
options.text: Milk fat sequesters zinc in the gut and suppresses erythropoietin production
options.rationale: Milk fat does not sequester zinc or suppress erythropoietin; this mechanism is fabricated.

options.label: B
options.text: Calcium competes with non-heme iron for intestinal absorption and milk displaces iron-rich solids
options.rationale: The professor explained that calcium binds the same intestinal transport pathway as non-heme iron, inhibiting absorption, and that milk-filled stomachs reduce intake of iron-rich foods - the dual mechanism behind milk-induced iron deficiency anemia; whole milk should be capped near 16 ounces per day.

options.label: C
options.text: Lactose accelerates gut transit time and prevents folate absorption in the jejunum
options.rationale: Lactose does not block folate absorption; folate deficiency produces macrocytic, not microcytic, anemia.

options.label: D
options.text: Casein binds vitamin B12 in the stomach and increases its renal excretion
options.rationale: Casein does not cause B12 loss; pernicious-type B12 mechanisms are not implicated in toddler milk overconsumption.

questions.sourceMapping: Week 3 transcript, milk-volume discussion ('calcium can bind and prevent the absorption of iron'); Slide 4 (whole milk no more than 16 oz/day); course nutrition table

stem: During a 14-month well-child exam, the clinician suspends the child forward and notes absent extension of the arms toward the surface. The professor highlighted this reflex as essential at this age. Its primary protective function is to:

options.label: A
options.text: Allow the head-heavy toddler to catch themselves and avoid facial injury when falling
options.rationale: Toddlers are head-heavy during rapid brain growth; the parachute reflex lets them extend the arms to catch themselves when falling forward, preventing face-first injury - the professor's explicit rationale for checking it at the 12-15 month exam.

options.label: B
options.text: Stimulate myelination of the corticospinal tracts during gait maturation
options.rationale: Primitive reflexes do not drive myelination; this reverses cause and effect.

options.label: C
options.text: Maintain upright trunk posture while the child learns to cruise furniture
options.rationale: Trunk posture in cruising relies on proximal strength and equilibrium reactions, not the parachute reflex.

options.label: D
options.text: Prevent aspiration by coordinating swallow and airway protection
options.rationale: Airway protection is mediated by swallow and gag coordination, unrelated to the parachute response.

questions.sourceMapping: Slide 4 (12-15 month physical exam, parachute reflex); Week 3 transcript, parachute reflex discussion

stem: A capillary lead screen at a 24-month visit returns 14 mcg/dL in an asymptomatic child. According to the confirmatory testing schedule taught in this course, the confirmatory venous specimen should be obtained:

options.label: A
options.text: Within 1 month of the capillary result
options.rationale: Capillary results of 10-19 mcg/dL require venous confirmation within 1 month; the professor stressed 'if you get somebody that has a 10 to 19, you've got to make sure you're seeing them within a month.'

options.label: B
options.text: Within 48 hours of the capillary result
options.rationale: Within 48 hours applies to capillary results of 45 mcg/dL or higher.

options.label: C
options.text: Within 3 months of the capillary result
options.rationale: Within 3 months applies to capillary results of 3.5-9 mcg/dL.

options.label: D
options.text: Within 2 weeks of the capillary result
options.rationale: Within 2 weeks applies to capillary results of 20-44 mcg/dL.

questions.sourceMapping: Slide 10 (Lead Exposure: Testing & Follow-up); NYC DOHMH Lead Guidelines (2023) confirmatory schedule; Week 3 transcript, lead follow-up discussion

stem: A 3-year-old with a confirmed venous blood lead level of 52 mcg/dL is asymptomatic, and the family reports ongoing renovation of a pre-1978 home. What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.label: A
options.text: Repeat venous lead in 1-3 months with dietary counseling only
options.rationale: Watchful waiting is inappropriate at 45 mcg/dL or above; that range requires urgent action, not interval recheck.

options.label: B
options.text: Referral to early intervention and repeat lead level in 6 months
options.rationale: Developmental referral is adjunctive; it does not address the urgent toxicologic threshold reached here.

options.label: C
options.text: Urgent expert consultation and chelation once ongoing exposure is controlled
options.rationale: A BLL of 45 mcg/dL or higher mandates urgent expert consultation and chelation, initiated after the environmental source is controlled; the child must not be returned to an uncontrolled exposure site. The professor flagged 'anything greater than 45' as an immediate-seeing threshold and 'really abnormal.'

options.label: D
options.text: Outpatient oral chelation today with discharge to the same home
options.rationale: Chelation before source control, with discharge to the same lead-exposing home, violates the core rule that treatment fails if the environment is not made lead-safe.

questions.sourceMapping: Slides 9 and 11 (Lead management by venous BLL; MUST KNOW pearls); NYC DOHMH Lead Guidelines (2023), BLL >=45; Week 3 transcript, lead levels discussion

stem: When managing a child with a blood lead level of 8 mcg/dL, the clinician orders ferritin and dietary review of iron and calcium intake. The physiological rationale for this step is that:

options.label: A
options.text: Calcium supplements bind circulating lead and renally clear the chelated complex
options.rationale: Calcium reduces absorption of ingested lead but does not chelate circulating lead.

options.label: B
options.text: Iron repletion activates a bone enzyme that demethylates and clears stored lead
options.rationale: No demethylation enzyme exists for lead; this option is mechanistically false.

options.label: C
options.text: Lead, iron, and calcium share an intestinal binding site, so deficiency increases lead uptake
options.rationale: The professor explained that lead binds in the small intestine at the same site as iron and calcium; replete iron and calcium stores competitively reduce gastrointestinal lead absorption - a MUST KNOW pearl on the treatment slide.

options.label: D
options.text: Lead chelates hepatic ferritin stores and produces a functional iron overload state
options.rationale: Lead does not chelate ferritin or cause iron overload; iron deficiency is the relevant association.

questions.sourceMapping: Slide 11 (Lead Treatment Pearls: evaluate iron deficiency, optimize iron and calcium); Slide 8; Week 3 transcript, iron/calcium/lead binding discussion; NYC DOHMH Lead Guidelines (2023)

stem: A 15-month-old's parent asks whether they should switch from whole milk to 2% milk to 'get ahead of cholesterol.' Per the course's dietary guidance, the most appropriate response is that:

options.label: A
options.text: Skim milk is preferred now, because caloric density must fall after the first birthday
options.rationale: Caloric density should not be reduced by skim milk in the second year; the restriction contradicts the table.

options.label: B
options.text: All milk should stop, because fortified soy beverage replaces dairy after 12 months
options.rationale: Fortified soy beverage is an alternative for dairy intolerance, not a mandated replacement after 12 months.

options.label: C
options.text: Whole milk should continue, because low-fat products are not recommended before age 2
options.rationale: The table specifies whole milk or milk products (2 cups/day) for ages 1-2 years and footnotes that low-fat products are not recommended under age 2; the professor noted the fat supports brain development.

options.label: D
options.text: 2% milk is preferred now, because saturated fat restriction begins at 12 months
options.rationale: Saturated fat restriction is not initiated at 12 months; dietary fat is essential for neural development in this window.

questions.sourceMapping: Course nutrition table (Dairy row and low-fat footnote); Week 3 transcript, whole-milk fat and brain development discussion

stem: At an 18-month visit the parent reports the child does not bring objects over to show the parent, plays mainly by mouthing toys, and falls frequently while walking. Which interpretation is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: Showing objects is a 30-month skill, so its absence is not yet concerning
options.rationale: Pulling a person to show something is an 18-month expectation, not a 30-month skill.

options.label: B
options.text: All three findings are 18-month warning signs requiring developmental evaluation
options.rationale: The 18-month warning-signs row includes 'does not pull person to show something,' 'primary play: mouthing of toys,' and 'not yet walking or frequently falls when walking' - all three reported findings are red flags.

options.label: C
options.text: Frequent falls are expected until 24 months and need no evaluation
options.rationale: Frequent falls at 18 months is explicitly a warning sign, not an expected variant.

options.label: D
options.text: Mouthing toys is normal at 18 months if the child also stacks two blocks
options.rationale: Mouthing as primary play is listed as abnormal at 18 months regardless of block stacking.

questions.sourceMapping: Slide 16 (developmental warning signs table, 18 months); Week 3 transcript, red-flag table discussion

stem: A 24-month-old says about 10 words, produces no two-word phrases, points to wants, follows simple commands, and has an older sibling who 'talked late.' Growth is normal. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.text: Order emergent neuroimaging as the first-line study for isolated expressive delay
options.rationale: Neuroimaging is reserved for regression or focal neurologic signs, not first-line isolated expressive delay.

options.label: B
options.text: Reassure the family and reassess expressive language at the 30-month visit
options.rationale: Reassurance alone misses a documented red flag and delays the early-intervention window that closes at age 3 in many jurisdictions.

options.label: C
options.text: Order audiologic testing and refer for speech-language and developmental evaluation
options.rationale: A 2-year-old should have roughly 50 words and two-word phrases; absent meaningful two-word phrases is a 24-month red flag, and the case discussion mandated hearing testing, autism/developmental screening (M-CHAT), and speech/early-intervention referral regardless of family history.

options.label: D
options.text: Attribute the delay to the sibling history and observe for another 6 months
options.rationale: A 'late talker' sibling history is worth noting but does not excuse evaluation; the professor explicitly rejected this reasoning in the case debrief.

questions.sourceMapping: Slide 14 (2-year language milestones); Slide 16 table (no meaningful two-word phrases at 24 months); Week 3 transcript, Case 1 debrief (speech eval, hearing test, M-CHAT, early intervention, lead level)

stem: A 20-month-old previously said 'mama,' 'dada,' and six other words but has lost all of them over four months. The parent attributes this to a new sibling. The single most important interpretation is that:

options.label: A
options.text: Regression is expected during family stress and resolves without workup
options.rationale: Psychosocial stress does not excuse regression; organic causes must be excluded first.

options.label: B
options.text: Selective mutism explains the loss and requires behavioral therapy only
options.rationale: Selective mutism is a consistent failure to speak in specific settings, not loss of acquired words.

options.label: C
options.text: Loss of acquired milestones is a red flag requiring prompt neurologic and developmental evaluation
options.rationale: The professor stated that gaining and then losing a milestone is 'a huge red flag' raising concern for a neurodegenerative or neurologic process warranting developmental-neurology evaluation.

options.label: D
options.text: Language loss before age 2 has no neurologic significance if motor skills are intact
options.rationale: Motor sparing does not exclude neurologic disease; regression in any domain is concerning.

questions.sourceMapping: Week 3 transcript, Case 1 twist ('when anybody gains a milestone and loses a milestone, it's a huge red flag')

stem: During an 18-month health maintenance visit, several findings are documented. select all findings that constitute red flags requiring further evaluation.

options.label: A
options.text: Uses mouthing of toys as the primary form of play
options.rationale: 'Primary play: mouthing of toys' is listed in the 18-month cognitive column as a warning sign.

options.label: B
options.text: Does not pull a person to show an object of interest
options.rationale: 'Does not pull person to show something' is listed in the 18-month psychosocial column as a warning sign.

options.label: C
options.text: Follows simple one-step directions such as 'jump'
options.rationale: Inability - not ability - to follow simple directions is the listed red flag; following directions is normal.

options.label: D
options.text: Scribbles spontaneously when given a crayon
options.rationale: Failure to try to scribble is the red flag; spontaneous scribbling is an expected 18-month fine-motor skill.

options.label: E
options.text: Falls frequently during independent walking
options.rationale: 'Not yet walking or frequently falls when walking' is listed in the 18-month strength/coordination column.

questions.sourceMapping: Slide 16 (developmental warning signs table, 18 and 24 months); Week 3 transcript, red-flag table walkthrough

stem: The parents of a 19-month-old ask whether they should begin intensive toilet training this month because a daycare requires trained children by age 2. Based on AAFP guidance, the best response is that:

options.label: A
options.text: Readiness emerges between 18 and 30 months, and a third are not ready until near 30
options.rationale: AAFP notes more than two-thirds of U.S. children achieve the physiologic, cognitive, and emotional prerequisites by 18-30 months, with as many as one-third not ready until closer to 30 months; expectations should be set accordingly and the approach kept positive.

options.label: B
options.text: Training begun before 18 months prevents later stool withholding and encopresis
options.rationale: Early training does not prevent withholding; stool toileting refusal is more common when training begins after 3.5 years, not before 18 months.

options.label: C
options.text: Daycare deadlines justify punishment-based methods to accelerate continence
options.rationale: Punishment and negative language are explicitly discouraged; temporary breaks are preferred over coercion.

options.label: D
options.text: Training should always finish by 24 months, so intensive effort now is appropriate
options.rationale: A universal 24-month completion deadline is unsupported; completion age varies widely.

questions.sourceMapping: AAFP Toilet Training: Common Questions and Answers (Baird 2019); Week 3 transcript, positive-reinforcement toilet training discussion

stem: A 4-year-old has bowel movements every four to five days, large painful stools, hides in a corner to defecate, and has small smears of stool in his underwear daily. The mechanism of the underwear soiling is best described as:

options.label: A
options.text: Absence of the urge to defecate from congenital sensory neuropathy
options.rationale: Congenital sensory neuropathy is rare; the typical pathway is pain-driven withholding after painful stools.

options.label: B
options.text: Secretory diarrhea from an undiagnosed carbohydrate intolerance
options.rationale: Secretory diarrhea would produce voluminous watery stool, not scant smearing with retained large stools.

options.label: C
options.text: Overflow leakage of liquid stool around a retained fecal impaction
options.rationale: In functional constipation with withholding, liquid stool seeps around the impaction producing overflow fecal incontinence (encopresis); the professor stressed the smearing 'is not an accident' and signals significant impaction.

options.label: D
options.text: Deliberate behavioral defiance requiring disciplinary consequences
options.rationale: Soiling is involuntary overflow, not defiance; shaming worsens withholding - the course insists on positive reinforcement.

questions.sourceMapping: Week 3 transcript, Case 5 (encopresis, overflow incontinence); AAFP Toilet Training (Baird 2019), complications section

stem: The mother of the constipated 4-year-old above adds that he did not pass meconium until 72 hours after birth and has 'never been regular' since infancy. This historical detail most strongly raises suspicion for:

options.label: A
options.text: Hirschsprung disease, warranting specialty referral and testing
options.rationale: Delayed meconium passage beyond 48-72 hours with lifelong constipation is the classic red flag for Hirschsprung disease; the professor said this twist makes suspicion 'go way up' and is a major concern.

options.label: B
options.text: Normal variation in the timing of neonatal gut maturation
options.rationale: Meconium beyond 48-72 hours is never normal variation and mandates workup.

options.label: C
options.text: Cow's milk protein allergy as the sole explanation
options.rationale: Milk protein allergy can cause constipation but is not the diagnosis signaled by delayed meconium.

options.label: D
options.text: Functional constipation from low dietary fiber alone
options.rationale: Fiber insufficiency contributes to functional constipation but does not explain delayed meconium passage.

questions.sourceMapping: Week 3 transcript, Case 5 twist (meconium at 72 hours, Hirschsprung); transcript red-flag list (Hirschsprung, hypothyroidism, celiac, spinal abnormalities)

stem: A 5-year-old snores nightly, mouth-breathes, is difficult to wake, and has 3+ tonsils on exam. The kindergarten teacher reports high activity and poor attention. The most appropriate management sequence is to:

options.label: A
options.text: Evaluate the sleep disorder with polysomnography and ENT referral before attributing symptoms to ADHD
options.rationale: Habitual snoring with mouth breathing, unrefreshing sleep, and tonsillar hypertrophy suggests obstructive sleep apnea; the course teaches that sleep disorders must be addressed before ADHD because roughly 35% of children with ADHD have a coexisting sleep disorder and treating sleep can improve attention symptoms.

options.label: B
options.text: Start stimulant therapy for ADHD and reassess snoring after a school term
options.rationale: Treating ADHD first inverts the taught sequence and risks misattributing sleep-deprivation behaviors.

options.label: C
options.text: Reassure the family that snoring is universal at this age and needs no workup
options.rationale: Habitual snoring with witnessed features is not benign primary snoring and warrants evaluation.

options.label: D
options.text: Prescribe a prolonged course of oral corticosteroids to shrink tonsillar tissue
options.rationale: Oral steroids are discouraged (they can activate children and disrupt sleep); intranasal steroids treat allergic rhinitis, and definitive airway management is ENT-directed.

questions.sourceMapping: Week 3 transcript, Case 3 (OSA vs ADHD, 35% coexistence, address sleep first); Slide 25 (school-age annual exam)

stem: The same child's parent now reports witnessed pauses in breathing followed by gasping during sleep. Community ENT wait times are three months. As the primary care provider, the best action is to:

options.label: A
options.text: Expedite care by ordering polysomnography now and contacting ENT directly
options.rationale: Witnessed apneic pauses with gasping escalate urgency; the professor directed students to take initiative - order the sleep study yourself and call ENT rather than letting the child wait months unprotected.

options.label: B
options.text: Schedule routine follow-up after the three-month ENT wait
options.rationale: Passive waiting through a three-month queue ignores an escalated red flag.

options.label: C
options.text: Begin intranasal steroids and defer any sleep testing indefinitely
options.rationale: Intranasal steroids address allergic rhinitis only and do not replace objective sleep testing.

options.label: D
options.text: Advise watchful waiting since gasping is a normal sleep transition
options.rationale: Gasping after apneic pauses is pathologic, not a normal sleep transition.

questions.sourceMapping: Week 3 transcript, Case 3 twist (pauses with gasping; PCP initiative to order sleep study and call ENT)

stem: A 4-year-old with eczema and seasonal allergies coughs at night and after soccer practice. The clinician suspects asthma. The most appropriate confirmatory test in this child is:

options.label: A
options.text: Spirometry with pre- and post-bronchodilator testing to demonstrate reversibility
options.rationale: The professor preferred spirometry pre- and post-bronchodilator over peak flow because peak flow depends on age, sex, and height and is technique-limited in young children; reversibility on spirometry supports asthma.

options.label: B
options.text: A trial of oral antibiotics to exclude occult bacterial bronchitis
options.rationale: Antibiotics have no role in diagnosing or treating asthma or exercise-induced bronchoconstriction.

options.label: C
options.text: Peak flow measurement as the standalone office diagnostic standard
options.rationale: Peak flow is 'a tricky thing' per the transcript and is not the better diagnostic test here.

options.label: D
options.text: Chest radiography to confirm the asthma diagnosis
options.rationale: Chest radiography does not confirm asthma and is not indicated for this presentation.

questions.sourceMapping: Week 3 transcript, Case 4 (spirometry pre/post bronchodilator vs peak flow); allergic march discussion

stem: When counseling the family of an infant with atopic dermatitis about future atopic disease, the clinician describes the 'allergic march.' Which additional exposure further increases this child's asthma risk?

options.label: A
options.text: Early-life respiratory syncytial virus lower respiratory infection
options.rationale: The course sequence is eczema, then allergic rhinitis, then asthma, and the professor identified RSV exposure as the viral exposure that further increases asthma risk.

options.label: B
options.text: Use of a household HEPA air purifier during infancy
options.rationale: Air filtration is an environmental control, not an asthma risk factor.

options.label: C
options.text: Introduction of peanut-containing foods at 4-6 months
options.rationale: Early peanut introduction reduces peanut allergy risk and does not drive the march.

options.label: D
options.text: Annual inactivated influenza vaccination after 6 months
options.rationale: Influenza vaccination is protective and unrelated to asthma causation.

questions.sourceMapping: Week 3 transcript, Case 4 (allergic march; RSV as added asthma risk)

stem: An 8-year-old presents for a well visit with BMI at the 97th percentile. No lipid panel has ever been obtained. Universal screening is scheduled between 9 and 11 years. The correct action today is to:

options.label: A
options.text: Order cardiac imaging instead of any lipid testing today
options.rationale: Imaging is not a screening substitute for a lipid panel in asymptomatic obesity.

options.label: B
options.text: Defer all lipid testing until the universal 9-11 year window
options.rationale: Deferral ignores the targeted-screening indication that exists before the universal window.

options.label: C
options.text: Screen now, because obesity indicates targeted screening before age 9
options.rationale: Before age 9, screening is indicated for children with BMI at or above the 85th-95th percentile thresholds, hypertension, diabetes, smoking, or positive/unknown family history; BMI above the 95th-97th percentile qualifies now.

options.label: D
options.text: Defer testing until age 17-21 unless symptoms develop
options.rationale: The 17-21 window is the second universal screen, not a substitute for indicated early testing.

questions.sourceMapping: Slide 28 (Cholesterol Screening, NHLBI/AAP); Slide 29 (CV risk factors); AFP HCM Part I (dyslipidemia screening)

stem: A fasting lipid panel on a 10-year-old returns total cholesterol 172 mg/dL, LDL 134 mg/dL, HDL 46 mg/dL, and triglycerides 96 mg/dL. Which value is abnormal by pediatric criteria taught in this course?

options.label: A
options.text: HDL of 46 mg/dL
options.rationale: HDL 46 is above the low threshold of 40.

options.label: B
options.text: LDL of 134 mg/dL
options.rationale: Pediatric abnormal thresholds are total cholesterol above 200, LDL above 130, HDL below 40, and triglycerides above 130; only the LDL of 134 crosses its threshold. The professor corrected the slide live to confirm these are 'abnormals.'

options.label: C
options.text: Total cholesterol of 172 mg/dL
options.rationale: Total cholesterol 172 is below the 200 abnormal threshold.

options.label: D
options.text: Triglycerides of 96 mg/dL
options.rationale: Triglycerides 96 are below the 130 abnormal threshold.

questions.sourceMapping: Slide 30 (Cholesterol Levels Pediatrics - abnormals); Week 3 transcript, live correction of abnormal lipid thresholds

stem: A parent asks why the lipid panel must be fasting. The clinician's best explanation is that:

options.label: A
options.text: Total cholesterol is unmeasurable in non-fasting serum
options.rationale: Total cholesterol is measurable regardless of fasting status.

options.label: B
options.text: HDL concentrations rise falsely after any caloric intake
options.rationale: HDL is not falsely elevated by meals in any clinically meaningful way.

options.label: C
options.text: LDL disappears from serum within four hours of eating
options.rationale: LDL does not vanish postprandially; it is relatively stable.

options.label: D
options.text: Triglycerides are the fraction most influenced by recent food intake
options.rationale: The professor explained fasting matters mainly for triglycerides, which are diet-sensitive; LDL changes little day to day, so a non-fasting normal panel rarely needs repetition, but elevated triglycerides or LDL require fasting confirmation.

questions.sourceMapping: Week 3 transcript, fasting labs discussion (triglycerides most diet-impacted)

stem: During counseling for a 7-year-old, the family reports two hours of daily recreational screen time, no organized activity, and bedtime at 11 pm. Which counseling statement aligns with school-age health maintenance guidance?

options.label: A
options.text: Screen limits are unnecessary when school performance is acceptable
options.rationale: Screen limits apply regardless of grades; individualized limits come from a Family Media Use Plan.

options.label: B
options.text: Sleep of seven hours nightly is adequate for school-age children
options.rationale: Seven hours is below the recommended 9-12 hours and is linked to behavior, attention, blood pressure, and obesity problems.

options.label: C
options.text: Thirty minutes of activity three days per week is sufficient at this age
options.rationale: Thirty minutes thrice weekly falls far short of the daily 60-minute recommendation.

options.label: D
options.text: Children should accumulate 60 minutes of moderate to vigorous activity daily
options.rationale: AFP Part II recommends 60 minutes of moderate to vigorous physical activity daily, a Family Media Use Plan for screens, and 9-12 hours of sleep for school-age children.

questions.sourceMapping: AFP HCM Part II (Locke 2019), healthy lifestyle counseling; Slide 25 (school-age annual exam)

stem: A 5-year-old presents for a kindergarten-entry visit. Records show four DTaP, three IPV, one MMR, and one varicella dose. Which vaccine set is due at this 4-6 year visit?

options.label: A
options.text: Tdap, meningococcal conjugate, and HPV dose 1
options.rationale: Tdap, MenACWY, and HPV belong to the 11-12 year visit.

options.label: B
options.text: DTaP dose 5, IPV dose 4, MMR dose 2, and varicella dose 2
options.rationale: The 4-6 year platform includes the DTaP fifth dose, IPV, MMR second dose, and varicella second dose before school entry, per the slide and AFP Part I.

options.label: C
options.text: DTaP dose 4, IPV dose 3, MMR dose 1, and varicella dose 1
options.rationale: Those are infant-series doses already completed or mis-sequenced for this age.

options.label: D
options.text: Hepatitis A dose 1, hepatitis A dose 2, and influenza only
options.rationale: Hepatitis A dosing occurs in the second year of life, not at school entry.

stem: At which well-child visit is blood pressure first measured as a routine component of the examination in this course's schedule?

options.label: A
options.text: The 18-month visit
options.rationale: centers on M-CHAT, ASQ, and HepA #1, not BP.

options.label: B
options.text: The 6-year visit
options.rationale: Waiting until 6 years misses three years of recommended screening.

options.label: C
options.text: The 24-month visit
options.rationale: The 2-year visit focuses on language, play, and HepA #2.

options.label: D
options.text: The 36-month (3-year) visit

stem: For school-aged children, the AAP recommendation for blood pressure screening frequency is:

options.label: A
options.text: Once between ages 9 and 11 only
options.rationale: The 9-11 window applies to universal lipid screening, not BP.

options.label: B
options.text: Every two years, matching vision and hearing
options.rationale: Every two years applies to vision and hearing screening.

options.label: C
options.text: Annually, or at every encounter when risk factors are present
options.rationale: AAP recommends annual BP measurement in school-aged children, or at every health care encounter for those with risk factors.

options.label: D

options.rationale: Risk-based-only BP screening contradicts the annual recommendation.

stem: In the absence of symptoms or known disease, the recommended interval for vision and hearing screening in school-aged children is approximately:

options.label: A
options.text: Every six months
options.rationale: Six-month intervals are unnecessary for asymptomatic children.

options.label: B
options.text: Every two years
options.rationale: AAP recommends vision and hearing screening approximately every two years during school age.

options.label: C
options.text: Every five years
options.rationale: Five-year intervals are far too sparse for detectable acquired deficits.

options.label: D
options.text: Once at school entry only
options.rationale: A single entry screen misses later-onset deficits.

stem: A 9-year-old presents with six months of recurrent abdominal pain and fatigue. Extensive GI workup is unrevealing, and the child has become restless and clingy about school separation. Per school-age guidance, the clinician should now:

options.label: A
options.text: Order universal depression screening, which is mandated for all children under 12
options.rationale: No mandate exists; evidence is insufficient for universal screening under 12.

options.label: B
options.text: Consider depression, which may present with somatic complaints, restlessness, or anxiety
options.rationale: Although routine depression screening before 12 lacks sufficient evidence, depression should be considered in children under 12 with unexplained somatic symptoms, restlessness, separation anxiety, phobias, or hallucinations.

options.label: C
options.text: Refer for diagnostic laparoscopy before considering any psychiatric diagnosis
options.rationale: Invasive surgery is inappropriate after a negative workup with a suggestive psychosocial pattern.

options.label: D
options.text: Repeat the gastrointestinal workup, because somatic symptoms exclude mood disorder
options.rationale: Somatic presentation does not exclude mood disorder; repeating negative workups delays care.

questions.sourceMapping: AFP HCM Part I (Riley 2019), depression in children younger than 12

stem: A 6-year-old drinks well water tested at 0.4 ppm fluoride. The child has no dental home. The appropriate preventive action is to:

options.label: A
options.text: Withhold fluoride to avoid fluorosis at any water level
options.rationale: Withholding fluoride in deficient areas increases caries risk.

options.label: B
options.text: Prescribe a daily fluoride supplement
options.rationale: Children in areas with inadequate water fluoride (0.6 ppm or less) should receive daily fluoride supplementation.

options.label: C
options.text: Advise brushing with non-fluoride toothpaste only
options.rationale: Fluoride toothpaste remains recommended; supplementation addresses the deficient water supply.

options.label: D
options.text: Refer for immediate professional sealing without supplementation
options.rationale: Sealants do not replace systemic fluoride in a deficient-water child.

questions.sourceMapping: AFP HCM Part I (Riley 2019), fluoride supplementation threshold

stem: A 10-year-old has BMI at the 96th percentile confirmed across three visits. Beyond counseling, the guideline-supported action is to:

options.label: A
options.text: Schedule annual recheck without intervention until adolescence
options.rationale: Surveillance alone undertreats established obesity.

options.label: B
options.text: Initiate pharmacotherapy as first-line treatment before behavioral programs
options.rationale: Pharmacotherapy is not the first-line step described in this guidance.

options.label: C
options.text: Refer for comprehensive intensive behavioral intervention with more than 26 contact hours
options.rationale: Children with obesity (BMI at or above the 95th percentile) should be offered referral for comprehensive, intensive behavioral interventions; evidence supports programs exceeding 26 contact hours.

options.label: D
options.text: Recommend a calorie-restricted 1,200 kcal diet without behavioral support
options.rationale: Restrictive dieting without behavioral intervention is not the recommended pathway.

stem: An 11-year-old presents for a health maintenance visit with the parent in the room. Guidance on sensitive-topic screening directs the clinician to:

options.label: A
options.text: Interview the child alone for sensitive topics after explaining confidentiality
options.rationale: Sensitive issues such as substance use and sexual activity (counseling begins at 11 years) should be discussed without the parent present, with confidentiality laws explained to both patient and parent beforehand.

options.label: B
options.text: Use written questionnaires only, with no verbal discussion at any age
options.rationale: Questionnaires supplement but do not replace direct confidential conversation.

options.label: C
options.text: Ask the parent to answer all sensitive questions on the child's behalf
options.rationale: Parent-proxy answers defeat the purpose of confidential screening.

options.label: D
options.text: Defer all sensitive topics until age 18 in order to preserve parental trust
options.rationale: Deferral to 18 contradicts the recommendation to begin at 11 years.

questions.sourceMapping: AFP HCM Part II (Locke 2019), confidentiality and sensitive issues beginning at 11 years

stem: When prioritizing injury counseling for a 9-year-old, the clinician notes that the leading cause of death in this U.S. age group is:

options.label: A
options.text: Unintentional injury
options.rationale: is the leading cause of death in school-aged children, anchoring accident-prevention counseling at every visit.

options.label: B
options.text: Congenital heart disease
options.rationale: mortality presents predominantly in infancy.

options.label: C
options.text: Malignancy
options.rationale: Cancer is a leading disease cause but not the overall leading cause of death.

options.label: D
options.text: Homicide
options.rationale: ranks below unintentional injury in this age band.

stem: A 8-year-old describes practicing soccer drills 'to be the best on the team,' builds elaborate models, and compares his accomplishments with classmates. Erikson's stage and central task for this child are:

options.label: A
options.text: Autonomy versus shame and doubt, built through self-care tasks
options.rationale: Autonomy versus shame and doubt is the toddler task.

options.label: B
options.text: Industry versus inferiority, built through mastery, teamwork, and peer competence
options.rationale: School age (5-11 years) is industry versus inferiority: building, creating, accomplishing, teamwork, and mastering reading, arithmetic, and sports skills.

options.label: C
options.text: Initiative versus guilt, built through exploration and purposeful play
options.rationale: Initiative versus guilt is the preschool task.

options.label: D
options.text: Identity versus role confusion, built through values exploration
options.rationale: Identity versus role confusion is adolescent, beyond this course's span.

questions.sourceMapping: Slide 23 (Developmental Theories - School Age, Erikson industry vs inferiority)

stem: A 9-year-old correctly explains that pouring juice from a short wide glass into a tall thin glass does not change the amount, and sorts cards by two sequential rules. Piaget's stage accounting for this reasoning is:

options.label: A
options.text: Sensorimotor, with object permanence mastery
options.rationale: Sensorimotor reasoning predates language-based logic.

options.label: B
options.text: Preoperational, with symbolic but egocentric thought
options.rationale: Preoperational children typically fail conservation tasks.

options.label: C
options.text: Concrete operational, with logical thought and conservation
options.rationale: Conservation of mass/volume and logical sequential organization define the concrete operational stage of school age.

options.label: D
options.text: Formal operational, with abstract hypothesis testing
options.rationale: Abstract hypothetical reasoning emerges later in adolescence.

questions.sourceMapping: Slide 23 (Piaget concrete operational: conservation, logical thinking)

stem: At a 5-year well visit, the clinician asks the child to draw a person as part of fine-motor and cognitive screening. The expected performance at this age is a person with:

options.label: A
options.text: At least nine body parts
options.rationale: Nine parts exceeds typical 5-year performance.

options.label: B
options.text: At least five body parts
options.rationale: The course schedule expects five body parts in a drawn person at 5 years (four at 4 years), and the drawings should be kept in the chart for comparison.

options.label: C
options.text: At least three body parts
options.rationale: Three parts underestimate the 5-year expectation.

options.label: D
options.text: At least two body parts
options.rationale: Two parts correspond to a much younger expected performance.

stem: Which cluster of findings is expected in a typically developing 6-7 year old?

options.label: A
options.text: Losing the first tooth, telling time, and differentiating right from left
options.rationale: Six- to seven-year-olds lose first teeth, read age-appropriate books, speak in complete sentences, understand numbers, differentiate right and left, tell time, and play cooperatively with same-gender friends.

options.label: B
options.text: Complete independent grooming and mixed-gender club participation
options.rationale: Mixed-gender clubs and complete self-grooming describe 8-9 year olds.

options.label: C
options.text: Riding a tricycle and speaking three-word sentences
options.rationale: Tricycle and three-word sentences are 3-year milestones.

options.label: D
options.text: Parallel play and two-word phrases
options.rationale: are 2-year milestones.

questions.sourceMapping: Slide 25 (Milestones 6-7 years)

stem: Which finding documented at a 5-year (60-month) kindergarten physical is a red flag requiring further evaluation?

options.label: A
options.text: Hopping on one foot for several seconds at a time
options.rationale: Hopping is expected; difficulty hopping or jumping is the listed red flag.

options.label: B
options.text: Accurate counting to 10 when the clinician requests it
options.rationale: Counting to 10 is expected; inability to count to 10 is the listed red flag.

options.label: C
options.text: A drawing of a person that includes a head and a body
options.rationale: Drawing a person with a body is expected at 60 months; inability to do so is the red flag.

options.label: D
options.text: Speech that strangers understand only about 75% of the time
options.rationale: At 60 months the speech pattern should be 100% understandable; partially intelligible speech is a listed warning sign prompting audiologic and speech evaluation.

questions.sourceMapping: Slide 26 (developmental warning signs table, 60 months); Week 3 transcript, red-flag table discussion

stem: Universal autism spectrum screening with the M-CHAT is performed at which visits in this course's schedule?

options.label: A
options.text: Every visit from 12 months through 5 years
options.rationale: Universal screening is visit-specific, not continuous at every encounter.

options.label: B
options.text: The 24-month and 48-month visits
options.rationale: The 48-month visit is not a universal autism screening point.

options.label: C
options.text: The 18-month and 24-month visits
options.rationale: M-CHAT screening is taught at the 18-month visit and repeated at the 2-year visit, matching AAP/Bright Futures universal autism screening at 18 and 24 months.

options.label: D
options.text: The 12-month and 36-month visits
options.rationale: The 12-month visit includes lead and developmental surveillance, not universal M-CHAT.

stem: At a 30-month visit, the clinician administers a parent-completed tool that screens global development across communication, motor, and problem-solving domains. This tool is the:

options.label: A
options.text: Bayley Scales of Infant Development
options.rationale: Bayley scales are a comprehensive diagnostic instrument, not a brief surveillance screener.

options.label: B
options.text: Pediatric Symptom Checklist
options.rationale: The PSC screens psychosocial/behavioral symptoms in school-age children.

options.label: C
options.text: Modified Checklist for Autism in Toddlers (M-CHAT)
options.rationale: M-CHAT screens specifically for autism risk, not global development.

options.label: D
options.text: Ages and Stages Questionnaire (ASQ)
options.rationale: The ASQ is the parent-completed developmental screening tool used at 18 and 30 months in this schedule; the professor emphasized early identification so intervention can begin before children age out of early-intervention services at 3.

questions.sourceMapping: Slides 12 and 19 (ASQ at 18 and 30 months); Week 3 transcript, ASQ and early-intervention window discussion

stem: A parent reports that their 2-year-old rejects every new vegetable after a single taste. The evidence-based anticipatory guidance is to:

options.label: A
options.text: Continue offering the food, since about ten exposures establish acceptance
options.rationale: The professor taught that it takes about ten exposures to a new food before a child's true acceptance or rejection is established; keep placing it on the plate without pressure.

options.label: B
options.text: Substitute a preferred food at every refusal to preserve caloric intake
options.rationale: Routine substitution trains the child to prefer the alternate food - the exact trap described in lecture.

options.label: C
options.text: Withhold dessert only on days when the vegetable is fully eaten
options.rationale: Contingent dessert withholding creates pressure and conflict contrary to positive feeding guidance.

options.label: D
options.text: Remove rejected foods permanently to avoid mealtime conflict
options.rationale: Permanent removal guarantees the food is never accepted.

questions.sourceMapping: Week 3 transcript, new-food exposure discussion ('ten different times to try a food')

stem: A mother with severe peanut allergy asks when peanut should be introduced to her 5-month-old infant. Consistent with the lecture's updated guidance, the best answer is:

options.label: A
options.text: Introduce small creamy amounts now, mixed into formula or breast milk
options.rationale: The lecture described the paradigm shift: allergenic foods such as peanut can be introduced in tiny creamy amounts around 4-6 months, mixed with formula or breast milk, especially in allergic-history families, with nuts/eggs/seafood around 6 months; whole nuts are a choking hazard under 3.

options.label: B
options.text: Delay all peanut products until age 3 years to avoid sensitization
options.rationale: Delaying allergens increases, rather than reduces, allergy risk.

options.label: C
options.text: Avoid peanut entirely because of the maternal allergy history
options.rationale: Maternal allergy is not a reason to avoid introduction; early introduction is favored.

options.label: D
options.text: Introduce whole peanuts at 6 months of age to build tolerance
options.rationale: Whole peanuts are a choking hazard for children under 3.

questions.sourceMapping: Week 3 transcript, early allergen introduction discussion; course nutrition table choking-hazard footnote

stem: A 2-year-old has three tantrums daily. The parents currently yell 'no' repeatedly and sometimes give the demanded candy to end the episode. Select all guidance consistent with the course's positive-parenting approach.

options.label: A
options.text: Praise good behavior when it occurs
options.rationale: Praising good behavior is the core positive-reinforcement strategy taught for this age.

options.label: B
options.text: Avoid giving in to tantrum demands
options.rationale: Giving in conditions the child to repeat tantrums, so demands must not be rewarded.

options.label: C
options.text: Give in quickly to shorten each episode
options.rationale: Giving in quickly is the exact reinforcement trap the professor warned against.

options.label: D
options.text: Remove all transitional warnings before changes
options.rationale: Transitional warnings ('in five minutes we're leaving') are recommended to preempt meltdowns, not removed.

options.label: E
options.text: Ignore misbehavior that is not dangerous
options.rationale: Inappropriate behavior is ignored unless harmful, with danger handled by calm redirection and a 'danger' cue.

questions.sourceMapping: Slides 5 and 13 (anticipatory guidance: praise good behavior); Week 3 transcript, tantrum and positive reinforcement discussion

stem: A 15-month-old shows extreme, prolonged distress whenever the parent leaves the room and does not search for a hidden toy. Per the warning-signs table and lecture, the cognitive domain of concern is:

options.label: A
options.text: Stranger anxiety, which is pathologic at any age after 6 months
options.rationale: Stranger anxiety is a normal developmental phenomenon, not pathologic here.

options.label: B
options.text: Object permanence, a sensorimotor achievement whose absence at 15 months is a red flag
options.rationale: 'Lack of object permanence' is listed as a 15-month cognitive warning sign; the professor linked object permanence to healthy separation - the child must know the caregiver returns - and absence warrants evaluation.

options.label: C
options.text: Conservation, a concrete operational skill expected by 15 months
options.rationale: Conservation is a school-age skill, not expected at 15 months.

options.label: D
options.text: Symbolic play, a preoperational skill required at 15 months
options.rationale: Symbolic/pretend play emerges later; its 15-month absence is not the listed flag.

questions.sourceMapping: Slide 15 (15-month cognitive warning sign: lack of object permanence); Slide 3 (Piaget sensorimotor, object permanence); Week 3 transcript, object permanence discussion

stem: A 2-year-old's environmental history is being updated. Select all exposures that the course identifies as potential lead sources requiring counseling or investigation.

options.label: A
options.text: Drinking water from lead service lines and older plumbing
options.rationale: Lead service lines, pipes, and fixtures contaminate drinking water (Flint was referenced in lecture).

options.label: B
options.text: A parent's stained-glass and furniture-refinishing hobby
options.rationale: Take-home exposure from hobbies such as stained glass and furniture repair is explicitly listed.

options.label: C
options.text: Cooking and storing food in imported clay pots
options.rationale: Imported clay pots and ceramics are named lead sources.

options.label: D
options.text: Peeling paint and renovation dust in a home built before 1978
options.rationale: Pre-1978 housing paint and renovation dust are the dominant exposure sources taught in the course.

options.label: E
options.text: Commercial iron-fortified infant cereal prepared at home
options.rationale: Iron-fortified cereal is protective nutrition, not a lead source; adequate iron reduces lead absorption.

stem: A parent asks which non-cognitive health effects of pediatric lead exposure the course emphasizes. The correct pairing is:

options.label: A
options.text: Pulmonary fibrosis and valvular heart disease
options.rationale: Pulmonary fibrosis and valvular disease are not depicted lead effects.

options.label: B
options.text: Pancreatic failure and adrenal insufficiency
options.rationale: Pancreatic and adrenal failure are not depicted lead effects.

options.label: C
options.text: Retinal detachment and skeletal dysplasia
options.rationale: are not depicted lead effects.

options.label: D
options.text: Hearing damage and kidney problems

stem: A child with a confirmed venous blood lead level of 6 mcg/dL is entering follow-up after source control. Per the follow-up schedule, the initial recheck interval is approximately:

options.label: A
options.text: Annually, matching the well-child schedule
options.rationale: Annual recheck is inadequate until exposure is controlled and levels decline.

options.label: B
options.text: Every 3 months, extending to 6-9 months as the level declines
options.rationale: For venous 3.5-9 mcg/dL, follow-up is about every 3 months initially, then every 6-9 months once the level is declining.

options.label: C
options.text: Every 48 hours until two normals
options.rationale: 48-hour confirmation applies to capillary results of 45 mcg/dL or higher.

options.label: D
options.text: Every 2 weeks, extending to monthly
options.rationale: Two-week-to-monthly intervals apply to the 20-44 mcg/dL range.

stem: A bilingual (Spanish-English) 24-month-old has a combined vocabulary of 25 words across both languages and no two-word combinations in either language. The most appropriate approach is to:

options.label: A
options.text: Attribute the deficit solely to the nanny's language use and observe
options.rationale: Caregiver language patterns inform the history but do not replace evaluation.

options.label: B
options.text: Test only English vocabulary before making any referral decision
options.rationale: Vocabulary must be counted across both languages; single-language testing misclassifies bilingual children.

options.label: C
options.text: Proceed with full evaluation now, since bilingualism delays speech but not red flags
options.rationale: The case debrief taught that dual-language exposure can delay expressive speech, but children with red flags must still be evaluated and referred; bilingualism modifies history-taking, not the referral threshold.

options.label: D
options.text: Defer evaluation for 12 months because bilingual children always normalize by 3
options.rationale: Automatic normalization is a myth; waiting risks missing the early-intervention window.

questions.sourceMapping: Week 3 transcript, Case 1 debrief (dual language, sign language, still refer)

stem: Dental counseling for a 6-year-old without caries should include which instruction?

options.label: A
options.text: Avoid fluoride toothpaste until all permanent teeth erupt
options.rationale: Fluoride toothpaste is recommended well before permanent dentition completes.

options.label: B
options.text: Use a full toothpaste tube length to maximize fluoride contact
options.rationale: Full-length paste risks excess fluoride ingestion without benefit.

options.label: C
options.text: Brush once weekly with fluoride rinse only
options.rationale: Weekly brushing is grossly inadequate for caries prevention.

options.label: D
options.text: Brush twice daily with a pea-sized amount of fluoride toothpaste
options.rationale: School-age guidance specifies brushing twice per day with a pea-sized amount of fluoride toothpaste.
