stem: A 4-year-old organizes siblings into building a blanket fort, assigns roles, and later confesses with visible distress after being scolded for 'bossing' the baby. Erikson's preschool crisis and its virtue are:

options.label: A
options.text: Industry versus inferiority, with the virtue of competence
options.rationale: Industry versus inferiority is the school-age crisis.

options.label: B
options.text: Autonomy versus shame and doubt, with the virtue of will
options.rationale: Autonomy versus shame and doubt is the toddler (1-3 year) crisis.

options.label: C
options.text: Trust versus mistrust, with the virtue of hope
options.rationale: Trust versus mistrust belongs to infancy.

options.label: D
options.text: Initiative versus guilt, with the virtue of purpose
options.rationale: Preschool (3-5 years) is initiative versus guilt: asserting control over the environment, exploration, and leadership in play; success yields purpose, while excessive disapproval produces guilt.

questions.sourceMapping: Slide 18 (Developmental Theories - Preschool, Erikson initiative vs guilt, virtue purpose)

stem: A parent hides a toy under a cup while a 10-month-old watches; the infant immediately lifts the cup to retrieve it. This behavior demonstrates mastery of:

options.label: A
options.text: Symbolic play within the preoperational stage
options.rationale: Symbolic play is preoperational and not demonstrated by hidden-object search.

options.label: B
options.text: Conservation within the concrete operational stage
options.rationale: Conservation emerges in concrete operations during school age.

options.label: C
options.text: Object permanence within Piaget's sensorimotor stage
options.rationale: Searching for a hidden object reflects object permanence, the sensorimotor achievement (0-2 years) that the lecture tied to separation trust; its absence at 15 months is a table red flag.

options.label: D
options.text: Egocentrism within the preoperational stage
options.rationale: Egocentrism is a perspective limitation, not a retrieval skill.

questions.sourceMapping: Slide 3 (Piaget sensorimotor, object permanence); Slide 15 table (lack of object permanence at 15 months); Week 3 transcript, object permanence discussion

stem: At a 30-month visit, the parent reports the child cannot follow two-step commands such as 'get your shoes and put them by the door,' and still cannot copy a circle. these findings represent:

options.label: A
options.text: Normal variation, since two-step commands emerge after 36 months
options.rationale: Two-step commands are expected by 30 months; the table lists their absence as abnormal.

options.label: B
options.text: A isolated fine-motor delay that requires no cognitive follow-up
options.rationale: The combination spans cognitive and fine-motor domains, not an isolated motor issue.

options.label: C
options.text: Two documented 30-month red flags warranting developmental evaluation
options.rationale: The 30-month row lists 'cannot follow two-step commands' (cognitive) and 'unable to copy a circle shape' (fine motor) as warning signs; two domain flags strengthen the case for formal developmental evaluation before the early-intervention window closes at 3.

options.label: D
options.text: Expected performance in children who attend daycare
options.rationale: Daycare attendance does not make these findings expected.

questions.sourceMapping: Slide 20 (developmental warning signs table, 30 months); Week 3 transcript, early-intervention age-out discussion

stem: A preschool physical on a 48-month-old documents that the child climbs stairs by placing both feet on each step, balances on one foot for 2 seconds, and copies a circle but not a square. the correct interpretation is:

options.label: A
options.text: Normal, because square copying emerges at 60 months
options.rationale: Square copying is a 4-year expectation; triangle copying is the 60-month item.

options.label: B
options.text: Abnormal, because 48-month-olds must balance on one foot for 10 seconds
options.rationale: The table's 48-month balance threshold is 4 seconds, not 10.

options.label: C
options.text: Normal, because alternating steps is a 6-year skill
options.rationale: Alternating stairs is expected by 4 years per the course milestones (4-year-old climbs stairs with alternating feet).

options.label: D
options.text: Abnormal, because 48-month-olds should alternate steps on stairs and copy a square
options.rationale: The 48-month row flags 'unable to alternate steps when climbing stairs' and 'unable to copy square'; both deficits are present, making this an abnormal pattern requiring evaluation.

questions.sourceMapping: Slide 21 (developmental warning signs table, 48 months); Slide 24 (4-year alternating stairs)

stem: A 12-month-old is transitioning off formula. The clinician's nutrition plan should specify:

options.label: A
options.text: Continued formula as the sole nutrition source until 18 months
options.rationale: Formula is not the sole source beyond the first year; table foods and milk replace it.

options.label: B
options.text: Skim milk introduction limited to about 24 ounces per day
options.rationale: Skim and low-fat milks are not recommended before age 2, and 24 ounces exceeds the cap.

options.label: C
options.text: Whole milk ad libitum as the primary calorie source
options.rationale: Ad libitum milk intake is the mechanism of milk-induced iron deficiency anemia.

options.label: D
options.text: Whole milk introduction limited to about 16 ounces per day with table foods
options.rationale: At 12-15 months the child should be off bottle/formula, transitioned to whole milk capped near 16 ounces daily (the table specifies 2 cups/day of whole milk for 1-2 years), and eating table foods; excess milk displaces iron and causes anemia.

questions.sourceMapping: Slide 4 (off bottle/formula; whole milk no more than 16 oz/day); course nutrition table (dairy 1-2 years); Week 3 transcript, milk volume discussion

stem: The parents of a 2-year-old report the child eats only crackers, pasta, cheese, and potatoes and refuses vegetables. Growth and activity are normal. The most appropriate counseling is to:

options.label: A
options.text: Start daily iron supplementation today regardless of laboratory testing
options.rationale: Empiric iron without laboratory confirmation is inappropriate; test first when pallor or other concern exists.

options.label: B
options.text: Prepare a separate preferred meal at each refusal to protect caloric intake
options.rationale: Substitution reinforces refusal and trains preference for the alternate food - the exact trap described in lecture.

options.label: C
options.text: Continue offering family foods, including rejected items, without pressure or separate meals
options.rationale: The case debrief endorsed everyone eating the same food, keeping rejected foods on the plate without pressure (about ten exposures), and avoiding substitution cycles; 'white food' phases are common and normal growth is the reassurance.

options.label: D
options.text: Withhold all snacks and milk until vegetables are accepted at meals
options.rationale: Withholding snacks and milk creates conflict and risks inadequate intake; structure without coercion is taught instead.

questions.sourceMapping: Week 3 transcript, Case 2 debrief (white-food diet, alternate-food trap, ten exposures, CBC if pale)

stem: A capillary lead screen returns 6.5 mcg/dL at an 18-month visit. Per the confirmation schedule, the venous confirmatory draw should occur:

options.label: A
options.text: Within 2 weeks
options.rationale: Two weeks applies to the 20-44 mcg/dL capillary range.

options.label: B
options.text: Within 48 hours
options.rationale: 48 hours applies to capillary results of 45 mcg/dL or higher.

options.label: C
options.text: Within 1 month
options.rationale: One month applies to the 10-19 mcg/dL capillary range.

options.label: D
options.text: Within 3 months
options.rationale: Capillary results of 3.5-9 mcg/dL are confirmed with a venous specimen within 3 months.

questions.sourceMapping: Slide 10 (confirmatory venous testing after capillary BLL); NYC DOHMH Lead Guidelines (2023)

stem: A confirmed venous blood lead level of 28 mcg/dL is returned on an asymptomatic 3-year-old. Which management plan is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: Environmental investigation, iron studies, close follow-up, and no routine chelation
options.rationale: For 20-44 mcg/dL the course adds complete history/physical, environmental investigation and lead-hazard reduction, iron-deficiency anemia evaluation, and PEHSU/poison control consultation - and explicitly states chelation is not routinely recommended in this range.

options.label: B
options.text: Reassurance and repeat venous testing in 6-9 months without intervention
options.rationale: Six-to-nine-month recheck without source control undertreats a reportable elevation.

options.label: C
options.text: Immediate inpatient chelation before any environmental assessment occurs
options.rationale: Inpatient chelation is reserved for 45 mcg/dL or higher or symptomatic disease.

options.label: D
options.text: Outpatient chelation today with discharge home to the same residence
options.rationale: Chelation in this range lacks neurodevelopmental benefit and home discharge without source control violates lead-safe principles.

questions.sourceMapping: Slide 9 (management 20-44 mcg/dL); Slide 11 (do not chelate routinely 20-44); NYC DOHMH Lead Guidelines (2023)

stem: A child presents with seizures, vomiting, and encephalopathy; the venous lead level returns 68 mcg/dL. The immediate disposition is:

options.label: A
options.text: Six hours of clinic observation, then home if the child is alert
options.rationale: Brief observation ignores a life-threatening emergency.

options.label: B
options.text: Outpatient chelation with reassessment in clinic the next day
options.rationale: Outpatient management of encephalopathic lead poisoning is unsafe.

options.label: C
options.text: Elective chelation once the home renovation is fully completed
options.rationale: Deferring chelation until renovation completes leaves ongoing exposure and active toxicity untreated.

options.label: D
options.text: Hospitalization and chelation per expert protocol with lead-safe discharge
options.rationale: Symptomatic severe toxicity (encephalopathy, seizures) requires immediate hospital care and chelation under expert protocol, with discharge only to a lead-safe environment after inspection.

questions.sourceMapping: Slide 9 (>=45 with symptoms requires immediate hospital care); NYC DOHMH Lead Guidelines (2023), BLL >=45 and chelation protocol

stem: Laboratory evaluation of a pale 2-year-old with 30 ounces of daily milk intake shows hemoglobin 8.4 g/dL and MCV 65 fL. Which additional pattern confirms iron deficiency rather than thalassemia trait?

options.label: A
options.text: Elevated ferritin with low TIBC and normal RDW
options.rationale: Elevated ferritin with low TIBC suggests iron overload or inflammation.

options.label: B
options.text: Low ferritin with elevated TIBC and elevated RDW
options.rationale: Iron deficiency depletes stores (low ferritin), raises binding capacity (elevated TIBC), and increases size variation (elevated RDW); the lecture tied ferritin to stores, TIBC to marrow activation, and RDW to size variation.

options.label: C
options.text: Low ferritin with low TIBC and low RDW
options.rationale: Low TIBC with low RDW does not fit iron deficiency physiology.

options.label: D
options.text: Normal ferritin with normal TIBC and normal RDW
options.rationale: A fully normal iron panel suggests thalassemia trait rather than iron deficiency.

questions.sourceMapping: Week 3 transcript, Case 2 debrief (ferritin, TIBC, RDW, reticulocyte count, Hgb 8.4/MCV 65)

stem: After confirming iron deficiency anemia in the child above, the most appropriate management bundle is:

options.label: A
options.text: Oral iron with vitamin C, less milk, iron-rich foods, and repeat hemoglobin
options.rationale: The debrief plan was iron supplementation for microcytic anemia with presumed low ferritin, milk reduction, iron-rich foods with vitamin C to enhance absorption, and hemoglobin recheck to document response.

options.label: B
options.text: Dietary change alone with no iron supplementation or recheck lab
options.rationale: Diet alone corrects established anemia too slowly and omits needed recheck.

options.label: C
options.text: Intravenous iron as first-line therapy without any dietary change
options.rationale: IV iron is not first-line for uncomplicated dietary iron deficiency.

options.label: D
options.text: Transfusion followed by discharge with no follow-up laboratories
options.rationale: Transfusion is reserved for severe symptomatic anemia and never replaces follow-up.

questions.sourceMapping: Week 3 transcript, Case 2 debrief (start iron, reduce milk, vitamin C, recheck hemoglobin)

stem: Using the lecture's bedside rule that hematocrit approximates three times hemoglobin, the expected hematocrit for a child with hemoglobin 8.4 g/dL is approximately:

options.label: A
options.rationale: would correspond to a hemoglobin of 11 g/dL.

options.label: B
options.rationale: Hemoglobin 8.4 x 3 equals about 25%, matching the lecture's 'multiply times three' rule and confirming a significantly anemic child (hemoglobin should be 10 or more).

options.label: C
options.rationale: is a normal adult-range hematocrit, inconsistent with this hemoglobin.

options.label: D
options.rationale: would correspond to a hemoglobin near 5.7 g/dL.

questions.sourceMapping: Week 3 transcript, Case 2 debrief (hematocrit equals hemoglobin times three)

stem: The parents of a 22-month-old ask whether their child is ready to begin toilet training. Select all findings that indicate developmental readiness per AAFP markers.

options.label: A
options.text: Copying a square with a crayon
options.rationale: Copying a square is a 4-year fine-motor skill, not a toileting readiness marker.

options.label: B
options.text: Following simple parental instructions and pulling pants up and down
options.rationale: Walking, dressing skills, and the ability to follow parental instruction are listed readiness markers.

options.label: C
options.text: Staying dry for about two hours at a time or during naps
options.rationale: Staying dry for two hours or during naps (75% achieve by 24-26 months) is a listed readiness marker.

options.label: D
options.text: Showing discomfort with soiled diapers and wanting to be changed
options.rationale: Discomfort with soiled diapers and desire to be changed is a listed readiness marker.

options.label: E
options.text: Climbing stairs with alternating feet
options.rationale: Alternating stairs is a 4-year gross-motor skill, not a toileting readiness marker.

questions.sourceMapping: AAFP Toilet Training (Baird 2019), readiness markers table

stem: Parents ask whether the Brazelton child-oriented method or the Azrin-Foxx structured behavioral method is superior. The evidence-based response is that:

options.label: A
options.text: No method is superior; the approach should fit the family and use positive reinforcement
options.rationale: AAFP counsels that no training method is superior to another; families should choose what suits their child, and all methods should rely on positive reinforcement - echoing the professor's insistence on positivity and no shaming.

options.label: B
options.text: Structured behavioral methods are superior for all healthy toddlers
options.rationale: No trial establishes behavioral methods as universally superior.

options.label: C
options.text: Elimination communication is the only method preventing enuresis
options.rationale: Elimination communication has no proven enuresis-prevention superiority.

options.label: D
options.text: Child-oriented methods are superior for all healthy toddlers
options.rationale: No trial establishes child-oriented methods as universally superior.

questions.sourceMapping: AAFP Toilet Training (Baird 2019), methods section; Week 3 transcript, positive reinforcement discussion

stem: A 3-year-8-month-old refuses to sit on the toilet for stool after training began at 3.5 years, with escalating family conflict. Per AAFP guidance, the best next step is to:

options.label: A
options.text: Pause training for a few weeks and observe psychosocial contributors
options.rationale: Stool toileting refusal is more common when training begins after 3.5 years; after excluding organic causes, AAFP advises pausing training advances for a few weeks and observing psychosocial contributors, avoiding negative language; temporary 1-3 month breaks are acceptable.

options.label: B
options.text: Add punishment contingencies around stimulant laxative dosing
options.rationale: Punishment is explicitly discouraged and worsens withholding.

options.label: C
options.text: Escalate to daily scheduled enemas to force toilet compliance
options.rationale: Enemas to force compliance are coercive and inappropriate.

options.label: D
options.text: Refer now for anorectal manometry as the first step
options.rationale: Manometry is not indicated before behavioral modification and organic workup.

questions.sourceMapping: AAFP Toilet Training (Baird 2019), stool toileting refusal and training breaks

stem: A 5-year-old has never achieved daytime continence despite completed training attempts. The appropriate interpretation is that:

options.label: A
options.text: Daytime incontinence at 5 years is normal and needs no workup
options.rationale: Labeling it normal delays detection of anatomic or metabolic causes.

options.label: B
options.text: Workup is deferred unless nighttime dryness is also absent at 7
options.rationale: Deferral to 7 years applies to enuresis thresholds, not persistent daytime incontinence.

options.label: C
options.text: Psychiatric causes alone are considered at this age
options.rationale: Organic causes must be excluded before attributing symptoms to psychosocial factors.

options.label: D
options.text: Daytime incontinence at 5 is unusual and warrants a secondary-cause workup
options.rationale: Failure to achieve at least daytime continence by 5 years is unusual and warrants investigation for infection, anatomic urinary tract abnormalities, metabolic disorders, and bladder dysfunction.

questions.sourceMapping: AAFP Toilet Training (Baird 2019), continence by five years

stem: A 6-year-old with habitual snoring has allergic rhinitis with a high-arched palate. To reduce nasal obstruction contributing to sleep-disordered breathing, the preferred pharmacologic option is:

options.label: A
options.text: A nightly sedating antihistamine given to induce sleep
options.rationale: Sedating antihistamines do not treat obstruction and degrade sleep architecture.

options.label: B
options.text: An intranasal corticosteroid, avoiding oral steroids that disrupt sleep
options.rationale: The debrief specified intranasal (not oral) corticosteroids to reduce nasal passage swelling from allergic rhinitis, since oral steroids can activate children and worsen sleep; the high-arched palate marks chronic mouth breathing.

options.label: C
options.text: A proton pump inhibitor as monotherapy for obstruction
options.rationale: PPIs treat GERD, not nasal obstruction from allergic rhinitis.

options.label: D
options.text: A prolonged oral prednisone taper repeated each semester
options.rationale: Repeated oral steroid tapers carry systemic toxicity and sleep disruption.

questions.sourceMapping: Week 3 transcript, Case 3 debrief (intranasal vs oral steroids; high-arched palate from mouth breathing)

stem: A 7-year-old with diagnosed ADHD continues to snore habitually and falls asleep in class. The course's sequencing principle is to:

options.label: A
options.text: Address the sleep disorder first, as 35% of ADHD children have one
options.rationale: About 35% of children with ADHD have a coexisting sleep disorder, and the course insists sleep is always addressed first because treating it can improve attention and behavior symptoms.

options.label: B
options.text: Assume a medication effect and stop the stimulant abruptly
options.rationale: Abrupt stimulant cessation without evaluation is unsafe and uninvestigated.

options.label: C
options.text: Increase the stimulant dose before any sleep evaluation
options.rationale: Dose escalation masks an untreated sleep disorder driving inattention.

options.label: D
options.text: Defer the entire sleep evaluation until adolescence
options.rationale: Deferral ignores a modifiable contributor to current symptoms.

questions.sourceMapping: Week 3 transcript, Case 3 (35% ADHD-sleep disorder coexistence; address sleep first)

stem: A 5-year-old with chronic nocturnal cough has normal spirometry with reversibility testing and no wheeze on exam. The clinician recalls the lecture's mimic list. Which condition can mimic or exacerbate asthma in this way?

options.label: A
options.text: Gastroesophageal reflux disease irritating the cough reflex
options.rationale: The professor noted GERD can mimic or exacerbate asthma because gastric content irritation sensitizes the cough reflex - a key distractor-resistant teaching point in the asthma case.

options.label: B
options.text: Vocal cord dysfunction visible on chest radiograph
options.rationale: Vocal cord dysfunction is diagnosed by laryngoscopy, not chest radiograph.

options.label: C
options.text: Celiac disease presenting solely with cough
options.rationale: Celiac disease does not present as isolated chronic cough.

options.label: D
options.text: Chronic bacterial sinusitis cured by antibiotics
options.rationale: Sinusitis is not the mimic emphasized, and antibiotics are not a diagnostic trial for cough.

questions.sourceMapping: Week 3 transcript, Case 4 debrief (GERD as asthma mimic/exacerbator)

stem: Spirometry on the 4-year-old with exercise-related cough shows a 15% increase in FEV1 after albuterol. This result:

options.label: A
options.text: Excludes asthma because reversibility requires a 50% change
options.rationale: No 50% threshold exists; clinically significant reversibility is far smaller.

options.label: B
options.text: Demonstrates reversibility supporting an asthma diagnosis
options.rationale: Pre- and post-bronchodilator spirometry demonstrating significant reversibility supports asthma; the course chose this testing strategy specifically to document reversibility.

options.label: C
options.text: Confirms exercise-induced vocal cord dysfunction
options.rationale: Vocal cord dysfunction produces inspiratory loop flattening, not bronchodilator reversibility.

options.label: D
options.text: Indicates the need for emergent intubation
options.rationale: A reversible spirometric response is not an airway emergency.

questions.sourceMapping: Week 3 transcript, Case 4 (spirometry pre/post bronchodilator to see reversibility)

stem: A family history reveals a paternal myocardial infarction at age 52. For lipid screening purposes, this history is:

options.label: A
options.text: Positive only if the relative was a first-degree female
options.rationale: First-degree male relatives count under the 55-year threshold.

options.label: B
options.text: Negative, because premature male disease is defined as under 45 years
options.rationale: The male threshold is 55, not 45.

options.label: C
options.text: Positive, because premature male cardiovascular disease is under 55
options.rationale: Premature cardiovascular disease family history is defined as under 55 years in male relatives and under 65 years in female relatives; a father with MI at 52 triggers targeted lipid screening before age 9.

options.label: D
options.text: Irrelevant to any pediatric lipid screening decisions
options.rationale: Family history is a core trigger for early screening.

stem: A 10-year-old's lipid panel shows HDL 38 mg/dL with all other values within normal limits. The correct interpretation is:

options.label: B

options.rationale: HDL does have a pediatric abnormal threshold.

options.label: C

options.label: D
options.text: Normal, because only LDL above 160 mg/dL is abnormal
options.rationale: The LDL abnormal threshold is above 130, not 160.

stem: The school-age annual examination taught in this course includes which components beyond the physical examination?

stem: Which behavior cluster best fits a typically developing 8-9 year old?

options.rationale: Eight- to nine-year-olds dress and groom themselves completely, enjoy competition, games, clubs, and groups, and begin mixing friends of both genders.

stem: Parents request splitting MMR into single-antigen components because of autism concerns. The most appropriate response is that:

stem: A 26-month-old enrolled in Medicaid has never had a blood lead test. Per the risk-assessment guidance, the correct action is to:

options.label: A
options.text: Defer testing until the 3-year visit
options.rationale: Deferral to 3 years misses both mandated windows.

options.label: B
options.text: Screen by questionnaire only and test if any answer is positive
options.rationale: Questionnaire-only misses mandated age-based testing.

options.label: C
options.text: Perform lead testing now, since Medicaid requires testing up to age 6
options.rationale: Mandated testing occurs at ages 1 and 2 (9-15 and 21-27 months), and Medicaid requires testing for children up to age 6 who were not previously tested; an untested 26-month-old is overdue today.

options.label: D
options.text: Test only if the child becomes symptomatic
options.rationale: Most exposed children are asymptomatic; waiting for symptoms defeats screening.

stem: Which household instruction correctly reduces ingested lead from tap water in a home with older plumbing?

options.label: A
options.text: Boil the tap water for 10 minutes before mixing formula
options.rationale: Boiling does not remove lead and concentrates it as water evaporates.

options.label: B
options.text: Run the tap at least 30 seconds until noticeably colder after non-use
options.rationale: Running the tap at least 30 seconds until noticeably colder after several hours of non-use reduces lead exposure for drinking, cooking, and formula preparation.

options.label: C
options.text: Use only hot tap water for cooking because heat destroys lead
options.rationale: Hot water leaches more lead from plumbing; lead is not destroyed by heat.

options.label: D
options.text: Store tap water in imported clay pots to filter out lead
options.rationale: Imported clay pots are themselves a lead source.

stem: A 2-year-old with confirmed venous blood lead level of 12 mcg/dL enters follow-up. Select all actions included in management for the 3.5-19 mcg/dL range.

options.label: A
options.text: Repeat venous lead testing in 1-3 months initially
options.rationale: Repeat venous testing every 1-3 months initially applies to the 10-19 mcg/dL range.

options.label: B
options.text: Assess and treat iron deficiency and counsel on adequate iron and calcium intake
options.rationale: Iron and calcium assessment and counseling are specified to reduce absorption.

options.label: C
options.text: Begin routine chelation therapy at this level
options.rationale: Chelation is not routinely recommended below 45 mcg/dL; it has not shown neurodevelopmental benefit at 20-44, let alone 12.

options.label: D
options.text: Assess development and refer to early intervention services when indicated
options.rationale: Developmental assessment with early-intervention referral when indicated is specified.

options.label: E
options.text: Report to the state or local health department and arrange environmental investigation
options.rationale: Reporting and environmental exposure history with home investigation as required are core actions in this range.

questions.sourceMapping: Slide 9 (management 3.5-19 mcg/dL); Slide 10 (follow-up intervals); Slide 11 (no routine chelation below 45)

stem: A child undergoing chelation for a blood lead level of 50 mcg/dL is ready for discharge. The mandatory discharge condition taught in this course is that:

options.rationale: The NYC guidance requires that a child receive chelation in, and be discharged to, a lead-safe environment, with home inspection before discharge - reinforcing the teaching pearl that treatment fails without source control.

options.rationale: Six-month observation is dangerous at this level.

stem: Which statement correctly describes the CDC blood lead reference value of 3.5 mcg/dL?

options.rationale: No safe level exists; the reference value is not a safety line.

options.label: C

options.rationale: Chelation is tied to 45 mcg/dL or higher, not 3.5.

options.rationale: The reference value applies to blood lead generally; capillary elevations simply require venous confirmation.

stem: A venous lead level of 4.2 mcg/dL returns on an asymptomatic 2-year-old. The correct interpretation and action is that:

options.label: A
options.text: The value requires chelation within 48 hours
options.rationale: Chelation is reserved for 45 mcg/dL or higher or symptomatic disease.

options.label: B
options.text: The value is normal because it is below the 10 mcg/dL toxicity threshold
options.rationale: No safe level exists and 10 is not an action threshold; 3.5 is the reference value.

options.label: C
options.text: The value requires no action until the next annual visit
options.rationale: Deferring a year ignores the required follow-up interval (about every 3 months in this range).

options.label: D
options.text: Above the 3.5 reference value, triggering follow-up and source assessment
options.rationale: Any confirmed level at or above the 3.5 mcg/dL reference value warrants action: exposure history, environmental control, iron/calcium assessment, developmental monitoring, and scheduled retesting; the professor stressed 'if we have a blood lead level greater than 3.5, we have to do follow-up.'

questions.sourceMapping: Slides 8-10 (BLL >=3.5 actions and follow-up); Week 3 transcript, greater-than-3.5 follow-up cue

stem: A newly elevated capillary lead level of 15 mcg/dL is reported from your office. Beyond venous confirmation, the mandated administrative action is to:

options.label: A
options.text: File an incident report with the laboratory only
options.rationale: Laboratory incident reporting does not satisfy public health reporting.

options.label: B
options.text: Report the elevation to the state or local health department for investigation
options.rationale: Elevated blood lead levels are reportable to state/local health departments, which assist with environmental investigation; the professor noted 'once you get an elevated lead, you report it to the Department of Public Health... and they can help with that piece.'

options.label: C
options.text: Await two consecutive venous elevations before any report
options.rationale: Reporting should not wait for repeat venous confirmation.

options.label: D
options.text: Notify child protective services as a report of maltreatment
options.rationale: Lead exposure is an environmental hazard report, not automatically a maltreatment report.

questions.sourceMapping: Slide 9 (report to state/local health department); Week 3 transcript, public health reporting discussion; NYC DOHMH Lead Guidelines (2023)

stem: The course states that routine chelation is not recommended for confirmed levels of 20-44 mcg/dL. The rationale taught is that:

options.label: A
options.text: Chelation is effective only when given before age 2 years
options.rationale: Age-based chelation efficacy cutoffs are not the teaching.

options.label: B
options.text: Levels in this range always normalize within weeks without treatment
options.rationale: Levels do not reliably self-normalize without source control.

options.label: C
options.text: Chelation in this range causes immediate renal failure in most children
options.rationale: Catastrophic renal failure 'in most children' is not the stated rationale.

options.label: D
options.text: Chelation lowers the level but has not shown neurodevelopmental benefit in this range
options.rationale: The MUST KNOW pearl: do not chelate routinely at 20-44 mcg/dL because chelation lowers BLL but has not demonstrated neurodevelopmental benefit in this range; source control, nutrition, and follow-up are the interventions.

questions.sourceMapping: Slide 11 (CHELATION/URGENT CARE pearls); Slide 9 (20-44 management)

stem: A family needs specialist consultation about a chronic residential lead exposure from a hobby workshop. The resource the course identifies for pediatric environmental health consultation is the:

options.label: A
options.text: Local health department dental division
options.rationale: Dental divisions do not manage environmental lead consultation.

options.label: B
options.text: Regional poison center's veterinary line
options.rationale: The veterinary line is irrelevant to pediatric exposure.

options.label: C
options.text: State occupational safety office for adult workers only
options.rationale: Adult occupational offices do not replace pediatric environmental consultation, though take-home exposure involves work settings.

options.label: D
options.text: Pediatric Environmental Health Specialty Unit (PEHSU)
options.rationale: The course lists PEHSU consultation (with Poison Control 1-800-222-1222) for pediatric environmental health questions and complex lead cases.

questions.sourceMapping: Slide 11 (Poison Control and PEHSU resources); Slide 9 (consult PEHSU or Poison Control)

stem: A 2-year-old with iron deficiency anemia is noted to eat paint chips and dirt. This behavior is best characterized as:

options.label: A
options.text: Pica signaling and perpetuating iron or nutrient deficiency and lead risk
options.rationale: The debrief identified pica as indicating iron/nutrient deficiency, and pica with nonfood items (paint chips, soil) is both a consequence and a driver of deficiency plus a direct lead exposure pathway requiring counseling and, when persistent, behavior referral.

options.label: B
options.text: A habit disorder unrelated to nutritional status
options.rationale: Pica is tightly linked to iron deficiency, not an isolated habit disorder.

options.label: C
options.text: Normal exploratory behavior with no clinical significance at 2 years
options.rationale: Persistent nonfood ingestion at 2 years is clinically significant, not benign exploration.

options.label: D
options.text: Evidence of intentional maltreatment
options.rationale: Pica is not itself evidence of maltreatment.

questions.sourceMapping: Week 3 transcript, Case 2 (pica indicates iron/nutrient deficiency); NYC DOHMH Lead Guidelines (2023), nonfood items and behavior referral

stem: When organizing the differential for microcytic anemia, the professor's four mechanistic categories are dietary intake, absorption, production, and loss. Celiac disease belongs to which category?

options.label: A
options.text: Absorption, because mucosal disease impairs iron uptake
options.rationale: The debrief placed celiac disease in the absorption branch ('is there some GI thing going on, celiac, something going on where they're not absorbing?'), prompting consideration when dietary iron deficiency does not fit or fails to respond.

options.label: B
options.text: Loss, because celiac disease always causes gross bleeding
options.rationale: Celiac rarely causes gross bleeding; malabsorption is the mechanism.

options.label: C
options.text: Dietary intake, because celiac disease reduces appetite
options.rationale: Appetite reduction is not the mechanistic category taught.

options.label: D
options.text: Production, because celiac disease suppresses marrow directly
options.rationale: Celiac causes malabsorption, not primary marrow suppression.

questions.sourceMapping: Week 3 transcript, Case 2 debrief (dietary, absorption, production, loss; celiac in absorption)

stem: In evaluating anemia response, an elevated reticulocyte count after starting oral iron indicates:

options.label: A
options.text: Marrow failure with inadequate reserve
options.rationale: Marrow failure would produce a low reticulocyte response.

options.label: B
options.text: Laboratory error requiring repeat only if symptomatic
options.rationale: A rising reticulocyte count is an expected therapeutic marker, not error.

options.label: C
options.text: Active marrow production of new red cells in response to therapy
options.rationale: The reticulocyte count measures immature red cells; a high or rising count signals the bone marrow is actively producing red cells - the expected healthy response once iron is replete.

options.label: D
options.text: Ongoing hemolysis requiring transfusion
options.rationale: Reticulocytosis after iron therapy reflects response, not hemolysis.

questions.sourceMapping: Week 3 transcript, Case 2 debrief (reticulocyte count meaning)

stem: A microcytic anemia fails to respond to adequate oral iron, and the family history notes Mediterranean ancestry with 'mild anemia' in a parent. The next consideration is:

options.label: A
options.text: Vitamin B12 deficiency as the cause of microcytosis
options.rationale: B12 deficiency causes macrocytic, not microcytic, anemia.

options.label: B
options.text: Immediate bone marrow transplantation evaluation
options.rationale: Transplant has no role in trait-level hemoglobinopathy.

options.label: C
options.text: Lead poisoning as the only alternative diagnosis
options.rationale: Lead is one consideration but not the only alternative; ancestry points to thalassemia.

options.label: D
options.text: Thalassemia trait, evaluated with a thalassemia panel
options.rationale: The debrief explicitly instructed considering thalassemia (and sickle cell) based on family history and ethnicity when microcytosis is out of proportion or iron-unresponsive, since the milk intake may not be the driver.

questions.sourceMapping: Week 3 transcript, Case 2 debrief (thalassemia/sickle cell considerations, ferritin and TIBC interpretation)

stem: Parents of a 20-month-old ask whether starting intensive toilet training now (more than three prompts daily) risks constipation or withholding. Per AAFP evidence, the correct answer is that:

options.label: A
options.text: Intensive training before 27 months guarantees later encopresis
options.rationale: No evidence supports guaranteed encopresis from earlier intensive training.

options.label: B
options.text: Training intensity has never been studied for complications
options.rationale: Complication data exist and are summarized in the article.

options.label: C
options.text: Any training before 30 months is contraindicated
options.rationale: Training before 30 months is not contraindicated; many children train between 18-36 months.

options.label: D
options.text: Intensive training before 27 months is not linked to constipation or withholding
options.rationale: AAFP reports intensive toilet training before 27 months is not associated with complications such as constipation, stool withholding, or stool toileting refusal - reassuring families who choose earlier starts while still emphasizing readiness and positivity.

questions.sourceMapping: AAFP Toilet Training (Baird 2019), intensive training before 27 months

stem: Toilet training has devolved into daily conflict with a 30-month-old who screams and hides from the potty. The AAFP-consistent recommendation is that:

options.label: A
options.text: Permanent abandonment of training until age 5 is required
options.rationale: A break is temporary, not permanent abandonment.

options.label: B
options.text: A temporary break of one to three months is acceptable to defuse conflict
options.rationale: Temporary one- to three-month breaks are acceptable to avoid negative attitudes and conflict, alongside positive language and praise; this mirrors the professor's positivity-first counseling.

options.label: C
options.text: Training must continue without interruption to avoid regression
options.rationale: Continuing through daily conflict entrenches withholding and refusal.

options.label: D
options.text: Punishment should be added to accelerate compliance
options.rationale: Punishment is explicitly discouraged.

questions.sourceMapping: AAFP Toilet Training (Baird 2019), breaks and positive approach

stem: Which comorbidity cluster reduces the likelihood of achieving full toilet training and prompts early subspecialty or therapy consultation?

options.label: A
options.text: Iron deficiency anemia without pica
options.rationale: Iron deficiency without pica does not change training prognosis.

options.label: B
options.text: Down syndrome, autism spectrum disorder, and cerebral palsy
options.rationale: AAFP notes medical comorbidities such as Down syndrome, ASD, and cerebral palsy lower the likelihood of full toilet training and often require early consultation with occupational therapy, developmental pediatrics, or other subspecialists.

options.label: C
options.text: Recurrent otitis media with tympanostomy tubes
options.rationale: Otitis media history does not affect toileting outcomes.

options.label: D
options.text: Asthma, eczema, and allergic rhinitis
options.rationale: Atopic disease does not impair continence acquisition.

questions.sourceMapping: AAFP Toilet Training (Baird 2019), comorbidities section

stem: For the 4-year-old with functional constipation, overflow soiling, and delayed meconium passage, the definitive diagnostic pathway for the suspected organic cause is:

options.label: A
options.text: Contrast enema and rectal biopsy via pediatric surgery or GI
options.rationale: Hirschsprung disease - signaled by delayed meconium beyond 48-72 hours with lifelong constipation - is confirmed via contrast enema and rectal suction biopsy through specialty referral; the case twist made this the major concern.

options.label: B
options.text: Anorectal manometry as the sole first test in primary care
options.rationale: Manometry may adjunct but does not replace biopsy-based confirmation via referral.

options.label: C
options.text: An empiric gluten-free trial without any testing
options.rationale: A gluten-free trial addresses celiac, not the meconium-delay pattern.

options.label: D
options.text: Serial abdominal radiographs every month for a year
options.rationale: Serial radiographs delay definitive diagnosis.

questions.sourceMapping: Week 3 transcript, Case 5 (Hirschsprung suspicion); transcript red-flag list of organic causes

stem: The first-line pharmacologic agent the course named to soften stool and reverse withholding in functional constipation with encopresis is:

options.label: A
options.text: Polyethylene glycol 3350 (MiraLAX) mixed in liquid
options.rationale: The debrief specified MiraLAX (PEG 3350) mixed in liquid to get the bowels moving and keep stool soft and easy to pass while withholding extinguishes; loperamide would worsen impaction.

options.label: B
options.text: Loperamide to reduce soiling episodes
options.rationale: Antimotility agents aggravate impaction and overflow soiling.

options.label: C
options.text: Prophylactic oral antibiotics to prevent fissure infection
options.rationale: Antibiotics have no role in uncomplicated fissures or encopresis.

options.label: D
options.text: Daily stimulant suppositories as maintenance monotherapy
options.rationale: Suppository monotherapy is not the taught first-line maintenance strategy.

questions.sourceMapping: Week 3 transcript, Case 5 (MiraLAX to loosen stool)

stem: A 5-year-old with stool withholding does not recognize the urge to defecate. Alongside osmotic therapy, the behavioral strategy the debrief endorsed is:

options.label: A
options.text: Immediate reward only for large-volume stools
options.rationale: Rewarding only large stools reinforces anxiety and holding.

options.label: B
options.text: Withholding all fluids to concentrate the urge
options.rationale: Fluid restriction hardens stool and worsens withholding.

options.label: C
options.text: Scheduled toileting about every two hours to retrain urge recognition
options.rationale: The debrief endorsed a toileting schedule about every two hours so the child practices feeling and responding to the urge instead of holding; soft stool from PEG makes responding painless.

options.label: D
options.text: Daily suppositories to manufacture the urge
options.rationale: Suppositories do not teach urge recognition and are not the taught strategy.

questions.sourceMapping: Week 3 transcript, Case 5 debrief (toileting schedule every two hours)

stem: A 6-year-old presents with habitual snoring. Select all history elements the course identifies as features of possible obstructive sleep apnea to probe during the visit.

options.label: A
options.text: Consistent sleep-through-the-night without any movement
options.rationale: Completely motionless sleep is not an OSA feature; restlessness is.

options.label: B
options.text: Excessive daytime sleepiness and difficulty waking
options.rationale: Daytime sleepiness (with screening tools available) and difficult morning waking are core features.

options.label: C
options.text: Nighttime awakenings and morning headaches
options.rationale: are listed OSA features.

options.label: D
options.text: Immediate sleep onset within seconds at bedtime every night
options.rationale: Instant sleep onset is not among the taught OSA probes.

options.label: E
options.text: Restless sleep with witnessed pauses and gasping
options.rationale: Restless sleep, witnessed not breathing, and gasping pauses are the taught red-flag history elements.

questions.sourceMapping: Week 3 transcript, Case 3 debrief (OSA history elements and daytime sleepiness screening tools)

stem: In evaluating the snoring 6-year-old, the clinician plots a BMI at the 96th percentile. The relevance of this finding is that:

options.label: A
options.text: Obesity excludes adenotonsillar disease as a contributor
options.rationale: Obesity and adenotonsillar hypertrophy frequently coexist.

options.label: B
options.text: Obesity is an OSA risk factor, so growth and BMI assessment belong in the workup
options.rationale: The debrief listed checking growth and BMI because obesity contributes to sleep apnea alongside adenotonsillar hypertrophy; both pathways inform referral and management.

options.label: C
options.text: BMI above the 95th percentile mandates immediate CPAP
options.rationale: CPAP is not first-line; adenotonsillar evaluation and sleep testing come first.

options.label: D
options.text: BMI has no relationship to pediatric sleep-disordered breathing
options.rationale: Obesity is a well-established pediatric OSA risk factor.

questions.sourceMapping: Week 3 transcript, Case 3 debrief (checking growth and BMI in OSA evaluation)

stem: The snoring child breathes through his mouth continuously, and the clinician suspects the adenoids are involved. The anatomic rationale taught is that:

options.label: A
options.text: Adenoids sit behind the nose and enlarge with tonsils, blocking airflow
options.rationale: The debrief explained adenoids sit at the back of the nose; habitual mouth breathing suggests adenoid hypertrophy, and big tonsils usually travel with big adenoids - informing the ENT referral.

options.label: B
options.text: Adenoids sit in the oropharynx beside the tonsils and rarely enlarge together
options.rationale: Adenoids are nasopharyngeal, and they commonly enlarge with tonsils.

options.label: C
options.text: Adenoids regress by age 3, so they cannot obstruct at 6 years
options.rationale: Adenoid tissue persists through early school age and commonly obstructs at 6 years.

options.label: D
options.text: Adenoid tissue is irrelevant unless the child has cystic fibrosis
options.rationale: Adenoid hypertrophy is common without cystic fibrosis.

questions.sourceMapping: Week 3 transcript, Case 3 debrief (adenoids at the back of the nose; tonsils and adenoids go hand in hand)

stem: When describing the atopic march to the family of a 4-month-old with new atopic dermatitis, the clinician states that the march typically begins with:

options.label: A
options.text: Food anaphylaxis in infancy, progressing to isolated eczema
options.rationale: Anaphylaxis is not the march's starting point.

options.label: B
options.text: Asthma in infancy, progressing to eczema and rhinitis
options.rationale: Asthma is the later step, not the infant onset.

options.label: C
options.text: Allergic rhinitis in infancy, progressing to eczema and then asthma
options.rationale: Rhinitis does not precede eczema in the march sequence.

options.label: D
options.text: Eczema in infancy, progressing to allergic rhinitis and then asthma
options.rationale: The allergic march as taught starts with eczema in babies, then allergic rhinitis, then asthma - framing early skin barrier disease as the first step of the atopic trajectory.

questions.sourceMapping: Week 3 transcript, Case 4 (allergic march sequence)

stem: A 7-year-old with confirmed exercise-induced bronchoconstriction asks whether he can keep playing soccer. The management consistent with the case discussion is to:

options.label: A
options.text: Advise breathing through the mouth in cold weather to prevent attacks
options.rationale: Mouth breathing in cold air worsens airway drying and bronchoconstriction.

options.label: B
options.text: Require clearance only after a negative chest radiograph each season
options.rationale: Radiographs do not gate sports participation in EIB.

options.label: C
options.text: Permanently restrict the child from all aerobic sports
options.rationale: Sport restriction is unnecessary with treated EIB.

options.label: D
options.text: Provide a reliever inhaler for use before and during play as prescribed
options.rationale: The case discussion supported keeping the child active with an inhaler available at soccer in case of an attack during play, alongside environmental trigger review; exercise restriction is not the goal.

questions.sourceMapping: Week 3 transcript, Case 4 (inhaler at soccer; environmental evaluation)

stem: Which differential set did the course attach to the child with nocturnal and post-exercise cough and atopic history?

options.label: A
options.text: Croup, epiglottitis, and bacterial tracheitis
options.rationale: Those acute infectious airway emergencies do not fit a chronic atopic cough pattern.

options.label: B
options.text: Asthma, allergic rhinitis, and exercise-induced bronchoconstriction
options.rationale: The debrief's differential was asthma, allergic rhinitis, and exercise-induced bronchoconstriction, with the added pearl that GERD can mimic or exacerbate asthma through cough-reflex irritation.

options.label: C
options.text: Foreign body aspiration as the sole consideration
options.rationale: Foreign body is a consideration in sudden-onset focal cough, not the taught differential here.

options.label: D
options.text: Pertussis, bronchiolitis, and bronchopneumonia
options.rationale: Those infectious diagnoses do not match the chronic atopic presentation.

stem: A 10-year-old screened at age 10 had a fully normal lipid panel and remains healthy with stable BMI. Per the course's screening logic, the next universal lipid screen is:

options.label: A
options.text: Annually beginning at age 12
options.rationale: Annual lipids are not recommended after a normal universal screen.

options.label: B
options.text: Never, because one normal childhood panel is lifelong clearance
options.rationale: The 17-21 window still applies; one panel is not lifelong clearance.

options.label: C
options.text: Between 17 and 21 years, sooner if weight or risk status changes
options.rationale: Universal screening occurs at 9-11 and again at 17-21; a normal childhood panel does not require repeat until the second window unless weight or other risk factors change - the professor's exact answer to 'why do we stop between 11 and 17?'

options.label: D
options.text: Every two years until age 21
options.rationale: Two-year intervals apply to vision/hearing, not lipids.

stem: A 17-year-old establishes care with no record of any lipid screening. The appropriate action is to:

options.label: A

options.rationale: Missing the first window does not forfeit screening; the second window exists.

options.label: B
options.text: Order coronary calcium scoring instead of a lipid panel
options.rationale: Calcium scoring is not a pediatric screening tool.

options.label: C
options.text: Screen only if the patient develops hypertension
options.rationale: Risk-based-only screening ignores the universal recommendation.

options.label: D

stem: When counseling a 7-year-old and family about diet and activity, the clinician recalls that school-aged children are concrete thinkers. The counseling style indicated is:

options.label: A
options.text: Abstract risk-probability discussions aimed at the child
options.rationale: Abstract probability framing exceeds concrete operational reasoning.

options.label: B
options.text: Written pamphlets handed to the child without verbal discussion
options.rationale: Pamphlets alone omit the direct conversation guidance recommends.

options.label: C
options.text: Direct and straightforward, with concrete instructions the child can follow
options.rationale: AFP Part II states school-aged children are concrete thinkers, so counseling should be direct and straightforward - matching Piaget's concrete operational stage taught on the slides.

options.label: D
options.text: Deferred counseling until adolescent abstract reasoning emerges
options.rationale: Deferral forfeits the age when lifelong habits form.

stem: Which dietary pattern statement matches school-age counseling guidance?

options.label: A
options.text: Emphasize whole foods and limit sugar and highly processed foods
options.rationale: The guidance specifies a diet high in fruits, vegetables, whole grains, low-fat or nonfat dairy, beans, fish, and lean meats, limiting sugar, fast food, and highly processed foods - consistent with the Dietary Guidelines' 'eat real food' reset.

options.label: B
options.text: Emphasize high-protein ketogenic restriction of all grains for all children
options.rationale: Universal ketogenic grain restriction is not pediatric guidance.

options.label: C
options.text: Emphasize calorie counting as the primary pediatric strategy
options.rationale: Calorie counting is not the primary counseling strategy; pattern change is.

options.label: D
options.text: Emphasize unrestricted fruit juice as the primary fruit source
options.rationale: Juice is limited (4-6 ounces at 4-6 years) and is not the primary fruit source.

stem: A 14-month-old has never seen a dentist. The oral health action indicated at this visit is to:

options.rationale: Waiting for permanent teeth misses the entire primary dentition risk window.

options.rationale: Waiting for complete primary dentition misses early caries prevention.

options.label: C

stem: When counseling families of toddlers and school-age children alike, the course cites strong research support for which routine practice?

options.label: A
options.text: Shared family meals, which support emotional well-being
options.rationale: The professor cited 'an exorbitant amount of research' that family meals - whichever meal - where people gather and talk are extremely beneficial for emotional well-being, and the school-age exam still asks about family dinner time.

options.label: B
options.text: Independent meals in front of television to build autonomy
options.rationale: Screen-distracted solitary meals contradict the guidance.

options.label: C
options.text: Elimination of all family snacks between meals
options.rationale: Snack elimination is not the teaching; healthy snacks are endorsed at 2 years.

options.label: D
options.text: Separate meal times for children and adults always
options.rationale: Separate schedules forfeit the documented benefit.

stem: Which language-promotion counseling is consistent with the course from infancy through preschool?

options.label: A
options.text: Delay reading until the child recognizes letters at 4 years
options.rationale: Waiting for letter recognition wastes the critical language window.

options.label: B
options.text: Read aloud daily and narrate routines constantly, starting in the newborn period
options.rationale: The course emphasizes reading from the newborn period (highlighting the Dolly Parton book program) and constant narrating talk as core language-building anticipatory guidance.

options.label: C
options.text: Use screen-based language apps as the primary language input
options.rationale: Screens are discouraged as language substitutes in early childhood.

options.label: D
options.text: Limit talking during routines to avoid overstimulation
options.rationale: Narration is encouraged, not limited.

stem: A toddler runs toward a hot stove. The discipline response the course recommends in dangerous moments is to:

options.label: A
options.text: Move the child and use a calm 'danger' cue, not repetitive 'no'
options.rationale: The lecture taught picking your battles: for genuine danger, move the child and say 'danger' calmly; repetitive 'no' and yelling are discouraged, and ignoring applies only to non-harmful misbehavior.

options.label: B
options.text: Ignore the behavior entirely regardless of danger
options.rationale: Danger is the explicit exception to planned ignoring.

options.label: C
options.text: Scream 'no' repeatedly to build lasting avoidance
options.rationale: Repetitive yelling dilutes the cue and models escalation.

options.label: D
options.text: Administer a brief spanking to encode the hazard
options.rationale: Corporal punishment is not endorsed anywhere in the course.

questions.sourceMapping: Week 3 transcript, pick-your-battles and danger-cue discussion; Slides 5 and 13 (praise and redirect)

stem: Anticipatory guidance at the 12-15 month visit includes ensuring the family has which safety resource immediately available?

options.label: A
options.text: The poison control number, because hand-to-mouth exploration escalates now

options.label: B
options.text: A home defibrillator for arrhythmia screening
options.rationale: Home defibrillators are not anticipatory guidance for toddlers.

options.label: C
options.text: A pulse oximeter for nightly saturation monitoring
options.rationale: Nightly oximetry is not indicated for healthy toddlers.

options.label: D

options.rationale: Universal auto-injectors are not indicated without allergy history.

stem: Select all components that belong to the school-age annual examination as defined in this course.

options.label: A
options.text: Annual universal depression screening before age 12
options.rationale: Routine depression screening before 12 lacks sufficient evidence; case-finding on somatic or anxiety symptoms is taught instead.

options.label: B

options.rationale: Head circumference is no longer routine in this age group absent concern.

options.label: C
options.text: Assessment of peer and family relationships and emotional health
options.rationale: Peer, family, and emotional health assessment are explicit annual components.

stem: Every well-child encounter in this age span begins by addressing which items before new guidance is given?

options.label: A
options.text: Growth plotting only after the complete physical examination
options.rationale: Growth assessment is an early core component at every visit.

options.label: B
