options.rationale: Immunizations come at the end of the visit sequence, not before history.

options.label: C
options.text: Parental concerns, prior-visit issues, and specialist evaluations
options.rationale: Each well-exam slide opens with continuing to address parental concerns, issues from the previous visit, and any specialist evaluations - and the transcript stressed re-evaluating prior recommendations and referral follow-through at every visit.

options.label: D
options.text: Screening questionnaires only if the parent raises concerns
options.rationale: Standardized screening tools are scheduled, not complaint-driven.

questions.sourceMapping: Slides 4, 12, 14 (well-exam opening items); Week 3 transcript, re-evaluate prior recommendations discussion

stem: A 12-month-old is seen for a health supervision visit. The provider reviews interval milestones, observes parent-child interaction, elicits caregiver concerns, and considers risk factors before deciding whether a standardized instrument is indicated. This activity, performed at every well and acute visit across the lifespan, is best classified as which of the following?

options.label: A
options.text: Developmental surveillance, because it is a continuous, longitudinal, elicitation-based process
options.rationale: Surveillance is the flexible, cumulative, ongoing process performed at every encounter from birth onward; it precedes and informs the decision to screen. The professor emphasized surveillance occurs 'at every single visit... birth to death.'

options.label: B
options.text: Developmental screening, because a structured process is applied at a scheduled visit
options.rationale: Screening refers to administration of a standardized, validated instrument at specified ages or when concern arises, not the global every-visit process.

options.label: C
options.text: Diagnostic evaluation, because it establishes the presence of a developmental disorder
options.rationale: Diagnostic evaluation is a comprehensive, usually specialty-based assessment that follows a positive screen or persistent concern; it is not performed in primary care at a well visit.

options.label: D
options.text: Case-finding evaluation, because it is triggered by a previously positive screening result
options.rationale: Case-finding or further evaluation follows a positive screen; here no prior positive result exists, and the described activity is universal and proactive.

questions.sourceMapping: Atypical Development transcript (surveillance vs screening); AAP Clinical Report, Lipkin & Macias, Pediatrics 2020 (surveillance at every health supervision visit); Cases deck Slide 8

stem: The American Academy of Pediatrics recommends standardized developmental screening with a validated instrument at which set of health supervision visits, in addition to screening at any visit when concern arises?

options.label: A
options.text: 6, 15, and 24 months of age
options.rationale: These ages do not correspond to any AAP-recommended standardized developmental screening schedule.

options.label: B
options.text: 9, 18, and 30 months of age
options.rationale: The AAP clinical report and its algorithm specify standardized developmental screening at the 9-, 18-, and 30-month visits, with additional screening whenever concerns emerge.

options.label: C
options.text: 12, 24, and 36 months of age
options.rationale: This schedule substitutes the 24-month autism-specific screen age for the 18-month dual screen and omits the 9-month screen.

options.label: D
options.text: 18, 24, and 30 months of age
options.rationale: 18 and 24 months are the autism-specific screening ages; the general developmental screen ages are 9, 18, and 30 months.

questions.sourceMapping: AAP Clinical Report (Lipkin & Macias, Pediatrics 2020), abstract and algorithm Figure 2, steps 3a-3d; Atypical Development transcript

stem: In addition to general developmental screening, autism-specific screening with a tool such as the M-CHAT-R/F is recommended by the AAP at which ages?

options.label: A
options.text: 9 and 18 months of age
options.rationale: The 9-month visit includes a general developmental screen but not a routine autism-specific screen.

options.label: B
options.text: 12 and 24 months of age
options.rationale: 12 months is not an AAP autism-specific screening age; loss of skills at any age, however, mandates evaluation.

options.label: C
options.text: 18 and 24 months of age
options.rationale: AAP recommends autism-specific screening at the 18- and 24-month visits; the professor reinforced this verbally as a mandatory recall item ('18 and 24 months is when we check with the M-CHAT').

options.label: D
options.text: 24 and 36 months of age
options.rationale: By 36 months the validated window for the M-CHAT-R/F has passed; concern at any age still warrants autism-specific screening.

questions.sourceMapping: AAP Clinical Report (Lipkin 2020) algorithm step 3c-3d; JAMA ASD Review (Hirota & King, 2023); Atypical Development transcript (verbal emphasis: 'just reinforcing 18 and 24 months')

stem: A 18-month-old with no identified risks arrives for a health supervision visit. According to the numbered algorithm in the figure, which standardized testing should be administered during this visit?
Figure from AAP Clinical Report algorithm (Lipkin & Macias, Pediatrics 2020), p. 4

options.label: A
options.text: Developmental screening only, because autism-specific screening begins at 24 months
options.rationale: Autism-specific screening begins at 18 months, not 24 months; the 24-month visit repeats the autism-specific screen only.

options.label: B
options.text: No standardized screening, because testing is indicated only when surveillance raises concern
options.rationale: Universal standardized screening at 9, 18, and 30 months is independent of surveillance concern; concern merely adds screening at other ages.

options.label: C
options.text: Autism-specific screening only, because the 9-month developmental screen was completed
options.rationale: The developmental screen is repeated at 18 months; it is not a single 9-month event.

options.label: D
options.text: Developmental screening and an autism-specific screen, per steps 3b and 3c
options.rationale: The algorithm's 18-month node pairs the standardized developmental screen with the autism-specific screen; this dual administration is unique to the 18-month visit.

questions.sourceMapping: AAP Clinical Report (Lipkin 2020), surveillance/screening algorithm (Figure 2, nodes 3a-3d); Atypical Development transcript

stem: According to the screening framework in the figure, which two conditions are identified through the newborn-care pathway rather than through later health supervision visits?
Figure from AAP Clinical Report screening framework (Lipkin & Macias, Pediatrics 2020), p. 3

options.label: A
options.text: Metabolic disorders and hearing loss
options.rationale: The figure places metabolic disorders (newborn screening) and hearing (newborn hearing screening) under the newborn-care branch; all other listed domains are surfaced during health supervision visits.

options.label: B
options.text: Autism spectrum disorder and motor disorders
options.rationale: Autism spectrum and motor disorders appear as subdomains of developmental disabilities identified at health supervision visits, not in the newborn period.

options.label: C
options.text: Vision impairment and behavioral-emotional problems
options.rationale: Vision and behavioral-emotional problems are health supervision visit screening domains in the figure's middle tier.

options.label: D
options.text: Specific language disorders and intellectual disability
options.rationale: Language and intellectual disabilities are subdomains branching from developmental disabilities, detected later through surveillance and screening.

questions.sourceMapping: AAP Clinical Report (Lipkin 2020), Figure 1 screening/identification framework; Atypical Development transcript (newborn screening, PKU history)

stem: Which statement correctly characterizes the M-CHAT-R as described in the assigned JAMA review?

options.label: A
options.text: A 10-item clinician checklist validated for children 36 to 60 months of age
options.rationale: The item count and age window are incorrect; the tool targets 16-30 months, not preschool-graduate ages.

options.label: B
options.text: A 20-item parent questionnaire for 16- to 30-month-olds in which a score above 2 triggers follow-up questions
options.rationale: The M-CHAT-R is a 20-item parent-completed screen for 16-30 months; a total score greater than 2 requires structured follow-up questions (M-CHAT-R/F), which raise specificity.

options.label: C
options.text: A diagnostic instrument whose sensitivity alone confirms autism in primary care
options.rationale: No screening tool diagnoses autism; a positive screen mandates comprehensive evaluation. The professor stressed 'screening identifies risk... it doesn't give a diagnosis.'

options.label: D
options.text: A structured observation that must be administered by two trained examiners
options.rationale: Two trained examiners describe the ADOS-2 diagnostic observation, not the M-CHAT-R screen.

questions.sourceMapping: JAMA ASD Review (Hirota & King, 2023), Screening section; Atypical Development transcript (ADOS by two observers)

stem: Per the assigned JAMA review, the M-CHAT-R with follow-up questions demonstrates which approximate operating characteristics?

options.label: A
options.text: Sensitivity 91% and specificity 76%
options.rationale: These are the reported values for the ADOS-2, a diagnostic observation tool, not the M-CHAT-R/F.

options.label: B
options.text: Sensitivity 99% and specificity 85%
options.rationale: Inverting the values overstates sensitivity; the follow-up process primarily protects specificity while retaining high sensitivity.

options.label: C
options.text: Sensitivity 85% and specificity 99%
options.rationale: With follow-up questions the M-CHAT-R achieves approximately 85% sensitivity and 99% specificity, which is why the follow-up step is integral to the tool.

options.label: D
options.text: Sensitivity 80% and specificity 72%
options.rationale: These are the reported values for the ADI-R caregiver interview, not the M-CHAT-R/F.

questions.sourceMapping: JAMA ASD Review (Hirota & King, 2023), Screening and Diagnostic Assessment sections

stem: A 24-month-old scores in the high-risk range on the M-CHAT-R/F. There are no other medical concerns. Which action sequence is most appropriate?

options.label: A
options.text: Repeat the M-CHAT-R/F in 6 months to confirm persistence before any referral
options.rationale: Repeating a positive screen delays time-sensitive early intervention and adds no actionable information.

options.label: B
options.text: Defer all intervention until the diagnostic evaluation formally confirms autism
options.rationale: Waiting for a definitive diagnosis before starting services directly contradicts AAP guidance and the lecture's central teaching point.

options.label: C
options.text: Order brain MRI and EEG in primary care before generating specialty referrals
options.rationale: Neuroimaging and EEG are not routine primary-care workups for a positive autism screen absent seizures or regression.

options.label: D
options.text: Refer for comprehensive diagnostic evaluation and initiate early intervention services now
options.rationale: A positive autism-specific screen warrants immediate comprehensive diagnostic referral plus concurrent early intervention referral; services must not wait for diagnostic confirmation. The professor flagged this repeatedly ('we don't wait to find out what's going on').

questions.sourceMapping: Atypical Development transcript (do not wait for diagnosis; EI referral); Cases deck Slide 5; JAMA ASD Review (positive screen -> comprehensive evaluation and developmental services)

stem: A 20-month-old used approximately 50 words at 15 months but now uses none, and has stopped responding to his name. Growth and prior milestones were normal. Which interpretation is most appropriate?

options.label: A
options.text: Developmental regression requiring prompt neurologic, genetic, and metabolic evaluation
options.rationale: Loss of previously acquired language or social skills is regression, a red flag demanding evaluation for neurologic, genetic, metabolic, and epileptic causes. The professor's stated pearl: 'any child who loses skills needs an evaluation... there is no reassurance here.'

options.label: B
options.text: A normal developmental variation that should be rechecked at the 24-month visit
options.rationale: Watchful waiting at a future visit is inappropriate; regression is never a normal variation.

options.label: C
options.text: An expected language plateau that warrants reassurance and continued surveillance
options.rationale: Reassurance is explicitly contraindicated when skills are lost; plateaus differ from true skill loss.

options.label: D
options.text: An isolated expressive delay manageable with speech therapy referral alone
options.rationale: Speech therapy may be part of the plan, but regression mandates a medical evaluation, not a single-therapy referral.

questions.sourceMapping: Atypical Development transcript (regression red flag; teaching pearl, verbal emphasis); Cases deck Slide 8; AAP Clinical Report (Lipkin 2020)

stem: Which findings identified during developmental surveillance should be treated as red flags prompting further evaluation? Select all that apply.

options.label: A
options.text: Loss of previously acquired language or social-communication skills
options.rationale: Regression of any previously acquired skill is a high-priority red flag for neurologic, genetic, or metabolic disease.

options.label: B
options.text: A consistent hand preference established before 12 months of age
options.rationale: Early hand preference suggests possible contralateral motor pathway injury (e.g., hemiplegic cerebral palsy); infants normally grasp bimanually.

options.label: C
options.text: Independent walking achieved at 13 months of age
options.rationale: Walking at 13 months is within the normal range and is not a red flag.

options.label: D
options.text: Persistent asymmetry of tone, movement, or hand use between sides
options.rationale: Asymmetry of tone or movement is an explicit red flag in the lecture and AAP framework.

options.label: E
options.text: Consistent orienting to name by 10 months of age
options.rationale: Responding to name by 10 months is expected; failure to respond to name by 9 months would be the concerning finding.

questions.sourceMapping: Atypical Development transcript (red flags list, verbal emphasis); Cases deck Slide 8; AAP Clinical Report (Lipkin 2020)

stem: During a 10-month visit, an infant consistently reaches for and holds objects using only the right hand, with no transfer to the left. Why is this finding concerning?

options.label: A
options.text: It indicates advanced fine-motor development that requires enrichment activities
options.rationale: Early hand preference is not a marker of advanced development and should never be praised as a milestone.

options.label: B
options.text: It suggests premature lateralization from possible contralateral motor pathway injury
options.rationale: Infants normally grasp bimanually; an early handedness implies the other side is underused, raising concern for hemiplegic cerebral palsy or another focal motor lesion.

options.label: C
options.text: It is an expected finding that removes the need for further motor surveillance
options.rationale: The finding heightens, rather than removes, the need for focused motor and neurologic surveillance.

options.label: D
options.text: It predicts a specific learning disorder and mandates neuropsychological testing now
options.rationale: No evidence links infant hand preference to later learning disability in a way that mandates neuropsychological testing.

questions.sourceMapping: Atypical Development transcript (early hand preference red flag, ~4-month bimanual grasp reference)

stem: A parent expresses persistent worry that her 16-month-old 'is not developing like his cousins.' Developmental surveillance and a standardized screen today are unremarkable. Per the lecture, the most appropriate response is to:

options.label: A
options.text: Discharge the concern because the validated screening instrument is negative
options.rationale: A negative screen does not override persistent informed concern; surveillance concern mandates screening or direct referral per AAP.

options.label: B
options.text: Repeat the identical screening tool next month before taking any additional action
options.rationale: Mechanical repetition of the same tool delays evaluation; the concern should drive targeted assessment or referral now.

options.label: C
options.text: Honor the concern, because persistent caregiver concern alone warrants further evaluation
options.rationale: Persistent caregiver concern is itself a red flag; the professor cited that parents are correct roughly 80% of the time and instructed never to minimize their concern.

options.label: D
options.text: Order chromosomal microarray in primary care before considering any referral
options.rationale: Microarray is pursued within a specialty evaluation when indicated, not as a first step in primary care for an unremarkable screen.

questions.sourceMapping: Atypical Development transcript (parent concern 80%; persistent caregiver concern red flag, verbal emphasis); AAP Clinical Report (Lipkin 2020)

stem: A 26-month-old is confirmed to have a global developmental delay after comprehensive evaluation. The family asks how to obtain services. Which statement is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: The school district's preschool special education committee is the entry point before age 3
options.rationale: School-based services (CPSE/school-age) begin at age 3, after early intervention eligibility ends.

options.label: B
options.text: Early intervention eligibility begins at age 4, concurrent with kindergarten entry
options.rationale: Age 4 is far past the early intervention window; the 3-year boundary shifts services to the school system.

options.label: C
options.text: Services require a documented diagnosis and formal disability designation before eligibility
options.rationale: Requiring a diagnosis first inverts the lecture's core directive: intervene while the diagnostic evaluation proceeds.

options.label: D
options.text: The early intervention program (birth to 3) evaluates and provides services without awaiting a diagnosis
options.rationale: Children under 3 are served by early intervention (e.g., home-based evaluation in New York); referral occurs at the point of concern and does not require a diagnosis.

questions.sourceMapping: Atypical Development transcript (EI birth to 3 vs school-based after 3, verbal emphasis); Cases deck Slides 3 and 5

stem: The professor warned against referring 'because you don't know.' Which practice best reflects appropriate referral behavior for an advanced practice provider?

options.label: A
options.text: Complete an appropriate primary-care workup and refer with an explicit clinical question
options.rationale: Referrals should carry a formulated clinical question the specialist is being asked to answer, built on a completed primary-care evaluation; the professor modeled this with the language-loss example.

options.label: B
options.text: Refer immediately upon any abnormal finding so specialty assumes responsibility
options.rationale: Referral without workup abdicates the provider's reasoning role and frustrates consultants, per the lecture.

options.label: C
options.text: Defer all evaluation until the specialist specifies which tests should be ordered
options.rationale: Providers may and should ask consultants what would help pre-referral, but initiating the workup remains the referring clinician's job.

options.label: D
options.text: Refer only after the family independently secures imaging and insurance authorization
options.rationale: Placing logistics before clinical action delays care; the provider drives the workup and coordination.

questions.sourceMapping: Atypical Development transcript (referral with a clinical question, verbal emphasis: 'I'm going to warn you...')

stem: A 9-year-old is brought in because teachers describe the pattern depicted in the figure: quietly off task, staring, and missing instructions, with no disruptive behavior. Which statement is most accurate?
Figure from Slide 3 (ADHD lecture deck)

options.label: A
options.text: The depicted pattern excludes ADHD because hyperactivity is required for the diagnosis
options.rationale: Hyperactivity is not required; DSM-5-TR recognizes a predominantly inattentive presentation.

options.label: B
options.text: The depicted inattentive pattern is frequently under-recognized, particularly in girls
options.rationale: Predominantly inattentive presentation lacks disruptive behavior, so it is missed more often; the lecture noted girls tend to present inattentively and are overlooked, sometimes until later school years.

options.label: C
options.text: The depicted pattern is pathognomonic of absence epilepsy and mandates an EEG first
options.rationale: Absence events are a differential to consider, but the depicted daydreaming pattern is not pathognomonic and EEG is not an automatic first step.

options.label: D
options.text: The depicted pattern represents willful misbehavior best managed with a discipline plan
options.rationale: Inattention is a neurodevelopmental symptom, not willful disobedience; punishing uncontrollable behavior is explicitly cautioned against.

questions.sourceMapping: ADHD deck Slide 3 and Slide 7; Rec_20260930 transcript (female inattentive under-recognition); Fred case deck Slide 2

stem: The DSM-5-TR defines autism spectrum disorder by persistent deficits in which two core domains?

options.label: A
options.text: Expressive language delay, plus intellectual disability of any severity
options.rationale: Language delay and intellectual disability commonly co-occur but are neither necessary nor sufficient for an autism diagnosis.

options.label: B
options.text: Inattention, plus hyperactivity-impulsivity present in two or more settings
options.rationale: These are ADHD symptom domains, not autism criteria.

options.label: C
options.text: Social communication and interaction, plus restricted and repetitive behaviors or interests
options.rationale: The two DSM-5-TR domains are persistent social-communication/social-interaction deficits and restricted, repetitive patterns of behavior, interests, or activities.

options.label: D
options.text: Sensory hyperreactivity, plus restricted interests in the absence of social impairment
options.rationale: Sensory features belong within the restricted/repetitive domain; social-communication deficits are required, not absent.

questions.sourceMapping: Atypical Development transcript (core domains); JAMA ASD Review (diagnosis); Cases deck Slide 5

stem: According to the assigned JAMA review, the estimated prevalence of autism spectrum disorder in the United States is approximately:

options.label: A
options.text: 1.1% of children aged 8 years, with equal sex distribution
options.rationale: 1.1% reflects the 2008 estimate; prevalence has since more than doubled with better ascertainment.

options.label: B
options.text: 0.9% of children aged 8 years, with female predominance
options.rationale: 0.9% is the female-specific prevalence, not the overall estimate, and ASD is male-predominant.

options.label: C
options.text: 2.3% of children aged 8 years, with an approximate 10:1 male-to-female ratio
options.rationale: A 10:1 ratio overstates the sex difference reported in current surveillance data.

options.label: D
options.text: 2.3% of children aged 8 years, with an approximate 4:1 male-to-female ratio
options.rationale: The review reports ASD in about 2.3% of US 8-year-olds (and 2.2% of adults), with male prevalence 3.7% versus female 0.9%, roughly a 4:1 ratio.

questions.sourceMapping: JAMA ASD Review (Hirota & King, 2023), abstract and prevalence section

stem: When families ask why autism 'seems more common now,' the explanation best supported by current science is:

options.label: A
options.text: Expanded diagnostic criteria, improved screening and diagnostic tools, and increased awareness
options.rationale: The JAMA review attributes rising prevalence to changes in diagnostic criteria, better tool performance, and public/professional awareness; the lecture echoed 'better recognition and understanding of the disorder.'

options.label: B
options.text: Childhood immunization schedules combined with dietary gluten exposure
options.rationale: No credible evidence supports vaccine or gluten causation; these are debunked attributions.

options.label: C
options.text: An epidemic rise in environmental neurotoxins within processed foods
options.rationale: Environmental factors contribute a minority of risk (14-22% in the review) and do not explain the prevalence trend as toxins in food.

options.label: D
options.text: Replacement of reciprocal caregiver interaction with recreational screen time
options.rationale: Screen time is not an established cause of autism; it may modify interaction but is not etiologic.

questions.sourceMapping: JAMA ASD Review (prevalence trend; heritability 81%, environment 14-22%); Atypical Development transcript (better recognition)

stem: A child with autism spectrum disorder and co-occurring intellectual disability carries a markedly elevated risk (approximately 21%, versus 0.8% in the general population) of which comorbidity?

options.label: A
options.text: Type 1 diabetes mellitus
options.rationale: Diabetes is not an established ASD comorbidity at this magnitude.

options.label: B
options.text: Epilepsy and seizure disorders
options.rationale: Epilepsy occurs in about 21% of individuals with ASD plus intellectual disability (8% without ID) versus 0.8% in general population samples; seizures are a lecture-emphasized comorbidity and red flag.

options.label: C
options.text: Congenital heart disease
options.rationale: Congenital heart disease is associated with specific genetic syndromes (e.g., trisomy 21), not with ASD per se.

options.label: D
options.text: Sensorineural hearing loss
options.rationale: Hearing impairment raises ASD prevalence estimates but is not the 21%-versus-0.8% comorbidity described.

questions.sourceMapping: JAMA ASD Review (comorbidities: epilepsy 21% with ID vs 0.8%); Atypical Development transcript (seizures as red flag and comorbidity)

stem: Which represents the criterion standard for establishing an autism spectrum disorder diagnosis?

options.label: A
options.text: A single positive ADOS-2 module administered by any available clinician
options.rationale: ADOS-2 requires trained examiners (per lecture, two observers) and cannot stand alone as a diagnosis.

options.label: B
options.text: Chromosomal microarray demonstrating a pathogenic copy-number variant
options.rationale: Genetic testing identifies etiology and recurrence risk in a minority; it does not establish the behavioral diagnosis.

options.label: C
options.text: Best-estimate clinical consensus by a multidisciplinary team using standardized tools
options.rationale: The criterion standard is best-estimate clinical consensus: multidisciplinary agreement based on detailed developmental history and standardized observation (ADI-R, ADOS-2), which inform but never supersede clinical judgment.

options.label: D
options.text: A parent-reported M-CHAT-R/F score above the validated risk cutoff
options.rationale: The M-CHAT-R/F is a screen that identifies risk; a positive result mandates evaluation rather than confirming diagnosis.

questions.sourceMapping: JAMA ASD Review (Diagnostic Assessment); Atypical Development transcript (PCP does not diagnose autism; ADOS by trained evaluators)

stem: A family asks whether you, as their primary care provider, can 'just diagnose autism today.' The most accurate response is that:

options.label: A
options.text: Primary care confirms the diagnosis using DSM-5-TR criteria during the well-child visit
options.rationale: DSM-5-TR criteria are applied within the comprehensive specialty evaluation, not by a primary-care screen.

options.label: B
options.text: Primary care must defer all screening until the specialty evaluation is completed
options.rationale: Screening is a primary-care responsibility and must proceed irrespective of specialty wait times.

options.label: C
options.text: Primary care diagnoses autism once hearing loss and language disorder have been excluded
options.rationale: Excluding mimics is necessary but insufficient; the diagnosis requires structured multidisciplinary assessment.

options.label: D
options.text: Primary care screens and refers; diagnosis is made by trained specialists using standardized evaluation
options.rationale: The professor was explicit: 'Do I diagnose autism? No.' Primary care identifies risk, screens, refers for comprehensive evaluation (neuropsychology, developmental pediatrics, neurology), and coordinates care meanwhile.

questions.sourceMapping: Rec_20260930 transcript (case discussion: 'Do I diagnose autism? No'); Atypical Development transcript (referral pathway)

stem: Genetic testing is recommended for individuals diagnosed with autism spectrum disorder. Which combination reflects current recommendations?

options.label: A
options.text: Chromosomal microarray and fragile X testing, with MECP2 sequencing in females with regression
options.rationale: AAP and ACMG recommend microarray for copy-number variants and fragile X testing for all individuals with ASD; females with developmental regression should be tested for Rett syndrome (MECP2).

options.label: B
options.text: Karyotype alone, and only when dysmorphic features are present on examination

stem: Regarding treatment of autism spectrum disorder, which statement is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: Risperidone is first-line, with behavioral therapy added if irritability persists

options.text: Behavioral interventions are first-line; risperidone and aripiprazole target irritability, not core symptoms
options.rationale: First-line therapy is behavioral (e.g., Early Start Denver Model and related NDBIs); FDA-approved pharmacotherapy (risperidone, aripiprazole) mitigates irritability and behavioral dysregulation but does not treat core social-communication deficits.

options.label: C
options.text: Melatonin is first-line disease-modifying therapy for social-communication deficits
options.rationale: Melatonin may help sleep onset but has no disease-modifying effect on core symptoms.

options.label: D
options.text: SSRIs are first-line for core symptoms, with behavioral therapy reserved for adults
options.rationale: SSRIs lack evidence for core ASD symptoms and are not first-line at any age.

options.label: B

options.rationale: Normal social presentation does not make a language delay unimportant; this exact trap was taught in Case 1.

options.label: C

options.rationale: Joint attention, pointing, eye contact, and name response argue against ASD; a screen-positive result, not this vignette, would drive ADOS referral.

options.rationale: Delaying 6 months for a communication device substitutes for, and postpones, the required hearing workup and referral.

stem: For a 10-year-old being evaluated for ADHD, DSM-5-TR requires which symptom count and setting distribution?

options.text: At least 6 symptoms in a domain, with symptoms present in at least 2 settings
options.rationale: For individuals under 17, at least 6 symptoms in a domain are required, with several symptoms present in 2 or more settings; ages 17 and older require at least 5.

options.label: C
options.text: At least 5 symptoms in a domain, with symptoms in at least 3 settings
options.rationale: Five symptoms applies to age 17 and older, and 3 settings is not a criterion.

options.label: D

options.rationale: Symptoms are counted per domain, and cross-setting presence is essential.

stem: A teacher Vanderbilt rates 7 of 9 inattentive symptoms with academic impairment; the parent rates 3 of 9 inattentive and 1 of 9 hyperactive-impulsive. Which interpretation is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: The diagnosis is confirmed because one informant exceeds the symptom threshold
options.rationale: A single elevated informant scale cannot confirm ADHD without cross-setting integration and differential analysis.

options.label: B
options.text: ADHD is excluded because the parent score falls below the threshold
options.rationale: A low parent score may reflect limited awareness, context differences, or parenting style; it does not exclude ADHD.

options.label: C
options.text: The discrepancy requires further inquiry, because rating scales do not independently diagnose
options.rationale: Informant discrepancy is common and informative; scales support but never establish diagnosis, and a low score from one informant does not exclude ADHD. This exact scenario was the Fred case's final twist.

options.label: D
options.text: A combined presentation is established by averaging the two informant scores
options.rationale: Scores are never averaged; presentation is determined by criteria met within each domain across settings.

stem: A 20-year-old college student requests stimulants, stating his ADHD 'finally showed up' this semester. He reports no childhood academic or behavioral concerns, and his family recalls none. Which conclusion is most defensible?

options.label: A
options.text: ADHD is confirmed because current impairment is documented by the university
options.rationale: Current impairment alone cannot satisfy the developmental-onset criterion.

options.label: B
options.text: ADHD is unlikely as presently framed, because several symptoms must predate age 12; evaluate alternatives
options.rationale: Onset before age 12 is required; a truly de-novo adult-onset pattern demands evaluation of sleep, mood, substance, and medical contributors. The professor stated late-onset likelihood is 'pretty much nonexistent' without childhood clues.

options.label: C
options.text: ADHD is excluded solely because the patient is over 18 years of age
options.rationale: Age does not exclude ADHD; the disorder is lifelong, but childhood onset must be demonstrable.

options.label: D
options.text: ADHD should be treated empirically with stimulants before further history is obtained
options.rationale: Empirical treatment without evaluation violates the core reasoning sequence taught (history, informants, mimics first).

stem: Teacher ratings are markedly elevated while home behavior appears unremarkable in an 8-year-old. Which principle governs interpretation?

options.label: A
options.text: Symptoms in a single setting confirm ADHD if impairment is academic
options.rationale: One-setting impairment fails the cross-situational criterion.

options.label: B
options.text: A negative home report invalidates all school-based observations
options.rationale: Parent reports can under-capture school demands; they do not invalidate teacher data.

options.label: C
options.text: Cross-setting presence is required; informant asymmetry warrants inquiry, not exclusion
options.rationale: DSM-5-TR requires symptoms in 2 or more settings; when informants disagree, the provider probes context (demands, structure, parenting awareness) instead of prematurely confirming or excluding, as modeled in the Fred case.

options.label: D
options.text: Setting requirements apply only to the hyperactive-impulsive domain
options.rationale: The setting criterion applies to the disorder's symptoms overall, not one domain.

stem: An 8-year-old snores most nights, gasps during sleep, is difficult to wake, and falls asleep at his desk. Teachers report inattention. Which evaluation step has the highest yield now?

options.rationale: Melatonin treats circadian sleep-onset problems, not obstructive breathing.

options.label: D

stem: A 11-year-old with inattention, restlessness, and worsening school refusal has prominent worry, somatic complaints, and reassurance-seeking. The professor's stated management sequence is to:

options.label: B
options.text: Start stimulants first, because anxiety is usually secondary to ADHD failure
options.rationale: Assuming secondary anxiety without a treatment trial of anxiety risks missing the primary driver.

options.label: C
options.text: Start both simultaneously at full doses to save visits
options.rationale: Simultaneous full-dose initiation obscures which intervention produced change and increases adverse-effect ambiguity.

options.label: D
options.text: Treat the anxiety first, then re-assess attention once anxiety is controlled
options.rationale: The professor described anxiety and ADHD as 'best friends' and her practice of quieting significant anxiety first, because anxiety can generate ADHD-like inattention; response then clarifies the residual picture.

options.rationale: Activity-responsive restlessness is consistent with ADHD or mismatch, not seizures.

stem: A 15-year-old on stimulant therapy admits to occasionally using a classmate's cannabis vape 'to sleep.' Which action is most appropriate?

stem: The neuroimaging montage in the figure illustrates distributed network differences. Which pharmacologic principle follows from the lecture's neurobiology framing?

options.label: A
options.text: Agents increase dopamine/norepinephrine; amphetamines are relatively more noradrenergic
options.rationale: Stimulants increase dopamine and norepinephrine; the lecture notes amphetamines add relatively more norepinephrine (more activating), while methylphenidate is comparatively dopaminergic—guiding class choice by tolerability, not imaging.

options.label: B
options.text: Effective agents act primarily on serotonergic pathways regardless of class
options.rationale: Serotonergic agents (e.g., SSRIs) do not treat core ADHD symptoms; centanafadine's triple action is the exception among newer agents, not the rule.

options.label: C
options.text: Neurotransmitter effects are irrelevant because ADHD is purely behavioral
options.rationale: Neurotransmitter mechanisms are central to pharmacotherapy even though diagnosis is clinical.

options.label: D

options.rationale: No imaging-guided prescribing exists for ADHD.

options.label: D
options.text: Place a gastrostomy tube as the first-line management step
options.rationale: Gastrostomy is reserved for refractory cases after behavioral/medical management.

questions.sourceMapping: Atypical Development transcript (start OT/speech/sensory work while evaluating; do not wait); Cases deck Slide 5

stem: Which coordination principle defines the primary care provider's role for families of children with developmental delays?

options.label: A
options.text: The school system replaces medical follow-up after age 3
options.rationale: School services complement, not replace, medical surveillance.

options.label: B
options.text: The specialist assumes all coordination after referral
options.rationale: Specialists evaluate and treat; the medical home retains coordination.

options.label: C
options.text: The medical home coordinates specialty, school, and early intervention services
options.rationale: The lecture opens by defining the primary care job as coordination of care for these families, with tracking progress and coordination as the final pathway step; chronic-condition management continues per the AAP algorithm.

options.label: D
options.text: Coordination ends when a definitive diagnosis is assigned
options.rationale: Diagnosis initiates, rather than ends, chronic-condition management (algorithm node 15).

questions.sourceMapping: Atypical Development transcript (coordination of care role); AAP Clinical Report (Lipkin 2020), node 15 chronic condition management

stem: A 5-year-old former preterm infant (28 weeks) with prior intraventricular hemorrhage shows persistent toe-walking, asymmetric tone, and delayed sitting historically. Which diagnosis best integrates these findings?

options.label: A
options.text: Phenylketonuria detected on newborn screening
options.rationale: PKU presents with regression and is screened at birth.

options.label: B
options.text: Duchenne muscular dystrophy from dystrophin mutation
options.rationale: DMD shows proximal weakness, Gowers, and pseudohypertrophy without prematurity linkage.

options.label: C
options.text: Autism spectrum disorder without motor features
options.rationale: Social-communication features are absent from this vignette.

options.label: D
options.text: Cerebral palsy related to prematurity and neonatal brain injury
options.rationale: Prematurity with IVH plus non-progressive asymmetric tone, toe-walking, and delayed sitting fits CP; the lecture ties CP to prenatal/perinatal injury with spastic/dyskinetic/ataxic patterns.

questions.sourceMapping: Atypical Development transcript (CP etiology: prematurity, perinatal injury; tone and asymmetry)

stem: Which statement about the ADOS-2 is correct per the lecture and JAMA review?

options.label: A
options.text: Semi-structured observation by trained examiners; sensitivity ~91%, specificity ~76%
options.rationale: ADOS-2 is a semi-structured direct observation performed by trained specialists (per lecture, two observers), with reported sensitivity 91% and specificity 76%; it informs but does not supersede clinical judgment.

options.label: B
options.text: A parent-completed 20-item screening questionnaire for toddlers
options.rationale: That describes the M-CHAT-R.

options.label: C
options.text: An instrument administered by primary care at well visits
options.rationale: Primary care screens and refers; ADOS-2 is specialty-administered.

options.label: D
options.text: An observation tool with sensitivity ~80% and specificity ~72%
options.rationale: Those values belong to the ADI-R.

questions.sourceMapping: JAMA ASD Review (ADOS-2 operating characteristics); Atypical Development and Rec_20260930 transcripts (two trained observers)

stem: The Vineland-3, referenced in the neuropsychological evaluation discussion (transcribed phonetically as 'violin three'), is used to:

options.label: A
options.text: Screen newborns for inborn errors of metabolism
options.rationale: Newborn metabolic screening uses biochemical assays.

options.label: B
options.text: Assess adaptive functioning within the comprehensive diagnostic battery
options.rationale: The transcript's 'violin three' is the Vineland-3 (Vineland Adaptive Behavior Scales), used within neuropsychological evaluation to assess adaptive functioning; JAMA lists Vineland among cognitive/adaptive measures supporting diagnosis and therapy planning.

options.label: C
options.text: Measure stimulant response during the dose titration period
options.rationale: Stimulant response uses rating scales and functional goals.

options.label: D
options.text: Quantify noise and distraction exposure within the classroom setting
options.rationale: This option is a distractor with no clinical basis.

questions.sourceMapping: Atypical Development transcript ('violin three' = Vineland-3, transcription correction); JAMA ASD Review (Vineland Adaptive Behavior Scales)

stem: Which agent, transcribed in the audio as 'valmoralone,' is a newer corticosteroid-sparing option approved for Duchenne muscular dystrophy from age 2 years?

options.label: A
options.text: Valproate
options.rationale: Valproate is an antiseizure medication and a teratogen.

options.label: B
options.text: Viloxazine
options.rationale: Viloxazine (Qelbree) is an ADHD nonstimulant.

options.label: C
options.text: Vamorolone
options.rationale: Vamorolone is the dissociative steroid referenced for DMD age 2+ with a more favorable bone/growth side-effect profile than classic glucocorticoids; the transcript phonetically rendered it 'valmoralone.'

options.label: D
options.text: Varenicline
options.rationale: Varenicline is a smoking-cessation agent.

questions.sourceMapping: Atypical Development transcript (transcription correction: 'valmoralone' = vamorolone; novel steroid age 2+)

stem: Which combination of actions completes the AAP algorithm's response to a 'concerning' standardized screening result (nodes 6-9)?

options.label: A
options.text: Reassurance with annual developmental surveillance only
options.rationale: Reassurance after a concerning screen violates the algorithm.

options.label: B
options.text: Repeat the screening in 3 months before any evaluation
options.rationale: Delay contradicts the algorithm's immediate evaluation pathway.

options.label: C
options.text: Direct school enrollment without medical or developmental evaluation
options.rationale: Educational placement follows, not replaces, medical and developmental evaluation.

options.label: D
options.text: Medical evaluation with genetic testing plus developmental evaluation and EI referral
options.rationale: A concerning screen routes to medical evaluation (genetic testing, chronic-condition evaluation) and developmental evaluation (early intervention and therapy referrals), per algorithm nodes 6-9.

questions.sourceMapping: AAP Clinical Report (Lipkin 2020), algorithm nodes 6-9; Atypical Development transcript (referral and evaluation pathway)

stem: Which components belong in the comprehensive diagnostic evaluation of suspected autism spectrum disorder? Select all that apply.

options.label: A
options.text: Structured caregiver interview and standardized observational assessment
options.rationale: ADI-R-style caregiver interviews and ADOS-2 observation are the standardized diagnostic core within best-estimate clinical consensus.

options.label: B
options.text: Cognitive and adaptive-function testing with speech-language assessment
options.rationale: Cognitive/adaptive testing (e.g., Vineland-3) and speech-language assessment establish diagnosis and therapy plans.

options.label: C
options.text: Sensory and motor assessment as supplementary functional information
options.rationale: Sensory and motor assessments add useful supplementary functional information per the JAMA review.

options.label: D
options.text: Serum neurotransmitter panels to biochemically confirm diagnosis
options.rationale: No biochemical or neurotransmitter test diagnoses ASD; diagnosis is clinical/behavioral.

options.label: E
options.text: Routine brain MRI and EEG as mandatory diagnostic criteria
options.rationale: MRI/EEG are reserved for specific indications (e.g., seizures, regression) and are not diagnostic criteria.

questions.sourceMapping: JAMA ASD Review (Diagnostic Assessment); Atypical Development transcript (neuropsych battery: ADOS, caregiver interview, Vineland-3)
